Preface 

XX 

Few people in the United Kingdom, let alone further afield, have 

heard of Argiva. But if you have lived in the UK in recent decades, 

or even just visited there, the chances are that you have used 

services that Arqiva plays a pivotal role in facilitating. Watch 

television? Listen to the radio? Use a mobile device? If you have 
done any of those things in the UK, Arqiva has likely enabled 
you to do so. 

Owned by a consortium of international investment institu- 

tions — of which, at the time of writing, the two with the largest 

shareholdings are the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board 

and the Australian financial services company Macquarie — 
Arqiva is a private telecommunications company. It controls 
much of the basic infrastructure of the UK entertainment and 
communications landscape: around 2,000 TV and radio broad- 

cast transmission sites, around 8,000 ‘macrocellular’ telecom 

towers, and four of the national ‘multiplexes’ through which the 

radio spectrum is licensed for the purposes of carrying radio and 
TV signals. 

What kind of company is Arqiva? When we think about 
companies, we tend to think in terms of the classic three-sector 
model that divides economies into three sectors of activity: 

extraction of raw materials (the primary sector), manufacturing 

XVI 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of products (secondary), and provision of services (tertiary). But 
Arqiva doesn’t really fit any of these three types. Arqiva doesn’t 
primarily extract or make or provide. In fact, the crux of its busi- 

ness model is not doing (extracting/making/providing) at all; 

rather, it is having. 

Consider who Argqiva’s main customers are and what they pay 

Arqiva for. It has two main customer groups: on the one hand, 

major UK terrestrial TV broadcasters such as the BBC and ITV; 

on the other, major UK mobile telephony operators such as 
BI-EE, Vodafone, Telefonica O2, and Three. The former pay fees 

to Arqiva to use its transmission sites and radio spectrum; the 

latter pay it fees to use its telecom towers. Arqiva makes money, in 
other words, thanks to what it controls rather than what it does, 
and the money handed over by its customers is accordingly remu- 
neration not for something received — a raw material, product or 

service — so much as for something accessed or used. The word 
typically used to refer to such an access or usage payment is rent 
(the transmission sites, spectrum and towers are essentially being 
rented out); and Arqiva, insofar as such rents are its lifeblood, is 
what is typically referred to as a rentier. 

Rents and rentiers are the particular types of economic trans- 

fers and actors, respectively, examined in this book. Arqiva is just 

one example among a bewildering array of contemporary rent- 

iers. What they all share is this same focus on rent as their mode 
of money-making. I will have more to say shortly on the ques- 

tion of definition, but, in essence, rent, at least as understood in 

this book, is payment to an economic actor (the rentier) who 

receives that rent — and this is the key factor — purely by virtue of 

controlling something valuable. The ‘something’, whatever it 
happens to be, is referred to generically as an ‘asset’: an ‘item of 
value owned’ (to borrow the standard dictionary definition) that 

is valuable precisely in view of the fact that control over it endows 
the owner with the capacity to generate future income. 

A house is a good example to help illustrate what is and is not 

rent, and who is and is not a rentier. Suppose a construction 

PREFACE 
XVI 

company builds a house for a landowner who then lets the house 

to a tenant. The house ‘earns’ money, in a sense, for both the 
construction company and the landowner. But fundamentally 

different types of economic activity, actor and payment are 

involved in each case. The construction fee is payment for the 

work involved in building the house, independent of the house’s 

ownership; if no work had been carried out, after all, there would 

be no house, and no payment. Thus, the construction company 

is not a rentier; it earns money not for controlling the asset, but 

for creating it. The letting fee, by contrast, is rent, and the land- 

owner a rentier, since she receives payment only because she is 

the owner of the house and thus has the capacity to charge some- 

one for the right to occupy it. 

Rentier assets are as varied as rentiers themselves. Some — 

housing, telecommunications infrastructure, digital platforms — 

are physically constructed, in virtual if not real space; others — 

intellectual property rights, outsourcing contracts — are purely 

legal rather than physical constructs; and others still — land, 
natural resources — are not constructed at all, but simply exist 
spontaneously. Some 
assets, such as natural resources and 
outsourcing contracts, are exhausted in the process of their utili- 

zation, either physically or simply with the passage of time 

(think, for example, of seventy-year copyright protection); in 

other cases, such as telecommunications transmission towers, 

housing, and even a digital platform like Facebook, use is likely 

to cause some wear and tear; and, in other cases still, such as 

radio spectrum, no amount of use occasions asset impairment. 

Whatever its particular qualities, however, there must be an asset 

for there to be rent. Rent is income to which control of a valua- 

ble asset is in some sense fundamental, and a rentier is the recipi- 

ent of such income. No asset, no rent, no rentier. 

While rents and rentiers are key concerns of this book, its 
primary concern is with the system of economic production and 
reproduction in which incomes are dominated by rents and 
economic life is dominated by rentiers. Following many others, I 

XVII 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

refer to such a system as rentier capitalism. Rentier capitalism is 

an economic system not just dominated by rents and rentiers 

but, in a much more profound sense, substantially scaffolded by 

and organized around the assets that generate those rents and 

sustain those rentiers. Assets, for instance, like those of Arqiva — 

a quintessential rentier. 

Pervaded by a proprietorial rather than entrepreneurial ethos, 

rentier capitalism can be usefully understood as a kind of 

‘balance-sheet 
capitalism’. Alongside 
the income 
statement 
(which details a business’s revenues, costs and profits) and the 
statement of cash flows (which shows the flow of cash in and out 
of a business), the balance sheet is one of the three main types of 
financial statements used to document the financial activities 
and position of a business — or indeed a household. It identifies 
for a particular point in time both future financial obligations to 
third parties (‘liabilities’) and our aforementioned ‘items of value 
owned’ that are expected to generate positive future economic 
benefits — that is, assets. 

A form of capitalism geared principally to ‘doing’ pays heed to 

the balance sheet only to the extent that assets facilitate and 

liabilities mitigate profitable making or providing, or whatever 

else a business does. For a form of capitalism structured by 

contrast around ‘having’ — rentier capitalism, in other words: a 
mode of economic organization in which success is based princi- 
pally on what you control, not what you do — the balance sheet 

is the be-all and the end-all. The assets held on household and 

(especially) corporate balance sheets are rentier capitalism’s basic 
building-blocks. When you hear corporate executives wax lyrical 
about the ‘strength’ and ‘health’ of a companys balance sheet, 
about ‘leveraging’ it, using it ‘efficiently’ and ‘putting it to work’, 

it is as sure a sign as any that that company is a rentier capitalist, 

a balance-sheet capitalist. 

Rentier capitalism is not a mere theoretical construct, existing 
only in the imaginations of economists and within the covers of 
books like this one. Rentier capitalism is real. It exists widely 

PREFACE 
XIX 

— but, I will argue, is manifest in an especially advanced and stark 
form in Arqiva’s territory of operation, the United Kingdom, 
where it has taken shape over the course of the past four decades, 

during thé era of what is commonly described as ‘neoliberalism’. 

Using the neoliberal UK as its primary focus, this book explores 

the forms that Western rentier capitalism takes, the factors 

accounting for its materialization, and the consequences of its 

ascendancy. 

In recent years, much has been written about Western rentierism 

and rentier capitalism by some of the world’s highest-profile 
commentators on the economy. ‘Thomas Piketty’s Capital in the 

Twenty-First Century, published in 2014, was a catalytic inter- 

vention in this regard.' It is not a book about rent and rentiers 

per se; its primary focus is inequality. But rent is a pivotal varia- 

ble in the book and in Piketty’s theorization of capitalism. As is 
by now well known, Piketty argues that, unless actively checked, 
wealth inequality tends under capitalism inexorably to rise 
because of the famous 7 > g dynamic, where g represents the rate 

of economic growth and r represents the rate of return on capi- 

tal, or the rate at which rents can be extracted from the existing 
stock of assets. In short, 7 > g puts rent squarely in the spotlight, 
Piketty positing that 7’s tendency to exceed g is the fundamental 

reason why inequality has been growing. 

Piketty’s book opened the floodgates. The rentier is now every- 

where. The rich whom we cannot afford, as identified by Andrew 

Sayer in Why We Cant Afford the Rich (2015), are the rentier 

rich.’ It is rentiers who, in Guy Standing’s 2016 account, are 

responsible for the ‘corruption of capitalism’.° And it is rentiers 

doing the ‘taking’ rather than the ‘making’ in Mariana Mazzucato’s 

The Value of Everything: Making and Taking in the Global Economy 

(2018).‘ So ubiquitously do the figures of rent and the rentier 

seem now to loom that, in 2016, Philippe Askenazy, shadowing 

William Harcourt in the nineteenth century (“We are all social- 

ists now) and Milton Friedman in the twentieth (“We are all 

XX 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Keynesians now’), submitted that, with the twenty-first century 

less than two decades old, we were now all rentiers.> Even the 

premier magazine and premier newspaper of global capitalism, 

the Economist and the Financial Times respectively, have been 

writing about rentierism — with, it must be said, barely more 

fondness than the illustrious scholars mentioned above.° 

One of the main problems one confronts when trying to get a 

handle on this post-Piketty burst of writing on the rentier, 
however, is that definitions and conceptualizations vary. Not 
only do different writers have different things to say about rent 
and rentierism; the object of their analysis is often not even the 
same. But this should not surprise us. Of all key economic terms 
and concepts, arguably none has been put to such varied termi- 
nological and theoretical use over the years as ‘rent’. To begin to 
make headway with my examination of rentier capitalism, there- 
fore, I must first be clear about how I understand the term ‘rent’, 
and why. From among the plethora of extant usages, it is possible 
to isolate two main understandings. I will examine these as a way 
to situate and contextualize the specific usage employed in this 
book. 

The first understanding, which I will refer to as the ‘heterodox’, 

originates in everyday usage. From there, it entered Western 
economic thought in its earliest variants, in the shape of classical 

liberal political economy. For the likes of Adam Smith and David 
Ricardo, as for the population at large then and now, rent was 
land rent: the payment to the landowner made by her tenant, 
whether in urban or rural locations. In developing their respective 

theories of rent, both Smith and Ricardo emphasized the monop- 

olistic character of landownership. The fact that the landowner 
enjoyed monopoly power over her asset meant, said Smith, that 
the price paid for use of this land — namely, rent — is ‘naturally’ 
(inherently) a monopoly price. Marx concurred, in his turn. For 
him, land rent was the form in which the monopoly that is landed 
property is economically valorized under capitalism. Though he 
gave 
it a different name 
(ground-rent’) 
and examined 
its 

PREFACE 
XX 

materialization in different sub-variants (so-called ‘absolute’ rent, 

and two types of ‘differential’ rent), Marx’s rent was essentially 

everyone else’s rent: payment to monopoly control of land. 

Crucially, this first understanding of rent has been dramati- 

cally widened in the period since Marx and his predecessors were 

writing. Rent remains, by this expanded understanding, payment 

for monopoly control of an asset, but the asset need not be land; 

it can be anything, if control of that thing generates some kind 

of access or usage payment. What Marx did not anticipate, writes 
David Harvey, was that 

new forms of capitalist rent might also evolve within the 

evolutionary structures of capitalism and that rent-seeking 
might go well beyond that which he found both necessary and 

functional as well as politically tolerable for a mature form of 

capitalist development. Rent-seeking through speculation in 

land markets and resource endowments (like oil wells) is bad 

enough. But what are we to make of rent-seeking through 
ownership of intellectual property rights? 

These are the types of questions that contemporary analysts of 

rent are asking, as the rentier’s terrain has widened to incorpo- 

rate, in Harvey’s words, ‘asset markets of all sorts’.’ 

In fact, there is one important type of asset that Harvey — who 

defines rent in this broadened sense as ‘a return to the monopoly 
power of private ownership of some crucial asset’ — excludes from 

his treatment of rentierism: financial assets.® Like Marx, Harvey 

regards rent (earned by rentiers) and interest (earned by finance 

capital) as categorically different from one another. Ironically, 

and confusingly, there are still other writers for whom the exact 

opposite applies: when they speak of rentiers, it is precisely finan- 

cial rentiers (and only them) that they have in mind. The most 

famous was John Maynard Keynes, with his legendary call for 

the euthanasia of the (financial) rentier, the owner of financial 

assets.” Today, the Economist, among others, defining rentiers as 

NLL 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

‘those who live off their savings or inherited wealth’, cleaves to 

this narrow Keynesian understanding." 

But the majority of those working these days within the heter- 

odox tradition conceptualize rent and rentierism much more 

expansively. The range of assets on which rent can be earned is, 

for them, essentially limitless (and includes financial assets). 
Piketty, Sayer and Standing, for example, all mobilize extremely 
capacious, classically rooted, asset-oriented definitions of rent. 
For Piketty, rent is ‘remuneration for ownership of [an] asset, 
independent of any labor’; for Sayer, it is a payment extracted ‘by 
those who control an already existing asset, such as land or a 
building or equipment, that others lack but need or want, and 
who can therefore be charged for its use’; and for Standing, it is 
income generated ‘from ownership, possession or control of 
assets that are scarce or artificially made scarce’.!! 

Before we turn to the second principal understanding of rent, it 

is worth mentioning some notable inflections that the heterodox 
conceptualization is frequently given. Not only, some heterodox 

writers argue, is rent asset-based income; it is income associated 

with the extraction rather than creation of value. The rentier, that is 

to say, is considered a parasite; asset control enables her to arrogate 

to herself value created elsewhere. This was very much Ricardo’s 

view, for example. Today, prominent Ricardians (at least on rent 
theory), wittingly or otherwise, include Mazzucato and Rutger 
Bregman, the latter of whom has written vividly of rentiers ‘sucking 
the rest of us dry’.’? Then there are those who give this parasite— 
host imagery a particular geographical and geopolitical spin: for the 
likes of Michael Roberts, many contemporary Western economies, 
including the UK’s, are rentierist specifically in the sense that they 

‘[live] off the productive development of other countries’."3 Such 
critiques hark back to the work especially of Lenin, who argued in 
the 1910s that European imperialism had led to the ‘extraordinary 
growth’ of ‘a stratum of rentiers, i.e., people who live by “clipping 
coupons’, who take no part in any enterprise whatever, whose 
profession is idleness. The export of capital . 
. . still more completely 

PREFACE 
NULL 

isolates the rentiers from production and sets the seal of parasitism 

on the whole country that lives by exploiting the labour of several 

overseas countries and colonies.’'4 

The second principal understanding of economic rent is very 

different, and belongs to a different epistemic community. Within 
mainstream (‘orthodox’) economics, rent is defined not on the 

basis of the type of asset in relation to which it represents a payment 

— land rents, financial rents, and so forth — but instead by the 
quantum of market power enabling its derivation: it is the profit 

attainable specifically due to a dearth of market competition. Thus, 

if ‘normal levels of profit are those that can be realized in a compet- 

itive situation, rents are the ‘excess’ returns afforded by any depar- 

ture from that idealized scenario — the abnormal profits occasioned 
by the capitalist power to monopolize a market.” 

Rents defined in this orthodox sense may derive from control 

of an asset, but, crucially, they need not; they can arise in the 
context of all types of market production and exchange. Citing 

the textbook definition of such rents (‘the difference between 
what a factor of production is paid and how much it would need 

to be paid to remain in its current use’), the Economist provides 
one example where asset control is absent: ‘A soccer star may be 
paid $50,000 a week to play for his team when he would be will- 

ing to turn out for only $10,000, so his economic rent is $40,000 

a week.’!° Jerry Epstein and Juan Antonio Montecino provide 

another: ‘in the case of bankers, the rent is the amount of their 

income that they are able to command over and above what 

would be required to get them to perform their activities’. The 

same authors usefully add: ‘More generally, we think of rent as 

an excess payment, excess in the sense that it is a payment not 

justified by the requirements of an efficient economy.” 

The definition of rent used in this book is firmly grounded in 

the heterodox tradition and its emphasis on assets. But it also 

incorporates the attention to market conditions that is central to 

the mainstream usage, because the heterodox understanding 

does not quite suffice in isolation. Recall that rent in the latter 

XXIV 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

tradition is the return to monopoly control of an asset. Does 

such monopoly control, combined with asset scarcity, guarantee 
income generation? No. An asset — a new, patented production 
technology, say, or a mineral fuel resource — can be scarce and in 

principle valuable; but the proprietor’s commercialization of it 

can nonetheless encounter competition of a degree that precludes 

rents from being earned. Other technologies might be available 

to produce better, cheaper substitute products; government 

intervention might serve to ‘strand’ mineral assets of one kind 

(such as fossil fuels) and to subsidize the production and marketi- 

zation of alternative fuel sources (such as renewables). 
Rent-bearing assets, in short, are those characterized by monop- 
oly power not just in ownership or control — the heterodox 
emphasis — but aéso in terms of their commercialization on the 
market. This, insofar as it denotes the significance of market 
power, is where the orthodox understanding of rent adds value: it 
underscores the fact that, in order to be successful, the rentier 
requires concrete market advantage, whether by virtue of the 
nature of the asset she controls or otherwise. Monopoly control of 
an asset is for naught economically if the owner lacks the power 
to monetize that asset in market exchange; think, for example, of 
the owner of an electricity-distribution network that lacks a 
government licence to operate that network and distribute elec- 
tricity through it on a commercial basis — or to subcontract those 
functions. One of the main explanations for the market power 
enjoyed by the successful rentier, as we will see, is that in most 
cases the barriers to entry — that is, the obstacles to securing 
competitive rent-generating assets — are formidably high. With 
maybe one or two partial exceptions, such assets do not come 
cheap, and they frequently remain unavailable by regulatory edict. 
The definition of rent I use here, then, is effectively a hybrid of 
the heterodox and orthodox: income derived from the ownership, 
possession or control of scarce assets under conditions of limited or no 
competition. As we will shortly see, this two-part definition fits all 
significant, commonly 
recognized 
forms 
of contemporary 

PREFACE 
CD 

rentierism. Both parts are critical. With mainstream economists, 

we can agree that market power is integral to rent and rentierism. 

But this condition, though necessary, is not sufficient, since 

monopoly’ profits can of course also be achieved without the 

control of scarce assets — for instance, in the case of cartelized or 

highly concentrated 
industries. Meanwhile, with heterodox 

scholars ranging from Harvey to Piketty, we can agree that 

control of scarce assets is also integral to rent and rentierism — 

but this condition is not itself sufficient either, because the owner 

of such assets may nonetheless be subject to competitive forces in 

the shape, for example, of substitute products or services. Both as 

asset proprietor and in putting the asset to commercial use, the 

rentier sweats monopoly from every pore. 

Though my preferred definition adds a qualifier regarding 
market conditions to typical heterodox definitions of rent, it 

remains broad. To recognize this is to raise an important ques- 

tion: If there are no restrictions on the nature of the asset on 
which the rentier earns rent, what capitalist income is not rent? 
What capitalist not a rentier? 

Ultimately, like all important economic concepts, ‘rent’ is blurred 

at the margins. There are no cut-and-dried distinctions. Most 
economic production of goods or services contains rentier elements. 

But in many instances these are merely trace elements. If no scarce 
and exclusively controlled assets are being leveraged in production 

— examples would be a manufacturer using widely available equip- 
ment to make products for sale off the shelf, or a company offering 

residential cleaning services on an on-demand basis — then no rents 

are being earned. Not all capitalists are rentiers. 

Where rent is being earned, meanwhile, it is unlikely to be the 

case that all of the rentier’s income takes the form of rent. With 

most of the varieties of rentierism I examine in what follows, 
income derives simultaneously both from control of an asset and 
from the work involved in delivery of the product or service 
underwritten by it. Few assets, if any, generate income automati- 

cally; they ordinarily need to be put to work. This holds even for 

XXUI 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

real estate, the archetypal rentier asset. Why else would landlords 

use letting agents? Consider, similarly, the example of a medicine 
protected by a patent. How much of the income earned from 

that medicine is payment occasioned by the monopoly control 
embedded in the patent, and how much is payment for the work 

involved 
in the medicine's 
manufacture 
and distribution? 
Ultimately, it is impossible to say for sure. 

In general, we can state: rent is typically only part of a rentier’s 
income rather than its totality. As will become clear, the degree 

of significance of asset control (the essence of rentierism) to the 
income generated by rentiers varies greatly. The key definitional 

point nonetheless is that in all cases of rentierism, such control is 

material; if it were not, which is to say, if the income could 
equally well be earned without the proprietary asset, then there 
would be no rent and no rentier. Rentierism consists therefore in 
scarce and exclusively controlled assets being not just leveraged 
in production but substantively so — that is, in such a way as to 
materially influence the nature of the economic activity and the 
amount of income it generates. In any event, in all of the forms 
of economic production investigated in this book, control of an 

asset is fundamental; without it, income-generation would be at 
least severely compromised, and in many cases inconceivable. 

If Marx, Keynes and mainstream (orthodox) economics differ in their 

definitions of rent and rentierism, what they share is perhaps more 

significant and striking. For all three, rent (and hence the rentier) is a 

marginal, residual or ephemeral phenomenon within capitalism. 

Marx, as I have said, emphasizes landed forms of rentier capi- 

talism, and thus treats the rentier as residual, harkening back to 

feudalism. It baffled Marx that under nineteenth-century indus- 

trial capitalism, the landed rentier hadn't yet passed into the 

night, but instead was still capable of extracting a share of the 
surplus value created by workers in production. 

Keynes, as I have also noted, focuses for his part on financial 

forms of rentier capitalism. His view was not so much that 

PREFACE 
NXVIL 

financial rentierism was an anachronism, a relic of a bygone age 

that should by right have dissipated, as land rentierism was for 
Marx. Rather, Keynes believed that under the right circum- 

stances, firiancial rentierism would soon dissipate. As we will see 

in Chapter 1, his argument was that a greater abundance of capi- 

tal — something of which he was strongly in favour — would bring 

about the euthanasia of the financial rentier. 

Meanwhile, orthodox economics treats rent as an aberration 
from an idealized norm, a phenomenon of the historical and 

theoretical margins. The entire mainstream edifice is structured 
around the expectation that competition will ultimately and 

ordinarily prevail in a market system. With the exception of a 
few particular sectors where monopoly is considered necessary 
and even functional, rentierism — understood in this tradition as 

the extraction of excess profits — will ineluctably be eroded away. 

Yet the reality of the early twenty-first century clearly belies all 

three — Marx, Keynes, and the mainstream. Land rents haven't 

faded away. Nor have financial rents. And nor — contra the main- 

stream — have rents in general. Rentierism has proven itself to be 
incredibly stubborn. It is a much more important phenomenon 

to contemporary capitalism than Marx or Keynes could ever 

have imagined, and than mainstream economics allows. 

Rentier Capitalism demonstrates this entrenchment. Further, 

it investigates the historical supports to contemporary rentier- 

ism, showing how it has been accelerated by a series of policy 
reforms typically named ‘neoliberalism’. Lastly, the primary 

implications of the rentier dominance of contemporary capital- 

ism are identified. Rentierism stifles innovation, depressing the 
dynamism of capitalist economies. And rentierism is a major 
mechanism producing inequality in our society; I explore this 
mechanism in significantly greater depth and detail than Piketty 

— using the abstract calculus of r > g — did in Capital in the 

Twenty-First Century. 

As such, this book is a political-economic critique of rentier 

capitalism. It asks what the secular advance of rentierism means 

XMXUILL 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

for macroeconomic outcomes and for the changing ‘microeco- 

nomic’ experiences of key actors in the rentier drama: workers, 

customers and investors, as well as rentiers themselves. This 

political-economic cast sets it decisively apart from the various 

Piketty-inspired accounts of Western rentierism identified above. 

It is worth briefly fleshing out the differences. 

In his Tous Rentiers!, Philippe Askenazy offers a largely ideo- 

logical or ‘ideational’ critique of rentier capitalism. Defining rent 

as income derived by capitalists not from control of an economic 

asset but from advantages conferred by powers that are as likely 

to be legal or political as they are ‘economic’ (involving forms of 
manipulation of the sociopolitical environment that are often 

referred to as ‘rent seeking’), Askenazy’s argument is essentially as 
follows. Recent decades have seen the ascendancy of an ideology 
(propriétarisme) that downplays or flatly denies ordinary workers 
contribution to wealth-generation, by designating their labours 
‘unproductive’. This ideology legitimizes wage deflation, and 
thus the channelling of income and wealth into the hands of 
manipulative capitalist rentiers. What is needed above all, then, 

is a fundamental revaluation of work and of what workers do. 

Notably, Piketty’s own follow-up to Capital in the Twenty-First 

Century, 2020's Capital and Ideology, treads similar eground.'® 
Where Capital in the Twenty-First Century examined how and why 
capitalism creates inequality (giving a starring if abstracted role to 

rent), Capital and Ideology examines how social elites — capitalist or 
otherwise — historically have ideologically justified such inequality; 
and although rent and the rentier barely merit a mention this time, 

it is indisputably rentier capitalist societies whose ‘inequality 

regimes’ (his term) Piketty is principally concerned to elucidate. In 
doing so, he uses the same concept as Askenazy, labelling the ideol- 
ogy that succours post-1970s rentierism and its attendant inequal- 

ities ‘neo-proprietarianism’ (néo-propriétarisme). 

Meanwhile, the three other important books on rentierism 
mentioned earlier — those by Mariana Mazzucato, Andrew Sayer 
and Guy Standing — are written very much in the tradition of ‘moral 

PREFACE 
XIN 

economy’. By this, I do not mean that they are concerned princi- 

pally with the moral norms embedded in rentier capitalism (although 
such norms do figure in the discussion). Rather, they bring primar- 

ily moral considerations to bear in their critique of that economic 

system. ‘The critique is predicated explicitly on moral claims. 

As Sayer explained in his powerful earlier writing on moral 
economy, such claims can take many possible forms.'? Arguments 

for or against, say, capitalism, or feudalism, or socialism, might 

be rooted in commitments to justice, to understandings of indi- 

vidual rights and responsibilities, to principles of ‘freedom’, or to 

conceptions of ‘the good’. In their unabashed diatribes against 

rentierism, Mazzucato, Sayer and Standing rely, more and less 

explicitly, on notions of justice and fairness, and they share 

exactly the same rationale for doing so. Rentier capitalism is 

unfair and unjust, they maintain, because, being predicated on 

‘having’ rather than ‘doing’, rentier income — unlike income 

received by workers or by what the authors in question refer to as 

‘productive’ capitalists — is unearned. 

Rentier Capitalism provides a fresh perspective, then, inas- 
much as its critique is concerned neither with ideology nor 

morality, neither with the inherent ethical status of rentierism 

nor the ideas animating it. Admittedly, it is impossible to draw a 

watertight distinction between political-economic and moral- 

economic critiques. Our objection to, say, increasing inequality 

is ultimately almost always a partly moral one; we do not think 

it is right. But the critique of rentierism levelled by Mazzucato 
and the other authors cited above is moralist tout court: Insofar as 

the rentier generates income from having rather than doing, that 

income is understood to be unearned and therefore undeserved. 

There is, I believe, a significant difference between on the one 

hand an ethical assessment of a political-economic outcome, 

such as rising inequality, and, on the other, a prima facie moral 

adjudication — for example, that the rentier does not deserve her 

income because she has not done the requisite ‘hard work’. 

XXX 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Another of this book’s principal claims is that rentierism is far 

more diverse in its forms than most analyses have suggested. 
Correspondingly, another of its distinctive contributions is to 

consider closely all of the main varieties of rentierism. Many of 

the heterodox scholars who use expansive definitions of rent 

refer to several discrete types of rentier asset — those identified 
most commonly tend to be land, intellectual property (espe- 

cially in pharmaceuticals), financial assets, and, increasingly, 

digital platforms — giving selected examples of prominent rent- 

iers in each of these domains. But none offers a comprehensive 

categorization of the main contemporary variants of rentierism, 

still less a detailed study of each one. That is what this book aims 

to provide. 

As well as being a study of rentier capitalism, then, this book 

is a study of a series of distinct rentier capitalisms — which, even 

as they share a common foundation in the generation of income 

based on the control of scarce assets, nonetheless vary to such an 

extent that broad generalizations about ‘rent’ and ‘rentiers’ of the 
kind we often read are ultimately inadequate. Factors such as the 
mechanisms of an asset’s creation and the nature of prevailing 
arrangements for its ownership and control indelibly shape how 
and by whom the asset is commercially exploited to realise rental 
payments. I identify seven core asset types, and I explore at 
length, in seven chapters, the form of the particular rentier econ- 
omy arrayed around each one. Table P.1 identifies those seven 
asset types. It also summarizes how private-sector rentiers gener- 
ally come to control such assets, and the types of rent that such 
control enables them to earn in each case. 

This compartmentalization should not be taken to suggest 

that there is no overlap between the seven forms of rent I iden- 

tify. There is considerable overlap. Many financial rentiers, for 

example, are also land rentiers, earning rents on real estate along- 

side financial assets. Yet the various types of assets and rentier- 

isms are sufficiently distinct to warrant separate, if connected, 
treatments. The seven chapters of the book therefore lay out its

political-economic critique in respect of those seven distinct 
rentier-dominated spheres of the economy, within each of which 

workers, customers, investors, and so on, have been affected in 
markedly different ways. Meanwhile, in the Introduction, I focus 

on what the rising tide of rentierism in general has led to at the 

level of the overall political economy of the UK. 

Chapter 1 examines Keynes's béte noire — the financial rentier. 

For Keynes, the primary form of financial rent was the interest 
income ‘earned’ by holders of financial assets. The quote-marks 

are necessary because, in Keynes's view, investors did not really 

earn this income. It came to them, he said, not by virtue of ‘genu- 

ine sacrifice’, but instead because the amount of capital was 

limited, and thus borrowers were required to pay to access it. As 
Keynes saw it, there were no ‘intrinsic reasons’ why capital should 

be scarce. It was scarce, he surmised, simply because financial 

rentiers managed to keep it that way; hence his description of the 

XNIL 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

ability of the financial-capitalist class ‘to exploit the scarcity-value 

of capital’ as a ‘cumulative oppressive power’.”° Interest income, 
however, is not the only form of rent earned by financial rentiers 

on the assets they control. Rents also accrue in the form of finan- 

cial dividends and capital gains. The relative contribution of these 

various types of financial rent is ever in flux, depending on rentier 

strategies, financial-market dynamics and interest-rate trends, 
among other things. Generally, across the Global North, interest 
income has declined in relative importance in recent decades as 

rentiers have actively diversified their earnings streams.”! 

In Chapter 2, I turn my attention to natural-resource rents: 

rents generated through exploitation of naturally occurring 

resources, including both energy products (oil, gas and coal) and 

other minerals (metal ores, stones, sands and salts). Natural 
resources are the specific source of rents for one of the most widely 
recognized types of rentier institution — the so-called ‘rentier 

state. But such rents do not only accrue to governments. They 

also accrue to capitalist firms, such as the major fossil-fuel and 
mining companies. Typically, the rent earned from natural 
resources is shared between the owner of the mineral rights — 
generally either the state or the landowner — and the organization 
that develops and extracts the resource and brings it to market in 
either unprocessed or processed form. It is this latter role that 
private corporate entities widely fulfil, especially in the West. The 
part played by such private entities is my main object of interest: 
the work and spoils of the capitalist natural-resource rentier. 

Chapter 3 considers rents derived from intellectual property 

(IP). Many of the most valuable assets in contemporary capital- 

ism are not physical assets such as natural resources, but rather 
creations of the mind or intellect, the proprietary ‘ownership’ of 
which is recognized in law. The most common examples of IP 

rights are patents, trademarks and copyright. A patent confers 
ownership of a product or process that a company or individual 

has invented; a trademark confers ownership of a produét or 
service identifier, such as a brand name; and copyright confers 

PREFACE 
XMXLIL 

ownership of an original creative work, such as a song, book or 

film. IP rents are a significant feature of all sectors of the modern 
economy in which creations of the mind represent meaningful 

sources of competitive advantage: patents figure prominently in 

the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors; trademarks are 

ubiquitous in the consumer products industry; copyright under- 

writes much of the entertainment and publishing sectors. Rights 

owners can generate rents either by exploiting the IP themselves 

(for example, a drug company manufacturing and selling one of 

its own patented medications) or by licensing it to a third party 

(as with copyright-protected proprietary software). 

Intellectual property is a significant feature of the burgeoning 

digital-platform business — the world of Airbnb, Facebook, Uber, 

and so on. Chapter 4 examines such platforms, placing them in 

the context of platform capitalism more generally. While the 
technology they use and their scale of operation may be new in 

the networked age, the core ‘service’ — intermediation and market- 
making via the provision of a ‘space’ of some kind in which inter- 

action between participants can occur — clearly is not. A high- 

street shopping centre is a capitalist platform operator no less 

than its online equivalents such as eBay. Platforms generate three 
main types of revenue for their owners. Insofar as those revenues 

are payments originated by virtue of control of the platform asset, 

rent is clearly what they represent. One is a simple membership or 

subscription charge; the second comprises fees or commissions 

levied on transactions initiated through the platform; and the 

third is advertising, whereby platform owners leverage the ‘atten- 

tion’ value of the traffic that the platform attracts. 

Chapter 5 analyses a very different type of asset and its corre- 
sponding form of rent. A longstanding mantra of the manage- 
ment-consultancy industry has been that clients in the public and 

private sector alike should focus exclusively on their so-called ‘core 

competences’, and outsource all other activities. Over the course of 

several decades, the result has been a veritable explosion in the 

outsourcing industry, and the emergence of a raft of companies 

XXXIV 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

with no core business of their own; but whose business rather is to 

undertake the non-core operations of other entities: catering, 

cleaning, IT, payroll, and so on. The alternative name for outsourc- 

ing, ‘contracting out’, is more revealing for our purposes, because 
when organizations outsource activities they generally do so by 
awarding contracts for the services to be provided, and those 

contracts become the principal, prized assets for companies in the 
outsourcing sector. These contract assets are scarce in the sense that 
each is unique, and they are by nature limited in number. Moreover, 
they frequently encompass the delivery of services for a period of 
years — even, in some cases, decades — and the income they gener- 
ate thus takes the form of rent: income guaranteed by virtue of 
possession of an asset that insulates the contractor from all compe- 
tition for the contract duration. 

In Chapter 6, I turn to infrastructure rents: rents issuing from 
control of the key frameworks, facilities and systems that under- 

lie the provision of major services, ranging from energy and 

water supply to communications and transportation. This, of 

course, is Argiva’s home turf; but it is also the turf of, for exam- 
ple, the owners of electricity and gas transmission and distribu- 
tion networks — and, less obviously, the owners of today’s vast 
cloud-computing 
infrastructures. What such infrastructures 
share is that they are indispensable to service-delivery, in much 
the same way that, say, a dwelling is indispensable to the ‘service’ 
provided by a residential landlord. Anybody wanting to’sell elec- 

tricity, broadcast a television channel, or run a significant online 
business requiring substantial storage and processing Capacity 
must either build the necessary infrastructure themselves — which 
is likely to be expensive, and will often, in heavily regulated 
contexts, simply be impossible — or pay to access and use existing 
third-party-owned infrastructures. If they do the latter, they pay 
rent, even if they do not call it that. 

Finally, in Chapter 7, I turn to land rent — the most venerable 
and widely recognized form of capitalist rent, and the one on 

which, in a sense, 
all subsequent forms of rent have been 

PREFACE 
XXXV 

modelled. Land rent is an occupancy rent — or, at least, it is 
understood as such in this book. For that reason — plus the diffi- 

culty, not to mention pointlessness, of trying to separate the two 

— we include here rents paid to the various properties ov the land, 
commercial or residential, that are occupied by tenants. When 
building tenants make rental payments to their landlords, after 

all, they are making a payment both for the physical property 
and for the location. A prosaic marker of the significance of the 

latter is the simple fact that landlords are, indeed, called land- 

lords. A more meaningful marker is the fact that the rent paid on 

a property in one location can be orders of magnitude higher 
than that paid on the exact same type of property located some- 

st 
where else. 

In most countries of the West, most of these various forms of 

rent are paid to corporate entities — either the state or, as is over- 
whelmingly the case, capitalist corporations. This, in itself, is 

striking: when we use the term ‘rentier’, it typically conjures an 
image of an individual — one living comfortably and passively off 

inherited wealth; but the reality is that most rentiers are not indi- 

viduals, but institutions. More precisely, the reality is that 
contemporary rentierism, in terms of the overall scale of rents 

being ‘earned’, is a predominantly corporate rather than indi- 

vidual or household affair. 

The two main types of rent that, to some extent, represent 

exceptions to this rule are those considered in the first and last 

chapters.** In many countries, individuals own substantial stocks 

of land and residential property, thus representing a significant 

class of individual land rentiers. Equally, in many countries, 

individuals also own substantial stocks of financial assets — espe- 

cially, though certainly not exclusively, in the form of pension- 

fund holdings. Frequently, financial rentierism is thus also an 

individual as well as corporate enterprise. 

In any event, both land and financial rentierism among house- 

holds are important phenomena in the country where my 

XU 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

examination 
of rentier 
capitalism 
is focused: 
the United 
Kingdom. ‘This is the final factor that sets this book apart from 

previous studies of rentier capitalism. Unlike the accounts 

referred to above, it is a case study of rentier capitalism in a 

particular place and time. 

Nonetheless, Rentier Capitalism strives — as its title suggests — 

to be substantively more than that. In examining rentier capital- 

ism in the UK, it explores a mode of economic organization that, 
by all accounts, is increasingly dominant across advanced capital- 

ist economies more generally. Rentier capitalism may not — 
indeed almost certainly does not — look the same from place to 
place. But it shares certain dynamics and outcomes, not to 
mention common asset forms and categories of rentier. In exam- 
ining the historical conditions, evolving forms and emerging 
consequences of rentier dominance specifically in the UK, this 
book advances claims that to one degree or another can be gener- 
alized beyond the UK’s territorial borders. 

Naturally, the configuration and weighting of asset portfolios 
and sectoral rentier forces will vary between countries. As we will 

see, finance (Chapter 1) and natural resources (Chapter 2) play a 
disproportionately significant role in the UK economy. Moreover, 

it is hard to imagine that any national government competes 
with the UK’s in the extent to which it has advanced down the 
road of enabling contract rentiers (Chapter 5) and infrastructure 

rentiers (Chapter 6) through outsourcing and _ privatization, 
respectively. On the other hand, it is also hard to think of any 
major capitalist economy in which all of the forms of rentierism 
explored in this book do not represent significant phenomena — 
with the possible exception of natural-resource rentierism. While 
the UK obviously has its idiosyncrasies, Rentier Capitalism is 
therefore written in the conviction that the UK experience is 
broadly representative of the wider system of Western rentier 
capitalism that the various existing studies by Piketty’s interlocu- 
tors have begun to bring into focus. 
: 

Introduction 

‘ 

One of the great ironies of the political-economic history of the 
United Kingdom is that, despite its status as the birthplace of the 

Industrial Revolution, it has never truly been an industrial nation 

— culturally, politically, or indeed economically. “Workshop to 

the world’ it may famously have been for a few short decades in 

the nineteenth century; but the reality is that, from the earliest 
days of its capitalist odyssey, the UK and those who steered and 

profited from its economy were predominantly rentierist, rather 

than industrialist — focused on having, rather than doing. 

Central to this issue were land and landowners. Noting the 

historical fact — some would say curiosity — that traditional agrar- 

ian classes ‘either led or survived every major political upheaval 

that opened the way to the modern capitalist state, not only in 

Europe but in North America and Japan as well’, Perry Anderson 

has argued that nowhere did those tenacious traditional land- 

owning classes prosper, both politically and economically, from 

the transition to capitalism more than in the UK: “The English 

estate-holders had no rivals in this regard.’ For reasons including 

the particular thoroughness with which peasants were divorced 

from the means of production in the countryside, agriculture in 

the UK assumed a capitalist cast more rapidly and more compre- 

hensively than anywhere else in Europe. So, consequently, did 

2 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the nation’s major landowners, who by at least a century in 
advance of the Industrial Revolution had become what Anderson 

describes as ‘a capitalist stratum proper.’ The UK was now char- 

acterised by a political economy later described by Martin 
Daunton as ‘aristocratic rentier capitalism’, dominated by a land- 
owning class that was ‘capitalist rather than feudal’ — or, in 

Martin Wiener’s words, ‘basically rentier, not entrepreneurial or 
productive’. 

When industry arrived on the scene, 
the UK’s landed- 
property establishment succeeded to a remarkable degree in 
reshaping the emergent industrial bourgeoisie in its own image. 
‘With his factory in a rural setting, with the ultimate social refer- 
ence group the great landowners, the successful industrialist had 
every incentive to assimilate to the existing status structure by 
buying a large block of land’, Eric Jones has written. ‘He had 
perhaps attained his wealthy eminence by novel means and untra- 
ditional attitudes, but to fix his children in the social firmament, 

as to the manner born, he would have to play by the rules of estab- 
lished, landed society’. Moreover, the landed rentier class retained 
its superiority; industry and the industrial bourgeoisie were subor- 
dinate. Owning predominantly small-scale firms, the UK’s leading 
industrialists were, says Anderson, ‘junior partners in the natural 
order of things’, while the nation’s ‘dominant bloc remained 
‘essentially landowning throughout most of the 19th century.“ 
Indeed, between 1809 and 1879, approximately 90 per cent of 
British millionaires were landowners.5 Industry, for all its raw 
productivity, was not even in second place. Beneath landowning, 
notes Anderson, ‘came commerce rather than manufacturing’, not 
just socially, but also ‘economically’.° 

Needless to say, undisputed landowner dominance did not last 

forever. Times were changing. But when a new dominant bloc 
eventually came to the fore, it was another rentierist bloc. By the 
nineteenth century, London had eclipsed Amsterdam as the 
world’s leading financial centre. The City’s main activities Were 
largely disconnected from domestic industry, with overseas 

INTRODUCTION 
3 

investment added to ‘its two principal pre-industrial activities: 

traffic in government securities, and discounting and insurance 

of foreign trade’ from mid-century onwards. Thus, ‘When agrar- 

ian property lost its weight it was not industry but finance which 

became the hegemonic form of capital, in a City socially and 

culturally in many ways closer to the wealth of estates than of 

factories.’ 
In fact, landed property was only ever partially 

displaced by financial capital. As Anderson remarks, it is truer to 

say that what the late Victorian epoch actually saw in the UK was 

the emergence of ‘an increasingly integrated plutocracy’ popu- 

lated principally by both financiers and ‘landed magnates’.’ 

In the UK, then, the rivers of rentierism run extraordinarily 

deep. Many writers on the country’s contemporary political 
economy have forgotten its profoundly rentierist past, or are 
simply oblivious to it. But not all. In launching the Kilburn 

Manifesto — designed to map the contours of neoliberalism 

specifically as it has materialized in the UK — with Stuart Hall 

shortly before Hall’s death in 2014, Doreen Massey and Michael 

Rustin argued that it was impossible to understand the contem- 

porary UK unless one attended to the longstanding influence of 

financial and landed-property interests. Both of these sets of 

interests, Massey and Rustin emphasized, sought to profit 

primarily from ‘the holding of assets’ rather than from produc- 

tion and human labour (in other words, both were explicitly 

rentierist); and both were ‘utterly embedded in the British class 

structure’.® Massey and Rustin argued that over the longue durée, 

rent had ‘been more important in the mentality and practice of 

Britain’s ruling class than industrial production’... In short, by 

historical disposition the UK — at least at the level of the capital- 

ist class — is a rentier nation. 

One possible reason for the widespread forgetting of rentier- 

ism’s deep roots in the marrow of the UK economy and its elite 

social structures is that the early to mid twentieth century in the 
UK saw a substantive if far from complete subduing of the rent- 

ier — just as it did, as Thomas Piketty has shown, in the majority 

4 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of the other advanced industrial nations in which rentiers of one 

kind or another had previously enjoyed economic and social 
prominence.’ In the UK, both financial and landed-property 

interests — the dominant rentiers of the past — were effectively 

shackled. Vast amounts of land were taken into public owner- 

ship.'’ By mid-century, Hugh Dalton, then chancellor of the 
exchequer in a Labour government, felt sufficiently confident 

about the direction of travel to predict full land nationalization.” 
Meanwhile, the “Big Five’ clearing banks were controlled by the 

state to the extent of receiving ‘precise instructions from the 

‘Treasury concerning not only their liquidity but also their lend- 
ing priorities’ 
.'* Nobody described the hobbling of the financial 

sectors commercial freedoms in this period better than Oliver 
Franks, chairman of Lloyds in the late 1950s. ‘It was like driving 

a powerful car at twenty miles an hour’, he later told the writer 
Anthony Sampson. “The banks were anaesthetised — it was a kind 
of dream life.’ 

Since the end of the 1970s, UK banks and bankers have clearly 
awoken from that dream state, and have enjoyed a period of 
almost unimaginable riches — rudely interrupted in 2008, to be 

sure, but to the long-term cost not of the banks and bankers 
themselves but rather of the government and taxpayers. Indeed, 

so vibrant and sustained has the awakening been that the revivi- 
fication of finance has been widely seen as the pre-eminent trans- 
formative story of the UK economy in the neoliberal age. Much 
like its US counterpart, the UK economy, it is argued, has been 
‘financialized’. Greta Krippner defines financialization in terms 
of profits increasingly accruing ‘through financial channels rather 
than through trade and commodity production’.!> In 2008, 
Ewald Engelen described the US and UK economies as those 
‘which arguably have moved furthest in the direction of being 
truly “financialized”’.'° 
More 
recently, Aeron 
Davis 
and 
Catherine Walsh noted: ‘the UK economy has become more 
financialised and has gone through a more pronounced process 
of deindustrialisation than any of its major economic rivals’ .!7 

INTRODUCTION 
5) 

Such declarations are no longer seriously questioned. That the 
UK's is a financialized economy is now more or less a stylized fact 
—a commonplace of current scholarship.'* 

But it is not true. Or, rather, it is true only in small part: finan- 

cialization represents only one vector of a wider structural shift 

in the UK economy under neoliberalism. For instance, the real 

estate sector, the crucible of land rentierism, also awoke from its 
induced coma from the 1970s, in the process returning land 

rentiers to their own historic position of economic and social 

power. And it is not only land rents that, alongside financial 

rents, have surged in significance in recent decades. All of the 
main varieties of rentierism identified in the Preface (see Table 

P.1, p. xxxi) and examined at length m this book have assumed 

greatly increased importance — some more or less from a stand- 

ing start. 

Two key observations follow. Firstly, if the past four decades in 

the UK have seen not so much the ascendancy of the rentier as 

the rentier’s return after a period of protracted dormancy, then it 

has been the return of a figure now displaying much greater 

diversity than during the earlier, pre-World War I, land-and- 

finance era of UK rentierism. A two-headed monster has returned 

as a many-headed hydra. 
_ 

Secondly, while it is indisputable that finance has become a 
bigger part of the UK economy since the beginning of the 1980s, 

it is deeply misleading to argue, as so many commentators now 

do, that that economy has become financialized. To do so is to 

privilege one strand of a broader structural transformation and 

ignore all of the others — several of which, data suggest, have 

been just as materially significant as the expansion of finance, if 

not more so. 

Financialization has been, at most, the leading edge of the 
economic transformation of the UK under neoliberalism. 

That overall process can be understood as one not of finan- 

cialization, but rather of rentierization, whereby, to paraphrase 

Krippner, one might say that profits have increasingly taken 

6 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the form of economic rents —including but not limited to 

financial rents — rather than income from trade or commodity 
production. 

To demonstrate the UK economy’s rentierization empirically is 

not a straightforward matter.’? The national accounts do not 
contain a line for ‘rent’ as defined in this book, or indeed for 
anything remotely approximating to it; nor does any other 
system of representation of the national economy. Nevertheless, 

a careful assessment of relevant data sources confirms the fact 
that rent is indeed now dominant. The UK economy has been 
transformed into one in which control of exclusive assets is ever 
more critical. We have seen the development of a full-fledged 
national rentier capitalism — or, more exactly, a system of rentier 
capitalism centred on the UK, but extending well beyond its 
territorial borders. In the UK today, the leading corporations are 
largely rentiers, and the biggest sectors of the economy are largely 
characterized by rentier dynamics. It is helpful to examine these 
two categories in turn — corporations, and then sectors. 

Table 0.1 enables us to consider the extent to which the UK’s 
leading corporations are rentiers. It shows the thirty companies 

listed on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) with the highest 
market capitalization (in order of market value) as at late 2019. 
In addition to listing each company’s capitalization, the table 

also provides a brief description of the companys main business 

activity. Finally, it indicates which, if any, of the seven types of 
rent examined in this book each company on the list substan- 

tially generates. The choice of showing only the top thirty is, 
admittedly, arbitrary. There are well over 2,000 companies listed 
on the LSE. The aim of the table is simply to depict the inci- 
dence and most common varieties of rentierism among the 
biggest companies. To that end, taking the leading twenty, or 

fifty, or one hundred companies would have served equally well 

— even if, as indicated below, each would have yielded slightly 

different results.

RENTIER CAPITALISM 

The primary message of the table is clear: the commanding 

heights of “UK plc’, as the nation’s commercial community as a 
whole is often labelled, are dominated by rentiers. Every single 

one of the thirty companies with the largest market value traded 

on the LSE earns substantial rents of some kind. Rents are what 

the companies listed in Table 0.1 are all designed to generate; 

rent is their shared raison détre, and rentierism is embedded in 

their individual and collective DNA. 

Note here that, in documenting which types of rent each 
company generates, I have erred deliberately on the side of 

caution, only indicating a company’s participation in a particular 

rent category where it is beyond dispute. I have been particularly 

circumspect, for instance, about intellectual property (IP) rents 

predicated on brand ownership. There can be little doubt that 

several of the companies that the table shows as not realising IP 
rents — Prudential, Tesco and Vodafone, for example — would 
argue that their brands possess substantial value and do enable 
rents to be earned (although they probably would not use that 
term). But the table does not include such rents. 

Nevertheless, even excluding these arguably marginal or tributary 

types of rent, there are several companies that unquestionably fulfil 

multiple rentier roles. BT Group is a good example. It operates and 

earns rents from a series of crucial telecommunications infrastruc- 

tures, both physical (the bulk of the UK’s fixed-line telephony and 
broadband networks) and virtual (in the form of valuable radio spec- 
trum holdings). It is also a leading IP rentier, operating three leading 
Internet-service-provider brands while also being a prolific generator 
of patents for information and communication technologies. Other 
multidimensional rentiers include CRH — whose revenues rely upon 

construction contracts alongside mountainous reserves of limestone, 
sand and gravel; and BAE Systems — one of the world’s largest defence 
contractors, whose competitive advantage rests on a vast web of 
patents, in addition to its vast contract book. 

In terms of the varieties of rentierism shown in Table 0.1 MMicre 

is clearly an imbalance between the most common (financial, 

INTRODUCTION 
gy 

natural resources, and IP-based) and those featuring less promi- 

nently. Only three of the thirty most valuable LSE-listed compa- 

nies earn infrastructure rents, the same number that earn contract 

rents; platform rents figure just twice; and land rents only once. 

Indeed, some might argue that the single land rentier identified in 

the list, Tesco, is not a land rentier at all. However, as I show in 
Chapter 7, the central role of land rents to the business of bricks- 
and-mortar retailers that, like Tesco, are themselves major land- 

owners, has long been recognized — including, in the UK context, 
by competition regulators. 

The disproportionate 
representation 
of finance, 
natural 

resources and IP certainly tells an important story: UK ple is 

decisively weighted towards them, espécially at the very top end. 

But the relatively low profile of infrastructure, land, contract 
and platform rents in Table 0.1 is largely a reflection of the arbi- 

trary selection of 
just the top thirty companies. If the list were 

extended beyond that point, it would rapidly fill up with rent- 

iers in those underrepresented realms, even if a degree of imbal- 

ance between the various types of rentierism would remain. 
Companies whose businesses consist largely of the generation of 

the four relevant types of rent — (1) infrastructure, (2) land, (3) 
contract and (4) platform rents — are notably abundant among 

the tier of companies hovering, in the latter part of 2019, just 
below the top thirty. If we limit ourselves to the top one hundred 
companies, the first category includes, among others, SSE 

(market value: £11.2 billion), United Utilities (€5.4 billion), 

Severn Trent (£4.8 billion) and Centrica (£4.3 billion); the 

second includes Segro (£8.3 billion), Persimmon (£6.4 billion), 

Land Securities (£5.9 billion), Berkeley Group (£5.0 billion) 

and British Land (£4.7 billion); the third includes Rolls-Royce 

Holdings (£16.3 billion), Rentokil Initial (£8.2 billion), Sage 

Group (£7.9 billion), Bunzl (£7.3 billion) and DS Smith (£4.7 

billion); and the fourth includes Just Eat (£5.2 billion), Flutter 

Entertainment (£5.1 billion), Auto Trader Group (£5.0 billion) 

and Rightmove (£4.7 billion). 

10 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

While the business models of the largest companies listed on 

the London Stock Exchange provide a useful window onto the 
dominant forms of rentierism in the contemporary UK econ- 
omy, it is far from the only or a perfect such window. At least two 

significant factors materially influence the view it offers, perhaps 
producing a distorted picture. 

Firstly, the fact that companies are listed in London does not 
mean they generate all their income in the UK. Many of the 
companies in Table 0.1 have extensive non-UK operations. This 

raises the question of how those operations and the rents or other 
income they earn should be treated. Do such operations form 

part of the UK economy, and does their income contribute to it? 
This is partly an empirical question: What happens to the income 
generated overseas? Does it get repatriated to the UK? But it is 
also a conceptual question: What do we even mean by ‘the UK 
economy, or a ‘national economy’ more generally?”° 

National accounts, the main statistical framework through 

which we have come to conceive of ‘national economies’ as such, 

effectively provide two alternative answers to this conceptual ques- 

tion: the most commonly accepted measure of the size of a national 
economy, gross domestic product (GDP), measures economic 
output produced within a country’s borders, whereas gross national 
product (GNP) measures output produced by a country’s resident 
companies and citizens, irrespective of where it takes place. What 

is important, however, is less these measures and their definitions 
of ‘the economy’ per se than the fact that there is no single correct 
answer. Io the extent that we choose to employ the concept, a 
national economy’ — the UK’s included — can be framed in a vari- 
ety of ways, each with its own merits and drawbacks, depending 
on what exactly we are trying to understand. 

‘The potential pitfalls of using just one framing or another have 
mounted in recent decades. As globalization has proceeded, 
economies like the UK’s have become increasingly entangled 
with economic structures and dynamics at larger scales. As David 

Edgerton has observed, between the 1950s and the 1970s the 

INTRODUCTION 
a 

UK’s arguably was a largely ‘national capitalism, protected by 
import controls, and closely tied to an interventionist and tech- 

nocratic state that wanted to increase exports of British designed 
and made‘goods’. But that national geo-economic ‘integrity’, 
which was of course never absolute, then rapidly crumbled: 

‘Since the 1970s things have changed radically. Today there is no 

such thing as British national capitalism. London is a place where 
world capitalism does business — no longer one where British 

capitalism does the world’s business.?! This is entirely correct. 

Edgerton’s own particular interest is in the expanded role of over- 

seas capital in the UK, and in how the dismantling of the rela- 

tively cohesive ‘UK economy’ from the outside in has reshaped 
UK politics, specifically in relation to Brexit — which is a ques- 

tion I will return to at the end of this book (see Coda). But as 
UK capital has expanded its own spatial footprint, the integrity 
of the ‘UK economy has also been dissolved from the inside out 

—as Table 0.1 and its list of UK-based transnational enterprises 

well illustrates. 

Secondly, not all companies with a major operating presence 

in the UK are listed on the London Stock Exchange. Some, such 

as INEOS (chemicals manufacture), Greenergy (fuel supply) and 
John Lewis Partnership (retail), are privately owned. Others, 

ranging from Goldman Sachs (banking and financial services) to 
Google, are listed on non-UK stock exchanges. Indeed, had I 
compiled Table 0.1 just twelve months earlier than I did, it would 

have contained at least two major rentiers missing from the snap- 

shot published here, by virtue of the fact that they were acquired 

in the interim by larger companies listed elsewhere: Sky, the UK 

media and telecommunications group, was acquired by Comcast 

(listed in the United States); and Shire, the UK biopharmaceuti- 

cals company, was acquired by Takeda (listed in Japan and the 

United States). Of course, even if all of the companies with a 

major operating presence in the UK were listed on the LSE, an 

analysis of the largest of them would only ever provide a partial 

picture of UK ple —still less the elusive “UK economy’ asa whole.

Table 0.1 with an alternative representation of the complexion of 

the UK economy that helps us consider things from a different 

angle: that of industry sectors, and their relative contributions to 

the ‘national economy’ specifically as conceived in the output- 

location sense associated with GDP”? To this end, Figures 0.1 and 

0.2 use Office for National Statistics (ONS) data on the UK’s 

gross operating surplus of corporations. This is the best available 
UK proxy for corporate profit, which in turn represents’ the 
preferred metric among economic analysts for investigating the

sectoral breakdown of an economy.” Gross operating surplus 

represents gross trading profits plus rental income from build- 

ings, minus inventory holding gains. By analysing the share of 

overall UK corporate gross operating surplus contributed by 

various economic sectors, we are able to assess the relative contri- 

bution of sectors with, and without, significant elements of 

rentierism. 

Figure 0.1 provides the picture for 2016 (the latest for which 

annual data were available at the time of writing). It shows the 

value of both the surplus generated by each of the major industry 

sectors identified by the UK standard industrial classification of 

economic activities (SIC), and, within those sectors, by each 

significant industry subsector. Figure 0.2 charts the respective 

shares of the same major industry sectors for each year between
