Although Figure 0.2 traces sectoral operating surpluses back 

to 1997, two decades clearly represents a relatively limited time- 

frame within which to consider the recent historic evolution of 

INTRODUCTION 
JES) 

the UK economy. To address the issue of possible structural 

transformation, it is important to extend the period over which 

the economy's development is examined. Hence, Figure 0.3 

charts the period 1970-2010. There are two important defini- 

tional points to bear in mind. Firstly, the industry groupings are 

not the same as in Figures 0.1 and 0.2; the latter use the UK’s 

2007 SIC codes, whereas Figure 0.3 uses the superseded 2003 

classification. Secondly, the sectoral shares shown are of gross 

value-added rather than gross operating surplus — as noted, the 
ONS provides a sectoral breakdown of the latter only as far back 

Asal 99720 

It is important to note that there is no straightforward mapping 

of our seven varieties of rentierism onto the sectoral breakdown 

used in these three charts. In some cases — most notably financial 

rents and land rents — there is certainly a close correspondence; 

in Figures 0.1 and 0.2, ‘Finance and insurance’ broadly corre- 
sponds with financial rents and ‘Real estate’ with land rents. 

Nonetheless, as the expanding literature on financialization has 
shown, and as we will see in Chapter 1, it is not only companies 

in the finance sector that earn financial rents; and neither does 

the ‘Real estate’ category capture all significant forms of land 

rent. 
} 
In other cases, meanwhile, there is no such correspondence. 

Several significant forms of rentierism are dispersed in each indi- 

vidual case across multiple economic sectors, featuring substan- 

tively in each one but without monopolizing any of them. 

Contract rentierism is a good example, although it is not alone. 
Not only is much of the activity in the manufacturing, wholesale 

and (especially) construction industries carried out today on a 

contract basis, but the work of the many outsourcing companies 

that have increasingly taken on activities deemed non-core to — 

and thus contracted out by — other companies is spread across 

numerous sectors. One unavoidable problem with Figures 0.1, 

0.2 and 0.3, then, is that, even if they contain evidence of rent- 

ierism, it might not always be clearly visible. 

16 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Still, the significance to the overall UK economy of sectors in 
which rentier dynamics are prominent is nonetheless evident. 

‘Real estate’ and ‘Finance and insurance’ are clearly the most 

striking examples; as Figure 0.2 demonstrates, their contribution 

to overall surpluses has increased strongly, from a combined 13.8 

per cent in 1997 to 19.6 per cent in 2016. Each of the other 
industry sectors that individually generated more than £30 

billion in operating surplus in 2016 (Figure 0.1) also has signifi- 

cant rentierist dimensions: 

* Manufacturing, 
as already noted, features 
a significant 

contract-rent element. IP rents are also integral to much of 

the sector. Its two largest subsectors — pharmaceuticals and 
motor vehicle manufacture, in each of which patents and 
branding play a crucial role — are examples of this. 

* Construction work is almost entirely contract-based. 

¢ The ‘Information and communication’ sector is likewise 

renowned rentier territory. Infrastructure and IP rents are 

extremely important in the telecommunications space (as 

discussed earlier in relation to BT), and IP is of course 
fundamental to computer programming and consultancy, 

as well as to film, television and music production. 

° 
‘Professional, scientific and technical’ and ‘Administrative 
and support services’ are the principal domains inhabited 
by the UK’s multitude of outsourcing companies — éven if, 

as I have noted, such companies seek out contract assets 
much more widely than that. 

* In ‘Retail and wholesale’, comfortably the most important 

rentier dynamic pertains to land, especially in retail. As 
Chapter 7 will explore, this is not so much a question of retail 
companies charging rent on land they own but do not use, 
although that does happen. It is more a question of their 
buying land in the vicinity of existing stores specifically to 

prevent competitors acquiring and building on it: an econontic 

rent generated negatively rather than positively, so to speak. 

INTRODUCTION 
WA 

In fact, the picture of the UK economy provided by Figures 

0.1 and 0.2 arguably underestimates the real extent of rentier- 

ism; it is no more perfect or objective a picture than the one 

provided by Table 0.1. The latter, as we have seen, shows that 

some of the very biggest companies — and rentiers — listed on the 

London Stock Exchange are mining, metals and oil and gas 

production companies (for example, BP, Glencore, Rio Tinto 

and Royal Dutch Shell), and manufacturers of tobacco (British 

American Tobacco and Imperial Brands) and munitions (BAE 

Systems). Yet these sectors barely feature in Figures 0.1 and 0.2. 

In 2016, for example, the combined gross operating surplus of 

the tobacco and munitions subsectors was less than £4 billion. 

To put that in context, British American Tobacco alone gener- 

ated profits of £4.7 billion that year. Similarly, ‘Mining and 

quarrying’ — which includes the extraction of oil and gas — 

accounted for just 2 per cent of total UK gross operating surplus 

in 2016. Earlier in the period covered by Figure 0.2, its share of 

surplus was much higher than that, peaking at 6.8 per cent in 

2000; but, even then, one might reasonably have expected to see 

a far stronger performance from this sector, given that it contrib- 

utes no fewer than six of the top twenty companies listed in Table 

0.1. How can we account for these discrepancies? The answer lies 

in income generated outside the UK’s borders. All of the compa- 

nies named in this paragraph generate a disproportionate share 

of their revenues and profits overseas, and those profits do not 

figure in Figures 0.1 and 0.2. This explains the anomalously 

lower values we see there. 

Ultimately, I suggest, it is precisely in the combination of 

perspectives offered by Table 0.1, on the one hand, and Figures 

0.1 and 0.2, on the other, that we can find the most meaningful 

picture of the role of rentierism in the contemporary UK econ- 

omy. Figures 0.1 and 0.2 demonstrate that the economy is today 
dominated by sectors in which rentierism is a significant factor, 

some of which are rentierist tout court. What Table 0.1 adds to 

this picture is information specifically about rentierism as a 

18 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

source of competitive advantage. It is not just rentier sectors that 
dominate the economy, but also rentier institutions. Every one of 

the top thirty companies listed on the LSE is a rentier. Rent, it 

can clearly be seen, is what the market values. Even if the econ- 
omy in general is not all about rent — and, of course, it is not — it 

is nonetheless rentiers who win out. 

Perhaps more important than the actual extent of rentierism 

in today’s UK economy, in any case, is the simple fact that rents 

are demonstrably much more material to corporate incomes now 

than they were in the not-so-distant past. To quibble over the 

precise level of contemporary rentier dominance is, in a sense, to 

split hairs. Clearly, the rentier has ascended — rentierization is the 

essential story. 

This historical story is the story of Figure 0.3, although it 

needs careful narration. As the figure shows, there was a modest 

increase between 1970 and 2010 in the share of value-added 

contributed by ‘other’ services; much of this growth, especially 
during the latter part of this period, represented the expansion of 

the real-estate sector and the proliferation of land rents. But 

clearly the most significant (and well-known) developments of 
the period that are visible in the chart were the decline of manu- 
facturing and the commensurate rise of finance and business 

services: the share of value-added of the former more than halved, 
while the share of the latter more than doubled. We can helpfully 
consider this ‘scissor movement in terms of our understanding 
of rentierism, beginning with manufacturing. 

Crucially, the third of the overall UK economy given over to 
manufacturing activity in 1970 looked very different from the 
manufacturing sector of today, and not just in terms of size. The 
country — indeed, the Global North as a whole — was on the cusp 

of, but had not yet begun to experience, revolutionary transfor- 
mations in the organization of production. On the way out were 
the vertically integrated manufacturing giants of the Fordist era. 
When 
‘flexible specialization’ and ‘just-in-time’ produétion 
became 
strategic watchwords 
of post-Fordism, 
from 
the 

INTRODUCTION 
HD) 

mid-to-late 1970s, the Fordist dinosaurs began relentlessly to 

disaggregate and outsource operations, thus spawning the web of 

complex 
contractual 
relationships 
— 
between 
end-product 

producers, contractors and subcontractors — that is more familiar 

today.” In 1970, that is to say, contract rents, at least in UK 

manufacturing, were rare. So also were IP rents: as we will see in 

Chapter 3, conditions in the UK manufacturing sector in the 

postwar decades were not conducive to IP rentiers, and the coun- 

trys leading manufacturers relied on IP rights for competitive 

advantage much less than they do today. 

None of this is to say that, in those pre-1980s decades, the 
UR’s leading manufacturers lacked monopoly power. They did 

not. But the power they possessed was not afforded — as it is 
much more today — by the control of scarce assets such as IP 

rights or secure, often long-term contracts. It was a categorically 

different type of monopoly power, occasioned chiefly by the use 

of cartels to fix prices. Stephen Broadberry and Nicholas Crafts 

have estimated that, in 1958, some 36 per cent of value-added in 
UK manufacturing originated in cartelized sectors, while approx- 
imately the same share was produced by industries ‘where there 

clearly were attempts at price-fixing but where this may have 

been rather less comprehensive’. Only an estimated 27 per cent 

of value-added derived from sectors that were deemed to be 
‘completely free of price-fixing behaviour’.* And only from the 
1960s did the UK’s freshly minted competition authorities even 

begin to take cartelization seriously and attempt to weed it out.” 
Why was manufacturer cartelization so rife? The obvious (but 

superficial) answer is that it provided monopoly power, and thus 

monopoly profit. But perhaps a fuller answer would be that it 

substituted for more robust sources of monopoly power — such 

as, most pointedly, scarce, rent-generating assets — that at the 

time happened to be in much shorter supply than they are today. 

One flipside to the post-1960s secular decline of a sector — 
manufacturing — that was not previously rentierist has of course 

been the rise of a sector that very clearly is. That sector — finance 

20 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

— has always been a rentier demesne. But, following the argu- 
ment I made earlier, it is vital not to overstate the contribution 

of finance to the post-1960s growth in the “Business services and 

finance’ component of the economy shown in Figure 0.3. The 

story traced by the rise of that line is not predominantly one 

about finance (or financialization). For all the rise of finance, the 

financial sector contributed only 9 per cent of UK gross value- 

added in 2010; the remainder (nearly three-quarters) of the 
cumulative 33 per cent of 2010 value-added accounted for by 

‘Business services and finance’ was contributed by non-financial 

business services. If the upward trajectory of the line in question 

is not principally a financialization story, however, it is certainly 

one of rentierization. Non-financial business services are the 
home territory of contract rents and of the UK’s army of outsourc- 
ing companies — those providing to other businesses services that 
those businesses elect not to carry out for themselves. 

Thus, Figure 0.3’s vivid illustration of the parallel decline of 
manufacturing and rise of finance and business services between 
1970 and 2010 shows, respectively, the decline of a fundamentally 
non-rentier economy — although what remains of manufacturing 

has itself become more rentierist — and the rise of a rentier economy. 
We see a shift, as it were, from cartelized to rentierized capitalism. 

How can we explain the rentierization of the UK economy? 
What have been its consequences? All seven chapters of this book 

offer distinctive answers to these questions. Each individual rent- 

ier capitalism is different in terms not only of its structural 
complexion and operating dynamics, but also in relation to the 

factors accounting for the rentier’s ascendancy and the implica- 

tions of such ascendancy for key stakeholders — customers, work- 

ers, investors, and so on. There are commonalities, and these will 
be abundantly clear. Still, even where common drivers of rentier- 
ism or comparable outcomes do pertain, they do not necessarily 
apply in equal measure in each rentier domain; and each domain 

is characterized by idiosyncratic dynamics not visible elsewhere. 

INTRODUCTION 
oF 

Yet, for all the importance of attending to these differences, 

there is also a critical story to be told about the whole picture. 
Why has the post-1970s era been such a propitious one not just 

for specific categories of rentier, but for rentierism in general? 

What has been the impact of the return of the rentier not just in 

the particular areas of the economy where rentierism has taken 

hold, but for the economy and its main sets of actors — and thus 
UK society — in general? What, in this latter sense, has been the 

cumulative outcome of our array of distinct-but-connected 

resurgent rentierisms? The remainder of this Introduction consid- 

ers, in turn, the questions of common causes and cumulative 

consequences. 

The word ‘neoliberalism’ is much abused, and is widely scoffed 

at beyond the Left. But if one wanted to sum up the reasons for 

the rentier’s resurgence in the UK since the 1970s, then one 

could do much worse than reach for this signifier. In other words, 

rentierization has not only been conterminous with neoliberal- 

ism; it has, to a large extent, been the result of neoliberalism — 

that is, of the particular constellation of ideas and actions that we 

have increasingly come to associate with that term, not least in 

the pivotal realms of monetary and fiscal governance, resource 

allocation and property rights. 

In an important essay, the economist José Palma has argued 

that, internationally, neoliberalism has served to facilitate ‘the 

ever-increasing rent-seeking practices of oligopolistic capital’. It 

has done so, he says, by effectively reducing ‘pressures on big 

agents to engage in competitive struggles in the real economy 

(while doing the opposite to workers and small firms)’, thus 

helping to ‘transform capitalism into a rentiers’ delight’.°° Palma’s 

analysis is helpful because this, I suggest, is essentially what has 

happened in the UK. Neoliberalism UK-style has created just 

such a rentier ‘delight’ — Jonathan Ford, at the Financial Times, 

has described the early-twenty-first-century UK as ‘a rentier’s 

paradise’ — and rentierization has been the more-or-less inevita- 

ble result.*! 

yy 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

I will turn presently to the principal mechanisms by which 

neoliberalism has encouraged and abetted rentierization. But 

first it is vital to note that, in the UK at least, neither neoliberal- 

ism nor rentierization came from out of the blue, suddenly taking 

hold, as it were, of an unprepared and inimical political economy 
when Margaret Thatcher took power in 1979. The historiogra- 
phy of the UK — indeed of the West more generally — has tended 

to draw sharp dividing lines between the pre- Thatcher (Keynesian, 

social democratic) and ‘Thatcherite/post-Thatcher (neoliberal) 

eras. And there are of course enormous differences: to take what 

is for our purposes the most pertinent phenomenon, rentierism, 
long endemic to the UK’s political economy, was, as I have said, 
subdued in the post-war decades, and it did burst forth with 
renewed vigour once Thatcher was in Downing Street. But some 
of the most important seeds of the rentier’s recovery had been 
sown already in the 1960s and 1970s, and green shoots of rent- 
ierism had already begun to appear well in advance of Thatcher's 
accession to the prime ministership. 

The fundaments of this ‘pre’ history of neoliberalism and rent- 

ierization in the UK are contained in an extraordinary, prescient 

essay written by E. P. Thompson in 1965.* It offered three main, 

striking observations, each of which has subsequently been borne 

out. Rentier capitalism was unequivocally on the way back. The 

state was deeply implicated in the enablement of its revivification. 
And this was assuredly not simply the UK rentier capitalism of old 

— in place of the ‘integrated plutocracy’ of landed and financial 
interests described by Perry Anderson for the late nineteenth 
century, Thompson described the emergence in the 1960s of a 
‘new, and entirely different, predatory complex’, one with ‘vast 
influence reaching into the Civil Service, the professions, and into 
the trade union and labour movement itself’, and characterized by 

its interpenetration of private industry and the State (Government 

contracts, especially for war materials, of an unprecedented size, 

subsidies, municipal indebtedness to private finance, etc.), its control 

INTRODUCTION 
AS 

over major media of communication, its blackmail by the City, its 

reduction of the public sector to subordinate roles, and its capacity 

to dictate the conditions within which a Labour Government must 

operate.*** 

If this new rentier complex wasn’t just about finance (or real 

estate), finance did — and would — play a hugely significant role; 
witness Thompson’s own reference to ‘blackmail by the City’. 

This role merits special mention. As Aled Davies has recently 
argued, the shift to neoliberalism that eventually occurred in the 
UK under Thatcher was facilitated by changes in the financial 
system in the 1960s and 1970s that weakened and undermined 
key components of the nation’s social democratic political econ- 
omy.** Not least among these changes were the breakdown of the 
post-war settlement model of voluntary cooperation between the 

state and an oligopoly of cartelized banks, the emergence of the 
London-centred Euromarkets, and the disintegration of the 
Bretton Woods international monetary system. As Davies also 

observes, in the 1970s, the UK’s social democrats ‘were not 

simply ignorant of the changes, or fatalistic in response to the 

challenges arising from them’. Rather, they ‘sought to reformu- 

late and reconstruct their economic strategy in the 1970s in an 

attempt to advance the social democratic project beyond the 

post-war settlement.” But they ultimately failed. 

To the degree that it is possible to disentangle the ideas that 
animate political actions from those actions themselves, my focus 

is on the latter in the following summary account of how neolib- 

eralism in the UK, flowering fully in the 1980s following prepar- 

atory developments in the 1960s and 1970s, has precipitated the 

rentier’s return. This is not because the ideas are unimportant; on 

the contrary, they are critical. But, as explained in the Preface, 

the nature of my critique is political-economic, not ideational. 

Furthermore, strong critiques of the neoliberal ideas that have 

buttressed rentiers’ enhanced capacity to earn rents already exist: 

not just Philippe Askenazy's and now Thomas Piketty’s analysis 

DA 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of the ideology of (néo-)propriétarisme (see Preface,) but also 
Andrew Sayer’s similar account of how neoliberalism has forti- 

fied the rentier and widened her ambit by presenting her role as 

one of ‘wealth creation rather than wealth extraction’.*° In their 

incarnation in the UK context, such ideologies no doubt have 

particular local inflections that would be worth exploring; but 

that is not the approach I take here. While mindful of the rele- 

vant ideologies and the ‘work they have consistently performed, 

I focus my explanation on actions taken and their impact on the 

conditions of possibility of rentierism itself. 

Nor do I linger here on what might be called the actions 

behind the action: the political manoeuvrings and private-sector 
lobbying that have contributed to forty-plus years of rentier- 

friendly governance and policy in the UK. To the extent that 
such influences are material and visible (they often operate 
behind closed doors and out of sight), I discuss them in the rele- 
vant chapters. In general, we can state: neoliberalism in the UK 
has endured and has worked to the advantage of private-sector 
rentiers partly because those rentiers have actively encouraged 
the UK’s successive governments to de rentier-friendly, have 
often put their money where their mouths are, and have found 
the administrations in question to be remarkably accommodat- 
ing. For example, it is of course no accident that the three indus- 
try sectors that dominate donations to the UK political party 
that has done most to advance rentier interests over the past four 
decades — the Conservative party — are rentier sectors one and all: 
the finance sector (Chapter 1), the oil and gas sector (Chapter 2) 
and the property sector (Chapter 7).?7 

There are four key respects in which shifts in political-economic 
governance and allied developments have had profoundly bene- 

ficial consequences for rentierism and the rentier in the UK 
under neoliberalism. The most visible, and probably most impor- 

tant, relates to the size of the pool of available assets for rentiers 

to rent out. The neoliberal era across the Global North hasbeen 

an era of unprecedented privatization, and nowhere more than 

INTRODUCTION 
DBS 

in the UK, which has been privatization’s undisputed trailblazer 

since the first Thatcher administration began. Vast quantities of 

public assets have been sold off to the private sector (often on the 

cheap), in‘the process massively expanding the territory, in 

particular, of infrastructure rents (Chapter 6) — through the 

privatization of water supply networks, energy transmission and 

distribution networks, telecommunications networks, and so on; 

and of land rents (Chapter 7) — through the privatization of land 
and property. 

But it is not only privatization that has substantially grown 

rentier portfolios. Other notable developments that have signifi- 

cantly swelled stocks of rent-generating assets include: a massive 
growth in levels of interest-bearing household, corporate and 
sovereign debt, driven by financial deregulation and liberaliza- 

tion (Chapter 1); major discoveries of fossil-fuel resources in the 
North Sea (Chapter 2); the emergence of new, rent-generating 

digital platforms enabled by new information and communica- 

tion technologies (Chapter 4); and the proliferation of contract 

rents associated with the relentless drive within both the public 
and private sectors to outsource non-core services (Chapter 5). 

In short, in more or less every rentier domain, the neoliberal era 

in the UK has seen incremental creation of privately-owned 

assets, and thus incremental opportunities for earning rent, on 

an enormous scale. 

The second general explanation for the latter-day rise of rent- 
ierism in the UK economy relates to policy-driven transforma- 
tions in the ability of rentiers to exploit commercially the assets 

that they control. It is not just that there are today more such 

scarce assets; those assets that exist have in many cases become 

effectively superior, because the rights they confer have been 

strengthened. Arguably, most important in this respect has been 

a long-term neutralization of competition policy. For a number 

of reasons — not least the growing influence of Chicago School 

orthodoxy within law and economics — UK competition author- 

ities have since the 1980s become considerably more tolerant of 

26 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

various forms of monopoly power, including that possessed by 

rentier institutions, whose ‘resources’ have increasingly taken on 

the quality of ‘assets’ — that is, entities capable of reliably generat- 

ing income — by virtue of their sheltering from competition.** If 

a secular decline in levels of antitrust enforcement has bolstered 

the commercial viability of rentier assets across the board, mean- 

while, a series of policy shifts pertaining to specific rentier sectors 

has had comparable effects for their respective asset types. These 

shifts include a widening and fortification of both IP rights 
(Chapter 3) and radio spectrum licensee rights (Chapter 6), and 

a tilting of the balance of power from tenants towards landlords, 

especially in the case of residential property (Chapter 7). 

Thirdly, as well as making it easier for rentiers to generate 

rents, policy developments have enabled them to maximize the 

rents they generate. Here, rentier-friendly fiscal and monetary 

policies have been particularly significant. Monetary policy has 
been especially important to the financial rentier: tight monetary 
policy underpinned high real interest rates from the late 1970s 
essentially until the onset of the financial crisis, sustaining in 
turn the levels of financial rents (Chapter 1). Fiscal policy, and 
especially the tax sphere, has had broader effects. For one thing, 
successive UK governments have offered substantial tax subsidies 
to certain types of rentiers, including those earning rents on 
natural-resource 
(Chapter 
2) and 
IP 
assets 
(Ghaptenas 
Furthermore, UK tax policy in general has in recent decades 
become increasingly accommodating to rentier income streams. 
‘The most significant example of this by far is capital gains tax 
(CGT), which is levied on the quintessential rentier income: the 
capital gain occurring upon asset disposal. As early as 1982, the 
Thatcher administration nailed its colours to the rentier mast by 
introducing a CGT indexation allowance that provided relief 
for the effects of inflation on asset values. Then, in 1988, the 
cost of all assets that had been held at 31 March 1982 was 
‘rebased’ to their market value at that date, thus ensuring’ that 
gains accruing prior to that would not be charged to tax. The 

INTRODUCTION 
AY 

first of these two forms of relief was amended in 1998, in a way 

that once again explicitly served rentier interests. For periods of 

asset ownership after April 1998, the relief afforded by indexa- 

tion was replaced by so-called ‘taper relief’, whereby chargeable 

gains would be tapered according to the length of time that an 

asset was held. The fundamental generosity of taper relief lay in 

the fact that the taper was (and still is) applied to net gains after 

the deduction of ‘allowable’ losses, which are set against gains in 

the order that produces the lowest tax charge. Moreover, as 
introduced in 1998, and in a further fillip for the corporate 

rentier, the taper was more generous for business assets than for 
non-business assets. On three subsequent occasions (in 2000, 
2001 and 2004), the definition of business assets has been 

widened.*” 

On top of all this, the UK has a dismal record on tax avoid- 

ance, which not only benefits rentier interests, but has also been 
shamelessly exploited by rentier institutions, to their great profit 

— not least in finance (Chapter 1) and infrastructure (Chapter 6). 

As a report by the Tax Justice Network recently showed, 

The UK with its corporate tax haven network is by far the 

world’s greatest enabler of corporate tax avoidance and has 

single-handedly done the most to break down the global 

corporate tax system, accounting for over a third of the world’s 

corporate tax avoidance risks . 
. 
. That’s four times more than 

the next greatest contributor of corporate tax avoidance risks, 

the Netherlands, which accounts for less than 7 per cent.” 

The sector most efficient in avoiding tax, according to this report, 

was finance. 

Fourth and finally, neoliberal governance 
has not only 
supported the incomes generated by rentier assets. It has also 

supported the value of those assets per se, with significant conse- 

quences for rentier fortunes. While this is true for all such assets, 

it is most easily measured, and most widely recognized, in the 

28 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

realms of finance (Chapter 1) and land (Chapter 7). Piketty has 

discussed this phenomenon in relation to the advanced indus- 

trial nations more broadly. As he writes, ‘the price of real estate 

and [financial] stocks fell to historically low levels in the after- 
math of World War II ... After 1950’, however, ‘these asset 

prices gradually recovered, with an acceleration after 1980’.*! 

Needless to say, there was nothing ‘natural’ about such accel- 

eration, which, in the UK, has in recent years been especially 
pronounced with respect to land values, and where unconven- 

tional post—financial crisis monetary policy, in the shape of 

so-called quantitative easing, has latterly played a crucial role. 

Asset price acceleration has occurred, as Piketty observes of 
Western societies under neoliberalism more generally, ‘in a polit- 

ical context that was on the whole more favourable to private 
wealth than that of the immediate postwar decades’.” In the UK, 
the most emphatic articulation of this greater favourability to 
private 
wealth 
accumulation 
came 
in 
1998 
when 
Peter 
Mandelson, during his brief tenure as secretary of state for trade 
and industry, famously expressed New Labour's standpoint thus: 
“We are intensely relaxed about people getting filthy rich as long 
as they pay their taxes.’ One imagines Mandelson would argue 
today that it is not his — or Tony Blair’s — fault that the UK’s 
rentier class readily absorbed the first part of this statement while 
— with active government connivance — widely ignoring the 
second. 
' 
When these four crucial sets of developments — bearing respec- 

tively on asset volumes, ease of rent extraction, rent levels, and 

asset values — are combined, they produce precisely the ‘rentier’s 

paradise’ referred to above by Jonathan Ford. Unsurprisingly, 

since the early 1980s, rentier institutions — and on a much 

smaller scale UK rentier households — have needed no further 
encouragement to fill their boots. 

What has the return of the rentier led to at the aggregate level of 

the UK and its overall political economy? 

INTRODUCTION 
BY 

Theory can help us greatly here. Marx opened Capital with the 
commodity because the commodity is the ‘elementary form’ in 

which wealth appears in capitalist societies, and is therefore the 

key to unlocking capitalism's secrets. If the commodity is in this 

sense capital’s ‘essence’, what is the essence of rent — and thus the 

key to understanding the effects of the rise of rentier capitalism? 

The answer is: monopoly. Monopoly — by providing the condi- 

tions under which an asset can generate an income — is the very 

sea in which the rentier swims. It is thus with monopoly that we 

begin. 

Much of the criticism of monopoly power, from both hetero- 

dox and orthodox economic perspectives, is based on the fact 

that it often, though not always, enables the realization of 
monopoly profits. This, after all, is a large part of the reason why 

capitalists attempt to secure monopoly power in the first place. 
As we will see, it is indisputably the case that many of the rentier 

institutions that dominate the UK economy today achieve levels 

of profitability that would be unimaginable without the monop- 
oly positions they enjoy. Where most capitalist companies would 

be delighted to achieve operating profit margins of 15 to 20 per 

cent, we will encounter rentiers that consistently post margins of 

30, 40, 50 per cent, or even higher. That is monopoly in action. 

But the most significant implications of the rise to dominance 
of the monopoly-enjoying rentier do not relate to monopoly 

profits, or at least not directly. They originate elsewhere, and can 

best be understood by referring to Marx and several of his later 

interlocutors. 

Only those who have never read Marx and Engels imagine 

that they were unremittingly critical of capitalism — and of what 

it had already achieved by the mid nineteenth century. Consider 

the opening pages of the Communist Manifesto, where they 

marvel at the ongoing revolutionization of industrial production 

across Europe. Capitalism, they recognized, had ‘created more 

massive and more colossal productive forces than have all preced- 

ing generations together; it had ‘accomplished wonders far 

BO 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

surpassing Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, and Gothic 

cathedrals’. It was a veritable engine of innovation: ‘Subjection of 

Nature’s forces to man, machinery, application of chemistry to 

industry and agriculture, steam-navigation, railways, electric 

telegraphs, clearing of whole continents for cultivation, canalisa- 

tion of rivers, whole populations conjured out of the ground — 
what earlier century had even a presentiment that such produc- 

tive forces slumbered in the lap of social labour?’ Marx and 

Engels remain open to interpretation, of course; but there can be 

little doubt that they saw positive consequences to all this. 
Where, today, capitalism’s apologists hail its ability to drag less 

‘developed’ nations out of poverty, Marx and Engels conceded 

that capitalism had ‘rescued a considerable part of the popula- 

tion from the idiocy of rural life ... The bourgeoisie, by the 
rapid improvement of all instruments of production, by the 
immensely facilitated means of communication, draws all, even 

the most barbarian, nations into civilisation.“? The downside to 
this ‘civilisation’, needless to say, was the exploitation that seem- 
ingly came as part of the bargain. 

If capitalism’s 
revolutionizing of production was 
to be 

applauded, it was clear to Marx where the driving force of this 
innovation economy lay: in the dynamics of competition. Like 
Adam Smith before him, Marx was acutely aware that competing 
was not what capitalists wanted to do. Given the choice, indi- 

vidual capitalists much prefer to be monopolists, enjoying, in 
David Harvey's words, ‘the certainties, the quiet life and the 
possibility of leisurely and cautious changes that go with a 
monopolistic style of working and living outside of the rough 
and tumble of competition’. The problem they face is that such 

a choice is not always available. If not in possession of robust 
monopoly powers, capitalists must innovate simply to remain 
competitive, and thus stay afloat. 

Marx's clearest statement of this existential sink-or-swim 
endeavour comes in volume 3 of Capital. The effort to stay Afloat 

is compelled by ‘the general competitive struggle and the need to 

INTRODUCTION 
Bul 

improve production and extend its scale, merely as a means of 

self-preservation, and on pain of going under’; it manifests as 

innovation, or ‘constant revolutions in methods of production 

themselves’ and it results in ‘the drive to expand capital and 

produce surplus-value on a larger scale’.“° In volume 1, mean- 

while, Marx repeatedly uses a striking word to describe the oper- 

ation of this ‘law’ of competition: ‘coercion’. ‘Under free compe- 

tition’, he writes, ‘the immanent laws of capitalist production 

confront the individual capitalist as a coercive force external to 

him ... and therefore enter into the consciousness of the indi- 

vidual capitalist as the motives which drive him forward’.“° 

Competition, in short, keeps capitalists honest. It forces Marx’s 

bad guys — capitalists, with their instinctive preference for 
monopoly — to do something he considered positive, namely 

innovate. 

The monopoly power inherent to rentierism, by contrast, is 

generally inimical to dynamism and innovation. Spared the coer- 

cive forces of competition buffeting other capitalists, the rentier 
ordinarily opts for a quiet life, focusing her energies on sweating 

existing income-generating assets — shoring up the defences 

arrayed around them, fighting any attempts to stem the flows of 
money they elicit — rather than, for example, innovating in the 

interest of developing new products or services. Lenin, following 
Marx, noted that the dulling impact of the rentier’s monopoly 
power ‘inevitably engenders a tendency to stagnation and decay. 

Since monopoly prices are established, even temporarily, the 

motive cause of technical and, consequently, of all other progress, 

disappears to a certain extent.’”” 

To be sure, Joseph Schumpeter famously contested this 

thesis, maintaining in his Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy 

that monopoly power does not in fact typically have such a 

‘soporific effect’ — a monopoly position, ‘especially in manufac- 

turing industry’, being ‘in general no cushion to sleep on. As it 

can be gained’, Schumpeter protested, ‘so it can be retained 

only by alertness and energy. “* But Schumpeter was wrong. 

SA 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

For one thing, the monopoly position enjoyed by the rentier 

very often is not gained by ‘alertness and energy’. In the UK 

case, for example, think of the natural monopolies in the elec- 

tricity, gas, water, rail and other sectors handed to private 
companies through privatizations in the 1980s and 1990s 
(Chapter 6), or the private lands handed down through genera- 

tions of aristocratic families (Chapter 7). Such monopoly posi- 

tions frequently require little by way of alertness or energy to be 

retained, either. Furthermore, Schumpeter did not so much 
underestimate as ignore the significance of competition as a 

coercive force: denying that monopoly power provides a cush- 

ioning effect, he elided the fact that competition does the 

opposite, and neglected to consider the implications of the 
removal of competition from the picture. 

In any case, it is not only that rentiers generally lack motiva- 

tion to innovate. In possession of ‘cash cows’, they also have 

active reasons, as Lenin commented, not to innovate, and to 
prevent others from doing so. David Hart refers to such 
obstructionism — overlooked by Schumpeter — in terms of rent- 

iers’ incentive to ‘slow the pace of technological change in order 

to increase their profits from existing products’.>° As always, 

there are exceptions. ‘Monopolists’, accepts Tim Harford, ‘can 
sometimes use their scale and cash flow to produce real innova- 
tions — the glory years of Bell Labs come to mind.’ But such 
exceptions are rare. Harford continues: ‘the ferocious cut and 
thrust of smaller competitors seems a more reliable way to 
produce many of the everyday innovations that matter’>! By 
nature, rentierism is inimical to all this. 

And so, precisely as one would expect, the return of the rentier 

to centre stage in the UK economy during the neoliberal era has 
had a demonstrably soporific effect. Figure 0.4 powerfully 
demonstrates this escalating torpor: increasingly beholden to 

rentier interests liberated from competitive coercion, and hence 
lacking the impetus to innovate, rates of capital investinent 

across the economy as a whole have plunged. In the 1970s, more

nothing that would bespeak the growing travails of the UK

rentierized. 

To be sure, rentierization is not solely to blame. The wide- 
spread and expanding availability in recent decades of cheap 

labour, arriving in the UK for example from Eastern Europe, has 

acted as a powerful dampener on the incentive for UK businesses 

to make investments designed to improve labour productivity. 
There is nothing surprising in this. As Marx might rhetorically 

have asked, why would a business invest in the hope of generat- 
ing relative surplus value (the extra profit that arises by shorten- 
ing the time required for a worker to perform a particular task) 
when it can generate absolute surplus value (the extra profit that 

arises when workers can be made to work for longer hours for the 
same pay) with no investment required? 

INTRODUCTION 
3D 

Nonetheless, as Michael Roberts has explained, rentierization 
has clearly contributed to the UK’s slowing productivity growth. 
To begin with, ‘productivity growth depends on capital invest- 
ment being‘ large enough’, which, as we have seen (Figure 0.4), it 

has not been in the UK in the period during which rentier domi- 
nance has intensified.” But that, says Roberts, is not all: ‘In the 

case of the UK, there is another particular problem: the UK is 

increasingly a rentier economy, relying on finance, business services 

and real estate. These are unproductive activities that do not boost 

the productivity of labour, but do reduce available profits for 

productive investment.’ To support his thesis, Roberts cites work 
by researchers at the Economic Statistics Centre of Excellence that 

identified the economic sectors primarily responsible for the drop 

in UK productivity growth between 2011 and 2015. The main 

culprits were, of course, rentier sectors: finance (Chapter 1, below), 
mining and quarrying (Chapter 2), telecommunications, electric- 

ity and gas (Chapter 6), pharmaceuticals (Chapter 3) and comput- 

ing and professional services (Chapter 5). 

It does not take a PhD in economics to figure out what the 

headline effect of all of this has been. If investment, and especially 
R&D investment, is falling, and if growth in labour productivity 

is also slowing, there can really be only one outcome: a slowdown 

in the economy as a whole; that is to say, declining growth in 
economic output. This, too, is demonstrated in Figure 0.5, which, 

alongside growth in productivity, charts annual growth in GDP, 

likewise on a three-year rolling-average basis. Like labour produc- 

tivity growth — which it inevitably tracks quite closely — growth in 
GDP has also swung quite violently in recent decades; but the 

general trend is likewise clearly downwards. 

Had the various major categories of recipient of UK national 
income absorbed the recent historic decline in income growth 

roughly proportionately with one another, that would be one 

thing; everybody would, 4 da David Cameron, have been ‘in it 

together’. But that is absolutely not what has happened. Parallel to 

56 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the long-run slowdown in economic growth, there has been a 

major ‘re-sorting’ of incomes such that the lion’s share of the pain 

of halting growth has been shouldered by workers, and especially 
low-income workers. In other words, the UK has seen growing 

inequality of income both between capital and labour and between 
workers at different ends of the income spectrum. Crucially, this 
growing income inequality has also been fundamentally — if not 

entirely — a function of economic rentierization. 

To understand how this has happened, let us first examine the 

relationship between capital and labour income. The distribu- 

tion of a nation’s income between these two constituencies has 

long been interpreted by heterodox scholars as an indirect meas- 

ure of the degree of labour exploitation taking place: the stronger 

the weighting towards capital, the more successfully workers are 

being exploited. Until relatively recently, the mainstream view — 

in which of course the word ‘exploitation’ is never used — was 

that this distribution was more or less an historical constant: 
whatever was happening in the economy, capital and labour’s 
respective shares of income tended to remain approximately the 
same. ‘This, for example, was very much John Maynard Keynes’s 
position. He famously described the longitudinal stability of 
labour's share as ‘one of the most surprising, yet best-established 
facts in the whole range of economic statistics’. 

But Keynes's observation no longer holds. Since the 1970s, 

labour’s share of national income has fallen precipitously. This, it 

should be noted, is not just a UK trend: the economists Loukas 
Karabarbounis 
and 
Brent 
Neiman 
have 
documented 
a 
5-percentage-point decline globally in the share of income 
captured by labour since the mid 1970s, showing that, of the 

fifty-nine countries with at least fifteen years of data between 
1975 and 2012, forty-two showed downward trends in their 
labour shares.*° But the UK has been an extreme example of the 
phenomenon. As the Bank of England’s Andrew Haldane has 
shown, whichever dataset one employs (they show slightly differ- 

ent things), the labour share of income in the UK has declined 

INTRODUCTION 
Byf 

dramatically since the early 1970s, from as high as nearly 70 per 

cent then to around 55 per cent today.” 

Several arguments have been advanced to try to explain this 

developmertt. Some authors 
— including Karabarbounis and 
Neiman — believe the substitution of technology for labour has 
played a role. The growing consensus, however — again, not just for 

the UK but more broadly — is that the key contributory factor is 

the phenomenon that, as we have seen, substantially defines rent- 

ierism: monopoly power. Traditionally, when economists have 

discussed monopoly power, they have focused on the effects of its 

exercise within the markets where monopolists sell their goods or 

services. In seeking to account for falling labour shares, however, 
they have turned their attention instead’ to the markets where 

goods and services are procured, and specifically to the labour 

market. A monopolist’s power to dominate labour markets, hold- 

ing down wages by virtue of the strength of its negotiating posi- 

tion vis-a-vis workers who lack choices of alternative employer, is 

referred to as monopsony. Growing monopsony power, it is argued, 

helps explain capital’s historic capture of income from labour.” 

The most persuasive application of this argument to the case of 

the UK and its own falling labour share in recent decades is found 

in the work of Will Abel, Silvana Tenreyro and Gregory ‘Thwaites 

on the effects of monopsony power in the UK private sector from 
1998 to 2017. Two aspects of their analysis are especially signif- 

cant. The first is that the impact of monopsony on wages is 
contingent: increasing monopsony drives down pay — and, 

extrapolated to the whole economy, labour’s share — only where 

workers are not covered by collective bargaining agreements. In 

other words, unionization, where present, serves as a bulwark 

against exploitation. But, as is well known, the neoliberal era has 

been one long period of union decline in the UK. In 1980, around 

70 per cent of employees’ wages were set by collective bargain- 

ing. By 2018, the figure had plummeted to just 26 per cent for 

the workforce as a whole, and even lower — a paltry 15 per cent 

— in the private sector.°' The bulwark, then, has been removed.

INTRODUCTION 
5g 

For our purposes, the second notable element of these authors’ 

analysis is more vital still. Monopsony power, they found, varies 

markedly by industry sector, with the highest levels of concentra- 

tion — that is, the lowest numbers of 
potential employers — found, 

without fail, in what this book identifies as rentier sectors. Figure 

0.6, reproduced from their analysis, provides a vivid demonstra- 

tion of this. Look towards the upper end of the chart, where the 

most concentrated industries are found, and you will see a veri- 

table roll-call of rentier strongholds: in particular, various itera- 

tions of infrastructure rentierism (Chapter 6), natural-resource 

rentierism (Chapter 2) and intellectual property rentierism 

(Chapter 3). We will be exploring the ‘local’ effects of this 
monopoly power in the respective chapters. Here, the key point 

is this: as the UK economy has rentierized since the 1970s, it has 

shifted increasingly into sectors characterized by monopsony, 

and thus, at the aggregate level, towards 
a more monopsonistic 

structural model. In that context, and with union power all the 

while being widely dismantled, anything other than a pronounced 

fall in labour’s income share would have been nothing short of 

remarkable. 

At the same time as capital, and especially rentier capital, has 
been capturing a growing share of the UK’s stagnating overall 

income, income inequality among workers has also been increas- 

ing. In a sense, this stands to reason based on what I have already 

discussed. If capital has been effectively squeezing labour, it 

would be exceptionally naive to believe that it has been squeez- 

ing all workers equally. Those at the top, after all, who decide 

workers’ salaries, are the ones carrying out the squeezing, and 

they are hardly likely to make themselves its victims. Granted, 

many big listed companies have ‘independent’ remuneration 

committees to set executive compensation, but everybody knows 

what a wretched job they have done in curbing executive salary 

inflation.” 

Rentierization has been integral to the increasing inequality of 
UK worker incomes. In fact, income inequality is to some degree 

40 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

baked into the rentier business model: growing inequality is a 
handmaiden to the emergent dominance of rentier capitalism. 
Rentierism 
is fundamentally about securing, protecting and 

sweating scarce assets, and these different roles — which we can 

think about in terms of different working ‘relationships’ to the 

asset — command vastly different pecuniary rewards. Within any 

rentier institution, the gains flow disproportionately to the small 

handful of individuals who create, capture or protect from compe- 

tition or impairment the all-important rent-generating assets: for 

instance, the ‘quants’ who design exotic new financial instru- 

ments; the oil industry executives who sign the licensing deals 

with the politicians of resource-rich states; the lawyers who secure 

patent approval for a blockbuster new drug; the ‘rain-makers’ 
who win ten-year outsourcing contracts. 

Indeed, the rise of rentier capitalism is the only credible expla- 

nation that we have for the fact that, as David Graeber has 

recently observed, lawyers and accountants account for ‘an 
extraordinarily high percentage of the working population’ in 
the UK, numbering some 150,000 and 312,000, respectively. 
For lawyers and accountants are quintessential, indispensable 
purveyors of balance-sheet capitalism. The former serve to secure 
the value of rentiers’ assets, litigating against any perceived or 
actual threat of devaluation. Accountants calibrate and audit the 
value of rentiers’ assets, rendering it legible, fungible and acces- 
sible to management and to the investment community. 

At the other end of the workforce spectrum, the 99 per cent 

perform the daily drudgery of sweating, or servicing, the assets 

that their bosses have heroically secured — manning call centres, 

fulfilling cleaning contracts, repairing network infrastructures, 
and so on. A striking example of this polarization is British 
American Tobacco, the London Stock Exchange—listed UK ciga- 

rette and tobacco manufacturer and intellectual property rentier 
whose market-leading brands include Dunhill, Lucky Strike and 
Rothmans (see Table 0.1). At the top of the company inéome 
hierarchy sits the chief executive and chief brand custodian, 

INTRODUCTION 
4] 

Nicandro Durante, whose total remuneration in 2017 was over 

£11 million. At the bottom are the up to 15,000 child labourers, 

some as young as three, believed to be working unpaid or for 

poverty wages harvesting tobacco for the company in the fields 

of Malawi. In 2018, the Chartered Institute of Personnel and 

Development produced a fascinating report on pay scales at 

FTSE 100 companies more generally. Those with the widest gaps 

between executive and average employee pay were, unsurpris- 

ingly, rentiers — many of which appear in the pages that follow.® 

In fact, there is one important corner of the rentier economy 

where something more particular still is going on. Chapter 5 

explores contract rents — the vast incomes that flow today in the 
UK to companies to which other organizations, in both the 

private and public sectors, have outsourced activities they no 
longer elect to perform in-house. This is probably the biggest 

rentier sector in financial terms. As we will see, one of the main 

reasons that so many organizations have chosen to outsource 
work to contract rentiers — though definitely not the reason they 

tend to offer when asked — 
is precisely to squeeze labour. 
Outsourcing, research has shown, widely strips workers of the 

benefits, including relatively decent pay, to which they would be 

entitled if they worked in-house. As one UK employment lawyer 

caustically observed, if conditions for workers at contractors 

were the same as for those at the companies for whom they 

contract, 
it would 
‘almost 
make 
outsourcing 
pointless’. 

Inequality is part of the raison d étre of outsourcing. 

Insofar as platform rentiers (Chapter 4) are able to treat those 

who secure employment — albeit precarious — through the plat- 

form as contractors rather than employees, the same capacity to 

squeeze labour is inherent to that rentier domain, too. The 

combined growth of contract rentierism and platform rentierism 

has been substantially responsible, at any rate, for the swelling to 

more than 5 million by mid 2019 of the number of people in the 

UK who, in Delphine Strauss’s words, were in ‘low paid, insecure 

forms of work — including short-term work and contracts with 

4D 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

unpredictable hours and pay — and were not earning enough to 
make ends meet’.”” This enlargement of the UK’s precariat is 

crucial in understanding what Torsten Bell and Laura Gardiner 
have recently described as the biggest change to the UK economy 

during the period since the financial crisis: the employment 

‘boom’ that has seen the proportion of the working-age popula- 

tion in work grow from 73 to 76 per cent. As they explain, the 
main reason people are working more is that most people are ‘a 

lot poorer than [they] expected to be’.

Meanwhile, at the top end of the income spectrum, those 

largely protected from the pressure on wages that has accompa- 

nied rentierization have added to their employment income by 
themselves becoming rentiers — whether or not they work at 

rentier institutions. They have done so by procuring in a personal 

or household capacity increasing quantities of financial and real 

estate assets (see Chapters 1 and 7, respectively), the latter 
primarily in the shape of buy-to-let residential property. This 
cumulative phenomenon, which, following Piketty, I refer to 

here as ‘petit’ rentierism, has further enlarged already widening 

INTRODUCTION 
43 

income gaps.”? Figure 0.7 shows annual investment income 

(including income from letting residential properties, but exclud- 
ing capital gains) for each decile of UK households, ranked by 

overall disposable income, between 1980 and 2016/17. It is a 

striking chart by any measure. Below the top two income deciles, 

essentially nothing has happened: here, among the bulk of UK 

households, rentiers are not to be found — if, as I have done, one 

excludes pension income.’! The ninth decile shows modest 
growth in investment income. But rentier income is essentially a 

feature of just the top decile, where annual investment income 
(combining financial and land rents) increased from an average 

of under £1,000 in 1980 to over £6,000 in 2016/17. 

For all these reasons, income inequality in the UK has surged 

as rentierism has tightened its grip. Such inequality is a veritable 

minefield of conflicting narratives that rely on different data 

sources. In a recent paper, Richard Burkhauser and his colleagues 

have helped clear the weeds somewhat.” As they say, whatever 

data one uses, it is clear that income inequality in the UK 

increased dramatically in the 1980s. The controversy concerns 
what happened next. Based on household survey data, inequality 

appears to plateau from around 1990 onwards, albeit at a much 
higher level than prior to the 1980s. Tax return data, by contrast 

— preferred by economists — show continued growth in income 

inequality, which has today reached a level considerably above 
where it was in the early 1990s, let alone the early 1980s.” 

But there is one final detail that deserves mention in this area. 

Even based on tax return data, it appears that the decade since 

the financial crisis has been characterised by falling inequality — 

which peaked, according to the official data, in 2009. But it 

should be borne in mind that this is only what the official data 

say. As many commentators have noted — including the late 

doyen of UK inequality studies, Tony Atkinson — these data are 

enormously problematic because they exclude various highly 

significant income sources, including much of the income going 

to non-domiciled residents, all capital gains, and tax-exempt 

44 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

returns on savings and investments. Not only are such incomes 
known to be heavily concentrated at the top of the income distri- 

bution; they are also overwhelmingly rentierist in nature.

If these missing income sources were included in measures 

based on tax return data, the share of UK income going to those at 

the top — and thus reported income inequality — would be substan- 

tially larger than is currently estimated in official statistics. As just 

one indication of the significance of the missing types of income, 
consider inequality in capital gains. Figure 0.8 shows the govern- 
ment’s estimates of the number of individual UK taxpayers realiz-

the upper end, some 9,000 individuals made gains of more than 
£1 million each. Meanwhile, some 99 per cent of taxpayers — those 
not registering on the chart — had no taxable capital gains at all.”4 
In a vital but as-yet unpublished study, the legal scholar Andy 
Summers has made provisional estimates of changes in UK income 
distribution with the various missing income sources included. He 
has found that such sources have grown relative to (observed) taxa- 
ble incomes over the past decade, driving ongoing increases in 
actually-existing income inequality.”°

INTRODUCTION 
A 

If the rise of rentier capitalism in the UK has led to growing income 

inequality, what of its corollary, wealth inequality? Here, of course, 

the key scholarly reference point of recent years is Piketty’s work, 
and his famous formula: 7 > ¢. Capital in the Twenty-First Century 

posited that the main driver of growing wealth inequalities under 
capitalism is the tendency of returns on capital to exceed the rate of 
economic growth. ‘The bigger the gap between 7 and g, the more 
pronounced the resulting increase in inequality: ‘when growth is 

low and the return on capital is distinctly greater than the growth 

rate, it is almost inevitable (at least in the most plausible dynamic 

models) that wealth will become [highly] concentrated’.”° 

What then of the UK under rentierization? We have discussed 

both rand g already. The former is rentierism’s cardinal metric — 

its pulse rate, the chief index of rentier viability. The higher r is, 

the better it is to be a rentier. The active amplification of 7 through 

a suite of rentier-friendly monetary and fiscal policies represents 

one of the key explanations for the revivification of the rentier in 

the UK under neoliberalism. Meanwhile, g, as we have just seen, 

has increasingly been suppressed — precisely as a consequence of 

the intensification of rentierism and the dulling impact on invest- 
ment of the monopoly powers it confers. 

In this sense, a rentier economy such as the UK has increas- 

ingly become represents the materialization, at least in theory, of 

perfect laboratory conditions for Piketty’s ‘law’ of growing wealth 
inequality to take hold. A rentier economy is by definition an 
economy of r-maximization and g-minimization. 

To some degree, the data bear this out. In charts illustrating 

wealth inequality in the UK over the past century, including 

Piketty’s, the line tracing the evolution of such inequality follows a 

classic hockey-stick path. From the early twentieth century through 

to around 1980, wealth inequality in the UK fell precipitously — 

further and faster, in fact, than in any of its peers among the 

advanced industrial nations. But then the course of UK history 
changed. Wealth inequality did not just stop falling; it began to 

rise (and is still rising), with the line tracing that rise departing 

46 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

almost at right-angles from the trajectory it had followed in previ- 

ous decades.”” The UK was now undergoing rentierization. 

Nonetheless, it is worth noting that the increase in wealth inequal- 

ity in the UK since the early 1980s has not been as substantial as in 

some other countries, such as the United States, Russia and China. 

The reason for this appears to have been to do with housing. In the 
UK, property prices have increased particularly sharply, and the 

distribution of housing is notably different from other asset classes. 

It accounts for only a relatively small proportion of total wealth at 

the top end; meanwhile, the mass conversion of social housing to 

owner-occupied dwellings over the past four decades has served to 

distribute significant amounts of property wealth across several 

wealth deciles. Thus, as Gabriel Zucman has noted, house price 

increases in the UK have ‘tended to boost the wealth share of the 

middle class, since most [of] its wealth is invested in housing, while 

upper groups mostly own financial assets .”* Or, as Facundo Alvaredo, 
Tony Atkinson and Salvatore Morelli note of the UK: ‘housing 
wealth has moderated a definite tendency for there to be a rise in 
recent years in top shares in total wealth apart from housing’.””

INTRODUCTION 
47 

But that is not quite the end of our account of the headline 
political-economic consequences of UK rentierization. This is 

because, in order to sustain the aforementioned house-price 

increases of‘ recent decades, it has been necessary for UK house- 

holds to take on sharply increasing amounts of mortgage debt. 
Moreover, as income and wealth inequality have increased, house- 

holds have, as a result, also taken on increasingly large quantities of 
unsecured debt (see Figure 0.9).*° This latter phenomenon is not 
only about households at the lower end of the income spectrum 

using debt to compensate for stagnant real wages. Growing 

inequality leads to growing debt burdens in more indirect ways, 

too. [he more that people at all levels of the income hierarchy see 

those above them pulling away, not least in terms of their consump- 

tion patterns, the more they are incentivized to try to keep pace. 

This ‘keeping up with the Joneses’ dynamic, which is inherent to 
inequality and powered by it, substantially propels debt accumula- 

tion. The overall result, in any event, has been a significant increase 

since the 1980s in the ratio of UK household debt to income 

(Figure 0.10) — one rendered tolerable, for the time being at least, 

only by a secular decline in interest rates (Chapter 1).

RENTIER CAPITALISM 

As accountants never tire of reminding us, though — and 

rightly enough — one person's liability is another’s financial asset. 

If the growth in the debt mountain pictured in Figure 0.9 looks 

positively daunting from the perspective of the UK household, 

there is inevitably a counter-perspective from which, by contrast, 

it looks positively appetizing. Whose perspective is this? Who 

has benefited from this explosion of household debt? The finan- 

cial rentier, of course — the creator, holder, and, through the 

charging of interest, exploiter of an asset pile that just three 

decades ago was worth around £200 billion, but on current 

trends will soon be worth ten times that sum. Appropriately 
enough, it is specifically with financial rents that I will begin my 

more detailed analysis of contemporary UK rentier capitalism. 

CHAPTER ONE 

The Functionless Investor: Financial Rents 

‘“ 

To announce great individual fortune in the midst of wider social 
and economic misery is invariably to court resentment and 
wrath. This was very much the scenario in February 2010, when 

Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, announced its results for 

2009. Group profit before tax had almost doubled from the 

previous year, reaching a record £11.6 billion. Given that the 
country had entered a period of painful austerity from which, a 
decade later, it has yet to recover, the news that annual Barclays 

staff bonuses had jumped to an eye-watering £2.7 billion was 
perhaps more poisonous still. Brendan Barber, general secretary 
of the Trades Union Congress, spoke for many of his country- 

folk when he raged, ‘Paying huge bonuses when people are still 

losing their jobs and businesses cannot get the loans they need 

because of a crash made in the finance sector goes against every 

concept of fairness.’! Just four months previously, the UK prime 

minister, David Cameron, notoriously had sought to democra- 

tize austerity, boldly proclaiming: “We're all in this together.”’ 

Barclays, evidently, was not. 

Dry it may be, but the annual report in which Barclays docu- 
mented its and its staffs unconscionable 2009 fortunes makes 

for essential reading.’ It tells us better than any financial jour- 

nalism or scholarly exegesis what type of business the modern, 

50 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

hyper-profitable Barclays, descended from a modest banking 

operation established in the City of London in the late seven- 
teenth century, has become. The report is shot through with 
what we might call asset vigilance. The superior performance of 

the business in 2009 is reported to be predicated on ‘efficient 

balance sheet utilisation’ and the improvement of ‘asset qual- 

ity’. The relative successes of the various divisions of the busi- 

ness are explained principally in terms of the size of their 

respective asset portfolios and each one’s ‘assets margin’ — a 

measure that quantifies Barclays’ efficiency in monetizing those 

assets. (Total group assets at the end of 2009, for what it is 

worth, were valued at £1.4 trillion.) Continued cultivation of a 

healthy balance sheet is identified as the secret to keeping the 

overall business on track. Having ‘increased the surplus of 
liquid assets’ in 2009, management pledged to remain ‘very 
attentive to the size and composition of our balance sheet’. In 

its preoccupation with the size, quality and productivity of its 
asset base, the modern Barclays is, I suggest, a quintessential 
rentier — an arch proponent of what I described in the Preface 

as balance-sheet capitalism. 

The original Barclays was a rentier institution of sorts, too. Its 

founders were ‘goldsmith bankers’: that is, goldsmiths — metal- 
workers specialized in working with (‘smithing’) gold and other 

precious metals — who were also bankers, in that their smithing 

activity enabled them to take on certain of the functions of what 
we now recognize as ‘banking’. Goldsmith banking in the seven- 
teenth century largely entailed currency exchange and the 
custody of valuable items, but over time these primitive financial 
institutions, Barclays included, branched out into a wider variety 
of financial services, one of which was lending money at inter- 

est.‘ Assets — gold, coins, bills of exchange — were their funda- 
mental stock-in-trade, and control over their circulation was 
Barclays’ prime source of competitive advantage. 

Thus began a long, upwards trajectory for Barclays and other 

British banking institutions that, by the late nineteenth century, 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
Sw 

had seen the sector move into a dominant economic position 

not just domestically, but globally — the latter thanks largely to 

the role of 
sterling in financing international trade. Led by gilt- 

edged names such as Barings, Coutts, Lloyds and Rothschilds, 

Britain had truly become ‘banker to the world’.° This economic 

dominance, not to mention the social privileges it afforded, 

spawned opprobrium comparable to that which poured forth 

in the wake of the financial crisis of 2007-09. In Capital, Marx 

described Britain’s ‘allegedly national banks and the big money- 

lenders and usurers that surround them’ as a ‘class of parasites 

[with] a fabulous power’.° His critique was taken up with 

particular vigour in the 1880s and 1890s by the bimetallists, 

who considered the growing influence of finance a curse and 

feared that the UK was ‘becoming a nation of “mortgagers and 

rentiers’ <7 

But the fortunes of the UK’s financial rentier class would 
subsequently slump. Two world wars, with the Great Depression 
sandwiched between them, put paid to the first, British-led era of 

financial globalization, and the domestic finance sector that 
re-emerged in the wake of World War II was a pale shadow of its 

brash, all-conquering, pre-war forebear. In the depths of the 
Depression, John Maynard Keynes had famously called for the 

euthanasia of the ‘functionless investor that was the financial 

rentier. In the Keynesian policy milieu of the 1950s the govern- 
ment was not about to let the finance sector regain its erstwhile 
power. The big banks (including Barclays and Lloyds) were kept 

on a tight leash — ‘anaesthetised’, as Lloyds’ chairman put it. 

Finance was now servant, not master.’ The result was a small, 

shrivelled financial sector. In only one year of the 1950s (1959) 

did financial corporations account for more than 2 per cent of 

the total gross operating surplus (essentially, profits) of all UK 

corporations, and the 1960s — when their share exceeded 2 per 

cent only in 1967 and 1968 — were not much better. Rentierism, 

in short, did not pay. 

What a difference the next half-century would make! By 2009, 

52 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Barclays’ record-breaking year, financial corporations’ share of 

total UK corporate operating surplus had surged to just shy of 20 

per cent (also a record), and their influence once again extended 

around the world in a second era of financial globalization. How 

can we account for this stunning revival of financial-rentier 

fortunes in Britain in recent decades? How and why during this 

period did today’s leading financial rentiers, epitomized by 

Barclays, become such vastly more complex animals than the 

simple clearing banks of the 1950s and 1960s — let alone the 
humble goldsmiths from which they originated? This chapter 

addresses these two questions, the answers to which turn out to be 

closely linked. If, as this book argues, the neoliberal period has 

seen the rise of the rentier across broad swathes of the UK econ- 
omy, the financial rentier has demonstrably been in the vanguard. 
This, after all, is the era of ‘financialization’.2 As such, it is the 
perfect place 
to 
begin our 
investigation 
of modern UK 

rentierism.

from 1990 to 2017. As the figure illustrates, asset growth 

significantly outstripped output growth during this period. 
The two series had, in fact, been diverging for some time 
already before 1990: although definitionally consistent Bank 
of England data for bank assets only go back as far as that

in the mid 1970s — in other words, the value of bank assets in 
that period broadly equalled the value of national annual 
economic output, which stood at £115 billion in 1975." In 
2017, at the end of which bank assets totalled £7.3 trillion, 
the ratio of assets to GDP was 3.6, this ratio having peaked at 

4.6 
in 2008, since when there had been limited net growth i
