At the core of Figure 1.1 is the story of a phenomenal mush- 
rooming in the stock of assets available for financial institutions 

in the UK to earn rent on. Appreciating this fact is the first step 

to understanding the revival of the financial rentier. Not only has 

this mushrooming been wholly divorced, as the figure shows, 
from the rate of growth in the wider economy; it has also seen 

the asset base of the UK banking system bloat to proportions far 

bigger, in relative terms, than those of other advanced capitalist 

countries. France, Germany, Japan, the United States — all have 
banking sectors that are considerably smaller than the UK’s when 

the assets they contain are measured against the output of their 

respective national economies.'' James Meek recently captured 

this particular ‘reality of Britain’s place in the world’ wonderfully 

well: ‘2 per cent of the global economy, less than | per cent of the 

world’s population, curating 18 per cent of the world’s interna- 

tional bank liabilities’.!? In terms strictly of asset volumes, the 

neoliberal era has generated a proportionately more bounteous 

harvest for financial rentiers in the UK than anywhere else. 

There are a number of interlocking explanations for this 
extraordinary expansion of the national territory of financial 

rent. In considering these various explanations, however, it is 

54 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

important not to let their individual features obscure what they 

share, which is a rootedness in policy and politics. The rise of 

financial rentierism in the UK in recent decades, and more 

specifically the asset growth underpinning it, has been neither 

‘natural’ — the inevitable ‘quaternary stage of progression for an 
economy that had historically passed through the primary (agri- 

cultural), secondary (manufacturing) 
and tertiary (services) 

sectoral phases — nor the consequence of exogenous market or 
technological forces beyond the influence or control of domestic 

institutions and policymakers. Rather, it has been driven by 

successive UK governments, and in particular powerful constitu- 

encies within them, that have actively privileged the financial 

sector and financial activities. 

As recent studies by Aeron Davis and Catherine Walsh and by 
Tami Oren and Mark Blyth have shown, such privileging began as 

early as the late 1970s, and has stubbornly endured.'? Davis and 
Walsh argue that the growing power within government of the 
Treasury, which from the mid 1970s increasingly eclipsed the 
Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), was especially significant: 

‘the Treasury's narrow, finance-linked economic worldview [came] 

to dominate the DTT’s wider industrial economic vision’.“ Whatever 
the force of this particular reading of Whitehall’s internal machina- 

tions, both Davis and Walsh's and Oren and Blyth’s accounts, based 
on interviews with key protagonists and analysis of newly declassi- 
fied documents, demonstrate clearly both that UK economic policy 
shifted in ways that abetted financial rentierism and that this shift 
was strategic. “This was not simply a lurch towards free markets’, 
write Davis and Walsh, ‘but a particular economic policy paradigm 
that advantaged finance and aided the financialisation of UK indus- 

try. It propelled the UK towards financialisation faster than almost 
any other leading economy of the time.’ 

Pivotal to the shift in question has been broadly based deregu- 

lation and liberalization — both of financial markets and of the 

financial institutions that operate in them. The most Widely 

cited, almost epoch-defining, example was of course the so-called 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
55 

Big Bang of the mid 1980s, the seeds of which had been sown in 

the immediate post-war period. In the 1950s and 1960s, large 
US banks were driven offshore from their home turf by exacting 

new domestic regulations, and they found the UK, which by 

contrast operated a laissez-faire regime, to be a remarkably oblig- 

ing host. The result was the rapid growth in those two decades of 

the London-centred, US bank-dominated Euromarkets, thus 

positioning the City perfectly to serve subsequently as the prin- 

cipal centre of petrodollar recycling in the early 1970s. However, 

as numerous commentators have observed, the second half of the 

1970s saw UK officials voice growing concerns that London in 

general, and the London Stock Exchange in particular, was losing 

its lustre for foreign banking institutions.’® Some types of busi- 

ness were beginning to emigrate, not least (back) to New York, 

and ‘the prospect that the Stock Exchange might be left on the 

sidelines ultimately proved too much for the Bank of England’.”” 

What followed was the Big Bang. 

Referring specifically to the London Stock Exchange's abandon- 

ment in 1986 of fixed commissions on securities transactions, the 
Big Bang, as John Plender noted the following year, was ultimately 
merely ‘the centrepiece of what has become known as the City 

revolution. Other contemporaneous measures with similarly revo- 

lutionary implications included the removal of barriers to foreign 

dealer entry to the Exchange and the cultivation among City regu- 

lators of ‘a more relaxed attitude to financial conglomeration ... 

in which commercial banking was closely combined with invest- 
ment banking’.'!® Banks were increasingly enabled and embold- 

ened to engage in a host of new activities. 

Nor by any means have major deregulatory initiatives been 

confined to periods of Conservative rule. It was New Labour that in 

the late 1990s shrunk the City’s regulatory system into the minimal- 

ist form of the Financial Services Authority (FSA). As Robert Wade 

has observed, the FSA’s architects and administrators were them- 

selves entirely up-front about just how hands-off and permissive this 

pared-down new regulator would be. Gordon Brown, the then 

56 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

chancellor, who established the FSA, said it heralded ‘not only light 

but limited regulation’; Howard Davies, the body’s first chairman, 

provided confirmation in the most arresting of terms: “The philoso- 
phy from when I set it up has been to say, “Consenting adults in 

PB 
eed 
KGS 
private? That's their problem, really”.’”? 
‘It set a new low bar for 

financial oversight’, was Adam ‘Tooze’s judgment two decades later, 

after the financial crisis had exposed the folly of such ‘light touch’ 

financial-sector regulation for all the world to see.”° 

A crucial way in which this history of financial deregulation and 

liberalization has contributed to the ever-expanding volume of 

assets swilling around the UK banking system is that it permitted 
and even encouraged what the financial geographers Andrew 
Leyshon and Nigel Thrift in 2007 dubbed ‘the capitalization of 
almost everything’! What they meant by this was that it had 
become possible for UK banks and other financial institutions to 
turn all sorts of regular income streams into assets that could be 
sold to investors on financial markets, effectively giving those inves- 
tors ownership of future flows of that income. The word ‘capitaliza- 
tion’ refers to the fact that, in creating new assets in this way, banks 
thus create capital — even if it is what Marx called ‘fictitious capital. 
Securitization is perhaps a better word because, legally and techni- 
cally, that — financial securities — is what is being produced. 

Some types of income stream, of course, have long been 

subject to such securitization — most notably company dividends 
(where the corresponding capital assets are equities) and institu- 

tional interest payments (bonds).?2 In the wake of the Big Bang 
and associated deregulatory initiatives, however, banks in the 
UK were able to extend longstanding techniques of securitiza- 

tion to a wide array of other, not previously assetized, future 
income streams, ranging from payments on infrastructure leases 

to those on households’ credit-card debts, electricity and gas bills 
and, last but definitely not least, residential mortgages. They 
capitalized, that is to say, ‘almost everything’. Thus were whole 
new asset classes conjured into existence, vastly expanding the 
financial rentier’s field of Operation. 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
Of 

Developments in housing finance warrant special mention in 

this regard, partly because they have been of particular signifi- 

cance socioeconomically. The colossal expansion of UK house- 

hold mortgage debt in the past few decades (see Figure 0.9, 

p. 46) has seen the financing and ownership of housing become 

increasingly pivotal not only to the UK financial sector but also, 

on some accounts, to the UK economy more widely.”’ But devel- 

opments in housing finance are also noteworthy because it was 

this space that saw the first big policy interventions bearing on 

financial rentierism under neoliberalism in the UK. 

Prior to the Thatcher era, the UK mortgage market was tightly 

regulated. Lending restrictions were exercised through the market 
dominance of specialist building societies operating an effectively 
unopposed interest-rate cartel. But, beginning in 1979 (the year 

Thatcher took power) with the abandonment of direct controls 

over building society lending, a multi-stage deregulatory process 

slowly but surely opened the mortgage market up to competition 
from banks, which became a permanent market presence from 
1983 onwards. ‘This elicited a major ‘broadening of access to 
mortgage finance, both in terms of the amount that could be 
borrowed and those who could borrow it’.** Lending for home- 
ownership boomed, and has continued to do so ever since, unre- 

mittingly swelling banks’ holdings of mortgage assets. Just during 

the decade beginning in 1995, mortgage lending increased by 

over 500 per cent.” Needless to say, the growth of mortgage 

securitization, enabling lenders to access the vast funding capac- 

ity provided by wholesale markets, was integral to this history.” 

Nonetheless, securitization — of mortgages and (almost) every- 
thing else — is not the only way in which financial deregulation 
and liberalization have fostered the massive diversification and 

accumulation of financial assets in the UK since the 1970s. 

Derivatives have been another obvious and much-debated focal 

point of financial innovation and expansion. | will say more in 

due course about the nature of the rents earned on these various 

asset classes (both new and old), but it is worth noting here that, 

yes 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

in many cases today, the rents are literal. Assets are, in effect, 

hired out — like an apartment, they are lent by their owners to 

third parties, the latter paying the former a fee for the temporary 

use of the asset. 

One scenario in which this occurs, for instance, is in short sell- 
ing — a market activity that has received a particularly bad press 

in recent times. Short selling usually involves selling a financial 

asset that has been borrowed (rented) for a fee from another 

party before later buying it back at — in theory — a lower price, 

and then returning it to the lender. Another pertinent example is 

a repurchase agreement (‘repo’ or ‘reverse repo’), which involves 
actually buying, rather than borrowing, a financial asset, but 
which in reality also amounts to the temporary renting of that 

asset, inasmuch as the buyer commits to sell the asset back to the 
original holder at an agreed price at a future date, or upon 
demand. Whether this agreement is called a repo or reverse repo 
depends simply on which side of the transaction you look at it 
from; they are two sides of the same coin. It is a repo for the seller 
— who contracts to repurchase the asset — and a reverse repo for 
the buyer. 

Esoteric these quasi-rental agreements may seemingly be, but 

it would be a mistake to imagine they are a marginal feature of 

the contemporary world of UK financial rentierism. Alongside 

derivatives, repos, in particular, figure prominently — often domi- 
nantly — in modern bank asset portfolios. ‘Only around half of 
UK-owned banks’ assets are loans to non-bank borrowers’, the 
Bank of England reported in 2014. ‘For the largest foreign 

subsidiaries in the United Kingdom, this figure is even lower: less 
than 10% of assets are loans to non-bank borrowers, with deriva- 

tives and reverse repos representing around 60% of assets.’2”? And 
on the eve of the crash of 2007-8, the proportion was even 
higher. 

In that regard, nothing spoke to the unparalleled latitude to 

create new assets on an essentially boundless scale that was 

afforded to financial institutions by the UK’s supine ‘regulators’ 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
5y) 

quite as strikingly as did the process known as ‘collateral rehy- 

pothecation’. Assume you are a bank that has ‘borrowed’ a finan- 

cial asset — say, a bond — from another financial institution under 

one of the aforementioned repurchase agreements. Then assume 
you decide to ‘lend’ that asset to a third party by selling it and 
repurchasing it before having to sell it back to the original holder. 

That’s collateral rehypothecation, so called because the asset 

serves as collateral for the cash that changes hands as a result of 

each of the sales and resales. Welcome to the brave new world of 

the financial rentier. Now, in the US, such rehypothecation has 

always been capped. But in the UK, prior to the crisis, it was not: 

as Manmohan Singh and James Aitken have noted, an ‘unlim- 

ited amount of assets could be rehypothecated there.*® And it 

was: to the tune, by late 2007, of some $4.5 trillion — additional 

assets conjured, in Adam Tooze’s words, ‘out of thin air’.” 

Collateral rehypothecation is not particularly interesting per 

se. But it is powerfully illustrative of the types of processes that 

historically have contributed to the fattening of the asset base of 

financial rentierism in the UK to the incomparably bloated scale 

depicted in Figure 1.1. It also shows the centrality of hands-off 

regulation to such fattening. And, last but not least, it demon- 

strates that however ‘complex’ modern finance has putatively 
become, it still consists in large part of folks lending stuff to one 

another. 

I argued in the Introduction that, if the policy-driven expansion 

of volumes of ‘rentable’ private assets of various types has been 

fundamental to the revival of the rentier in the UK under neolib- 

eralism, so too has been the policy-driven cushioning of rentier 

incomes 
— 
for example, through generous 
tax 
treatment. 

Although I discussed these two drivers separately from one 

another, the reality, of course, is that they are linked. From the 

licensing of natural-resource extraction (Chapter 2) to the privat- 

ization of social housing (Chapter 7), and from the outsourcing 

of public services (Chapter 5) to the privatization of energy 

60 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

infrastructures (Chapter 6), growth in stocks of private rentier 

assets has resulted from the ‘pull’ of private-sector demand as 

well as the ‘push’ of government policy — and the ‘pull’ has been 
strong precisely because policy has favoured rentierism. In other 

words, government actions such as the progressive weakening of 

capital gains tax (see Introduction) have contributed to the UK’s 

rentierization partly directly — by inflating rentier incomes — and 

partly indirectly — by encouraging companies and households to 

seek to expand their asset portfolios in the knowledge that doing 

so will pay off. 

This reciprocal relationship certainly applies in the UK finan- 

cial sector. Financial institutions have expanded their balance 

sheets to what would not long ago have been considered unfath- 
omable proportions partly because the government has enabled 
them progressively to grow the incomes that the assets on those 
balance sheets will on average generate. For example, in attempt- 
ing to account for the UK’s outsized banking system, the Bank of 
England identified one such mechanism: implicit state subsidy. 
‘The fact that large banks expect the government to prevent them 
from failing (as it did during the financial crisis) means that they 
are effectively in receipt of an insurance subsidy, encouraging 
them to invest in asset accumulation to a greater extent than they 
would if they were fully exposed to the risk associated with that 
investment. The International Monetary Fund suggests that, in 
2011-12, the total value of this implicit subsidy — which econo- 
mists refer to as a form of ‘moral hazard’ — was somewhere 
between $20 billion and $110 billion for major UK banks.*! 

But it is unlikely that this policy — if ‘policy’ is the right word 

for an implicit state commitment to ensure that systemically 
important banks do not fail — has been the most materially 

significant of those UK policies that have served to encourage 
financial asset growth by subsidizing financial rentierism. Tax 

policies have almost certainly played a greater role. I discussed a 

tax of more general importance earlier — capital gains tax, which 
through the 1980s and 1990s was repeatedly revised in ways that 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
61 

actively abetted maximization of rentier gains, and hence stimu- 

lated rentierism. 

A tax of more specific significance to the financial sector, 
meanwhile,‘has been stamp duty, which is a tax on share transac- 

tions in UK-incorporated companies. It was stamp duty (set at 

the time at 2 per cent) that militated most substantively against 

the competitiveness of the London Stock Exchange in the late 

1970s and early 1980s.** The reduction of this tax — to 1 per cent 

in 1984, and then 0.5 per cent in 1986 — revived the Exchange's 
fortunes and, more importantly, substantially lowered the abso- 

lute costs of financial rentierism in Britain. In the same period, 

other tax adjustments reduced the relative costs of being a finan- 

cial rentier. While increases in rates of value-added tax (VAT) 

were imposed on goods and (non-financial) services, financial 

and insurance services were made VAT-exempt.** And in a move 

that benefited sectors, such as finance, that are light on physical 

assets as much as it disadvantaged manufacturing, the govern- 
ment funded cuts in corporation tax rates by removing capital 

investment allowances for machinery and plants.* 

Finally, the UK government's position on tax havens is critical. 

In policy terms, the government has not, of course, given explicit 
support to what is euphemistically called ‘efficient tax planning’ 
by UK-based banks; but until very recently, at least, it has done 

precious little to address the issue. As the tax campaigner John 

Christensen has noted, around half of all recognized tax havens 

are directly linked to the UK, through their status as Overseas 

Territories or Crown Dependencies, or through membership of 

the Commonwealth. While these jurisdictions 
‘project the 

impression of autonomy’, many ‘act simply as booking centres 

for instructions issuing out of the City of London and other 

major financial centres’.”” 

These facts led Christensen, writing in 2011, to a striking 
conclusion: in reality, the UK government essentially ‘allows its 
Crown Dependencies to persist with facilitating tax evasion; 

and, accordingly, the UK ‘merits being placed high on the list 

62 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of most corrupt countries’.*° Research conducted in 2013 by 

the charity Action Aid into the use of tax havens by the UK’s 

100 largest public companies found that the financial sector 

was comfortably ‘the most prolific user’. No fewer than six of 

the ten UK companies with the most subsidiaries in tax havens 
were financial institutions, four of them banks (Barclays, 
HSBC, Lloyds and RBS). Barclays had nearly 500 such subsid- 

iaries — including, incredibly, over 120 in the Cayman Islands 

alone.*” More recent research, published in 2017 by another 

charity, Oxfam, showed that the situation was little improved: 
Uk-based banks were still widely reporting assets, and the rent- 

ier profits they generated, in countries ‘with very low, or zero, 
corporate tax rates’. Again, Barclays was a striking example, 

registering €557 million of 
its 2015 profits in Luxembourg, for 
instance — on which it paid taxes of just €1 million (0.18 per 
cent). 

Whatever the real extent of ‘efficient’ tax planning by UK-based 

financial institutions, 
it is clear that the governments 
lax 
approach to the use of tax havens over many years helps explain 

not only the resurgence of UK-based financial rentierism but 

also one of its most notable and significant characteristics — that 

is, its extensive spatial footprint. Interestingly, the Bank of 
England emphasizes an altogether different geographical feature: 

the significant role of foreign-owned banks within the UK. 
Indeed, the Bank regards this heavy international presence as 
‘arguably [the] defining feature’ of the UK banking system, 
noting that around half of all assets held by banking institutions 
located in the UK are accounted for by banks headquartered 
elsewhere.” This, as we have seen, is not a new development by 
any means, but has its historical roots in the post-war flowering 
of the Euromarkets. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Bank — and UK 
officialdom more generally — has much less to say about the flip- 
side to this geographical feature — the side that interests us here 

— concerning not the role of foreign-owned banks in the UK, but 
the role of UK-based (and frequently also Uk-owned) banks 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
63 

outside it. This feature is equally important, and is arguably no 

less definitive of the UK financial system. 

In her 2007 book on London's place in the contemporary 

world, World City, the late Doreen Massey argued that, in the 

early twenty-first century, the City’s institutional financial rentiers 

extract rents from international dependencies in an era of finan- 

cial globalization that, like the first such era, is in reality an era of 

financial imperialism, noting that in recent decades UK-based 
banks had ‘pick[ed] up the threads of old Empire to build a new 

one through which financial 
tribute could once again be 

collected’.“° Whether the imperialism framing is appropriate or 

not — and Massey was certainly not alone in believing it is — the 

fact that the City’s financial rents accrue largely overseas 
is 

indisputable.*! 

They do so partly through the export of services supported by 

assets held mainly domestically. Thus, in 2017, financial (includ- 
ing insurance) services accounted for nearly one-third of the value 

of overall UK service exports when measured in gross terms, and 

over half of their value when measured in net terms (that is, 

exports minus imports), at £78 billion (28 per cent of the gross 

total) and £61 billion (55 per cent of the net total), respectively.” 
But vast rents are also earned on assets held overseas. The dispro- 

portionate significance of financial assets located overseas for 

banks operating out of the UK is illustrated in Figure 1.2, which 
shows that, both in absolute terms and relative to assets held 

domestically, the value of cross-border loans and debt securities 

— in other words, those originating overseas — is larger for banks 

based in the UK than for those in any of the other advanced capi- 

talist countries with internationally significant financial services 

sectors. And this, of course, is where tax havens are crucially rele- 

vant. It is clearly not the only pertinent consideration, but UK 

banks have been emboldened to grow their overseas asset hold- 

ings on the colossal scale shown in Figure 1.2 partly because they 

know that, in many places where those assets are held, they can 

escape or at least minimize their tax commitments.

There is not much about the neoliberal period that would have 

surprised John Maynard Keynes if he had lived to see it. He was an 

extraordinarily astute observer of the era of high liberalism that 
stretched from the mid nineteenth century to the early twentieth 

century, as well as of liberalism’s subsequent, wretched descent into 

illiberalism and fascism. He knew, too, that the liberal world was 

not the utopia that many of its champions have claimed it to be; 
Western liberal ‘civilization’ was haunted by poverty in the midst 
of plenty. Keynes would have recognized both the impulses that, 
from the late 1970s, led Western societies to reject post-war 
Keynesian political economy, and the social and economic conse- 
quences of the return to market-led orthodoxy. 

But there is one thing about the neoliberal era that would have 

surprised, and perhaps even puzzled him: the return to rude 

health of the financial rentier. This rentier was Keynes's béte noire. 
He used the rentier label to refer to a particular financial activity: 
earning interest on loaned funds. This is arguably the classical or 

quintessential — and certainly the most venerable — fo#m of 

financial rentierism. In principle, it depends on scarcity of 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
65 

loanable capital. “The owner of capital can obtain interest because 

capital is scarce’, Keynes wrote, straightforwardly, in The General 

Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. If capital were abun- 

dant, after all, its owners’ ability to charge for access to it should 

be diminished accordingly. Keynes's most important, even radi- 

cal, insight was that there is nothing natural about the scarcity 

that underpins financial rents — ‘whilst there may be intrinsic 

reasons for the scarcity of land’, he insisted, ‘there are no intrinsic 

reasons for the scarcity of capital’.“4 Rather, as Geoff Mann has 

recently written of the Keynesian theory, ‘scarcity is socially 
produced so as to generate prospective and real yield . 
. 
. capital 

is made scarce because it must be scarce’.“” And the making of 

capital scarcity, Keynes realized, is very much a class project; he 
described the ability of banks ‘to exploit the scarcity-value of 

capital’ as a ‘cumulative oppressive power’.“° 

Given, moreover, that, in Keynes’s estimation, rent in the form 

of interest rewarded ‘no genuine sacrifice, any more than does 

the rent of land’, he believed that society’s goal should be to put 

in place the necessary conditions such that the generation of this 

financial rent would be impossible. How could this be done? By 
increasing the quantity of capital in circulation to such a point 

that it was no longer scarce. “Ihus we might aim in practice 

(there being nothing in this which is unattainable) at an increase 

in the volume of capital until it ceases to be scarce, so that the 

functionless investor will no longer receive a bonus’, Keynes 

wrote. This could be done, he ventured, ‘within one or two 

generations 
.*” 
Here we get the clearest understanding of exactly what Keynes 
meant when he described the financial rentier as ‘functionless’. 
He did not mean that the business of issuing loans served no 

useful purpose in a capitalist economy; it was obvious to him 

that it did. Indeed, in intermediating between those with surplus 

capital and those wanting to borrow it by channelling funds 

from the former to the latter, the banking system was an indis- 

pensable component of a monetized, capitalist economy. Keynes's 

66 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

point instead concerned the lack of ‘sacrifice’ on the part of the 

banker, even when acting as intermediary; financial rent, for 
Keynes, was ‘unearned’ in precisely the same sense that land rent 

was for Ricardo. Intermediation is a crucial function, but the 

intermediary is functionless because she gets paid handsomely — 
Keynes's ‘bonus’ — for fulfilling this function only because the 

asset she controls is artificially rendered scarce. 

Society could thus do away with the rentier, or at least the 
bonus (rent) she enjoyed, without doing away with intermedia- 
tion per se. In the scarcity-free, and hence rent-free, utopia 
Keynes envisioned, intermediaries would clearly still exist, and 
loaned capital would clearly still command a price; banks would 
continue to have to charge a modest rate of interest to cover ‘risk 
and the exercise of skill and judgment’. But, crucially, the 
fortune-generating interest rates — that is, scarcity-based rents — 
charged by banks in Keynes’s day would disappear; so too, there- 
fore, would the commercial institution and practice of financial 
rentierism itself. Increasing the volume of capital in the way 
Keynes recommended ‘would mean the euthanasia of the rent- 
ier, and thus an end to ‘the rentier aspect of capitalism 
’.* 
What would have surprised and probably puzzled Keynes, 

therefore, is that, while, as we have seen, the volume of capital in 

circulation during the neoliberal period, not least in the UK, 
would indeed increase dramatically — as he had urged — the clas- 

sical, interest-earning financial rentier did not in fact perish, as 
Keynes had predicted she would in such circumstances. On the 

contrary; the classical financial rentier has flourished: even if 

interest income contributes a lower share of UK-based banks’ 
revenue today than it did thirty or forty years ago, its share 
remains substantial (see Figure 1.4), as indeed does the absolute 
income amount (see Figure 1.3). The salient questions are why 
and how this comes to be the case. Why was Keynes wrong? 
Unravelling this puzzle is essential in telling the wider story of 
the return of the financial rentier. The answer, unsurprisingly, 
comes in several parts.

68 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Today, banks based in the UK earn interest rents on four main 

types of assets: loans, bonds, repos (including reverse repos) and 
money-market instruments — the last of which are primarily 

vehicles that banks use to lend to and borrow from one another 

for short periods. But, for all the exotic new financial assets that 

recent decades have ushered in, simple loans remain banks’ 
bread-and-butter, even in countries, such as the UK, with 

‘advanced’ financial systems. Over the past two decades, the 

share of UK-based banks’ gross interest received in any year 
accounted for by loans has typically been around 70 per cent 
(ranging from 64 to 73 per cent). The share accounted for by 
money-market instruments has consistently been small: less than 
5 per cent in every year since 2000. Bonds and repos combined 
have accounted for anywhere between 22 per cent (in 2000) and 

34 per cent (in 2007) of gross interest — the repo market having 
increased in scale through to 2007, before collapsing in 2008 
and 2009, and the bond market picking up the slack. 

The first part of the answer to the question of why Keynes's 

prediction concerning the likely fate of the financial rentier under 
conditions of massive capital expansion was wrong is a relatively 
simple matter of supply and demand. Keynes ultimately reasoned 

not only that the rate of interest charged by banks is in reality 

largely a function of supply and demand for capital — a contention 
I will consider shortly — but that significantly increasing supply 
would successfully bring the interest rate down, thus euthanizing 
the rentier, because demand would not increase commensurately.” 
In other words, he thought capital was demand-constrained. ‘I feel 
sure’, he wrote, perhaps anticipating objection, ‘that the demand 
for capital is strictly limited in the sense that it would not be diffi- 
cult to increase the stock of capital up to a point where its marginal 
efficiency had fallen to a very low figure.’ 

‘This was Keynes's first big mistake. Demand for capital among 
corporations, governments and households alike has proved far 
more expansive than Keynes could surely ever have imagined. 

Or, if he had been able to imagine something of the future 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
69 

growth in demand from corporations and governments, burgeon- 

ing household demand for credit on the scale seen in Britain 

since the 1970s would have been beyond his ken (see Figure 0.9). 
When Keynies died, in 1946, less than one-third of British homes 

were owner-occupied; Thatcher’s vision of a homeownership 

society fuelled by widely available mortgage credit lay beyond 

the ideological horizon of the time. So too did the prospect of a 

consumerist society fed by credit-card debt — the first credit card 

did not appear in Britain until two decades after Keynes died. 

What Keynes ignored or simply did not appreciate, then, is that, 

just as scarcity of capital supply is socially produced, so also are 

the consumer appetites — for houses, holidays, cars, and all 

manner of other goods — that feed demand for capital. And those 

appetites have clearly not proved to be limited. They have gorged 

seemingly without satiation. This has driven ever-escalating 

demand for capital; and banks — freed by deregulation and liber- 

alization from their former shackles — have increased supply to 

meet that demand without having to forfeit high interest rates. 
Of course, the story is not quite so straightforward. Banks 

ordinarily must borrow in order to lend (if not necessarily in that 

order), and if, because of buoyant demand for capital, they are 

able to charge high rates to those they lend to, then one might 

imagine they would have to pay high rates to borrow themselves. 

There is, surely, no free lunch. But capital is not just capital; it 

comes in different forms, and banks tend to borrow and lend 

capital of different types. In particular, they typically borrow 

short-term (capital with a short ‘tenor’) and lend long-term — 

this is their so-called ‘maturity transformation function — and in 

‘normal’ times interest rates are lower for short-term than for 

long-term borrowing. The ‘yield curve’ slopes upwards. Indeed, 

what ultimately matters to banks’ bottom line, at least where 

they fulfil the classic rentier role described by Keynes, is not the 

rate they are able to charge borrowers, but the differential, or 

‘spread’, between their own borrowing and lending rates. Healthy 

lending rates of 5, 10, 15 or even 20 per cent are for nothing if 

70 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

banks must pay the same or more to borrow. Analysts of bank 
performance are therefore less interested in the amount of inter- 

est banks earn than in net interest income: the difference between 

interest received and interest paid. 

Numerous studies have shown that, in view of the importance 

to banks of their ability to realize a spread between borrowing and 
lending rates, the interest rate environment in which they operate 

is highly significant. If market interest rates — and especially ‘real’ 

interest rates, which is to say interest rates relative to inflation — 

are high, that generally buttresses bank profitability.°! This stands 

to reason. In such an environment, there is ‘headroom’ for a prof- 

itable spread, say between a lending rate of 4 per cent and a 
borrowing rate of 2 per cent. If, however, market rates were to 

trend towards zero, the risk for banks would be that their scope to 

insert this all-important profit-generating spread between borrow- 
ing and lending rates would be progressively squeezed. 

While demand for capital is a significant determinant of the 
complexion of the interest rate environment, it does not fashion 

that environment independently. Monetary policy also plays a 
fundamental role”? — and monetary policy has been enormously 

significant in the neoliberal era. For the entirety of that era up until 

the global financial crisis, real interest rates in the UK remained 
high in the face of rapidly expanding capital supply not only because 
demand for capital also boomed, but because distinctly non- 
Keynesian monetary policy helped to maintain those high rates. In 
the words of Jerry Epstein and Arjun Jayadev, ‘the shift to tight 
monetary policies in the UK and US around 1979 or 1980, imple- 
mented by the “monetarists” of the Thatcher regime and by Paul 
Volcker, Chair of the US Federal Reserve at the end of the Carter 
presidency . 
. 
. ushered in an era of much lower inflation and high 

real interest rates’. Figure 1.5, which charts the ‘real’ rate of inter- 
est represented by the Bank of England’s base rate (the rate paid on 
reserves held at the Bank by commercial banks), demonstrates the 
point. Up to and including 2007, real rates were consistently higher 
during the neoliberal period than they had been on average in the 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
ve 

1970s. This kept the classic financial rentier in business: analysing 

the UK for the years between 1992 and 2009, Piergiorgio Alessandri 

and Benjamin Nelson found a positive ‘systematic effect of market 

interest rates‘on bank profitability’.

V2 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

That said, as Figure 1.5 shows, UK real interest rates did begin to 

drift downwards from the beginning of the 1990s — and UK-based 
banks definitely felt the effects. Their spread between borrowing 

and lending rates was indeed squeezed. Figure 1.6 shows the extent 

of this squeeze between 1997 and 2007 for lending to households, 

and between 2002 and 2007 for lending to businesses. The ratio of 

banks’ net interest income to total interest-bearing assets (the ‘net 

interest margin’) therefore declined — an effect to which, according 

to Alessandri and Nelson, the downward drift in market rates 

charted in Figure 1.5 ‘contributed strongly’.*° 

But the decline in rates and spreads was relatively modest. 
More importantly, as Figure 1.3 demonstrates, the negative 
impact of the squeezing of bank interest spreads on the absolute 
quantum of banks’ net interest income was more than offset by 
the positive effect on it of contemporaneous growth in the quan- 
tum of capital assets on which banks were earning their interest- 
based rents: net interest income increased very healthily from the 
early 1990s through to 2007. Indeed, the former trend (in inter- 
est rates) actively stimulated the latter (in asset volumes): ‘declin- 
ing interest rates prompted banks to expand credit provision, 
scaling up their balance sheets’.°° Notably, declining rates also 
prompted banks to increase their leveraging to protect their 
return on equity — the pre-eminent metric by which banks were 
judged by the markets in the pre-crisis era — as their interest 
margin and return on assets fell.°” 

But this all changed with the onset of the financial crisis. 
Demand for capital did not exactly dry up, but its upward 
momentum was certainly checked — reflected in the post-2008 

trend in UK-based bank asset volumes shown in Figure 1.1. 
More significantly still, monetary policy entered entirely new 

territory. Out went the contractionary bias of neoliberal conven- 

tion, to be replaced by its very opposite, an expansionary mone- 

tary policy known as quantitative easing (QE). 

I will have more to say about QE and its relation to financial 

rentierism later in the chapter, but its explicit aim was to lower 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
%) 

interest rates in order to stimulate borrowing in the ‘real’ (non- 

financial) economy. If the latter objective has met with only 

limited success — again, see Figure 1.1 — the former one has been 

resoundingly successful. As Figure 1.5 shows, UK real interest 

rates plummeted in 2008, and have been deep in negative terri- 

tory since 2009. Capital, in short, is no longer scarce. Neither of 

the factors that kept it scarce in the neoliberal period through to 

2007 — buoyant demand and tight monetary policy — continues 

to apply. If ever there was a conjuncture conducive, after all these 

years, to Keynes’s euthanasia of the rentier, one would think, 

therefore, that this is it. Surely, now, with interest rates at rock- 

bottom, precisely where Keynes wanted them to be, his prognos- 

tications would be proved correct, and financial rentierism in its 

classic form would fade quietly into the night. 

Yet, once again, nothing of the kind has happened. As the 

Economist, 
in head-scratching mode, remarked 
in 2014 in 

response to a call from Martin Wolf at the Financial Times ‘for a 

policy that will “wipe out rentiers with cheap money” ’: ‘So how’s 

that working out? We have had a near-zero rates policy and 

quantitative easing for five years now [but nevertheless] the rent- 

iers are not being wiped out; they are making out like bandits.’”® 
And they have continued to make out like bandits. By way of 

evidence, consider the net interest income trend in Figure 1.3: 

remarkably, the post-crisis era has been a positively bounteous 

one for the classical financial rentier. The functionless investor 

continues to receive her bonus, notwithstanding the apparent 
absence of capital scarcity. How can that be? To answer this ques- 

. 
eas 
° 
* 
’ 
tion, we must revisit the very notion of ‘scarcity’. 

In truth, the economics of rent have never been only about the 

scarcity of the asset that the rentier controls. Indeed, the clue is 

right there in the word ‘controls’: the conditions under which an 

asset is held and commercialized are just as important to its 

capacity to generate rents as the conditions of its materialization 

in the world. An asset can be both highly valuable and incredibly 

74 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

scarce and yet wholly incapable of generating rents if scarcity 

cannot be attached to the rights to access and commercially 

exploit it. Equally, rent is out of the question if an asset can be 

readily protected by secure private property rights but it exists 

and is accessible in abundance. Opportunities to earn rent are 

predicated on the scarcity both of an asset and of the power to 

monetize it. 

Recognition of such power is another key ingredient that was 

missing from Keynes's famous critique of the functionless inves- 

tor, and his call for her euthanasia. To be sure, Keynes knew the 

rentier had power. But this was the power specifically and only to 

control the supply of capital, and thus maintain its scarcity.” 
Absent from the General Theory and Keynes’s other writings is 
any sense that the rentier has power to control the price of capital 

other than through maintaining its scarcity — or, more generally, 
through shaping the wider currents of supply and demand. As 

we have seen, Keynes believed supply (of cash) and demand (for 

credit) determined the rate of interest: this was why increasing 
supply to the extent required to end the scarcity of capital was 
deemed sufficient to put paid to the rentier’s ‘bonus’. Do banks 
have the power to command interest-based rents in a world 
where capital is no longer scarce? Keynes, at least implicitly, 
suggested not. 

But he was wrong about this — a fact of which the performance 

of UK-based banks in the period since the financial crisis provides 

unequivocal evidence. Capital is no longer scarce — post-crisis 
UK monetary policy has seen to that, having ‘flooded the market 
with cheap money’, in the words of one commentator.” Real 

interest rates, as we have seen (Figure 1.5), have been stuck for a 
decade at lows not seen since the 1970s (and then only fleet- 

ingly). But the classical financial rentier has continued to make 
hay (Figure 1.3). 

The principal proximate explanation for the post-crisis surge in 

net interest income is obvious enough, and is illustrated clearly in 

Figure 1.6: beginning in the middle of 2007, banks rapidly and 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
7S) 

massively increased the all-important spread between their borrow- 

ing and lending rates. Here, a line from the Bank of England’s 
webpage explaining its official base rate (Bank Rate’) merits quota- 

tion: ‘banks* zormally pass any changes in Bank Rate onto their 

customers. When we raise Bank Rate, they usually increase the 

interest customers have to pay on borrowing and the interest they 

earn on savings, and vice versa.’*' The reason I have emphasized 

the words ‘normally’ and ‘usually’ should be clear: during and after 

the financial crisis, rate-setting by the UK’s banks was not what the 
Bank deems normal/usual. The official rate fell precipitously; 
UK-based banks were thereby enabled to borrow considerably 

more cheaply than they had previously been able to; and yet, as 
Alessandri and Nelson observed, they were singularly ‘unwilling to 

pass on rate cuts to borrowers’. This unwillingness was what 
wedged the borrowing/lending spread wide open.

The implications for the banks’ respective flows of interest 
payable and interest receivable really have been nothing short of 

extraordinary (and, one might add, nothing short of scandalous). 
Look at Figure 1.7. On the face of it, the banks’ lending business 

fell off a cliff after the crisis, with interest received declining from 

76 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

£378 billion in 2008 to £139 billion just five years later. But if 

official rate cuts had been passed on, this decline in (gross) inter- 

est income would obviously have been much steeper still. And, as 

it was, the banks availed themselves of the glut of newly available 

cheap money to ensure that their interest costs fell by a far greater 
amount. The result was, firstly, an increase in the ratio of net to 

gross interest income from 15.5 per cent in 2008 to 39.3 per cent 

in 2013, and fully 50 per cent by 2016; and, secondly, growing 

absolute levels of net interest income in spite of the dramatic fall 

in gross interest receipts (Figure 1.3). The classic financial rentier, 

let us be clear, has not just survived the end of capital scarcity; the 

classic rentier is thriving. 

If substantially stretched spreads represent the proximate 

explanation for this good fortune, the more interesting and 
important question concerns how, in turn, we should under- 

stand them. How, in short, has it been possible for UK-based 
banks to realize these spreads? It plainly has nothing to do with 
supply (which is plentiful) and demand. This is not asset scarcity 

in action; rather, the only credible explanation is scarcity of 
power. What the above developments highlight is the enormous 
power of the UK banking sector to subvert the dynamics of 
supply and demand by virtue of the fact that this power is itself 

scarce. The Bank of England’s error in assuming or trusting that 
commercial banks would pass on its rate cuts to their borrowers 
was in thinking, like Keynes, that supply and demand rule — or, 
in other words, that financial markets, where supply and demand 
for capital interact, have power over the banks operating in those 
markets. Developments of the past decade show that they do 
not; big banks are not meek price-takers, but price-makers. They 
can take the low borrowing rates available from the market with 
one hand and also take (charging their own borrowers rates 
appropriate for a scenario of capital scarcity, but in a world where 
capital is not scarce) with the other. 

The capacity to pull off this trick is in fact largely thnate. 
Under capitalism, private banks have long had almost complete 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
Je 

control over the supply of new credit. ‘In modern economies, 

such as the UK’, Laurie Macfarlane and his colleagues note, 
‘money in circulation created by the state — physical cash — only 
represents atound 3% of the total money supply. The remaining 
97% is lent in to economies as the digital IOUs of commercial 
banks — the deposits that are entered in to our bank accounts 
when banks make new loans.’ In theory, competition between 
banks should prevent them from abusing this innate, privatized 
power. But that is only the theory. Ownership of the vast stock 

of UK banking system assets pictured in Figure 1.1, and with it 

control over the pricing of those assets at the moment of their 

creation, is highly concentrated — and it has become more so in 

the past two decades. That is to say, the inherently scarce power 

to create, price and monetize credit has become scarcer. 
Numerous studies attest to this growing asset concentration. 

Crucially, levels of concentration increased particularly strongly 

during the financial crisis — that is, at the precise moment when 

the gap between bank borrowing and lending rates suddenly 
became a gulf (Figure 1.6). The acquisitions of ABN AMRO by 
RBS, HBOS by Lloyds, and Standard Life by Barclays saw the 
Herfindahl-Hirschman Index — the most commonly used meas- 

ure of industry concentration — for total UK bank assets, which 

had been below 1,000 at the turn of the millennium and around 

1,360 as recently as 2006, jump to approximately 1,900 by the 

first half of 2010. Reflecting on these striking numbers, Bank of 

England economists observed: “The ability of the banks to extract 

market rents seems to have continued over the crisis and into the 

post-crisis period.” Indeed it had.°° By 2016, the seven largest 

UK banks accounted for over 75 per cent of total domestic bank- 

ing system assets — higher than the equivalent shares in Japan (71 

per cent), Switzerland (71 per cent), Germany (48 per cent) or 

the United States (48 per cent).°” In short, limited and declining 

competition had translated into limited and declining pressure 

on the UK’s dominant banks to offer competitive borrowing 

rates. Rent, as we have seen, represents income derived from the 

Joh 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

control of assets under conditions of limited or no competition. In 

the case of financial rents, clearly, when competition is sufh- 

ciently limited, the assets in question need not even be scarce. 

For Keynes, as we have seen, the rentier was specifically an entity 

earning interest on loaned funds — that is, the classical incarna- 

tion of the financial rentier. But in the neoliberal era financial 

rentiers have branched out. They have diversified rental income 
streams — and they have done so partly because of interest rate 

trends. While UK-based banks were never solely the simple 

deposit-taking, loan-making intermediaries of popular lore, and 
had already somewhat reduced their traditional reliance on inter- 

est income by the time of the Big Bang, their expansion of non- 
interest-based activities gathered pace thereafter, and it picked 
up a powerful head of steam once interest rates began their secu- 
lar decline in the 1990s. 

The modern-day revival of the financial rentier in the UK 
would not have been anything like as strong as it has been had it 

not been for this income diversification, which has been under- 
written by the growth in financial assets, itself driven by a differ- 

ent kind of diversification — the proliferation of derivatives, 
mortgage-backed debt securities, reverse repos, and so on. In 
1984, non-interest income accounted for only a little over a third 

(35.6 per cent) of the total net income of UK-based banks; by 
1990, this proportion had increased to 38.7 per cent; and by 
1995, it was 42.7 per cent.® As Figure 1.4 demonstrates, growth 
then went into overdrive, with the share of non-interest income 
peaking at just under two-thirds (64.6 per cent) in 2006, before 
the financial crisis precipitated something of a return to business 
staples as interest income’s share recovered to around the 50 per 
cent mark. 

If, by opening the capital floodgates and driving down real 

interest rates, UK monetary policy since the financial crisis has in 
theory (if not in practice, and certainly not by design) mifitated 

against classical 
financial 
rentierism, 
it has simultaneously 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
ye 

operated in explicit favour of another important variety of finan- 

cial rentierism based not on interest income, but on capital gains 

driven by appreciation in asset prices. Concentrated in the period 
2009-13, QE saw the Bank of England purchase some £375 

billion in financial assets. This intervention had a strongly posi- 

tive effect on asset prices: Philip Bunn and his colleagues at the 
Bank have estimated that, without QE, real prices of equities 

listed on the London Stock Exchange would have been some 25 

per cent lower in 2014 than they actually were. We can see the 
concomitant rentier gains in Figure 1.4. Having declined to only 

a sliver of overall sector income in 2007, and then gone deeply 

into the red in 2008, income from UK-based banks’ proprietary 
trading activities quickly recovered to robust levels once the 

effects of QE had kicked in, exceeding £10 billion in each of the 

four years beginning in 2010. 

With only one partial exception (fees and commissions), all of 

the non-interest-based categories of bank income charted in 

Figure 1.4 derive, like interest, from asset ownership — only in 

these cases, of course, the rentier exploits qualities of those assets 

other than their interest-bearing potential. Still, somewhat differ- 
ing rentier dynamics are nonetheless at play in each case, and it 

is important to tease these out. 

Trading income, 
as we have seen, represents 
a relatively 

straightforward brand of financial rentierism, predicated simply 

on the gain — or loss — in capital value during the period of 
ownership of various types of financial asset. The overall figures 

for trading income in Figure 1.4 hide considerable variation 

between asset classes. During the immediate pre-crisis period of 

growth in trading income, between 2004 and 2006, most of the 

gains realized by UK-based banks were on securities (equities, 

bonds and others, including those backed by residential mort- 

gages); trading in foreign exchange and derivative assets, while 

profitable, generated much less income. Needless to say, 2008 

was a special year, in which foreign exchange was quiet and all 

the action took place in securities and derivatives. Banks suffered 

50 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

epic trading losses in the former category, to the tune of £73 

billion, and these were only partly compensated by gains on 

derivatives (£43 billion), many of which had been acquired to 
hedge securities trading positions. In the period since the depths 

of the crisis (2009-17 inclusive), the pattern of 2008 was essen- 

tially reversed: cumulative gains on securities totalled £141 

billion as capital markets brushed off the crisis to scale record 

heights; £76 billion of cumulative derivatives losses substantially 

pared these gains; meanwhile, foreign-exchange trading was 
steady if unspectacular, yielding cumulative income of £24 

billion. 

Dividend income is also a straightforward brand of rentierism, 

likewise predicated on the ownership of financial assets, but in 

this case only one particular type of asset — equities, or company 

shares, which represent fractional ownership of corporations. A 
dividend is not a capital gain, but rather a periodic payment 
made by a company to the holders of its equity assets, usually as 
a distribution of profits. It is, in this sense, a direct corollary of 
an interest payment: a recurring cost of capital paid by compa- 

nies to those they have, in effect, borrowed from. 

For banks, changes in UK taxation policy shortly prior to and 

then during the neoliberal era served to subsidize and thus 

increase the attractiveness of dividend-based institutional finan- 

cial rentierism, just as they did with regard to rentierism taking 
the form of capital gains. First, in 1973, the UK abandoned its 

classical system of taxation of dividends, under which corporate 
shareholders were fully subject to corporation tax on dividend 
payments, and which thus represented a system of 
‘double taxa- 
tion’ insofar as dividends were paid out of company profits, on 
which tax had already been paid. It moved to an imputation 
system. This, as John Kay and Mervyn King have explained, 
gave shareholders credit for tax already paid by the dividend- 
issuing company, which could be used to offset some of the tax 
liability on dividends. Imputation thereby eliminated a pdrtion 
of the double taxation.” Then, from 1988, corporation tax 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
81 

simply ceased to be chargeable on dividends paid by any 
Uk-resident company.’' While the rules were rewritten again in 
2009, 
the 
reality remained 
that 
‘dividends 
received 
by 
[UK-based] ‘companies will nearly always be exempt from UK 
tax.” Since the early 2000s, dividends have accounted for 
anywhere between 9 and 20 per cent of the annual net income 
of UK-based banks (Figure 1.4). 

The ‘Other’ category of net income in Figure 1.4, meanwhile, 

also derives principally from asset ownership. Like dividends, 

interest and trading income, it thus also largely represents rent. 

It has two main components. One is literal rent received on land 
and buildings. Insofar as investment in land and buildings by 

financial institutions is a strictly financial investment, the rents it 

yields could arguably be treated as financial rents, like the other 

types of financial rents discussed in this chapter. But they are 

better understood as what they actually are, which is land rents 

(see Chapter 7). Some rentier institutions generate more than 

one of the types of rent examined in the various chapters of this 
book (see Introduction), and this is certainly true of UK finan- 

cial institutions, for which land rents have been an important 

part of their business since the 1970s. Writing in the latter part 
of that decade, Doreen Massey and Alejandrina Catalano were 
among the first to analyse what they described as the ‘financial 
form of landownership’.”’> UK-based financial institutions have 

continued to invest heavily in land in the decades since, becom- 

ing major landowners in London, in particular.” 

The second principal component of the ‘Other’ category is 

receipts on finance leases. This, once more, constitutes arche- 

typal rentierism on the part of Uk-based banks: that is, owning 

an asset — though not, in this case, a financial asset — and extract- 

ing rental payments from it. A finance lease is essentially like any 

other asset-leasing agreement; 
the ‘finance’ modifier merely 

signals that the asset, which might for example be a vehicle or an 

item of plant or machinery, is owned by a finance company. A 

third party (the lessee) has use of the asset during the lifetime of 

52 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the lease, and typically has the option to acquire the asset when 

the lease comes to an end. The finance company (the lessor) 

receives periodic rental payments from the lessee. Inasmuch as 

the finance company’s investment in the asset is a financial invest- 

ment, these rental payments, like those that financial institutions 

receive on land, can be regarded as a financial rent. Indeed, they 

are treated precisely as such by the UK tax authorities: ‘gross 

rentals due under a finance lease [equate to] “interest” plus “capi- 

tal” repayments.” Purchasing sundry non-financial, non-land 

assets only to lease them out to third parties may seem like a 

curious way for banks to operate — but finance leases have become 

big business. For example, the present value that Barclays’ 
accounts placed upon minimum future payments receivable 
under finance leases as at the end of 2017 was £2.9 billion.” 
What are the specific attractions of this brand of financial rent- 
ierism? Given the ground this chapter has so far covered, readers 
will not be surprised to discover that preferential tax treatment is 
a major one. In the UK, the capital cost of the leased asset 
normally qualifies for capital allowances. 

The final item to address from Figure 1.4 is fees and commis- 

sions. These are of myriad types, ranging from arrangement fees 
charged to homebuyers taking out mortgages to advisory fees 

charged to corporations undertaking mergers and acquisitions; 
from overdraft fees charged to current-account holders to under- 
writing fees charged to corporations raising equity or debt capi- 

tal; from annual account fees charged to credit-card holders to 

issuing, underwriting and servicing fees associated with ‘exotic’ 

assets such as mortgage-backed securities. While it might not be 
immediately self-evident, these also are all ultimately forms of 

financial rent. 

In some cases, the rent is formally equivalent to those discussed 

in the preceding paragraphs: that is, it derives, like them, from 

asset ownership. This is true, for example, of the overdraft fee 

‘earned’ on the current-account asset, or the annual servite fee 

‘earned’ on the credit-card-account asset, or the arrangement fee 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
8&3 

‘earned’ on the mortgage asset. In a very real sense, these fees are 
simply capitalized interest: the alternative to levying them would 

be to charge a higher interest rate. Indeed, in the UK, certain 

types of financial regulation now explicitly recognize this equiva- 

lence of rental forms: since 2016, for example, mortgage lenders 

have had to include mortgage-related fees as part of the quoted 

annual interest rate. 

In other cases, however, something different is going on. An 

investment bank, for instance, does not own all the shares that 

are created when it manages and underwrites a corporation’s 

initial public offering (stock-market listing); yet it gets paid 
handsomely for its work — a typical fee would be 7 per cent of the 

value of the capital raised. This example therefore reveals some- 
thing extremely important: the rents generated by a financial 

asset (here, a company share) do not accrue only to those who 

directly control or own that asset, but also to those with the 
power to partake substantively in the wide array of service activi- 

ties that bear directly upon that asset’s life: its creation, adminis- 

tration, safekeeping, trading, and so on. Controlling the vital 

financial infrastructures of asset issue, underwriting and dealing, 

these asset gatekeepers perform a similar role to the infrastruc- 

ture rentiers we will examine in Chapter 6, and the rents they 

earn derive from similar capacities and dynamics. Monopolistic 

tendencies are critical: the scarcer the power over the infrastruc- 

tures of asset circulation — that is to say, the more concentrated it 

is in a small number of hands — the greater the ability of the asset 

gatekeeper to participate in the rents flowing from the asset. 

Just as recent decades have seen significant consolidation in the 
UK of ownership of financial assets (see above), so also have they 

seen parallel consolidation, often in the self-same corporate hands, 

of control of the aforementioned asset-market infrastructures.” In 

2012, in an influential report dealing specifically with UK equity 

markets, John Kay explained this consolidation trend as follows: 

‘Since “Big Bang” removed obstacles to the consolidation of finan- 

cial services businesses in 1986, regulation has not concerned itself 

84 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

with issues of market structure. Indeed, the application of compe- 

tition policy, the main policy tool for influencing market struc- 

ture, has been restricted in financial services.’”* It has been restricted 

in financial services in non-equity markets, too — and with the 

same implications for the ability of leading gatekeepers to extract 

rents.” Strikingly, John Plender, in his early reflections on the Big 
Bang back in 1987, foresaw exactly this outcome. ‘In general’, he 

remarked, ‘deregulation tends to favour the giants.’ Scale, he 

reasoned, would be essential to surviving and prospering in the 
world of financial-asset gatekeepership. “Unless those who play the 

new conglomerate game of issuing, distributing and making 

markets in securities across the globe can generate a high level of 

activity, he suggested, ‘they are likely to fall by the wayside.’®° This 

was one prediction concerning financial-rentier fortunes that, 

unlike Keynes’s, would be thoroughly vindicated. 

While the neoliberal era has provided a rich harvest for the 
Uk-based institutional financial rentier, it has of course done no 

such thing for most UK households. This is the much better- 
known aspect of the two-sided story of modern financial rent: 

the fact that, while the financial corporations earning rents have 
flourished, the households paying them — either directly as finan- 

cial consumers, or indirectly as taxpayers of a debtor state or 
customers of debtor corporations — have increasingly floundered. 

Levels of UK household debt, secured and unsecured, have 
skyrocketed (Figure 0.9). Household indebtedness was consider- 
ably worsened by the financial crisis, ensuing recession, and asso- 
ciated downward pressure on real wages, which had still not 
recovered to their early-2008 level a decade later.’! It has also 
been exacerbated by spiralling house prices. As we will see for the 
UK (see especially Chapter 7), and as Thomas Piketty has 
observed for the advanced capitalist countries more generally, it 
is not only financial assets that have seen substantial price infla- 
tion since the 1980s in political contexts described by Pikétty as 
‘more favourable to private wealth than that of the immediate 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
85 

postwar decades’.*’ With the ratio of median residential property 

price to median annual earnings in England and Wales increas- 
ing from 4.62 to 9.68 on new dwellings, and from 3.44 to 7.57 
on existing dwellings, between 1997 and 2017, households took 

on increasing sums in mortgage debt, younger generations inevi- 
tably shouldering the main burden.* 

Clearly, though, not all households have been caught up in the 

debt spiral. Furthermore, financial rents, alongside land rents 
(Chapter 7) and to a much lesser extent intellectual property 

rents (Chapter 3), occupy a special place among the seven differ- 

ent types of rent and rentierism that this book examines, insofar 

as these rents are not exclusively corporate rents, which the other 

types all are. Where they are owners of land and housing, or of 

financial assets, households can also be rentiers. We therefore 

need to consider their own particular forms of participation in 

the landscape of rentier capitalism. 

Indeed, in the specific case of financial rents that I have 

addressed in this chapter, the picture is even more complicated. 

Financial rentiers include not just financial corporations (see 

above) and some households (addressed below), but also some 

non-financial corporations. One of the main propositions of the 
burgeoning literature on financialization is that the contribution 

of financial rents to the profits of non-financial corporations has 

been increasing since the end of the 1970s. In other words, the 

non-financial corporation has itself purportedly been “financial- 

ized’. If this is indeed true, this development represents another 

important dimension of the revival of the financial rentier — only 

in this case camouflaged, so to speak, under another's skin. 

Most of the discussion of this latter form of financialization 

has focused on US corporations, where the tendency does appear 

quite striking.** But data for the UK suggest a comparable, albeit 
somewhat less pronounced, trend. Figure 1.8 shows, for the 

period between 1987 and 2017, the proportion of the gross 

operating surplus of UK non-financial corporations represented 
by financial rents, where the latter comprise the distributed

income of corporations (dividends plus withdrawals from the 
income of quasi-corporations) and interest income (shown in 
both gross and net terms). Although the profit contribution of 

financial rents has fluctuated, the overall tendency during the 
neoliberal period is clear enough, especially when interest income 

is netted out. Income from financial sources has become increas- 
ingly important to non-financial companies. 

What, then, of financial rentierism in the UK household 

sector? It is helpful to examine this form of rentierism with 

explicit reference to Piketty’s work. Piketty argues that many 
of today’s advanced capitalist countries, including the UK, in 

the nineteenth century were classic ‘rentier societies’, in the 
sense that they had extreme concentrations of wealth, while 
the overall income hierarchy was dominated by high incomes 
from capital ownership — in other words, rents — at the very 
top of the income spectrum. Then, between World War ] and 
the 1970s, rentierism became a much less significant phenom- 
enon among households (as well as among corporations), for 
three main reasons. First, household as well as corporate and 
public wealth holdings — the grist to the rentier mill — were 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
87 

ravaged by the two world wars. Second, in the immediate 

post-war decades, the economy, and with it labour-based 
household incomes buttressed by effective trade unionism and 
wage bargaining, grew relatively strongly, thus increasing the 

relative significance of income from labour across the income 

distribution. And third, relatively high taxes on wealth prevail- 
ing between the 1920s and 1970s substantially dampened 

returns on capital. 

Since the beginning of the neoliberal era, however, the pattern 
described by Piketty for the 1910s—1970s has effectively gone 

into reverse in the Global North. On the one hand, economic 
growth has slowed, while workers’ capacity to participate in any 

such growth has been weakened by the transnational political 

assault on organized labour. On the other hand, rentier house- 
holds have profited from two phenomena that we have already 
encountered in the UK context: reduction in taxes on wealth and 

the asset-price inflation it has helped to stimulate. 

But if this process has precipitated the re-emergence in 
Western states of a rentier society — as both a counterpart to and 

a vital component of rentier capitalism — it is, Piketty rightly 

notes, a markedly different rentier society from the one that 

pertained in the late nineteenth century. For one thing, the 

assets on which rentier households ‘earn’ rents look very differ- 

ent today: in place of agricultural land, the key rent-generating 

assets for households now are typically housing land (see Chapter 

7) and financial assets. Intimately connected to this change in 

key asset classes is the significantly higher proportion of house- 

holds that are rentiers today than was the case a hundred or 

more years ago. Private pensions — the main form in which 

contemporary households own financial wealth — generally did 

not exist; or, if they did, they were the preserve of a tiny elite. 

Nor — as we have seen in the UK case — did ‘homeownership 

societies then exist. 

The spreading-out or relative ‘democratization’ of household 
renticrism is well illustrated by a statistic that Piketty cites for 

38 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

France. He predicts that the share of the French population 

inheriting more wealth than the average lifetime earnings of the 

poorest 50 per cent will have increased from just 2 per cent for 

the cohort born between 1910 and 1920 to approximately 12 

per cent for those born between 1970 and 1980.® Piketty 

captures this sea-change with his concept of ‘a society of petits 

rentiers. Contemporary Western capitalism, he argues, is merely 

‘patrimonial’, in contrast to the more egregious ‘hyperpatrimoni- 

alism’ of the nineteenth century. We have, in short, ‘a less extreme 
form of rentier society [that has] moved from a society with a 

small number of very wealthy rentiers to one with a much larger 
number of less wealthy rentiers’.*° 

The UK today closely fits this picture of a society of petits 

rentiers, not least where financial wealth and financial rents are 
concerned. ‘The majority of households have some net financial 
wealth — and are thus financial rentiers in the strict sense of the 
term. ‘This is not to suggest, though, that financial wealth is 
evenly distributed. In fact, it is more unevenly distributed than 
any other form of wealth: for the period July 2014—June 2016, 
the Gini coefficient — the most common measure of inequality, 
where 0 expresses no inequality and 1 expresses maximal inequal- 
ity — for private pension wealth was 0.72, and for net other 
financial wealth (bank accounts, stocks and shares, and so on) it 
was 0.91; for net property wealth and physical wealth, the figures 
were 0.67 and 0.46, respectively.*” Figure 1.9 illustrates this 
inequality of distribution graphically for the period July 2012— 
June 2014. As it shows, financial wealth was heavily concentrated 
at the top end, with all percentiles in the bottom quarter of the 
wealth distribution having negative total net financial wealth. 
The skewing of the distribution is well highlighted by the figures 
for the total net financial wealth holdings of the fiftieth, seventy- 
fifth and ninety-ninth percentiles, which, respectively, were 
£53,000 (£47,000 pensions and £6,000 other), £237,000 
(£197,000 and £40,000) and £2.2 million (£1.5 milligh and 
£0.7 million).

Given this inequality of household financial asset ownership, 

it is inevitable that the rents flowing from such ownership are 
unequally realized. The concentration of financial rentierism 
among the wealthiest households is illustrated, for example, in 

the report by Bank of England researchers into the effects of 

post-crisis monetary policy on equity prices that I discussed 

earlier. The top household wealth decile, the report estimated, 

realized an average gain in private pension wealth of over 
£200,000 between 2007 and 2012-14 purely as a result of mone- 

tary policy changes, versus an average household gain of less than 

£40,000.*° The uneven distribution of financial rentierism and 

its fruits was also evident — at least indirectly — in Figure 0.8 

(p. 44). This showed an inverse relationship between the average 

size of individual taxable capital gain and the number of indi- 

viduals realizing gains of those different sizes. ‘The capital gains in 

question were those reported on disposal of all asset types; but, 

given that primary residences are exempt from capital gains tax 

in the UK, it is probably safe to assume that the bulk of the gains 

shown were derived from the sale of financial assets. 

However, to grasp the overall scale of household financial rent- 

ierism in the UK today, it is necessary to recall a key point | made 

90 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

in my original discussion of Figure 0.8: the 260,000 or so indi- 

viduals declaring taxable capital gains of more than £10,000 in 

2017-18 
represented less than 1 per cent of the roughly 31 million 

total individual UK taxpayers. It is true that a much higher propor- 

tion of UK individuals (and households) receives non-capital- 

gain-based financial rents, and thus that rentierism is today much 
more widely in evidence than it was in Piketty’s hyperpatrimonial 

era. But, for the most part, this more diffuse and broadly based 
household financial rentierism is demonstrably ‘petit’. As Figure 

1.10 shows, even for higher-earning households, recurring non- 

capital-gain-based rents derived from ownership of financial capi- 

tal — a combination of private pension income, interest income 

and dividends, the last two of which are included in the ‘Other 
income’ category alongside income from letting residential prop- 

erties — are dwarfed by income from employment. 

Indeed, this chart gestures towards one of Piketty’s central 

points about the differences between today’s society of petits 

rentiers and the nineteenth century's society of rentiers: ‘today 
one has to climb much higher in the social hierarchy before 
income from capital outweighs income from labour’.®® In France, 

in the late nineteenth century, rent (that is, income from capital) 
exceeded income from labour for around the top 1 per cent of 
the income distribution. Today in France, by contrast, only the 
top 0.1 per cent of the income distribution meets this criterion. 
While publicly available Office for National Statistics data do 
not allow us to identify precisely the size of the equivalent social 
group in the contemporary UK, Figure 1.10 suggests that, where 
income from financial capital is concerned, it is likely to be simi- 
larly small. So also does Figure 0.8: the proportion of individual 
UK taxpayers declaring capital gains of more than £250,000 in 
2017-18 was precisely 0.1 per cent; meanwhile, a total annual 
taxable income of nearly £650,000 was required to be in the top 
0.1 per cent of UK taxpayers.” This indicates that, even at that 
rarefied level of the income distribution, income from labour 

still exceeds financial rents.
