The one complicating factor here is that at that top end of the 
UK income distribution, the distinction between income from 

labour and financial rents is anything but clear-cut. Many of the 

UR’s highest income earners are financial sector workers, and 

while the income such individuals earn from employment is not 

in a direct sense financial rent as conceptualized in this book — it 

is not derived from their ownership of financial assets — it is 

certainly an indirect form of such financial rent, paid as it is out 

OY 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of the rents accrued by their employing institutions and which 

we have been examining in this chapter.”! 

Indeed, these indirect financial rents represent a significant 
component of the story of increasing income inequality in the 
UK during the neoliberal era. Between 1979 and 2007, the share 

of total household income captured by the UK’s top income 

decile increased from 28 to 43 percent. No less than two-thirds 

of this gain went to the top percentile.’ Using public-use tax 

return files available only from the mid-1990s, Brian Bell and 
John van Reenen have examined who belongs in that top percen- 

tile and what types of income they earn. In the decade between 
1998-9 and 2007-8, during which period the top percentile 
increased its share of the income pie by 3 percentage points, 
some 60 percent of the increase in income share went to finance 

sector workers, with this entire rise occurring in the form of 
bonuses rather than salary.”* For bonuses, then, read inequality. 

This financial rent-induced exacerbation of inequality has 
precipitated a vicious, self-reinforcing cycle. As I noted in the 

Introduction, increased inequality has encouraged UK house- 

holds to take on more debt (Figure 0.9). And as James Wood has 

recently shown, the growth of household debt has in turn led 
inexorably to still greater levels of inequality: 

[providing] a revenue stream from indebted households to the 

financial sector, where it is distributed to managers, sharehold- 

ers and employees at the top of the income scale. . 
. the expan- 

sion of household debt in Britain between 1966 and 2016 

increased the income share captured by the top 5% of the 

distribution, while also increasing the level of inequality 
between the top and the middle of the income scale.” 

So, today, it continues to go. ‘The significance of Bell and van 

Reenen’s analysis is to underline that this debt-and-inequality cycle 

operates principally via corporate rents and employment ificome 

rather than capital income flowing directly to households: less 

THE FUNCTIONLESS INVESTOR 
Os) 

than 15 percent of the top income percentile’s gain in income 

share between 1998-9 and 2007-8 consisted of increased invest- 
ment income, and all of the gain was among those of working age 
who had not retired from employment.” 

In short — other than among pensioner households, where 
almost by definition it becomes the principal income-generating 
mechanism — financial rentierism of a direct kind is ultimately a 

relatively marginal feature of the contemporary UK social land- 

scape. To all intents and purposes, today’s petit financial rentier 

class is identical with the pensioner ‘class’, and household financial 

rentierism with pension collection. The latter, to be sure, is a highly 

significant social and economic phenomenon in its own right: 

aggregate private pension wealth in Britain is valued at over £5 

trillion; around 20 per cent of individuals are in receipt of private 

pension payments at any one time; and total annual private 

pension disbursements currently total in the region of £120 

billion.*° Yet one could make a credible case that pension payments 

are not really financial rents at all, but rather delayed income from 

labour. If one were to take this position, then, in the low-interest- 

rate world that the financial crisis has bequeathed, the proportion 

of UK households earning significant financial rents — still less 
surviving on them — is very small. At the end of the day, financial 

rentierism, and especially financial rentierism at scale, is a corpo- 

rate phenomenon. So, too, is the brand of rentierism we turn to in 

the next chapter: the generation of natural-resource rents.

CHAPTER TWO 

Carbon Neoliberalism: 
Natural-Resource Rents 

In September 2013, the mining company Anglo American 
announced that it was withdrawing from the Pebble mine project 

in Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Anglo was vague about its reasons for 
doing so, though commentators speculated that it might have 
had to do with uncertainty over whether the US Environmental 

Protection Agency would approve its controversial plans to 

extract the region’s vast gold and copper deposits, which happen 

to be located underneath one of the world’s largest wild salmon 

fisheries. What the company did divulge, however, were the 

expenses it had incurred during its six years of involvement in 

the project, which had yet to see a single ounce of gold or copper 

mined. A total of $541 million invested in getting the project 

‘nearly to the point where it could begin applying for state and 

federal permits combined with an exit cost of $311 million to 

take overall expenses to not far short of $1 billion.’ Anglo walked 

away. 

Seemingly not in the business of walking away from trouble- 

some mining projects is another major mining company, BHP 

Billiton. In early 2017, trouble flared in Chile at Escondida, the 

world’s largest copper mine. Escondida has produced copper 

concentrate since the early 1990s, and currently accounts for 

96 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

about 5 per cent of global copper output, and BHP is its major- 

ity owner. Objecting to BHP’s proposed new labour contract, 

designed to reduce the mine’s operating expenses, unionized 
workers went on strike for forty-four days — the longest indus- 

trial action in the country’s mining sector for over forty years. 
The strike not only cost BHP and its partners an estimated $1 

billion in lost revenue; such is the scale of the mine that the 

dispute ‘rocked the global copper market and dragged on Chile’s 
economic growth’.* But the company stood its ground: though 

the miners returned to work at the end of the strike on their 

existing pay and benefits, BHP continued to push for the new 
contract, and the dispute remained unresolved at the time of this 
writing. Why this costly intransigence? Because, while ‘painful’, 
the dispute was, according to the company, ‘necessary to safe- 
guard the site’s future. In the words of the head of BHP’s 
Americas business: “We have to protect the competitiveness of 
Escondida not just in the short term but over the next five to ten 
years and the decades to come.” 

Meanwhile, on the other side of the Atlantic, in the Democratic 

Republic of Congo (DRC), another big mining company, 

Glencore, has been dealing with difficulties of an altogether 

different kind. In March 2018, Congolese President Joseph 

Kabila signed into law a new code that substantially raised royal- 

ties and taxes on mining companies operating in the country, 
which is Africa’s leading copper producer. While it is unclear 
exactly how much the new code will cost Glencore, which oper- 

ates in the country through its subsidiaries Katanga Mining and 
Mutanda Mining, it will clearly be a significant amount. ‘This 
much is apparent from the lengths to which Glencore went to 

try to prevent the code being adopted. The new legislation was 
preceded by no less than five years of ‘on-off negotiations 
between Congolese government officials and the mining indus- 

try, in which Glencore executives played a leading role. In January 
2018, 
‘miners 
including 
Glencore, 
Randgold 
and Rehing 
Molybdenum Co. sent a letter to the presidents of the two houses 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
7 

of parliament asking them to suspend the adoption of the new 
code and promising they would defend their investments “by all 
domestic and international means at their disposal”’. This letter 

having fallen on deaf ears, Glencore’s chief executive, Ivan 

Glasenberg, flew to DRC for personal, last-ditch talks with 

Kabila himself. These, too, failed: the country’s parliament passed 

the code at the end of the month. (‘Even Glencore’, commenta- 

tors reflected, in a sign of the company’s renowned clout, ‘was 
unable to talk the president down’.)’ All that remained was for 
Glencore and its peers to try to convince Kabila to reopen nego- 

tiations before he personally put pen to paper — which, in a six- 

hour meeting two days prior to his signing the code into law, 
they were unable to do.° 

Nominally unconnected to one another except insofar as they 

all concern mining, these three episodes from three different 
continents each highlight in their own ways a common, crucial 

feature of contemporary capitalism: companies will go to great 

lengths, and often incur great costs, either to convert naturally 

occurring mineral resources into exclusively controlled revenue- 

generating commercial assets (Anglo American’s aborted mission 

in Alaska), or to defend the ongoing revenue and profit-generating 
capacity of resources already successfully converted into that 

asset form (BHP Billiton’s and Glencore’s mission). In pursuing 

these particular strategic imperatives, Anglo American, BHP 

Billiton and Glencore all represent purveyors of natural-resource 

rentierism. But there is something else common to all three: 

nationality. They are UK rentiers — or at least semi-UK rentiers 

(Anglo American 
is Anglo-South African; BHP 
is Anglo- 

Australian; and Glencore is Anglo-Swiss), and all three list shares 

on the London Stock Exchange. 

Natural-resource 
rentiers 
are organizations 
involved 
in the 
commercial extraction, processing and sale of naturally occur- 

ring mineral fuels (coal, oil and gas, uranium) and other mineral 

resources (metal ores, stones, sands, salts). Part of the reason that 

8 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

such organizations often have to invest vast funds just to get to 

the point where the resources in question can even be thought of 

as their ‘assets’ (‘items of value owned’, according to the diction- 

ary definition), let alone legally and profitably extracted, is that 
numerous conditions first have to be satisfied — and in the case of 

Pebble mine and Anglo American, not all of them were. First, of 

course, the resources have to be discovered. At Pebble, this 

occurred in the late 1980s, through a combination of soil 
sampling, drilling of exploration holes and geophysical surveys. 
Second, it has to be believed that the resources are economically 

worth developing. This was never in doubt at Pebble: even on 
withdrawing from the project, Anglo reiterated its ‘belief that 
Pebble is a deposit of rare magnitude and quality.” Third, 

however, would-be rentiers must secure, if not de jure ownership 

of the resources, then at least de facto ownership, in the form of 

secure rights to extract and market whatever the commodity is. 
And this is where Anglo American’s Pebble dreams foundered: 

not only did it not secure such rights; it clearly came to the view 

that its prospects of doing so were negligible. It was then that it 
cut its losses. 

The rules and regulations governing the assignment and form 

of rights to develop mineral resources represent a veritable mine- 

field in their own right. They vary between countries; and they 

often vary within individual countries between different mineral 

types. Much depends, needless to say, on who owns the resources 

in the first place. In the UK, for example, the state owns all gold 
and silver deposits and fuel rights, while all other mineral rights 

are held privately — usually (though not always) by the owner of 
the surface land. For those resources under UK government 
ownership, a licence is required for any exploration or develop- 
ment activity, and the licences specify which of these activities — 
exploration or development — the permit covers. There is no 
specific UK national licensing system for the exploration and 
development of mineral resources that are privately owned, but 
planning permission must be obtained for their extraction. 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
Og) 

More generally, mineral rights owners around the world typi- 

cally use one of two different types of arrangement for outsourc- 

ing resource-extraction rights to specialist third parties. The first 

isva. concessionary arrangement, whereby companies are granted 

the exclusive right to explore for and/or develop resources at 

their own risk and expense in a fixed geographical area, and 
generally for a specific period of time. The company in posses- 

sion of the concession takes legal ownership of the resources at 

the point of their extraction (the wellhead in the case of oil, for 

example). The alternative is a contractual arrangement, which, 

while it can take multiple forms, typically sees the rights owner 

retain title to the resources but share the proceeds of production 
with the company (or often, companies) contracted to undertake 
development. Contractual arrangements, which generally trans- 

fer less risk and ownership away from the resource owner than 
concessionary systems, are more common outside the Global 
North, where, by contrast, concessions tend to be the norm. 

There is one other important point: the companies granted 

concessions or contracts are not always private companies. They 

can be state companies, and, in the oil-rich nations within the 

Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (Opec), 

they very often are. 
, 
In any event, only when all three of the above criteria — discov- 

ery, demonstration of economic viability, securing of develop- 
ment rights — have been satisfied does the natural-resource rent- 

ier recognize resources as assets. [hese assets have a special name 

— ‘reserves’ — and the term for recognizing them as such is ‘book- 

ing’. In other words, to ‘book’ reserves is formally to acknowl- 
edge their existence as proprietary assets with the potential to 

generate rents. The ‘booking’ terminology makes sense, because 

the recognition that naturally occurring mineral resources have 

been transformed into things of capitalist value (that is, assets) 

occurs through the primary representational apparatus of capi- 

talist valuation: accounting, and, in particular, the process of 

bookkeeping at its heart. To report reserves is, in short, to book 

100 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

their value — to affirm its actuality. Read any annual report or set 

of financial accounts published by a major mining or oil and gas 
company, and you will find literally dozens of pages of reserve 
statements, documenting the reserves the company owns in each 

minerals category, what additions to reserves have been made in 

the latest financial period, and what ‘depletions’ or ‘impairments’ 

— for example, through successful extraction, or, heaven forbid, 
expiry or loss of rights — these reserves have suffered. 

It would be only a slight exaggeration to say that the business 

of natural-resource rentierism is all about the rentier’s precious 

reserves: securing them, as Anglo American tried in vain and at 

great cost to do in Alaska; and defending their capacity to gener- 

ate maximum rents, as BHP Billiton and Glencore have fought 
ferociously to do in Chile and DRC, respectively. Reserves are 
also the fundamental basis for investors’ assessment of resource 
rentiers’ progress and prospects. Asset vigilance, in short, is as 
much of a strategic priority for these rentiers as for their peers in 
the financial sector. As BHP acknowledged with marvellous 
understatement in the section of its 2018 annual report on 
Business Risks that, as a listed company, it was required to 
provide for investors: ‘Failure to discover or acquire new resources, 
maintain reserves or develop new assets could negatively affect 
our future results and financial condition.’ 

But if, as I argued in Chapter 1, finance capital is not just 

finance capital, neither are reserves simply reserves. It is clear 
from those company reserve statements that reserves are distin- 
guished from one another not only according to the type of 
mineral resource to which they pertain, but also according to the 
extent of a company’s participation in the rents that the reserves 

are expected to generate (based partly on the particular conces- 
sionary or contractual arrangement through which the reserves 

are held) and the degree of certainty attached to the realization of 
future rental streams. In terms of the last of these differentiating 

factors, reserves are generally categorized as ‘proven’, ‘probable’ 

or ‘possible’. The UK’s Oil and Gas Authority, which in 2015 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
101 

replaced the Department for Energy and Climate Change as the 

entity responsible for domestic oil and gas licensing, defines 

these categories as follows: proven reserves are those that, ‘on the 

available evidence, are virtually certain to be technically and 
commercially producible, i.e. have a better than 90% chance of 

being produced’; probable reserves ‘are estimated to have a better 
than 50% chance of being technically and commercially produc- 

ible’; and possible reserves are those for which this chance is 

‘significant — but less than 50%’. 

Given that subjectivity and discretion are necessarily involved 

in the assigning of these labels — there is in reality no objective 
means of determining whether the chanee of a reserve being 

developable is closer to 88 or 92 per cent — it should be clear 

that reserve statistics are not so much practical facts as perform- 

ative artefacts. The production and publication of reserve state- 
ments is, literally, a performance of value: an attempt to perform 
company value by pledging the existence of a certain quantum 

of reserve value. We should be in no doubt about the signifi- 

cance of such performances. The stakes could scarcely be higher: 
when in 2004, for instance, the Anglo-Dutch oil major Royal 

Dutch Shell (hereafter, ‘Shell’) announced that it had previ- 

ously overstated by 40 per cent the proven reserves of 
its minor- 

ity-owned Petroleum Development of Oman, it led to the 

resignation of both its chairman and its chief executive of 

exploration and production." The actual amount of oil in the 

ground had not changed, and nor had Shell’s financial and legal 

interest in that oil. In fact, nothing of importance had changed, 

other than a number in a reserve statement. But these numbers 

matter. From the perspective of those who own shares in capi- 

talist companies, value is always a future-oriented phenomenon 

tied to expectations regarding the income that such share 

ownership will occasion. Reserve estimates are essentially narra- 

tions of that future: when the story changes, so too does value 

itself, and everything — careers included — that depends upon it. 

The most egregious example of false futurity in the annals of 

102 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the mineral resources sector was the infamous 1990s Bre-X scan- 

dal, when the eponymous Canadian company announced to the 
world that it had discovered gold reserves of 57 million ounces at 
Busang on the island of Borneo. Its market value soared to more 
than $4 billion; but later the company admitted that it had over- 

stated these reserves 
— by, essentially, 57 million ounces." 
(Independent analysis found that there was no gold.)!? Bre-X 

was an attempt to conjure a rentier into existence by conjuring 

an asset into existence. The. episode highlighted better than 
any other the crucial importance of the performative dimension 
of reserve booking. No wonder, in its aftermath, that actual 
natural-resource rentiers are as vigilant about the credibility of 
their reserve statements as they are about stewardship of the 
assets to which those statements refer — as the following entry in 
BHP Billiton’s 2018 annual report nicely demonstrates: 

The Petroleum Reserves Group (PRG) is a dedicated group that 

provides oversight of the reserves’ assessment and reporting 

processes. It is independent of the various operation teams 

directly responsible for development and production activi- 

ties 
... The manager of the PRG . 
. 
. is a full-time employee of 
BHP and is responsible for overseeing the preparation of the 

reserve estimates and compiling the information for inclusion 

in this Annual Report. He has an advanced degree in engineer- 
ing and more than 35 years of diversified industry experience in 

reservoir engineering, reserves assessment, field development 
and technical management ... The estimates of petroleum 

reserves are based on and fairly represent information and 
supporting documentation prepared under [his] supervision. 
He has reviewed and agrees with the information included in 

[this report] and has given his prior written consent for its 
publication. No part of the individual compensation for 
members of the PRG is dependent on reported reserves." ia

What is the scale of natural-resource rentierism in relation to 

the modern UK economy as a whole? Figure 2.1 provides one 
way — perhaps the most common — of picturing this scale. For 

the entire neoliberal period and — for historical context — the 

decade preceding it, the chart shows the share of overall UK 

gross value-added (GVA) contributed by mining and quarrying 

activities, which encompass the extraction of mineral resources 
including oil and gas. An industry sector's GVA represents its 

net contribution to national economic output — in technical 

terms, its gross output minus the value of its ‘intermediate 

consumption’. If you sum GVA across all industry sectors and 

adjust for taxes and subsidies, you arrive at a better-known 

measure: gross domestic product (GDP). In essence, what 

Figure 2.1 tells us is the relative importance of the activities of 

natural-resource rentiers to the UK economy in each year since 

LO703 

Two features of Figure 2.1 merit close consideration. The first 

is what appears to be an anomalous period of a decade and a half, 
beginning in the mid 1970s, during which the GVA contribu- 

tion of the mining and quarrying sector firstly rose sharply, and 

104 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

then declined just as rapidly as it had risen, before settling at a 

level much lower than its mid-1980s peak, but nonetheless 

significantly higher than the level achieved in the first half of the 

1970s. I will return to this anomalous period shortly. 

The second important feature of Figure 2.1 is the absolute 

level of the mining and quarrying sectors GVA contribution 
during the past three decades: the period since the late 1980s. 

As the chart shows, this depends somewhat on how one defines 

the sector — SIC codes are a means of industrial classification. 
But either way, the message of the chart seems clear enough: 
mining and quarrying are only marginal economic activities in 

the UK, consistently contributing less than 3 per cent of 
overall 
economic output — and in some years considerably less than 
that. 

On the face of it, Figure 2.1 raises a rather fundamental ques- 

tion: Why include natural-resource rentierism in a book on rent- 

ier capitalism in the modern UK — why, indeed, devote a whole 
chapter to it — when the reality appears to be that, save for a 

relatively brief period that ended some three decades ago, this 
form of rentierism does not play a significant role in the UK 
economy? ‘The question is an important one, and much of the 

rest of this chapter represents, indirectly at least, a series of 
answers. For a variety of reasons that will become apparent, any 
account of the contemporary UK economy that aspires to come 
meaningfully to grips with that economy, and especially one that 

is interested chiefly in predominant rentier dynamics, must pay 
close attention to the extractive industries. 

The answer I want to begin with concerns the issue of how we 

should even endeavour to conceptualize, frame and measure a 
national economy in the first place. What is the ‘UK economy? 
We cannot begin to discuss how significant this or that sector is 

to the national economy until we know what form this larger 
entity takes. Unfortunately, this question does not have a.simple 

or single answer. As I noted in the Introduction, the ‘UK econ- 
omy can be defined, and thus measured, in various ways. The 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
105 

GVA data plotted in Figure 2.1 represent an example of one type 
of geo-statistical framing of the economy, which we can call the 

territorial framing. Like GDP, GVA refers to the value of goods 
and services produced within a particular country, irrespective of 
who carries out this production. Thus, in the specific case of 

Figure 2.1, the economic output represented could equally well 

have been generated by a French or Canadian company as by a 

British one. All that matters is that the production occurs within 

the territorial boundaries of the UK. 

But a territorial framing is not the only way to envision a 

‘national economy’, or necessarily the most meaningful, or the 

closest we can get to satisfactorily pinning down the elusive real- 

ity that ‘national economy’ refers to. No less meaningful, for 
many purposes, is a residency-based framing, where output is 
deemed to be part of a national economy if it is generated by 
people or corporations normally residing in that country. ‘This 
framing is the one used for the other main metric ordinarily 

invoked, alongside GDP and GVA, as the measure of an econo- 

my’s size: gross national product (GNP). Where GDP is the 
value of goods and services produced domestically, GNP is the 

value of goods and services produced by a country’s residents 

(‘nationals’), irrespective of where in the world this production 

takes place. 

For some sectors of the economy, it does not greatly matter 
whether one adopts a territorial or residency-based framing: 

the sector’s relative importance appears more or less equivalent 
whichever lens one uses. Indeed, this is broadly true of the 

sector I considered in the previous chapter: finance. A substan- 

tial quantum of financial sector output is generated within the 
UK by non-nationals — recall the discussion of the longstand- 

ing major presence in London of leading US banks; but there 

is also a substantial quantum of output generated internation- 

ally by the likes of Barclays, HSBC and Lloyds. As the Bank of 

England’s own economists have noted in discussing the fact 

that banking systems, like economies, can be defined on the 

106 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

basis of either place (where financial assets are located) or 

nationality (of the asset owner), the key features of the UK 
banking system appear essentially the same regardless of the 

definition used.“ 

For the UK mineral-resources-extraction sector in the period 

since the mid 1990s, however, it matters enormously which 
framing of the ‘national economy’ one uses. Regrettably, the 
UK’s Office for National Statistics (ONS) does not publish 

data for industry shares of GNP; but, if it did, the sectoral 
contribution of the extractive industries would be substantially 

higher than the same sector’s contribution to GDP. Many of 
the world’s largest natural-resource 
rentiers 
are UK-based 
companies that list their shares in London. Indeed, in late 
2019, no fewer than six companies falling into this category 
featured among the twenty companies listed on the London 
Stock Exchange with the highest market value: in descending 
order of 
size, Shell, BP, Rio Tinto, BHP Billiton, Glencore, and 
Anglo American (see Table 0.1, p. 7).!° The reason that mineral- 
resource extraction has made only a relatively small annual 
contribution to UK GDP since the late 1980s, despite the fact 
that many of Britain’s biggest companies are engaged in precisely 
that activity, is simply that only a small subset of these compa- 
nies’ vast mineral reserves are found in the UK, and thus only a 
correspondingly small share of the rents generated through 
exploitation of those reserves is recognized in UK GVA or GDP. 
UK-based banks themselves have a famously high exposure to 
international markets (see Chapter 1), around 40 per cent of 
their assets being located outside the UK (Figure 1.2, p. 64). 
But this overseas exposure pales beside that of the big UK-based 
natural-resource 
rentiers, whose UK-based 
assets 
— which 
include significant deposits of nickel, salt and potash, but 
which, as we shall see, are dominated by petroleum reserves — 
are dwarfed by their overseas holdings. In no other smajor 
industry sector is the asset base of the UK’s corporate rentier 
class so heavily skewed to non-UK locations.

Figure 2.2 makes this international concentration vividly 

apparent. It shows the geographical distribution of the assets of 

five of the aforementioned “Big Six’ corporations at the end of 

their 2016 and 2017 
financial years, splitting those assets between 

the UK (or, where the company in question does not specifically 

identify the UK portion, the next-smallest regional scale for 

which data are available) and other territories. The only one of 

the Big Six missing from Figure 2.2 is BP, which, rather unhelp- 

fully, has since 2009 reported asset location only as US or 

non-US. At the end of the 2008 financial year — the last for 

which a more granular territorial breakdown is available — 17.8 

per cent of BP’s $228 billion of assets were located in the UK." 

Notably, this is higher than the 2016 and 2017 UK shares of 

assets for all of the other Big Six rentiers — in most cases, comfort- 

ably so. All told, Figure 2.2 provides a striking visual explanation 

of why there is such a significant mismatch today between the 

modest contribution of natural resource 
rents to UK GDP 

(Figure 2.1) and the major presence of natural resource rentiers 

108 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

among Britain’s leading corporations. Briefly stated, the rentiers 

are earning their rents elsewhere. 

In this respect, there would appear to be something of an 
imperial flavour to UK natural-resource rentierism. Essentially, 

there is a constellation of giant capitalist firms headquartered in 
Europe extracting both natural resources and the rents they 

afford primarily from other parts of the world — regions that in 
many cases are in fact former European colonies, British or 
otherwise. I have already touched, for example, on BHP and 

Glencore’s operations in Chile and DRC. Shell’s long and contro- 

versial presence in Nigeria is also well known; Anglo American’s 
main country of business is South Africa; BP has substantial 

operations in Angola — the list goes on. 

Imperialism clearly helps to explain how UK-based natural- 

resource rentiers came to enjoy such a strong overseas presence in 

the first place. If one digs into the histories of the likes of Anglo 
American, BP, Rio Tinto and Shell, one finds them to be saturated 
by the political economy of empire. This is especially true where 

oil is concerned — and thus where BP and Shell are involved.!7 Not 

for nothing did anticolonial voices long refer to the interpenetra- 

tion of empire and the activities of the Western oil majors in the 

era prior to decolonization in terms of ‘petroleum colonization’. 
Indeed, they argued that structural inequality — colonialism — was 
embedded both economically and symbolically in the concession- 

ary model that the likes of BP and Shell typically employed. 
Christopher Dietrich quotes Opec’s first Secretary General, Iran’s 
Fuad Rouhani, who in 1962 described concessions as transactions 

in which the non-Western countries from which Western compa- 

nies extracted oil ‘gave too much for too little’ ‘Casting an even 
darker pall’, says Dietrich, ‘was the way the term captured the gist 
of the relationship between the oil nations and the companies. As 
Rouhani put it, the problem was simple. A concession was by defi- 
nition “a giving of the weak to the strong." 
as 

It was not just oil. Anglo American was founded in 1917 in 

South Africa, at that time still a British colony, albeit not for 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
109 

much longer; and Rio Tinto’s rise to prominence in the inter-war 

period owed much to the opportunity that arose to invest in the 

copper belt of what was then British Rhodesia.!? Like BP and 

Shell, these two rentiers established enduring positions far from 

the UK partly because British imperialism enabled them to do so. 

Nicholas Shaxson has argued, however, that the image of 
Western oil companies as ‘agents of imperialism’ is in reality an 
increasingly outdated one.”” He is partly right. Even before 
Rouhani made the abovementioned comments, oil-rich non- 
Western nations had begun in some cases to claw back economic 
ground vis-a-vis the erstwhile petroleum colonizers, not least in 

Iran itself. A noteworthy 1957 agreement between Iran and the 

Italian oil company, ENI, for instance, would see the former 

receive fully 75 percent of the total profit from the development 

of three new oil fields — far higher than traditional cuts, and 

hardly a measure of subjugation.” 

The US, in particular, long held to the view that as decoloniza- 

tion proceeded, it was smarter (and more profitable) for Western 
producers to make compromises on tax and royalty rates — as 
ENI had in Iran — than risk the nuclear alternative: nationaliza- 

tion of their oil production facilities. Notably, BP and Shell were 

refuseniks, and, as late as 1970, were lobbying the Nixon admin- 

istration to take a harder line against the erosion of producer 

profit shares.” It was somewhat karmic, then, that among the 

first Western holdings to be nationalized were BP’s in Libya, in 

1971; and that — with Libya, like Iraq, using the Cold War to 

beat blacklisting of its supplies by doing deals with Moscow and 

its allies — BP received little by way of compensation.” 

Certainly, today, Western natural-resource rentiers operating 

in the Global South are not generally in positions of colonial- 

type dominance over host-nation governments. President Kabila, 

after all, successfully called the tune on mining taxes and royal- 

ties in DRC; and BHP has so far failed to get its way in its dispute 

with Chilean labour unions. Shaxson himself, meanwhile, relates 

the interesting case of when ‘BP, responding to transparency 

110 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

campaigns, promised in 2001 to’ publish financial information 
about its oil operations in Angola — and was threatened by the 
Angolan government with termination of its contract. What 
happened? “BP jumped smartly back into line.’ 

Nevertheless, to focus only on the relationship between Global 

South host governments and Western fossil-fuel or mining 
companies is to ignore the position of local inhabitants — and in 

particular to neglect the position of indigenous peoples. The 

latter have often found themselves doubly dispossessed: first by 

imperialism proper, and more recently by what, from their 

perspective at least, irrefutably represents fossil-fuel imperialism. 

Penelope Anthias’s brilliant 2018 study of indigenous disposses- 

sion and ongoing struggles over territory in Bolivia places the 
political economy of mineral-resource governance and extraction 

— including, in that country, by a subsidiary of BP — at the very 
centre of the narrative. That is where it belongs not just across 
resource-rich parts of the Global South, but also in resource-rich 
settler-colonialist societies of the Global North, such as Canada 
and Australia.” 

The question remains, though, of which picture provides the 
more fitting or meaningful representation of the present-day UK 
economy, and of the role of natural-resource rentiers within it. 
The rather underwhelming Figure 2.1? Or a residency-based 
framing, which would include rather than exclude the colossal 
non-Uk-generated output of the Big Six (see Figure 2.2)? I have 
no definitive answer to this question; both pictures tell interest- 
ing and important stories. But, in order to gain an understand- 
ing of the complexion of the contemporary economy of the UK, 

it seems to me that the latter picture is just as pertinent as the 
former; certainly, there is no reason to discount it. Think of the 
issue this way: What is more part of the UK economy — rent 
generated in the UK by a foreign company that then repatriates 

its profits rather than reinvesting them locally, or rent generated 
overseas by a British company that repatriates its profits to the 
UK? ‘There is a reason, ultimately, why national statistical offices 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
ILI 

such as the ONS typically publish both GDP and GNP metrics: 
both the territorial and residency-based pictures are significant 
and instructive. This is definitely true, at any rate, where natural- 

resource rentierism and the UK economy are concerned. 

In a country preoccupied over the past five years by Europe, it 
would be understandable if June 1975 is best remembered in the 
UK for the Common Market referendum. In that vote — the first 

ever referendum held throughout the nation, and the only one to 

be held on the UK’s relationship with Europe until 2016 — two- 

thirds of voters expressed support for staying in the European 
Community, which the UK had joined twovyears previously. But 
what was arguably a more significant event occurred later the 
same month. On 18 June, at what the then energy minister Tony 
Benn described as the ‘ravaged, desolate, industrial landscape’ of 

the River Medway estuary in south-east England, the first oil 

extracted from the UK sector of the North Sea — specifically, the 

Argyll field off the north-east coast of Scotland — arrived for 

processing onshore. Benn described not only the local physical 
landscape but, just as notably, the social congregation the event 
had elicited: ‘a complete cross-section of the international capi- 

talist and British Tory establishment’.” 

That the capitalist and right-wing political classes were well- 
represented at the Medway that day was both appropriate and 
prophetic, for North Sea oil and gas would fundamentally shape 

the fortunes of both over the coming decades — the ‘bump’ from 

1975 in the extractive industries’ share of UK economic output 
shown in Figure 2.1 was just one manifestation of a much wider 

political-economic transformation associated with the rise to 
prominence in the UK of a hydrocarbon economy. Substantial 

oil and gas fields had been discovered in the North Sea section of 

the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS) — the region of waters 

surrounding the UK in which the country has mineral rights — in 

the late 1960s and early 1970s. The first substantive profits from 
UK oil and gas extraction came on-stream in 1976, flowing both 

IM 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

to UK companies (most notably ‘BP and Shell) and to interna- 

tional, especially US, operators. By 1980, as Figure 2.1 demon- 

strates, the burgeoning domestic oil-and-gas industry had lifted 

the extractive sector’s share of total UK GVA from 1.6 per cent 

to over 6 per cent in the space of just five short years. The natural- 

resource rentier had long been one of the UK’s most successful 

economic actors overseas; all of a sudden, it had become a major 

actor locally as well. 

To a large extent, of course, these newly minted rentier fortunes 

were simply fortuitous. The domestic rise of oil and gas, and of 

natural-resource rents, was in one respect quite unlike the contem- 
poraneous rise of finance and financial rents (Chapter 1), inas- 
much as it depended wholly upon the identification and harvest- 
ing of valuable physical resources, which either were there to be 
discovered or were not. Finance is different. As numerous scholars 
have noted, especially since the financial crisis, the connection 
between financial assets and any underlying tangible commodity 
has in many instances become increasingly tenuous. Financial 
assets can be created out of thin air.”” This is not true, however, of 
resource rentiers’ reserves; an underlying substance is required. 
On the UKCS it materialized, and was harvested in vast volumes 
from the 1970s onwards. By 1980, the industry had produced 
approximately 2 billion barrels of oil and the same amount of gas 
(‘barrels of oil equivalent’); by 1990, cumulative production had 
reached 10.5 and 4.4 billion barrels, respectively.”® 

But in another crucial respect, the rise of natural-resource 

rents and rentiers was not so unlike what happened in the finance 

space; there was much more to it than pure fortuitousness. As we 

have seen, the UK government owns all UK oil and gas rights. 
There was therefore nothing inevitable about the discovery of oil 
and gas on the UKCS benefiting private-sector rentiers — whose 

net output is represented in Figure 2.1, and whose profits from 

oil and gas production are shown in Figure 2 
pian the.way it 

has. For comparison, consider the case of Saudi Arabia, for exam- 

ple, where oil was first discovered much earlier (in the late 1930s),

— just as it has in the financial sector.

government and government policy ebbed somewhat in the

‘LOil] policy in the UK since 1979 has been driven unashamedly

Little wonder, then, that private rentier interests have consist- 
ently been privileged and cossetted. Errol’s determination to 
freeze out the public sector was replicated by most of his succes- 
sors. What direct state involvement there was in North Sea oil 
and gas was gradually, but relentlessly, whittled away. BP — which, 
as Cumbers says, was originally ‘largely a creation of the British 
state — was progressively privatized. Setting out her stall almost 
immediately upon taking office in 1979, Thatcher sold 5 per 
cent of the company — taking the government’s equity interest 
from 51 to 46 per cent; by the end of 1987 the government had 
liquidated its holding entirely? Then there was the ill-fated 
British National Oil Corporation (BNOC). Created by Benn in 
1975 explicitly as a means to exert public control over oil and gas 
development, and to enable direct state participation in the

monetary proceeds, BNOC just about managed to ‘annoy the

across the entire spectrum of the British economy’. Since then, 

the upstream component of the UK oil and gas industry — explo-

If the private sector was given an advantage by the squeezing 

out of the public sector, furthermore, it also benefited from 
government 
policies that converted mineral resources 
into 

reserves more robustly, expansively and generously than in almost 
any other country. As we have seen, a rentier’s ability to generate 

rent depends, among other things, upon the strength and scope 

of her rights to the rent-generating asset; and in the UK oil and 

gas sector, the concessionary licensing system has consistently 

served up rights of the very highest quality. “The first huge areas 

of the sea, of a hundred square miles each’, the Public Accounts 
Committee of the House of Commons noted with barely 

concealed incredulity in 1972, ‘were leased to the companies as 

generously as though Britain were a gullible Sheikhdom, with 
concessions running for forty-six years’.*° 

Equally incredulous was 
the legendary US wildcatter- 
turned-corporate oilman T. Boone Pickens, who built the 
company he founded, Mesa, into one of the world’s largest 

independent oil companies. Pickens later recalled how, in the 

late 1960s, when he and Mesa had been focused on the Gulf 

of Mexico, he had looked with envy at what was happening in 

the North Sea: ‘I couldn't help thinking about the great possi- 

bilities across the Atlantic, especially when I learned that 

50,000-acre tracts were being given free to companies willing 

to explore them. To oilmen used to paying millions just for 

the privilege of drilling, that was a real incentive.” Pickens 

was not about to pass the incentive up. Mesa grabbed what 

North Sea tracts it could, and in 1976 it discovered there the 

largest oil field in its history, the Beatrice Field.

RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Over time, however, the biggest and most significant incentive 

of all, and the one that more than anything else served to make 

the North Sea an enduring corporate rentier’s paradise, would be 

the tax system developed by the UK government to enable the 

state to participate economically in the country’s natural-resource 
bounty in the absence of a proprietary state exploration and 
production enterprise. 

In general terms, it would be hard to overstate the significance of 

the fiscal arrangements that a country implements to structure 

the distribution of natural-resource rents in situations where 

rights-holding governments outsource the extraction of those 
resources in part or in full to private-sector operators. The name 
given to the system of taxation of mineral-resource production is 

‘fiscal regime’. This regime can take numerous different forms, 
and usually incorporates one or a combination of royalties (ordi- 
narily payable per unit of output), income taxes (with relief often 
available for capital expenditure), and special mineral taxes 
(generally levied on a project or field basis, and based on cash 
flows).°* The reason it matters so much is that it is typically the 
main determinant of the proportions in which host governments 
share the spoils of natural-resource wealth with private-sector 
rentiers. 

Taxation can range from extremely light to highly punitive, 

with profound consequences for both government receipts and 
company profits. In this respect, it is telling that when natural- 

resource rentiers like BHP Billiton and Glencore document the 
main risks to which their businesses (and profits) are exposed, 
the fiscal regime always appears at the very top of the list — rivalled 
only by natural disasters and indigenous land claims. Here, 

again, is BHP’s instructive 2018 annual report: 

Our operated assets and non-operated joint ventures are based 
: 
. 
on material long-term investments that are dependent on 
long-term fiscal stability, and could be adversely affected by

changes in fiscal legislation, changes in interpretation of fiscal 

legislation, periodic challenges and disagreements with tax 

authorities and legal proceedings relating to fiscal matters. The 

natural resources industry continues to be regarded as a source 

of tax revenue and can also be adversely affected by broader 

fiscal measures applying to businesses generally. 

The report went on to note that BHP was at the time ‘involved 

in a number of uncertain tax and royalty matters’.*’ So, as we 

have seen, had Glencore been, in DRC — and it had suffered 

precisely the types of adverse effects alluded to by BHP. 

The UK, by contrast, for the vast majority of the period of 

extraction of North Sea oil and gas, has offered an altogether 
more 
accommodating 
and business-friendly 
fiscal 
regime, 
redounding forcefully to the advantage of the private sector. 

Figure 2.3 provides a graphical representation of the evolving 

nature of that regime since the mid-to-late 1970s, showing, for 
each year, total industry income and total tax revenue from UK 

oil and gas production, and the effective tax rate (the ratio of the 

latter to the former). As Bernard Mommer has written, ‘the fiscal 

regime in British oil expanded until 1982, and then began to 

shrink.” 

Even when the tax rate was at its most stringent, in the early 
1980s, it was only in the region of 50 per cent. That might sound 

like a high number, until one compares it with the 70 to 90 per 

cent typically earned by the governments of the largest oil- 
producing nations in Africa.‘ In any event, rates of around 50 

per cent were only fleeting. From the mid 1980s, royalties came 
under what Juan Carlos Boué describes as ‘a sustained attack’ by 

the Thatcher government, and were progressively eliminated.” 

In addition, the government pushed to the extreme allowable 

relief on capital investment, eventually introducing 100 per cent 

depreciation in the year of expenditure, thereby ensuring that no 

project paid tax until payback was secured — ‘a uniquely attrac- 

tive feature for investors’, as Carole Nakhle later noted.”

Thus, by the early 1990s — by which time the tax yield had 

fallen to only around 10 per cent — what Boué refers to as the 

Conservative government’ longstanding ‘vision of a low tax 
hydrocarbons sector had well and truly materialized. The North 

Sea oil fields, Boué remarks, now enjoyed ‘the same fiscal arrange- 
ments as a bakery or a bike shop. Or, to put it another way, the 

British government was content to receive 
a compensation of 

precisely zero from the exploitation of certain hydrocarbon 

resources belonging to the Crown.” 

It is worth pausing at this point to consider the wider meaning 

of the aggressive reduction of UK tax rates on North Sea produc- 

tion from the mid 1980s. Writing with Philip Wright and draw- 
ing on Mommers work, Boué usefully counterposes ‘proprieto- 

rial’ with 
‘non-proprietorial’ 
fiscal 
regimes 
for petroleum 

industries, and argues that during the 1980s the UK effectively 

shifted from the former to the latter, becoming ‘increasingly 
non-proprietorial’. In proprietorial regimes, ‘like a landlord who 
rents out an apartment to a tenant’, the state requires ‘rent for 
the use of a country’s hydrocarbon resources’ — quite rightly, one 
might say, given, after all, that it owns those resources. Under a 
non-proprietorial 
regime, by contrast, 
‘the 
state 
becomes 
concerned about the relationship between its taxation practices

nies producing from its sovereign resources’ 
.”° 

This is what seems to have happened under Thatcher's Tories. 
From having put the state and its right to rent first, under Labour, 

the UK government switched to prioritizing the private sector 
and its ‘right’ to rent. Beginning in the mid 1980s, the guiding 

principle of the UK’s fiscal regime was not to secure a fair share 
of rent for the state, and thus the taxpayer, so much as not to 
jeopardize the private sector’s enthusiasm for exploring and drill- 
ing. ‘That this transformation fundamentally diminished the tax 
regime itself, turning it into a mere ‘adjustment variable,, to be 
fiddled with in order to secure the profitability of sub- -marginal 

investment projects, was, as Boué says, the very least of the

implications. As he points out, ‘saying that fostering investment 

is the role of a fiscal regime is tantamount to turning on its head 

the political relationship between resource owners, on the one 

hand, and the companies exploiting such resources, on the 

other’.“© No longer the steward of a valuable, publicly owned 

natural resource arbitrating private-sector access on its own, 

take-it-or-leave-it terms, the state becomes the oil industry’s 
lapdog, promising to do whatever it takes fiscally to safeguard 
both investment and profitability. 

Boosted, among other relatively marginal measures, by the 

introduction in 2002 of a supplementary charge to corporation 

tax to reflect the recovery of oil prices frona the mid 1990s, the 
UK government’s tax take on oil and gas production did recover 
somewhat from its early-1990s nadir; but it has never again 

exceeded 33 per cent. Notably, low upstream oil-and-gas taxa- 

tion combines in the UK with high downstream taxation: UK 

petrol prices have for decades been among the highest in Europe. 
The ratio of downstream-to-upstream hydrocarbon taxes peaked 

at approximately twelve-to-one in 1999, when the £2.5 billion 

in upstream taxes levied on producers that is shown in Figure 2.3 
compared with £30 billion in downstream

A number of interlocking factors account for the UK’s excep- 

tionally obliging oil-and-gas fiscal regime since the early 1980s. 

Partly, of course, the explanation is ideological: that is, the 

neoliberal state’s longstanding commitment to low taxation of 

capital, whatever the industry sector. Then there is the influence 

of lobbying, as we have seen. Mommer, for example, notes that 

the Conservatives’ move to shrink the fiscal regime from the mid 

1980s coincided with the government’s ‘[falling] prey to the 

permanent lobbying of the industry to bring down taxation 

levels’.“8 Indeed, UK petroleum tax policy is arguably the pre- 

eminent arena within which lobbying by the UK fossil-fuel 

sector has been most consistently practised, and most reliably 

120 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

efficacious — at least until climate change began to enter the 

conversation. 

As Wright and Boué have observed, the oil-and-gas ‘company 

lobby’ was utterly successful in shaping the contours of public 

debate on the fiscal regime in the 1980s, riding roughshod over 

the Labour Party’s vocal opposition to the Tories’ reduction of 

the tax take.” As Greg Muttitt and his colleagues have pointed 

out much more recently, the types of practices through which 

the UK’s fiscal regime has historically been made and remade 
have left it singularly open to corporate capture. Policy is made 

‘in close coordination with the oil companies and their tax advis- 

ers, and with almost no consultation with other stakeholders’. 
Meanwhile, periodically constituted ‘expert groups’ are also 
‘made up entirely of oil companies and their associations and tax 
advisers’ 
.°° 

The UK’s denuded fiscal regime for oil and gas can also be 

explained in terms of the historic geopolitical context. In the 
1970s and 1980s, the government was in a singular hurry for the 
North Sea’s oil and gas to be extracted as quickly as possible, 

largely because of a desire to undercut Opec, whose influence 

over global energy supplies and prices had been substantially 
heightened by the 1973 oil shock.*' One way to expedite rapid 
extraction was through SHEERS tax policy — 
and, as Mommer 
would later write, there is ‘no doubt that the lower level of taxa- 
tion had a positive impact on production’. 

Last but not least, the performative dimension of reserve esti- 
mation (see above) has also played a significant role. As it became 

ever clearer, through the 1970s and 1980s, that the North Sea 
harboured vast amounts of oil and gas, the industry went out of 

its way to underplay the real extent of these resource riches lest 

the government ramp up the tax burden. I suggested earlier that 
natural-resource rentiers make great play of their reserves wealth 

— but this can be a double- -edged sword: if it can increase cgmpa- 

nies’ attractiveness in the eyes of investors, it can also increase 
their perceived value as sources of potential tax income in the 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
IBA 

eyes of governments. As such, the rentiers in question always 
walk a fine line: ‘Oil companies [like] the idea of increases in 

reserves , observed Harvie. ‘But not huge increases; that might 
mean governments being a lot more choosy about policy.” The 

insistence that North Sea stocks were not, in fact, abundant, but 

actually quite marginal, was designed to keep the government's 

hands off the taxation trigger; increase taxes, the industry was 

effectively saying, and production might become unviable. 
Experts who attempted to publicize the true extent of the compa- 

nies’ reserves therefore made themselves deeply unpopular — 
none more so than a certain Peter Odell: “Odell claimed that 

there might be as much as 78 billion barrels in reserve, perhaps 

as much as 100 billion (10.5 to 13 billion tons). This did not 

meet with oil company approval. At all. Odell would become a 

close runner-up to Tony Benn as licensed offshore bogeyman.”™ 

In any case, the government did not listen to Odell; taxes would 
remain minimal, and thus industry profits maximal. “The British 
North Sea’, Mommer wrote at the turn of the millennium, ‘is 
nowadays by far the lowest-taxed and most profitable oil prov- 

ince of the world’. The UK government had committed to ‘a 

radical liberal fiscal regime’, becoming ‘the textbook example 
and the model pupil of liberal governance in oil’.” Indeed, there 

is an argument to be made that, from the early 1980s, the UK 

oil-and-gas sector was not only a model of radical liberal govern- 

ance specifically in hydrocarbons and, as such, a prototypical 

example of a privatized natural-resources rentier regime, but also 

a model of and for (neo)liberal rentierism much more generally, 

both in the UK economy and further afield: it was the domain in 

which this model was first fully developed and perfected. 

This development was never just about low taxes and the 

serving up by the government of robust and expansive private- 
property rights — although these were unarguably its key mecha- 

nisms. It was also characterised by two crucial phenomena that

tend to accompany rentierism in view of the rentier’s inherent

RENTIER CAPITALISM 

monopoly power. One is weakened labour; the other is a throt- 

tling of innovation. Both have been persistent features of the UK 

oil-and-gas industry, and integral elements of its status as liberal 

rentier archetype. 

Insofar as monopoly power is inherent to the exclusive North 

Sea concessions granted to oil companies, competition in oil- 
and-gas production is by nature restricted, just as it is in all cases 

of rentierism. There have nonetheless been sporadic attempts to 
introduce elements of competition to the sector, if only at the 

margins. In the early 1980s, for example, Thatcher's first energy 

minister, David Howell, tried to encourage smaller companies 

onto the Continental Shelf, to break the stranglehold of the BPs 

and Shells of the world. But Howell made no progress, discover- 
ing that ‘his Conservative colleagues’, Thatcher included, ‘saw 
privatization and competition as two quite different things’.*° 
(Howell, in other words, actually believed the Tories’ public- 
facing profession that privatization would lead to increased 
competition, which in reality has always been based more on 
ideology than fact.)”” 

Thus the ‘oil regime’ that materialized in the North Sea in the 
1970s and 1980s was, in Harvie’s words, ‘frankly oligopolistic’;°8 
and anti-labour practices were stitched into this oligopoly model. 
The major oil companies were ‘aggressively anti-union’ from the 

outset. Workers experienced ‘disempowerment, blacklisting and 
victimization whenever they posed a challenge to the non-union 
structure of industrial relations’.°? ‘In no other sector of British 
industry’, Harvie wrote, were the unions ‘put so firmly in their 
place’. It is true that some industry workers, in key specialist 
and management roles, are well remunerated; but it is also true 
that the deeply and inherently unequal rentier wage model that 
I outlined in the Introduction — very high incomes for those who 
create or capture assets; precarious and low-paid employment for 
those who sweat them — very much persists. Employee turnover 
rates have always been high. In recent years, moreover, a number 
of significant workplace protections and conditions have been 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
123 

eroded.®! Zero-hours contracts have proliferated, pension provi- 

sion has been reduced — and the fact that UK employment law 
only applies within twelve miles of the shoreline means that 

those working further from shore can be, and sometimes are, 

paid less than the national minimum wage. 

Disinclined on principle to regulate the sector meaningfully, 

on matters of health and safety as much as labour relations, 

successive Tory administrations have in fact engaged in a series 

of deregulatory initiatives, inspired by the growing discourse of 

globalization and the associated common-sense that imposing 

regulatory 
‘burdens’ 
would 
precipitate 
capital 
flight. 
Furthermore, when the industry was required to regroup in the 

early 1990s in the aftermath of the Piper Alpha tragedy, which 

killed 167 people, its Cost Reduction Initiative for the New 

Era was a quintessentially ‘oligopolistic response’ that further 

attenuated competition — ‘generating barriers to entry; ensur- 

ing the dominance of large, existent companies; encouraging 
bureaucratic inefficiency, stifling innovation; and creating the 

conditions for possible price-fixing and cartelisation’.”* Here, 

in short, was a paradigmatic example of neoliberal-era rentier- 

ism: an offshore prototype of a monopolistic, asset-based, 
profit-maximizing economic model that, in due course, would 

also become the norm onshore. 

Had it levied the kinds of taxes that represent the norm for oil- 

and-gas fiscal regimes outside of the UK, the government clearly 
could have earned considerably more from the private-sector-led 

exploitation of the North Sea Continental Shelf than it has done 
—even if the pace of remuneration might have been slower. When 

oil prices surged after 2000, the differential between the amount 

the government earned each year in petroleum taxes and the 

amount it would have earned with tax rates comparable to those 

levied by other producing nations in the North Sea, assuming no 

change in production volumes, reached what Juan Boué calls 

‘astonishing proportions’. He estimates that, had the UK’s 

124 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

effective tax rate been the same as Norway's between 2002 and 

2012, its oil-and-gas tax receipts would have been some £111 

billion higher.” 

That said, however, it would be wrong to think that the overall 
UK tax take from the North Sea has been trifling. It could have 

been much higher, but it has nonetheless been substantial — 
approaching a cumulative £200 billion to date (see Figure 2.3). 
Comfortably the biggest tax haul in real terms was achieved in 

the 1980s, when the government received a total of £65 billion. 

In the peak years of the early-to-mid 1980s, easily the largest 
component of government revenue from oil-and-gas production 

was the Petroleum Revenue Tax.” This tax, which was based on 
the accumulated cash flow arising from individual fields and 
became payable once the latter turned positive, was introduced 
by the Labour government in 1975; but it declined in impor- 
tance from the mid 1980s as the applicable taxation rate was 
progressively reduced, and because fields given development 
consent after March 1993 were exempted. 

In the period since what we might call ‘peak oil taxation’ — that 

is, the early-to-mid 1980s, when effective tax rates stood at 
around 50 per cent — a powerful narrative has coalesced concern- 
ing the government's use, and perceived abuse, of those peak tax 

receipts. Strikingly, it is a narrative rehearsed by commentators 

on both the left and the right. This narrative is essentially one of 
failure and waste, and those who rehearse it typically contrast the 
UK government’ alleged wasting of oil-and-gas tax revenue with 
the Norwegian government’s much more prudent and produc- 

tive utilization of its own equivalent hydrocarbon tax proceeds.” 
Indeed, the argument has been sufficiently stylized to become 
somewhat clichéd. It runs approximately as follows. 

The situation facing the UK and Norwegian governments 
from the late 1970s, it is said, was comparable to the one that 

had faced the Netherlands several years earlier, when it, too, 

discovered oil; and the challenge was precisely to avoid wane had 

happened there, because the Dutch experience was sufficiently 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
12D) 

deleterious to prompt the coining of a new economic term: the 
‘Dutch disease’. ‘As oil exports boomed’, Doug Sanders has writ- 

ten of the Netherlands, ‘the flood of money into the domestic 
economy inflated the currency, provoked price increases and 
destroyed exports, leading to a decade of joblessness and rising 
inequality 
.°* But while Norway, by all accounts, did successfully 

evade the Dutch disease, the UK did not. According to Sanders, 
and countless others, ‘the same thing happened, on an even 

larger scale, in Britain in the 1980s. After North Sea oil was 
discovered, the British industrial economy was virtually oblite- 

rated, leaving four million people jobless.” During Thatcher’s 

first two years in office, the UK economy actually contracted by 

2.5 per cent, while its — largely oil-less — peers were roaring ahead. 

It was manufacturing that was hit hardest: between 1979 and 

1986, the value of manufacturing as a share of UK GDP collapsed 
from over 25 per cent to under 20 per cent.” 

The principal proximate cause of this decline in the nation’s 
manufacturing base, and of the rising unemployment that 

resulted, was a diversion of investment into the North Sea. 
Between the mid 1970s and mid 1990s, the Continental Shelf 
consistently absorbed an extraordinary 10 to 20 per cent of all 
UK industrial investment.?! But the underlying cause of the 

UK’s travails, historians of the era suggest, was policy failure 

specifically in relation to North Sea oil and gas — failure of two 

main kinds. First, the Tories’ monetary policy exacerbated the 

oil-induced currency inflation that the UK experienced, like the 

Netherlands before it: ‘Between 1979 and 1981 [Thatcher] took 

a petro-pound which was already overvalued ... and forced it 

further up by policies dogmatically directed at curbing the 
money supply ... 
[This] throttled industrial investment, and 
decimated exports.” Second, the Tories failed to use their oil- 
and-gas tax revenues judiciously. Unlike the Norwegians — widely 
applauded for incorporating the lion’s share of their oil-and-gas 

tax receipts into a long-term investment fund, not to mention 
applying a much higher tax rate to hydrocarbon production in 

126. 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the first place — the UK government treated these revenues as a 

windfall to offset current expenditure. 

One major item of such expenditure was meeting the costs of 
economic restructuring, most notably in the form of unemploy- 

ment benefit. In a sense, this particular expenditure item was 
unavoidable; but others were not — not least, as Guy Lodge has 

noted, the ‘expensive tax cuts to woo middle England’ on which 
much of the oil ‘windfall’ was squandered.”* The key point that 
Lodge and others make is that, had the UK government used its 
oil-and-gas tax receipts more productively — investing for exam- 
ple in infrastructure (which, Lodge says, was ‘left to rov), public 
services (‘starved of resources’) or, most pertinently, in ‘find[ing] 
future employment for those industries deemed beyond the pale 
of the Thatcher revolution’ — then the substantial spending on 
social security payments might in fact have been avoided, just as 
it was in Norway.” But the Tories failed: ‘Exploiting the oil to 
benefit the British manufacturing economy required organiza- 
tion of a “war socialism” sort: centralized, specialized, committed 
to long-term planning and the integration of the trade unions 
into the decision-making process. This sort of planning was 
patent in Norway. But it was ruled out in Britain’, Harvie says, 
because the political compass had ‘moved sharply away from 
planning and towards a free marker’ 
.”° 

While there is much to agree with in this standard narrative, it 

suffers from two key, linked problems, which are more to do 

with perspective than substance. The first is the emphasis on 

destruction; the second, the imputation of intent, or rather lack 

of intent. In this conventional narrative, the Tories essentially 
screwed up. Voted into office in 1979 in the midst of a North Sea 
oil-and-gas boom that served up abundant tax revenues on a 

platter, Thatcher’s Conservatives mishandled the former and 
misused the latter, and thereby inadvertently eviscerated Britain’s 
industrial economy, putting 4 million workers on the dole. The 
narrative is largely a lament for what had been lost — destroyed 

— in the frittering-away of the nation’s natural-resource wealth. 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
HWA 

But what had been produced? This has become somewhat lost in 

the mists — which is a pity, because what the oil-and-gas-induced 
transformation of the UK’s political economy produced was 
nothing less than the fundamental ingredients of the version of 

capitalism we now habitually refer to as ‘neoliberalism’. 

At this point, it is instructive to turn to the work of the politi- 

cal theorist Timothy Mitchell on what he terms ‘carbon democ- 

racy’.’° Mitchell’s general argument is that, in order to under- 

stand structural political outcomes in a society, it is necessary to 
pay close attention to the way in which, literally, that society is 
powered — in other words, to its main sources of fuel and the 
manner in which they are owned, controlled and exploited. It is 

not that fuel regimes dictate political regimes deterministically; 

but, for Mitchell, they do indelibly shape the terrain of the possi- 

ble. Political possibilities, he says, are ‘opened up or closed down 
by different ways of organising the flow and concentration of 

energy. There is, he claims, a particularly intimate historical rela- 

tionship between hydrocarbon-based energy systems, on the one 

hand, and democratic political systems, on the other. ‘Fossil 

fuels’, he writes, ‘helped create both the possibility of modern 
democracy and its limits’.”” Hence: ‘carbon democracy’. 

It is not only different -political possibilities that different 

forms of energy, and different ways of organizing their use, open 

up or close down. They also open up or close down different 

political-economic possibilities. The UK in the early 1980s stands 

as a case in point. What materialized there was not carbon 

democracy, but rather a carboniferous iteration of that which, on 
Wendy Brown’s reading, is antithetical to democracy: that is, 

neoliberalism.”® Let us briefly explore this ‘carbon neoliberalism’, 

as I will call it, and the main lineaments of its historical 

development. 

Thatcher's Tories, it should be recalled, came to power in 1979 

against the immediate backdrop of ‘radicalization of the trade 

union movement, the cycle of rising expectations in wages and 

the Leftward shift of the Labour Party’.” If David Harvey is right 

128 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

that neoliberalism is chiefly about the restoration of the power of 

the capitalist class — and the evidence that he is indeed right 
grows stronger by the year — then the conditions prevailing in 

late-1970s Britain were about as unfavourable to neoliberalism’s 
emergence as it is possible to imagine.*? Half a decade later, 

however, the political-economic landscape had been thoroughly 
transformed, and in a way that was singularly productive for 

capital and its political sponsors in the Tory party. The working 

class had been brutalized and immiserated, and was ripe for the 

type of exploitation that would have been impossible in the 

1970s, but which has since become a neoliberal hallmark.

Ordinarily, perhaps, one might have expected immiseration 

on the scale that occurred in early-1980s Britain to incite wide- 
spread social unrest — maybe even revolution; but this did not 
happen. A significant part of the reason is that the North Sea tax 

receipts came to Thatcher's rescue. They allowed the government 

to meet the substantial rise in social-security costs that resulted 
from the industrial dislocation that mismanagement of the oil- 
and-gas boom had itself effected. Figure 2.4 illustrates those 
rising costs: between 1980 and 1987 (by which time the nation’s 

CARBON NEOLIBERALISM 
NAY 

transformation was largely complete, Thatcher had achieved her 

third consecutive general election victory, and the taps could be 

safely turned off), the UK state’s benefit expenditure increased 

strongly, both in real terms and as a proportion of Total Managed 
Expenditure, though somewhat less strongly as a percentage of 
GDP. The North Sea really did bail the Thatcher administration 

out — proving, in the words of one Tony Blair, ‘utterly essential to 
Mrs ‘Thatcher's electoral success’ in 1983 and 1987.*' As Terry 
Brotherstone has since noted, the social safety net afforded by oil 
money enabled ‘Thatcher to ‘ride out the crises generated by the 
economic policies of her early years’.*? 

There was a neat if tragic symmetry to allthis. The North Sea 
boom was both a cause of and solution to the problem of indus- 

trial decline. Needless to say, ‘solution’ is in reality too strong a 
word for what was actually achieved with the tax income; it was a 

mere sticking plaster. Indeed, even the metaphor of patching up 

is itself inadequate. The UK’s body politic had not suffered an 

injury or succumbed to a disease that might be ameliorated in 

time. Rather, it had undergone what Charles Woolfson and his 

colleagues later described as ‘radical surgery’ of a kind that ‘perma- 

nently [changed] the balance of forces’ between capital and labour. 

Insofar as this surgery would probably have failed in the absence 
of the oil-tax safety net — the body politic simply would not have 

tolerated its new configuration — those tax proceeds made the 

surgery feasible.** ‘Oil revenues’, notes Brotherstone, ‘helped 

make Thatcherite neoliberalism possible’.™ 

There was, of course, an additional, equally tragic symmetry 

involved. It was not just in manufacturing that large numbers of 

jobs were lost; hundreds of thousands of coalminers also lost 

their jobs in the 1980s. As well as helping the UK government to 

weather the storm of manufacturing industry dislocation, the 
development of the North Sea oil and gas fields helped it to end 

the country’s longstanding reliance on domestically-mined coal 

for electricity generation.®° One type of hydrocarbon essentially 

took the place of another; but the extraction and marketization 

130 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of these hydrocarbons were associated with radically different 

political economies. The UK’s emergent oil and gas sector, as we 
have seen, was a neoliberal prototype characterized by large, 

oligopolistic private capital and fragmented, non-unionized 

labour. The dying coal sector was its diametric opposite — the 
seedbed of Thatcher's ‘enemy within’, the once-mighty miners’ 
union, which was precisely why Thatcher was determined to 

obliterate it.8° If the Thatcherite neoliberalism that the UK’s oil 
and gas revenues helped to make possible was a form of carbon 

neoliberalism, what it supplanted — in the form of the coal- 
powered manufacturing nation — was arguably a form of carbon 
social-democracy. 

We will learn much more about post-1970s UK neoliberalism 

in the following chapters. But it is clear enough that neoliberal- 

ism, as it developed in the UK in the 1980s and thereafter, was 
neoliberalism of an explicitly rentierist variety. That is what the 
North Sea misadventure precipitated and buttressed: a radical 

national neoliberal rentier regime, with finance — the epitome of 

a minority rentier establishment earning rents from an enfeebled 
and indebted majority working class — installed by Thatcher at 

its beating heart. There was more than a hint of symbolism in the 

first North Sea oil coming ashore in the south-east. The road 
from the Medway to the City, from big oil to the Big Bang, is a 
short one, and it extended on into other rentier spheres. The 
concentration of a wide swathe of rent-generating assets — from 
radio spectrum to intellectual property and land — in a small 
number of privileged, private hands, which rapidly gathered pace 
in the 1980s and 1990s, would have been inconceivable before 
the radical surgery on the body politic overseen by Thatcher. Oil 
and gas in the UK, in short, provided much more than just a 
model or prototype for the wider rentier economy that has subse- 
quently emerged in the country — their effect was to enable it. 

Was this mere happenstance — 
the inadvertent outcome 

posited by the standard narrative of events? It seems unlikely. 
One does not need to be a conspiracy theorist to believe that the
