HSI 

devastation not only of coalmining country but also of the 
manufacturing sector— the other traditional heartland of Britain’s 
unions — and the mass unemployment it seeded were precisely 
what the Tories intended would result from the oil-and-gas boom 
and their (mis)management of it. To be sure, ‘some sections of 

industry’, and thus of capital, would suffer, as Woolfson and his 
colleagues noted. But the Thatcher government presumably 

considered this a price worth paying, these localized travails 
being ‘temporary difficulties 
. 
. 
. of little significance besides the 
long-term gains for British capital as a whole’.*’ ‘The sectors in 
question would take one for the team, as it were. 

Indeed, Brotherstone argues that the monumental shifting of 

the balance between capital and labour that occurred in early- 
1980s Britain was exactly what the then energy minister, later 

chancellor of the exchequer, Nigel Lawson was referring to when 

he claimed in a 1982 speech that North Sea oil had arrived on 

the scene when it was of ‘unprecedented value and strategic 

importance’.** It was, in other words, no mere accident that 

rising unemployment costs in that period were more or less 
matched by rising government revenues from hydrocarbon taxa- 

tion.®’ Anticipation of the latter, suggests Brotherstone, had been 

crucial to the strategy of actively fomenting the former. The 
North Sea was both breeding ground and operating theatre, 

then, for the ‘massive “market clearing” operation’ planned and 
executed by Tory strategists: “Ihe oil money would provide the 

safety net while [the government] applied the shock therapy of 

mass unemployment.”° What ensued was not failure; it was 

resounding, calculated success. Laissez-faire, and everything that 

went with it, was, as Karl Polanyi famously insisted, planned — 

and in the UK, natural-resource rentierism underwrote the Tory 

blueprint.” 

In recent years, of course, there has been increasing talk of a new 

threat to the business of natural-resource rentiers — and especially 

to those, like the UK’s leading protagonists, for whom mineral 

132 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

fuels represent a significant source of rents. The threat of climate 
change represents a very different type of threat from those 
mentioned so far. It does not threaten to impair the resource 

itself, or a company’s ability to access and extract it safely, as a 

natural disaster might. Nor does climate change threaten primar- 

ily to cut a company’s share of the rent generated by the resource 

asset, as a tax-hungry host government might (although a more 
expansive fiscal regime for hydrocarbons might well be one state 
approach to addressing climate change). 

Rather, the principal, almost existential threat to hydrocarbon 

rents posed by climate change is that it will choke consumption, 
most obviously through state regulation designed to help keep 

fossil fuels in the ground, rendering hydrocarbon assets ‘stranded’ 

and valueless. As discussion of this threat has expanded, talk of 
‘peak oil’ (the idea that the world might run out of quality oil 
reserves) has increasingly been replaced by talk of ‘peak demand’. 

‘To date, the response of the oil-and-gas majors to this perceived 

threat has been the classic response of the rentier, which is to 

defend to the hilt the asset and its continuing ability to generate 

rents. ‘They have done this privately by lobbying governments not 

to take the types of action that would make the theory of peak 
demand come true;” and they have done it publicly by essentially 
denying that the threat exists. For many years, this meant — at 

least in public — denial of climate change itself? But beyond the 
point at which it became essentially impossible to continue to 
peddle this anti-scientific line, the discourse has shifted to denial 
that climate change meaningfully threatens the value of oil and 
gas reserves. Yes, climate change is real, oil and gas companies 
have said, but our assets are not threatened, because we will have 
developed them long before any substantive changes in the land- 
scape of energy demand resulting from climate change have taken 
effect; if assets do become stranded, they will not be ours. Both 
BP and Shell explicitly make this argument.” This, once again, is 
the performativity of reserves and reserve values in action,

CHAPTER THREE 

Evergreen: Intellectual Property Rents 

~ 

What have been the most successful industry sectors in the UK 

in recent times? In 2010, in a report commissioned by the 
governments Department for Business, Innovation and Skills, 
Nicholas Crafts, the doyen of British economic historians, 
hazarded an answer. In stark contrast to textiles, which had been 

‘the pre-eminent British success story of the Industrial Revolution’ 

but had suffered an extended decline in the second half of the 
twentieth century, Crafts identified four especially buoyant areas 

of the UK economy today. One, financial services, we have 

encountered and examined already (Chapter 1) — although the 

irony of naming financial services as a ‘successful’ sector, in 2010 

of all years, appeared lost on Crafts. The other three were aero- 

space, pharmaceuticals and the creative industries. ' 

As well as naming these four success stories, Crafts also offered 
some thoughts on the reasons for their success: 

The most obvious common factor in success is the impor- 

tance of human capital both in terms of the factor intensities 

of the sectors and the availability of the relevant expertise in 

the UK. Aerospace, pharmaceuticals, financial services, and 

creative industries all can be described as intensive in the use 

of high-skilled labour. By contrast, textiles is a low-skilled 

138 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

sector and therefore much more vulnerable to low-wage 

competition.’ 

The UK is successful in these industry sectors, Crafts opined, 

because each one relies disproportionately on skilled workers, 
and this is where the UK has competitive advantage over its 

international peers. It is rich in all-important ‘human capital’. 

In this chapter I provide a very different set of explanations — 
emphasizing a very different type of ‘capital’ — for the undoubted 
importance to the contemporary UK economy of sectors such as 

aerospace, pharmaceuticals, and the creative industries (financial 

services are not my concern here). Perhaps all three are indeed 

intensive in their use of high-skilled labour. But all three are also 
highly intensive in their use of something else — not human capi- 

tal, but intellectual capital or property, such as patents (ubiqui- 

tous in aerospace and pharmaceuticals) and copyright (funda- 
mental to the creative industries). During the neoliberal era, the 
UK has become an unusually accommodating milieu for the 
creation, protection and economic exploitation of intellectual 
property. Moreover, the revenues earned by the corporate owners 
of intellectual property are not just any type of revenues. Rather, 
like the revenues earned by the UK’s financial services compa- 
nies, they are very clearly rents. 

Many of the most valuable assets in contemporary capitalism are 

not physical assets such as land and non-land natural resources, 

but instead intangible creations of the mind or intellect. Most 

creations of the mind, of course, are not ‘assets’ in the sense used 

in this book — nobody owns the concept of love or the knowl- 
edge of how to boil an egg. But some creations of the mind are 
indeed owned, insofar as the law recognizes and polices exclusive 
property rights over them. This is the terrain of so-called ‘intel- 
lectual property’ — a term used to refer both to the intellectual 

creation in question and to the property rights attached ea it, 
which serve to make it a proprietary asset. 

EVERGREEN 
139 

The most common examples of intellectual property (IP) 

rights are patents, trademarks, designs and copyright. A patent 

gives ownership of a product or process that a company or indi- 

vidual has invented; a trademark gives ownership of a product 

or service identifier, such as a brand name; a registered design, 

similar to a trademark, gives ownership of a product’s physical 
appearance (including its shape, configuration and ornamenta- 

tion), which is obviously another type of product identifier; and 
copyright gives ownership of an original creative work, such as 

a song. 

Why, in capitalist societies such as the UK, do IP rights and 

the laws that safeguard them exist? Policymakers and scholars 

have offered a range of justifications, of which the most commonly 
invoked is a utilitarian economic one. IP rights, say advocates, 

increase overall social utility because they stimulate investment 

and innovation.’ The key premise here is that if IP rights did nor 

exist, novel products, processes, designs, works of authorship 
and so forth would be less likely to be produced in the first place 

because their creators could not be sure of controlling them and 

profiting from their commercialization: others could freely repli- 

cate the product, adopt the identifier, or copy the creative work. 
Providing an exclusive property right ensures that the creations 

to which such rights are attached actually get created. As Keith 
Maskus glosses the argument, an absence of IP rights or ‘an 

excessively weak system could reduce innovation by failing to 

provide an adequate return on investment .4 

Whatever the rationale for IP rights, their crucial effect is to 

fashion monopoly powers for their owners. This has long been 
recognized as being the case for patents and copyright, in particu- 

lar. Thus, Edward Chamberlin, developer of the theory of 

monopolistic competition, was in a position in 1933 to write 

that patents ‘are instances where the principles of monopoly 

value are true without qualification . 
. 
. It is the same with copy- 

rights. Copyrighted 
books, 
periodicals, 
pictures,

compositions, are monopolies. 2

There had been more debate about trademarks and designs. As 

Daniel McClure would later note, things were arguably ‘less 

clear-cut’ with trademarks, since, although competitors could 

not use ‘similar marks’ or other ‘identifying symbols’, they could 
produce similar products® — generic cola drinks, for example. But 
Chamberlin essentially buried this debate, arguing that ‘the 

protection of trade-marks from infringement 
. 
. 
. is the protec- 

tion of monopoly’, inasmuch as the trademark ‘stands for a 

certain quality, a certain product, not a certain producer, and to 
permit only one producer to use the name is to grant him a 
monopoly of this product’.’? Today, in any event, economists 

typically view IP rights in general as ‘legal instruments that create 

monopolies’.’ Indeed, those critical of such rights use 
this 
monopoly quality as a stick to beat them with. Michele Boldrin 

and David Levine, for example, suggest that ‘what is commonly 

called intellectual property might be better called “intellectual 
monopoly”’.’ 

Chamberlin provided one further vital insight when it came 

to IP. Whether or not IP rights fuelled innovation (Chamberlin 

was ambivalent about this), there was one thing that, in his view, 

they undoubtedly did underpin: 
profit. More exactly, the 
monopoly power inherent in IP rights underpinned what he 
described as ‘sustained monopoly profits’. Cataloguing a series of 

court decisions in which companies had been successfully sued 

for infringing competitors’ trademarks — ‘“Gold Dust” was held 
infringed by “Gold Drop,” “Lacto-Peptine” by “Lactopepsine,” 
“Uneeda” by “Iwanta,” etc.’ — Chamberlin excoriated fellow 
economists for their belief that the law was hereby preserving 
competition. Nonsense, he said — and his logic was ironclad: 

When one producer copies the name, symbol, package, or 
product of another, the result is goods more nearly standard- 

ized, and, if the imitator is successful, a reduction in the profits 

of his rival. These profits (in so far as they exceed the necessary 
minimum) are . 
. 
. due solely to monopoly elements. For if the 

EVERGREEN 
14] 

goods were perfectly standardized, buyers would have no basis 

for discrimination; one producer could secure no larger volume 

of sales than another and hence no larger profits . 
. 
. [The prof- 

its] are due to the dissimilarity, not the similarity, of the goods, 

hence to the monopolistic, not the competitive, elements. 

Unlike the temporary ‘excess’ profits a producer might earn by 

dint, for example, ‘of his advantage in being first in the field’, the 
monopoly profits accruing specifically to the IP owner are endur- 

ing — lasting as long as the IP protections remain in place — 
because they are incapable of being competed away: ‘the law 

prevents it’.'° 

Derived from the control of scarce assets and under conditions 

of limited or no competition, the monopoly profits enjoyed by 
Chamberlin’s IP owner and preserved by IP laws are, of course, a 

specific example of what I have referred to as rents. Such IP rents 

can take two main forms. The first is where the owner itself 

exploits the IP — an example would be a drug company manufac- 

turing and selling one of its own patented medications. ‘The 
second type of rent arises where the owner licenses the IP to a 

third party, enabling the latter to do something that, without the 

licence, would constitute an infringement of the owner's prop- 

erty rights. Here, the rent generally takes the form of a royalty or 

fee paid by the licensee. One important example is the licensing 
and third-party use of proprietary software protected by copy- 

right of the source code, and sometimes also by patents. (To 

recognize this second model of IP rentierism is to appreciate that 

Microsoft is probably the most prolific rentier in capitalist 

history.) Another is the licensing of IP to restaurant franchisees 

by companies such as McDonald's and Subway. A brief consid- 

eration of this latter example will help to clarify the key dynam- 

ics of the IP rentier business. 

If you were to ask one hundred people what the primary busi- 

ness of McDonald’s is, ninety-nine would doubtless say some- 

thing along the lines of ‘fast-food production and retail’. But this 

142 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

is simply not the case. McDonald’s is chiefly a rentier. Worldwide, 

approximately 93 per cent of McDonald’s restaurant businesses 

are owned and operated by franchisees — independent individu- 

als or companies — rather than by McDonald’s Corporation itself. 

This begs the question: if those franchised restaurants are inde- 

pendent of McDonald’s as a corporate entity, how does the latter 
make money from them? 

‘The answer is by licensing its intellectual property: letting its 

franchisees use its brand name, its design features (the famous 
Golden Arches, for example), its restaurant layout templates, its 

menus, its recipes — in short, its intellectual assets. For the privi- 

lege, McDonald’s franchisees hand over an initial franchise fee 

(giving them franchise rights for a typical term of twenty years) 
plus an ongoing royalty calculated as a percentage of net sales 

(gross sales minus any local sales tax), which in the UK case is 
currently set at 9.5 per cent, comprising a 5 per cent ‘service fee’ 
and a 4.5 per cent contribution 
to company advertising. 
Significantly, because McDonald’s restaurant buildings are ordi- 
narily owned by McDonald’s itself rather than by franchisees, the 
latter are usually tenants, and must also therefore pay rent on 
their premises. This is significant because, in 2018, real estate 
rents paid by McDonald’s franchisees worldwide, totalling $7.1 
billion, were nearly double their royalty payments of $3.9 billion." 
Thus, if McDonald’s is an IP rentier, which it clearly is, it is also, 
unbeknown to most observers, a major land rentier (Chapter 7). 

McDonald’s is a heavyweight franchise-based IP rentier in the 
UK, but in terms of franchisee numbers it is not the largest. That 
honour goes to Subway. In fact, the UK is a somewhat anoma- 

lous territory for McDonald’s: while 93 per cent of its restaurants 
worldwide are franchises (and the company’s stated strategic goal 

— ‘to help optimize overall performance’ — is to be approximately 

95 per cent franchised in the long term, which tells you every- 
thing you need to know about the relative profitability.of the 

respective rentier and own-and-operate business models), only 
around half of its roughly 1,200 UK restaurants are franchised, 

EVERGREEN 
143 

This means that it lags far behind Subway, which has around 
2,500 current franchised UK restaurants, whose operators pay 

significantly higher royalties than their McDonald’s counter- 

parts: 12.5 per cent of net sales, split between an 8 per cent 

service fee and the same 4.5 per cent contribution to advertising 

— plus rent. 

Since average sales are substantially lower at Subway than at 
McDonald’s restaurants, Subway may not be a bigger IP rentier 

in the UK than its rival; but it is certainly purer. Every single one 

of its restaurants is franchised; Subway itself, which remains 

privately owned, does not get its hands dirty operating a single 

one. Economic rent, not food, is Subway’s business: it owns and 

constantly fine-tunes an asset in the form of the concept of the 
Subway restaurant, and what such a restaurant should look and 

feel like and offer to its customers; and it sells privileged access to 

that concept to those who want to mobilize it. 

Needless to say, IP rents are a significant feature of all sectors 

of the modern economy in which ownable creations of the mind 
—and yes, the idea of a six-inch meatball Subway” sandwich is an 
ownable intellectual creation — represent meaningful sources of 

competitive advantage. Patents figure prominently, for instance, 

in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors; trademarks are 

ubiquitous in the consumer products industry; copyright scaf- 

folds much of the entertainment and publishing sectors. And, as 

we have seen, such IP-intensive sectors are veritable bulwarks of 

the contemporary UK economic landscape. 

It is difficult to attach any exact numbers to the value of IP to the 
UK economy, however. There have been various attempts to do 

so but all the approaches used have drawbacks. Firstly, there are 

any number of studies suggesting, like Crafts, that industries in 

which IP plays a crucial role are especially significant in the UK. 

Thus, for example, a 2016 joint report by the European Patent 

Office and the EU Intellectual Property Office estimated that 

IP-intensive industries generated on average 44 per cent of

A second way of quantifying the importance of IP is by exam- 

ining industry investment trends. Here, the picture is striking. 

Figure 3.1 shows investment in intangible and tangible assets in 

the UK market sector (which excludes public sector and real 

estate) between 1990 and 2015 (although, prior to 1997, data 

are only available for 1990 and 1995). As we can see, investment 

in tangibles exceeded investment in intangibles up until the turn 
of the millennium; but from that point on the latter amount has 
been larger in every single year except 2015. The centre of gravity 
of the UK economy seems to have shifted in the direction of 

intangibles, in other words. 

ae 

It should be noted that not all intangible investment is 

protected by proprietary rights, though much of it is. The UK 

EVERGREEN 
145 

Intellectual Property Office estimates this proportion to be 

approximately half, and believes this share has been relatively 

stable over the past two decades. Again, though, this is just an 

estimate based on a series of eminently contestable assump- 

tions.'* One debatable aspect of its estimates, for example, is that 

it calculates the amount of intangible investment protected by 

the various types of IP rights in mutually exclusive terms: thus, 

of the estimated £63.5 billion of total protected 2015 invest- 

ment (out of £134 billion invested in intangibles, protected or 

unprotected), some £25.9 billion was estimated to be protected 

by copyright, £15 billion by design rights, £7.6 billion by patents, 

and £15 billion by trademarks.'” But the reality, as we shall see 

below, is that much investment in intangibles today is protected 
by overlapping IP rights. 

In theory, another way to gauge the importance of IP would 

be to examine trends in IP applications and grants. But such an 

exercise would be fraught with complexity. To begin with, it 
would have to exclude copyright. In the UK, as in much of the 

rest of the world, copyright protection is automatic (creators of 

original work do not have to apply for it, and there is no copy- 

right register); assessing trends in copyright generation is thus far 
from straightforward. Moreimportantly still, the application for 
and granting of other forms of IP occurs in ways that make it 
extremely difficult to discern trends specifically at the scale of a 

nation-state such as the UK. As will be explored in more detail 

below, IP governance is international. Briefly stated, there are 

both national and transnational IP regimes and treaties, and 

both national and transnational IP-granting institutions. These 

institutions grant IP to a range of both national and interna- 

tional IP applicants, and it is protected — through those regimes 

and treaties — at a number of different territorial levels. 

This means that examining trends in IP applications and 

grants at, say, the UK Intellectual Property Office does not neces- 

sarily reveal anything meaningful in terms of changes in the 

intensity of IP creation in the UK or by UK companies. For 

146 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

example, between 1995 and 2017, trademark applications to the 
UK Intellectual Property Office more than doubled, but design 
and patent applications were essentially flat.'° Does this mean 

the UK economy was not becoming more design- and patent- 

intensive during this period? No. Patent applications filed at the 
European Patent Office, and particularly applications designat- 

ing UK protection, had risen sharply; applications filed using the 

Patent Co-operation Treaty, which confers patent rights across 
many countries from a single filing, had also increased. In other 

words, applicants for UK patent protection were seemingly 

‘choosing to seek protection through alternate routes’, instead of 

via the UK’s own IP office.” The story appears to be similar for 

designs, not least because, since 2003, applicants to the EU 

Intellectual Property Office have been able to seek EU-wide 

protection in the shape of a Registered Community Design.

The body at number ten on the list obviously stands out, and 

merits comment: the University of Oxford. Universities and 

other research institutions play an increasingly important role in 
the production — and indeed the privatization — of economically 

valuable intellectual products and processes.'* In the UK, Oxford 
seemingly leads the way. It has had a ‘technology transfer’ office 

for more than thirty years. Now called Oxford University 
Innovation (OUI), this wholly-owned subsidiary of the univer- 

sity is a private company that files patent applications on behalf 
of the university and manages its IP portfolio, which currently 

contains more than 4,300 patents. OUI also advises the univer- 

sity’s researchers on commercializing their work, manages the 
formation of the spinout companies through which such 
commercialization is frequently effected, and, last but not least, 
manages the university's holdings in these companies. Those 

holdings are now worth well north of £150 million. 

In all this, OUI works closely with Oxford Sciences Innovation 

(OSI), which provides much of the funding to those spinout 
companies. Founded in 2015, OSI is also a private company. In 

its case, however, the University of Oxford is only a minority 

shareholder; most of its shareholders are venture capital firms 
from around the world, including Google Ventures, from whom 

collectively OSI has to date raised more than £600 million in 

seed capital. OSI has invested in approximately 70 university 

spinout companies so far, mainly in the field of medical and 

health technologies; at the time of this writing, its holdings in 

these companies were valued at over £200 million. Companies 

such as OSI and OUI, and behind them universities such as 

Oxford, are central actors in the wider commercialization of the 

UK higher education system; IP and IP rentierism is the vehicle 

through which much of that commercialization takes place.

Placing a value on IP assets, as on natural resource 
‘reserves 

(see Chapter 2), is arguably as much art as science. Nevertheless, 

for all the immateriality of the ideas being valued, the values 

150 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

themselves could scarcely be more material. For one thing, the 

value of IP is unquestionably real, not ‘fictitious’. Chamberlin’s 

words — ‘sustained monopoly profits’ — should be ringing in our 

ears at this point. Patents, after all, furnish monopoly conditions 

for as long as they provide legal protection (which is precisely 
why companies that own significant patents are obliged to 

divulge patent expiry dates to investors); the same applies in rela- 

tion to copyright. As for trademarks, once so doubted by econo- 

mists, these never expire (unless the owner forgets to renew 
them) — hence they occasion perpetual monopoly conditions 

given sufficient brand recognition and marketing support. 
Chamberlin referred to ‘the permanent profits made possible by 

trade-mark protection’, and GlaxoSmithKline, as if enacting his 

theory, today has a category of ‘Indefinite life brands’ on its 
balance sheet.?! 

On the topic of performativity, furthermore — and as in the 

case of mineral-resource reserves — IP values are also quintessen- 

tially material in the sense that they help enact real-world invest- 
ment decisions. Mutual funds and other asset managers base 

their investment choices on these balance-sheet numbers. It is 
perhaps little wonder, then, that an entire industry sector has 
sprung up around the estimation of these values. There are now 
approximately forty companies providing specialist IP valuation 

services in the UK.”” 

In short, valuations such as those shown for IP in Figure Bron 
though they may be social constructions, have obvious material

important companies, which deploy those assets and the valua- 

tions of them to shape both domestic and international econo- 

mies in profound ways.

Simultaneously, the legal strength of such protections has been 

reinforced, augmenting the ability of rentiers to monetize their 

proliferating IP assets. The upshot of these twin developments 

has been a burgeoning of IP rentierism. 

The list of specific ways in which IP developers and owners 

have thus increasingly been cossetted is a long one. Products or 

processes that in the past existed outside the ambit of IP have 

been brought within its proprietary confines, including perhaps 
most famously the genetically modified and subsequently 
patented “Harvard mouse’ used in laboratory cancer research. 

Periods of patent and copyright protection have been extended. 

Restrictions on obtaining IP rights have been swept away. Courts 

have lowered the bar at which defendants are considered to have 

infringed IP, and in parallel reduced the burden of proof of 

infringement on the plaintiff. Courts have also become more 

indulgent of IP rights from the perspective of competition law. 
Meanwhile, the range of attributes of a product or process 

considered eligible for IP protection has also been widened, 

increasing owners’ options for suing alleged infringers. Consider 

the example of patentable-pharmaceutical attributes: ‘In the 

1980s, the list of relevant drug properties was relatively limited. 

In the 1990s, the list extended protection in relation to range of 

use, methods of treatment, mechanism of action, packaging, 

delivery profiles, dosing route, regimen and range, drug combi- 

nations, screening and analytical methods, drug chirality, biolog- 

ical targets and field of use.’”° 

This widening and strengthening of IP rights has not been 
unique to the UK. As we have seen, IP protection and its govern- 

ance are thoroughly internationalized phenomena; while many 

national IP authorities have bolstered their respective IP edifices, 

transnational authorities have done likewise. Between the mid 

1970s and the late 1990s, the EU, through the issuing of a series 

of directives, substantially toughened and expanded the range of

the global level, most 
notably through the World Trade 
Organization (WTO) and its 1994 Trade Related Aspects of 

Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) agreement, which tight- 

ened protections, weakened existing exceptions and limitations, 

and extended rights to new subject-matter categories.” 

Indeed, UK rules have largely followed what has happened 

elsewhere. For example, the UK’s 1977 Patents Act reflected the

Valbona Muzaka has described TRIPS as the most significant IP 
agreement ever, ‘as it signals the moment in time when the vast 
majority of states agreed to adopt roughly similar and rather high 
IP protection and enforcement standards, despite the very differ- 
ent economic and _ socio-legal-political conditions prevailing 
within them’.’® 

In two vital respects, however, there is a specifically UK dimen- 

sion to this history. In fleshing them out, it will become clear 
both why the UK is a pivotal territory in the story of the rise of 
IP rentierism more widely, and, no less importantly, why IP rent- 

ierism has been a pivotal element of the story of the development 

of the UK economy over recent decades. 

‘The first specifically UK dimension concerns the country’s 
own role in the formulation and ratification of those transna- 

tional (EU and WTO) IP rules and agreements that the UK itself 
has subsequently adopted or observed. The UK was no hapless 

bystander, watching impotently from the sidelines as foreign 

EVERGREEN 
fia\s} 

bureaucrats devised new, expansionist IP protections that it then 
had no choice but to implement. Rather, the UK helped author 
and drive the endorsement of many of these transnational rules 
and agreements. And it did so for good reason: it answered an 

obvious economic interest of the country — or, more exactly, of 

its corporate sector. Certainly, the UK’s most IP-intensive indus- 

tries, such as aerospace, biotechnology, consumer goods, phar- 

maceuticals and the creative industries, were not as prominent in 

the 1980s and early 1990s as they are today; but neither were 
they insignificant. Many UK companies had a huge amount to 

gain from stronger IP protection both at home and abroad, and 

they were thus vigorous advocates for transriational agreements 

to support precisely such stronger protection, as well as for 

national rules serving the same purpose at home. 

To these ends, the UK’s IP lobby has long relied upon arguments 

revolving around concepts of ‘competitiveness’. It has insisted to 

policymakers that the success and competitiveness of the economy 

— UK or European, depending on the audience — is contingent on 

the success of its most IP-intensive industries and firms, and that 

the success of these depends in turn on strong IP protection. As 
Muzaka remarks, this logic ‘can be roughly stated as “higher IP 

protection = more innovation = improved competitiveness” ’.”” 

The UK IP lobby is widely recognized to be exceptionally 

strong. In his 2011 
review of the UK's intellectual property frame- 

work (commissioned by the then prime minister, David Cameron), 

Ian Hargreaves, 
a professor of digital economy, noted that 

IP-intensive industries contained ‘some of the most skilful and 

influential lobbyists on the UK political scene’. Sir Robin Jacob, 

professor of intellectual property law, when asked the following 

year by the House of Commons Business, Innovation and Skills 

Committee to comment on Hargreaves’ view, concurred.”! 

Arguably the strongest lobby group within the UK's IP firma- 
ment is the pharmaceutical lobby. The Association of the British 

Pharmaceutical Industry (ABPI) has a permanent lobby — the 

Intellectual Property Committee — dedicated specifically to IP

The second specifically UK dimension to the story of the 

strengthening and widening of IP rights in recent decades 

concerns their enforcement. It was all very well for the UK, EU 
and WTO to put in place new legislation, guidelines and treaties 

containing expanded IP protections; but if the latter were not 

effectively administered by the bodies responsible for enforce- 

ment, then it would all ultimately be for nothing. Laws are 

subject to courts’ interpretation, and treaty obligations to regula- 

tory implementation. Not for nothing, for example, does the 
WTO have a formal dispute-settlement mechanism standing by 

to sanction member governments that fail to apply properly the 

trade rules — including TRIPS — to which WTO membership 

implies adherence. Sometimes, members do not toe the line. 
Enforcement is uneven. 

But enforcement is another area in which the UK has long 

been in the vanguard. Moreover, UK courts have over time aggres- 

sively expanded their claims to jurisdictional reach in relation to 

IP law, thus enlarging the sphere of practical influence of their 

interpretations of how, when and where IP protections should 
and (less commonly) should not be enforced. For all the range of 

territorial levels on which IP is issued and administered, the 
enforcement of IP rights remains mostly confined within the 

nation-state. Consider the instructive example of ‘European’ 

patents. Although ‘granted under the European Patent Convention 
by the European Patent Office’, a European patent ‘is, in fact, a 
bundle of national patents, registered in each country of designa- 

tion, with each designation taking a life of its own after grant. 

That means that European patents must, generally, be enforced 

(or invalidated) nationally.“ 

What is true of ‘European’ patents is largely true of IP more 

generally. Nation-states have jurisdiction over nationally circum- 

scribed and registered rights: the UK, for instance, over UK 

copyright, UK patents, and UK trademarks and designs. 

Historically, moreover, the prevailing legal perception has been 

that IP registered in one country cannot be infringed by acts 

158 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

occurring in another. National courts have therefore not consid- 

ered justiciable either claims for overseas infringement of domes- 

tic IP or claims for infringement (wherever the alleged infringe- 
ment takes place) of overseas-registered IP.4” The UK courts, 

however, have led the way in beginning to break down this tradi- 

tional logic of rigid geo-legal IP scaffolding. In the process, the 
UK’s own enforcement norms have been ever more widely 

imposed. There have been two main vectors of encroachment. 

On the one hand, the presumption that an act performed over- 

seas will not amount to an infringement of UK IP has come under 

challenge — most notoriously in Menashe Business Mercantile Ltd 

v William Hill Organization Ltd (2002). The latter company (the 
Uk-based claimant) alleged that the former had infringed its UK 

software patent by supplying the software unlicensed to UK-based 

online gaming customers. Menashe’s domicile in Antigua nomi- 
nally put it beyond the reach of UK courts — as did the fact that 
bets were placed via the host server, also located in Antigua. But 
the UK Court of Appeal begged to differ: even though the server 
was in Antigua, the patented invention was, it said, put ‘into 
effect’ in the UK because the user was the punter, and the UK was 
where the user was based. The court ruled against Menashe. ‘Since 
the UK Court of Appeal judgment in Menashe v William Hill’, 
the attorney John Leeming wrote in 2017, ‘it has not been safe to 
assume that infringement of a patent claim including a processor 
or a processing step can be avoided by performing the processing 
on a server outside the UK’. 

Meanwhile, UK courts have also undermined the longstanding 

perception that claims for infringement of overseas IP are not 

justiciable in the courts of England and Wales. Here the most 

celebrated case is that of Lucasfilm Ltd v Ainsworth (2011). 
Ainsworth, the claimant, alleged that Lucasfilm Ltd, a UK-based 
prop-maker, had infringed its copyright by producing and selling 
without consent replicas of storm-trooper helmets used 
in the 

Star Wars films. Again, precedent seemed to weigh against the 
claimant, insofar as its copyright was US-based. In this case the 

EVERGREEN 
ipo 

UK Court of Appeal stuck with precedent, judging that it did not 

have jurisdiction to decide the claim. But the UK Supreme Court, 

on appeal, disagreed: the case was indeed justiciable in the UK, it 

decided, because Ainsworth operated from England. Lucasfilm’s 
copyright, in other words, may not have been under the court’s 

jurisdiction, but the defendant was. Like Menashe v William Hill, 

then, this decision has significant implications for IP enforcement 

and its shifting geographies. “Where a UK court has personal 

jurisdiction over a potential defendant and where issues of valid- 

ity of the right at issue are not put in question’, the lawyers 

Charters Macdonald-Brown and John Colbourn wrote in 2011, 

‘the UK courts now have a “green light” to exercise jurisdiction 

for infringement of overseas intellectual property rights.” 

If the new millennium has been notable for the UK courts’ 
expansion of the scope of applicability of their adjudication of IP 

rights, the 1980s and 1990s had been notable for a significant 

tightening of the enforcement norms embedded in such adjudica- 

tion. By the mid 1990s, the UK had already established a reputa- 

tion as a place where companies from around the world could do 

business safe in the knowledge that their IP rights — so long as they 
were registered locally — would be afforded forceful protection. 

In calling in 1997 for a new international system of IP protec- 

tion, for instance, Lester Thurow — who was alarmed among other 

things by spiralling rates of computer software piracy, which 

suggested to him that in some countries ‘computer makers have 

the tacit approval of local governments to violate patents and 

copyrights’ — nodded approvingly to the fact that the UK had the 

lowest estimated rate of piracy in Europe.” The UK has consoli- 

dated its reputation for stringent IP enforcement in the decades 

since, the government recently boasting: “The UK is recognised 

internationally for its world leading IP enforcement framework.” 

In Taylor Wessing’s influential Global Intellectual Property Index, 

the UK ranks as the third-strongest national IP regime (of forty- 

three that were assessed), behind only the Netherlands and 

Germany.” It does one better in the US Chamber International 

160 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

IP Index, ‘Create’, ranking second to the US, but close enough to 

it ‘that it has become clear the countries stand side-by-side as 

global leaders in IP protection and enforcement.” 

A particularly important reason for the substantial variation 

that exists between countries in the degree of protection they 

afford to IP holders concerns the varying treatment of IP under 

different national regimes of competition law. IP rights have long 
represented a thorny matter for the theory and practice of anti- 

trust. If economists consider IP rights as sources of monopoly 
power, should the law do the same? And, if so, does such monop- 

oly power warrant intervention on competition grounds, thus 

jeopardizing the harvesting of monopoly rents? 

Different countries, and their respective competition authori- 

ties, have offered different answers to these questions at different 

times, with direct consequences for levels of de facto IP protec- 

tion.“ The more relaxed the attitude towards monopoly, the 

better, in general, for IP owners. Notably, 1994’s TRIPS agree- 
ment, despite calling for national competition policies to be 
consistent with the principles of IP protection that it specified (a 
stipulation read by Hans Ullrich as ‘a caveat against an excessive 
exercise of competition policy’), nonetheless reserved IP-related 
competition policy to sovereign national determination.’ Even 
in the brave new world of globalized — and putatively harmo- 
nized — IP protection, in other words, there would remain lati- 
tude for competition authorities to shape significant national 
differences in IP enforcement outcomes. 

In the postwar decades, the UK’s competition authorities had 

generally taken a dim view of IP rights, considering them to be 
monopolistic and injurious to competition, which they sought 
where possible to encourage.* During the 1980s and 1990s, 

however, as IP became increasingly important to UK ple, and 

successive domestic governments legislated stronger and wider 

IP rights, domestic competition policy progressively effected a 

volte-face. This is perhaps unsurprising: there were few places 
where the tentacles of the IP lobby did not reach; and it would 

EVERGREEN 
161 

have been odd if the government had fortified IP rights with one 
hand while wielding a contrarily inclined competition policy 

with the other. By the mid-to-late 1990s, at any rate, the UK’s 
competition authorities no longer considered that the ownership 
and use of IP rights automatically created monopoly conditions. 
More strikingly still, in the rare circumstances where monopoly 
was deemed to be present, IP rights were nevertheless usually 
viewed as pro- rather than anti-competitive.” Adopting this 
exceptionally benign view of IP rights, then, the UK competi- 

tion authorities now seldom interfered with their commercial 

exploitation or their legal enforcement. The UK submission to a 
1997 OECD roundtable on competition issues relating to IP 

rights caught the prevailing mood: 

IP rights are designed to be exploited. Parliament (and, in the 

case of copyright, international convention) has granted these 

rights to companies as a reward for their innovation and crea- 

tivity, and in order to provide an incentive for future innova- 

tion and creativity by other firms. The whole point of creating 

IP rights is to allow firms to exploit that asset.” 

In short, the UK’s latter-day renown for strict enforcement of IP 

rights is based partly on the distinctly hands-off approach to 

IP practised by its competition policy regulators. 

Although the UK had proved itself, by the late 1990s, to be a 

consistently assiduous enforcer of IP rights, the nation’s leading 

IP rentiers remained far from satisfied. To understand why, it is 

essential to pause momentarily to consider the geography of the 

rents they earn. Rents derived from finance, natural resources 

and IP are grouped together in the first three chapters of this 

book not only because of their particular importance for the 

UK’s biggest public companies (see Table 0.1), but also because, 

in the UK at least, these three forms of rentierism share a key 
dynamic that is not shared by any of the types of rentierism 

162 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

explored in later chapters — namely, the earning of a significant 

(and in the cases of many companies, dominant) share of income 

overseas. Figure 3.4 quantifies this phenomenon as it pertains 

specifically to IP, showing the small share of revenue derived by a 

selection of leading UK rentiers from the domestic market.

The one exception among the rentiers shown in Figure 3.4 is 

BT’ Group, which is not heavily reliant on international markets. 

As we have seen, however, BT is not primarily an IP rentier; its 

rents are predominantly infrastructure rents, which have a consid- 
erably greater domestic concentration. Perhaps the quintessential 
export-oriented sector among the UK’s IP-intensive industries is 

the creative industries (value of 2015 exports: £21 billion), to 
which the government has long provided direct support 
for inter- 
nationalization, most recently through the establishment of a 
Creative Industries Trade and Investment Board.*® Quintessential 
assets created and exploited internationally by this sector include 
Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? — an entertainment format 
produced by the UK production company Celador and eventu- 
ally licensed to over 150 countries, with producers in each terri- 
tory paying royalty rents to the format (IP) owner.™ 

The heavy weighting of the business of UK IP rentiers towards 

international markets — which to some extent also applies to IP? 

rentiers based in other rich nations, including the US — has led 

EVERGREEN 
163 

historically to accusations of what Richard Stern once called 

‘intellectual property imperialism’. His chosen example, from 
what feels like a bygone age, was floppy-disk patents, and concerns 

in the mid 1990s about the ‘likely effect of such patents on the 

legal cultures and economic growth of developing countries on 
which they might be foisted’.°' As Hector MacQueen observed at 

around the same time, the international strengthening of IP then 
underway disproportionately served Western economic interests, 

since it was Western rather than non-Western economies that 
were increasingly based on ‘the production of ideas and their 

expression in various forms, whether technical or cultural’. 

It was, MacQueen said, ‘unsurprising’ that Western-led attempts 

to ensure protection of largely Western IP through global frame- 

works such as TRIPS met with resistance in the rest of the world, 
‘which sees yet another device by which the developed world seeks 

to maintain the technology, education and culture gaps and to 

control information transfer on its own terms’.° Even the law firm 

Taylor Wessing, an active champion of IP enforcement, concedes 

that there is — or, at least, was — a degree of truth to the unflattering 

picture of IP as ‘a tool of rich nations to oppress poorer nations, 

with the imposition of the former's laws on the latter so as to stem 

flows of counterfeits and pirated goods’. After all, the goods in 

question are not all frivolities like Millionaire. Where the Western 

products to which IP protections legally apply are medicines that 

can mean the difference between life and death, the issues are 

deadly serious. Often, the enforcement of Western IP ‘rights’ has 

led to the unaffordability of patented drugs where they are needed 

most. Joseph Stiglitz relates a famous example: “When the South 

African government attempted to amend its laws in 1997 to avail 

itself of affordable generic medicines for the treatment of HIV/ 

Aids, the full legal might of the global pharmaceutical industry 

bore down on the country, delaying implementation and extract- 

ing a high human cost’. 

In any event, the reason why the UK’s leading IP rentiers 
remained dissatisfied in the late 1990s was that, despite the UK’s 

164 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

chart-topping performance in terms of domestic enforcement of 

IP rights, the enforcement of those companies’ rights overseas — 

that is to say, in the markets that provide the vast bulk of their 
customer demand — was widely considered substandard. Menashe 

v William Hill was yet to come — and, in any event, it pertained 
only to the alleged infringement overseas of IP registered in the 
UK. A much bigger issue was — and remains — the enforcement 

overseas of IP that UK companies had registered with overseas IP 

offices, or endeavoured to do so. In this regard, the WTO 
dispute-settlement system had been hearing a steady stream of 

complaints initiated by the European Community or the United 

States, or both, under the TRIPS agreement, on behalf of Western 
companies that claimed their rights had been infringed.“ In the 
UK, a particularly vehement complainant was the BIA, which, 
through its Intellectual Property Advisory Committee, would 

claim in 2003 that in Asia, with the exception of Japan and 
Singapore, ‘copying and counterfeiting are endemic’, and that 
even where ‘enforcement provisions are in place, there is little 
business appreciation of the positive role of IP in a modern econ- 
omy and of the need to respect and enforce IP rights’.°” 

In his 2006 review of the IP system for the Blair government 

in the UK, Andrew Gowers picked up on such misgivings: ‘It is 
important that Governments and patent offices in developing 

countries are aware of the potential benefits available to them 
within the current international IP framework.’ The colonialist 

tone — they dont know whats good for them — was mirrored bya 

colonialist impulse. While recognizing that there was a limited 
amount that the UK government — or the UK courts — could 
do to enforce IP protection overseas, Gowers did not [shy] 
away from making recommendations with European or broader 
international import when they seemed necessary’. His recom- 
mendations included, in the short term, provision of ‘technical 
assistance to aid developing countries [especially in Aftica] to 
take a more strategic approach to IP’ — those countries being 
deemed unstrategic as well as unaware — and, in the longer 

EVERGREEN 
165 

term, ‘to enable the least developed countries to “strengthen” 
IPepimes 
°° 
The government was listening. In fact, it had not been wholly 

inactive before then; as Gowers admitted, the UK had already 

‘forged strong relationships with foreign patent offices, for example 

in China, to assist them with application procedures and enforce- 
ment policies’, and the Intellectual Property Office already had 

‘good contacts with offices in developing countries. But there was 
much more to be done; and, though Gowers envisaged ‘further 

joint working’, the steps that the UK government subsequently 
took were essentially unilateral. Its key innovation was to establish 

in 2011 an overseas network of IP attachés through the Intellectual 
Property Office. (Given the role of colonial ‘attachés’ in the admin- 

istration of the British Empire, this had obvious colonial under- 

tones.) The fact that ‘UK businesses sometimes find it difficult to 

control the use of their IP overseas’ was the main rationale provided 

for the appointment of these attachés, who, ‘working with local IP 

rights enforcement agencies, would ‘focus on promoting and 

protecting UK business interests within host countries’.” 

The first attaché, to be based in China, was recruited in 
December 2011. India, Brazil and South East Asia then followed. 
By early 2016, the Intellectual Property Office estimated that its 

attachés had helped some 14,000 UK businesses to protect £440 

million worth of IP assets in those four key markets.”! Bill Russell, 

the head of global cooperation at the Intellectual Property Office, 

has explained that the attachés are expected to ‘influence percep- 

tions around IP in host countries’ and provide support to indi- 

vidual companies, describing this crucial ‘diplomatic’ work as 

follows: “This is an often lengthy process of building trust, mutual 

respect and understanding. 
It involves breaking down pre- 

conceived ideas that IP is only beneficial to wealthy, Western 

companies and is often enforced at the expense of local workers 

and local businesses and local economies.’”” 

An external evaluation of the attaché network published in 
2014 noted 
that UK businesses 
had found 
the network 

166 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

invaluable for the recognition and enforcement of their IP in the 

territories where the attachés had been active. The evaluators 

usefully revealed some of the details of how enforcement was 

effected on the ground in daily practice: “Businesses can access 
government officials with the attaché’s help and the attachés 

facilitate meetings with in-market officials, where businesses’ 
own actions have proved fruitless. They access higher enforce- 
ment potential than would otherwise be possible. British consu- 

lar “muscle” via governmental letters is especially valued.’ 

‘Muscle’ is an appropriate metaphor, perhaps, with which to 

square the circle on the question of how the extraction of rents by 
UK IP rentiers has been progressively expedited. As we have seen, 

muscle of a sort was pivotal to the efforts of the nation’s corporate 

IP lobby, and the policymakers it corralled to its cause, to drive 

the fortification and widening of IP protections at both national 
and supranational levels in the 1980s and 1990s. Now we know 
that, having successfully lobbied for stronger and expanded rights 
(and thus stronger and expanded assets), UK IP rentiers such as 
GlaxoSmithKline, availing themselves of a different brand of 
muscle, have also increasingly been rewarded through the 1990s 
and beyond with singularly robust enforcement of those rights — 
both at home and abroad. The UK, in short, has led the way on 
the policing as well as fashioning of a globalizing arena for IP 
rentierism that is especially hospitable to its own rentiers. 

The mechanisms for enabling the extraction of rents that I have 
examined so far in this chapter all fundamentally pertain to the 
nature of the asset exploited by the IP rentier, The range of 
phenomena and attributes capable of being constituted as an 

asset (as, that is, intellectual property) has been broadened; the 
monopoly powers vested in intellectual property have been 
strengthened; and, through improved enforcement, intellectual 

property's resilience in the face of threats to such monopoly 
powers has been augmented. Yet there are other important ways 

in which IP rentierism in the UK has been indulged, which work 

EVERGREEN 
167 

not on the asset itself but rather on the fiscal environment within 
which the asset is commercialized; they work, in other words, on 

the tax regime. These mechanisms, in contrast to those discussed 

above, have served to facilitate not the extraction of rents so 
much as their maximization. They warrant brief investigation 

because they continue to be extremely significant. 

Some of these fiscal mechanisms are targeted not at IP rents as 

such, but rather at industry sectors that happen to be IP-intensive, 

thus buttressing such rents by default rather than by design. The 

best example concerns the array of tax incentives available to oper- 

ators in the creative industries — which can be compared with the 

tax subsidies on oil-and-gas exploration, and thts with the natural- 

resource rents discussed in Chapter 2. “The UK’s suite of creative 

tax reliefs, the government recently trumpeted, ‘are among the 

most competitive in the world.‘ It was not wrong. At the time of 

writing, there are seven main categories of creative industry tax 

relief available. They are listed in Table 3.1, together with their 

date of introduction, the number of claims up to July 2018, and

Other fiscal mechanisms, meanwhile, are targeted at IP rents 

themselves. They take two main forms. ‘The first came into being 

with the introduction in 2002 of the Intangible Fixed Assets 

(IFA) regime, which fundamentally changed the way the UK 
corporation tax system treated assets such as copyrights, patents 

168 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

and trademarks. Prior to the introduction of the IFA regime, the 

tax system did not allow relief for amortisation or impairment of 

such assets; changes in the value of an asset were generally only 
recognized in the tax system when an asset was sold. By contrast, 

in a move designed (familiarly) to support ‘UK competitiveness’, 

the IFA regime provides companies with relief for the cost of 
acquiring intangible fixed assets by allowing each year a deduc- 

tion from income — that is, from the rents on which tax is paya- 

ble — for the amortisation and.impairment debits recognised in a 
company’s accounts. 

Further changes to the UK corporation tax treatment of IP, 
complementing rather than replacing the IFA regime, were 

effected in 2013 through the introduction of the UK’s Patent 

Box. The Patent Box is the UK’s intellectual property box regime 

— an increasingly popular tool of fiscal policy that provides for 

substantially reduced rates of corporation tax on income derived 
from specified forms of IP” In the UK’s case, companies have 
since 1 April 2013 been permitted to apply a lower tax rate (10 
per cent, versus the standard rate of 20 per cent) to profits earned 
after that date that are specifically ‘attributable to patents and 
equivalent forms of intellectual property’. The stated policy aim 

is to increase the level of patenting of IP developed in the UK, 
and to ensure that new and existing patents are further devel- 
oped and commercialized in the UK.” A less charitable but argu- 
ably more credible interpretation would see the introduction of 
the Patent Box as a form of national tax competition precipitated 
by concerns that companies had been taking advantage of the 
fact that IP ‘does not have a clear geographical location’ to shift 
— in accounting terms — both IP assets and the rents they gener- 
ate to low-tax jurisdictions.” 

The immediate effect of the introduction of the UK’s Patent 

Box, needless to say, has been to make it easier for IP rentiers to 

profit from the exploitation of their assets. In 2016/17, the most 

recent financial year for which data were available at the time of 

writing, the total value of this UK tax subsidy, falling directly to 

EVERGREEN 
169 

the corporate bottom-line, was £943 million; 96 per cent of the 

total relief was claimed by what the government categorized as 

‘large companies’.”* GlaxoSmithKline, in particular, has profited 
prodigiously. Indeed, its accounts provide valuable insight into 

the geographies of taxation of IP rentierism, as seen from the 

rentiers perspective. On one hand, the company bemoans the 

fact that much of its profit is ‘earned in countries with tax rates 

higher than the UK statutory rate, the most significant of which 

in 2017 were the US, Belgium, and India’. On the other hand, it 
appreciates the fact that this ‘adverse impact was partly offset by 

the increased benefit of intellectual property incentives such as 

the UK Patent Box’, which collectively reduced its annual tax bill 
by a cool £458 million.” Whether the Patent Box will have the 
intended effect of stimulating UK-based innovation remains to 
be seen. But research conducted so far, at the wider European 

level, is not encouraging, suggesting instead, perhaps unsurpris- 

ingly, that the main effect of such incentives is to facilitate and 

accelerate the very trend — the shifting of corporate income to 
lower-tax jurisdictions — to which it presumably represented a 

response in the first places 

If there is reason to doubt the positive effect of national IP-oriented 

tax incentives on levels of innovation in the UK, there is also 

reason to doubt the innovation-related claims made for the very 

institution of intellectual property itself. At the beginning of this 

chapter, I articulated the following basic premise of advocates of 

intellectual property: IP rights and their protection are necessary 

to incentivize ideas-related innovation because people and compa- 

nies would not go to the trouble of creating commercially valua- 

ble new products or processes if they could not be sure of profit- 

ing from those creations. The threat of losing control of intellectual 

creations — the threat, that is, of those creations having no propri- 

etary status — would inhibit innovation. 

In recent years, however, an increasing groundswell of research 

has forcefully questioned this premise — though questioning the 

170 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

merits of intellectual property is not entirely new. As a 2015 
arti- 

cle in the Economist noted, it dates back at least to 1851, when 

that magazine lent its enthusiastic backing to abolitionists in a 

parliamentary debate over patent reforms, on the grounds — 

alleged and factual, respectively — that patents fail to encourage 

innovation and had not been required to stimulate the great 

technological breakthroughs of the Industrial Revolution, ‘from 
mule-spinning to railways, steamships to gas lamps’.*! For much 

of the modern period during which IP rights have been strength- 

ened and broadened, however, the presumed positive social util- 

ity of robust IP has gone largely unquestioned, at least in the 

mainstream. 

Only from around the turn of the millennium did influential 

voices begin to dissent. ‘They did so initially in relation to IP forti- 

fication at the margins: when the Sonny Bono Copyright Term 

Extension Act of 1998 extended US protection from life-plus- 

fifty years 
to 
life-plus-seventy, 
for instance, 
commentators 

observed that, from the point of view of incentives, the legislation 
was worthless.*’ Thereafter, questions increasingly began to be 
asked about the worth of IP itself — most notably by Michele 
Boldrin and David Levine.*’ Numerous studies of historic waves 
of innovation, they say, indicate that the orthodox thinking about 
IP and innovation has essentially been back-to-front. Patents are 
a result of, rather than stimulus to, successful innovation, the real 
engine of which (as Karl Marx once argued) is competition. 

In fact, there is plenty of evidence to suggest that the modern 
system of IP protection is actually counterproductive — when 
measured, that is, against the avowed purpose of stimulating 

innovation. Precisely because rights are now so strong and so well 

enforced, they encourage instead what is often referred to as 

‘rent-seeking’. 

Rent-seeking is a tricky concept to operationalize in a book all 

about rent. Are not all rentiers rent-seekers, by definition? ‘That 

is certainly one possible interpretation. Nonetheless, if ‘rent’ as 
defined in this book encompasses all types of income derived 

EVERGREEN 
WHA 

from the control of scarce assets under conditions of limited 

competition, then rent-seeking, as I understand it, entails a 

particular mode of rentierism: investing time and money more 

in sweating existing rent-generating assets than in carrying out 

the research and development necessary to create new ones. 
Arguably, all rentiers have such a regressive tendency. But some 

display it much more emphatically than others, not least, in 

recent times, IP rentiers. The current, expansionist system of IP 

rights is clearly partly responsible. That that system promotes 

rent-seeking is the crux of Stiglitz’s argument against it: ‘Research 

is often directed not at producing new products but at extend- 

ing, broadening and leveraging the monopoly power granted 
through the [existing] patent’.™ 

Indeed, Stiglitz believes that the current IP system is config- 

ured precisely with the purpose of generating rent-seeking oppor- 

tunities. In his view, the utilitarian justification invariably given 

for robust IP protection is nothing more than a sham: “The IP 
standards advanced countries favour typically are designed not to 

maximise innovation and scientific progress, but to maximise the 

profits of big pharmaceutical companies and others.” Whether 

or not this conspiratorial reading is correct, what is clear is that, 

with the monopoly powers conferred by IP rights now being so 

robust, rent-seeking is incentivized and widely pursued. Recalling 

Joseph Schumpeter’s words cited in the Introduction, then, the 

IP rentier’s monopoly position has indeed become a ‘cushion to 

sleep on’. Or, to use an alternative metaphor — this time from law 

professor Robert Merges — capital has for some time now been 

‘“pigging out” at the IP trough’.*° 

The trough offers ample sustenance. One thing that it is 

impossible to miss when researching IP rentierism is the extraor- 

dinary level of profitability that strong IP assets tend to generate. 

The most infamous example is academic publishing. Here, again, 

the Economist has been a critical voice. More than two decades 

ago, it marvelled at the 40 per cent profit margins — returns on 

sales — achieved by the ‘quasi-monopolistic’ owners of academic 

NZ 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

journal copyrights such as the LSE-quoted RELX, and expressed 

the hope that, with the advent of electronic publishing, the days 

of such exorbitant profitability ‘may soon be as dead as Robert 
Maxwell [who had made his early fortune in the industry]’.*” But 

that has not happened. In a recent analysis of the accounts of 

Elsevier (RELX’s forerunner), Informa and Wiley, the three goli- 

aths of the business, David Matthews found their margins to be 

37, 38 and 30 per cent, respectively.** 

Nor are sky-high margins among IP rentiers confined to schol- 

arly publishing. AstraZeneca’s core operating margin in 2017 was 

31 per cent; Diageo’s organic operating margin was also 31 per 

cent; BAT’s operating margin was 32 per cent; GlaxoSmithKline’s 

adjusted operating margin was 28 per cent; Reckitt Benckiser’s 

adjusted operating margin was 27 per cent — and the list goes on. 

Certainly, there are relative laggards: Unilever had to make do 
with an underlying operating margin of 18 per cent, and Rolls- 
Royce with a paltry 16 per cent. But even these poor relations 

enjoy margins far superior to the average in the publicly quoted 

corporate sector in general, which tends to hover around the 10 

per cent mark in both the US and the UK.®? It is little wonder 
that IP rentiers do all they can to gorge themselves at the trough 
when the monopoly powers occasioned by strong property rights 
make such inflated margins available. 

The evidence that rent-seeking — or ‘pigging out’ — afflicts IP 

rentierism in the UK is compelling. One way to examine this 

issue is through headline figures. Despite the fact that IP-intensive 

businesses, so often lauded for their innovativeness, play such an 
important role in the UK, levels of R&D across the economy as a 
whole are very low. Relatively little, in other words, is invested in 

activities that spawn innovation. The OECD tracks R&D inten- 

sity (expenditure on R&D asa percentage of GDP) for all OECD 
countries, and Britain consistently performs abjectly. In 2016, the 
average intensity across the OECD was 2.3 per cent; Israel and 
Korea had the highest R&D intensities, of 4.3 per cent and 4.2 
per cent, respectively. Britain’s R&D intensity stood at 1.7 per 

EVERGREEN 
173 

cent, and has not risen higher in more than a quarter of a century. 

Indeed, the period from 1981 to 1997 saw a long, gradual decline 

in R&D intensity (from 2.2 to 1.5 per cent) — precisely the period, 

of course, during which IP rights were being fortified.°? The 

usefulness of Stiglitz’s observation about rentier priorities is that it 

helps us to rationalize this underperformance. Flushed with 
increasingly sturdy existing IP assets yielding hugely profitable 

rents, why would UK capital go to the trouble and hard work of 

trying to innovate? It is easier, and probably more profitable, to 

focus efforts instead, in Stiglitz’s words, on ‘extending, broaden- 

ing and leveraging’ existing sources of monopoly rents. 

This, it transpires, is exactly what we see happening if we divert 

our attention from headline figures to attend to the activities of 

the rentiers in question. In research carried out in the late 1990s, 
Robert Pitkethly compared attitudes to new IP development 
among UK and Japanese companies; he found the latter to be 

altogether more dynamic than the former, for whom cushion- 

sleeping appeared to be the norm.”' This is to suggest not that UK 
companies are not concerned with IP, but rather that they are 
disproportionately focused on existing IP — in particular, on 

sweating it relentlessly. They do this in multiple ways, very often 
supported by domestic courts and regulators that — in line with 

their penchant for strict enforcement — appear to be more accom- 

modating to ‘pigging out’ than their peers in other jurisdictions. 

In this regard, the example of US company Unwired Planet is 

an instructive one to begin with. It is an example of what has come 

to be referred to as a non-practising entity — or, more pejoratively, 

a ‘patent troll’: a company that exploits patents not by producing 

the patented product or using the patented process, but solely by 

licensing its patent rights and/or enforcing those rights against 

alleged infringers. Non-practising entities arguably represent the 

very apotheosis of IP-related rent-seeking, inasmuch as there is not 

even a pretence of innovation or economic production. In Unwired 

Planet’s case, its more than 2,000 patents — many of which were 

acquired from Ericsson in 2013 — pertain primarily to mobile 

IMLS 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Internet technologies, and it has fought a multi-year battle to sue 

alleged infringers in the shape of major smartphone manufacturers 

including Apple, Google, Huawei and Samsung. 

The significance of Unwired Planet’s story lies not in the 
company and its patents per se — it is not even 
a UK company 

— but rather in how its litigation efforts have fared in courts in 

various territories. Having failed in its attempt to sue Apple in a 
US federal court in 2013, it turned to what it hoped would be a 

more conducive jurisdiction for litigation — the UK.” In 2015, 

it sued Samsung and Huawei in London, and won, in a decision 
upheld at subsequent UK appeals. Its attorney opined that the 
UK ruling went ‘a considerable way towards validating the 
Unwired Planet [patent] portfolio’.°’ He might also have said 

that it served in the process to validate the company’s business 
model — that is, rent-seeking. 

This business model has been validated in many other ways in 

the UK in recent years, lending encouragement to all companies 

intent on operating the model in some form. Perhaps the most 

notable methods for extending the limits of an existing intellec- 

tual property asset's ‘rentability’ are the strategies of ‘evergreen- 
ing used by pharmaceutical companies in particular. Sandeep 
Rathod defines evergreening generically as a strategy by which IP 
owners ‘keep their product sales protected for longer periods of 
time than would normally be permissible under the law — and, 
specifically in the pharmaceutical context, as a strategy by which 
‘a drug patent holding company protects the product sales/royal- 
ties flowing beyond the original patent covering the active phar- 
maceutical substance’. In his 2006 IP system review, Andrew 
Gowers identified a relatively innocuous example of evergreen- 
ing from beyond the world of pharma: ‘Increasingly, firms are 
using overlapping IP rights to protect their products. For exam- 
ple, new bands, whose artistic output will be protected by copy- 
right, will often trade mark their name so that when their.works 
fall out of copyright protection, their brand will still entitle their 
estates to some remuneration.” But it is in relation to the

far-from-innocuous world of medicines that evergreening has 

received most attention and criticism. 

There are numerous ways in which pharmaceutical patent 
holders can evergreen their products. They can recycle existing 

drugs in slightly new forms protected by fresh patents; indeed, 

the drug itself does not necessarily have to be new — the life of the 
product can be extended simply by introducing, and patenting, 

say, a different drug delivery system, or a different dosage form 

(so-called ‘secondary patents’).”° They can sign ‘pay for delay’ 
agreements with generic drug manufacturers to stop them enter- 
ing the market, or collude with them in other ways but towards 

the same end. They can launch repeated patent infringement 

suits or ‘citizen petitions’, which in many territories trigger auto- 

matic delays in the processing of generic product applications. 
And there are other techniques as well.” 

Whatever the mechanism, the result of pharmaceutical ever- 
ereening, observes Rathod, tends to be the same: delayed generic 
market formation, resulting in higher drug prices (and higher 
incumbent profits) for a longer period. What is also the same, 

needless to say, is the underlying motivation and logic: 

Although creating a successful new product from . 
. 
. scratch 

is a lot of effort, adding minor variations on an existing 

successful product is less resource intensive and a much more 

certain way to protect revenues. In the pharmaceutical busi- 

ness, creating a completely ‘new product requires a lot of 

research, coupled with the uncertainty of a very high failure 

rate. Hence, brand-name pharmaceutical companies instead 
work on existing, successful products and add ‘bells and whis- 

tles’ to them, so as to prolong the market life of these success- 

ful products.”* 

In the sheltered economy of IP rentierism, such adding of ‘bells 
and whistles’ is increasingly what passes for ‘innovation’. The 

more such ‘innovation’ is allowed to succeed, of course, the lower

‘the incentive on the nasi sector to develop truly innovative 
new chemical entities’.”” 

In the UK, evidence of evergreening by major pharmaceutical 
companies has been abundant since at least the early 2000s. ‘The 

British Generic Manufacturers Association presented evidence to 

the House of Commons Health Committee in 2004 of several 
examples of delay in the launch of generics that were caused ‘at 

least in part [by] the influence or actions of the originator 
branded pharmaceutical industry’, including by ‘changing the 

active ingredient, formulation or pharmaceutical form shortly 

before patent expiry’.!°° The Committee was persuaded by the 

evidence, deeply concerned by it, and called for ‘a systematic 

review of so-called evergreening and other practices that impede 
the entry of generic drugs on to the markev’.'°! 

But the review never happened, and the practices continued. 
Only very rarely, moreover, have the UK courts or competition 

regulators intervened — but two instances stand out. In 2008, 

the Court of Appeal for England and Wales ruled against the 
validity of a highly lucrative UK patent for a ‘new form of 
perindopril (a drug used in the treatment of hypertension) held 
by a French pharmaceutical company, Servier, after it had alleged 
infringement by the manufacturer of a generic version. This 
secondary patent was, the court ruled, an egregious example of 
evergreening: 

The market for the product is vast; UK sales alone are about 

£/70m per annum at Servier’s patent protected price. It is not 

surprising that Servier have sought to exploit the patent system 

as far as possible to protect that vast income stream.

the patent valid, Servier’s monopoly in practice would last 

until 2020. But. . 
. it is invalid. And very plainly so. It is the

It is right to observe that nothing Servier did was unlawful. It 

is the court's job to see that try-ons such as the present patent 

get nowhere.!”
