Iwo years later, the Office of Fair Trading fined Reckitt 
Benckiser £10 million for restricting competition in the supply of 
heartburn medicines to the NHS.' But it required a company 

whistleblower, who took his story to the BBC Newsnight 
programme, and a subsequent broadcast exposé for this abuse of 
market position even to come to light. It transpired that the 
company had used a whole suite of evergreening tactics to fore- 

stall the development of generic competition for Gaviscon, its 

bestselling drug, until long after the expiry of the original patent.'™ 

With such interventions occurring so infrequently, the broader 

reality is that practices of evergreening — or of rent-seeking more 
generally — are in fact sustained, and even fuelled, by the existing 
UK regime of IP governance (which, as we have seen, is one that 

the companies and their lobbyists have themselves played a 

significant role in helping to fashion). Consider the EU phenom- 
enon that is the supplementary protection certificate (SPC). The 
SPC is a sui generis IP right that extends for up to five years the 

duration of certain rights associated with a patent. Available for 

various human or veterinary medicaments and plant protection 
products (including insecticides), it enters into force after expiry 

of the original patent upon which it is based, thus prolonging the 
monopoly conferred by it. The SPC was introduced by European 
Community regulation in 1992, and implemented by statutory 

instrument in the UK shortly thereafter, directly in ‘response to 

pressure to extend the well-established protection of patents... 

For many years the pharmaceutical industry [had] been concerned 

that the 20-year period of patent protection is insufficient to 

guarantee drug producers a full return on their research and 

development costs.’!”” 

Significantly, applications for SPCs must be filed and approved 

on a country-by-country basis, requiring national intellectual 

property offices (and sometimes courts) to offer their own inter- 

pretations of the EU regulation. One notable case on which they 

have been required to do so in recent years concerned the drug 

Truvada, used in HIV treatment and prevention. ‘The key patent 

178 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

covering the main active ingredient (tenofovir disoproxil) expired 

in July 2017 in most countries. Naturally keen to protect annual 

sales of around $3 billion per annum, Truvada’s producer, the US 

biotech company Gilead, applied for SPCs in those European 

countries where this was the case. Some countries, including 
Greece, Italy and the Netherlands, declined to grant an exten- 

sion; there, Truvada soon became available in generic forms and 

the price fell sharply — from €344 for a thirty-day supply of the 
branded product to just €48.for the generic product in the case 

of the Netherlands, for example. Other countries, however, 
approved the application — including the UK, which extended 

patent protection to 2020. When generic manufacturers chal- 

lenged this decision, the UK deferred the case to the EU Court 
of Justice. “Will the European Court of Justice put a stop to the 

evergreening of Truvada patents?’, asked one commentator plain- 

tively, in early 2018.1 Later the same year, it effectively did, 
ruling against Gilead.” In the UK context this was probably just 

as well, because the domestic regulatory and legal environment 
remains, for now, heavily tilted in favour of IP rent-seekers. 

CHAPTER FOUR 

Making and Shaping Markets: 
Platform Rents 
. 

Everyone knows the image. It is iconic — era-defining, even. It is 
of a cluster of men — and it is always men — in strangely coloured 

jackets. They are standing close together, but looking in different 

directions. They wear varied expressions: some look calm, others 

excited, and a few positively frazzled, but all appear to be concen- 

trating deeply. Then there are the hand signals: clenched fists, 

hands with one finger raised, others with two or three raised. 

And sometimes, in the background, we see screens, whole banks 

of them, across which flicker endless rows and columns of long 

numbers. What does the image depict? The stock market, of 

course — that quintessential expression of testosterone-fuelled, 

greed-is-good, 1980s capitalism. 

The UK is home to one of the world’s leading stock markets 

— the London Stock Exchange — and one of the world’s leading 

stock-market operators — London Stock Exchange Group ple 
(LSEG), which, 
in addition 
to 
the eponymous London 

exchange, also owns and operates 
Italy’s leading financial 

exchange, Borsa Italiana. All companies wishing to have their 

securities (shares, bonds, and so on) admitted to and listed on 

one of these two markets — thus enabling third parties to buy 

and sell those securities — must pay fees to LSEG, both for 

180 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

admission and for ongoing membership. Such fees represent 
LSEG’s core income stream. In the year to 31 December 2018, 

during which nearly 200 new companies joined LSEG’s 

markets, taking the total number of companies whose securi- 

ties it listed to approximately 2,500 from over sixty countries, 

these fees totalled £407 million.' 

What kind of business is LSEG? Fundamentally, it is a plat- 
form rentier. Let us examine the two elements of this term in 

turn. 

First, LSEG operates platforms — in essence, that is what the 
London Stock Exchange and Borsa Italiana are. The Oxford 
English Dictionary lists multiple definitions of the word ‘plat- 

form’. The two that are most pertinent to the phenomenon of 

platform rentierism are ‘a discrete structure intended for a 

particular activity or operation and ‘the ground, foundation, or 

basis of an action, event, calculation, condition, etc.’. A stock 
exchange is, precisely, a foundation or structure intended for a 
particular activity — the buying and selling of financial assets. 
LSEG does not create financial assets, or trade in them itself: 
rather, it furnishes platforms where such trading can safely and 
smoothly occur. It thereby facilitates exchange — it helps to make 
financial markets. 

Second, LSEG is a rentier, both literally and economically 
speaking. Literally, it hires its platform out, in the sense that it 

creates a forum enabling third parties to conduct business with 

one another, and then charges for the use of that trading plat- 
form, which is nothing if not a rental charge. Economically, 
LSEG earns rents in exactly the form in which I have been fram- 
ing them in this book, inasmuch as the fees it receives for admis- 
sion and membership are occasioned by the asset that it owns 
and operates. That is to say, companies pay LSEG those fees in 
respect of not so much anything LSEG does as the attributes of 

its proprietary platform. The key such attribute is traffic =yor 
what is referred to in the retail trade as ‘footfall’. After all, compa- 
nies can issue and sell shares privately, instead of using a 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
181 

platform-operating market intermediary such as LSEG. But list- 
ing on one of the world’s leading stock exchanges exponentially 
expands the reservoir of potential owners of a company’s securi- 

ties, simply because everyone who is anyone in the financial 
world trades there. 

This illuminates perhaps the crucial point about platform 

rentiers — the general subject of this chapter. If they share one 
common feature beyond the fact that they control platforms of 
some kind that generate rents, it is that they — and the platforms 
they mobilize — are all intermediaries. They intermediate trade 

(broadly defined) that often could and does take place without 

the benefit of their intermediation, but which one or more 

parties to that trade believe is sufficiently facilitated by such plat- 
form intermediation that they are willing to pay the intermedi- 

ary for the service. And the core service — or at least the one for 
which platform rentiers are principally remunerated (a vital 

qualification, to which I will return shortly) — is indeed interme- 

diation. Platform intermediaries stand apart from the intermedi- 
ated trade per se, even as they usually shape the conditions on 

which it occurs. They are not parties to it, but enablers of it, 
connecting the main trading participants, and thereby expedit- 

ing the interactions between-them. 

Platform rentierism is not new. The stock exchange itself 

provides ample evidence of this: the first such exchanges can be 

traced back as far as the late sixteenth century. And what is the 

humble shopping centre, if not a platform in exactly the terms 

identified here — that is, a structure generating intermediation- 

based rents for its owner? Retailers compete for floor space and 

pay the centre owner rents to secure access to the consumer traf- 

fic circulating through the centre. ‘The owner effectively interme- 

diates between the shopper and the shop, bringing them together 

in one, concentrated space. One of the UK’s largest shopping- 

centre rentiers, for example, is Intu Properties, which owns and 

operates cight of the country’s top twenty centres, attracting, 

cumulatively, an average of 1 million visitors per day. In 2018, 

182 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the various UK shopping centres owned wholly or partly by Intu 
—led by the 2 million square-foot, 100 per cent-owned Trafford 

Centre — generated £495 million in rental income.’ One could, 

with some justification, classify these rents as land rents (see 
Chapter 7); but this would be to misdiagnose the essential 

‘service’ for which the centre owner is being paid, which is not 

the provision of 
space but the provision of connectivity — that is, 

intermediation. 

If platform rentierism is not new, however, it has indisputably 
become vastly more significant in our increasingly digitized, 
networked world — and it is easy to see why. The very largest 

physical shopping centres in the UK individually attract a maxi- 
mum of around 4 million visitors per month; eBay UK, the 

country's largest online marketplace, by contrast, has around 24 

million monthly visitors. Anyone with an Internet connection, 
anywhere in the world, can visit eBay. The Trafford Centre is not 

so easy or cheap to access, unless one lives locally. It is not just a 
question of relative footfall potential, either. Space is limited at 
physical shopping centres — the biggest in the UK host around 
300 retailers. No such restrictions apply online; eBay UK has, 

literally, millions of unique sellers. And because platform operat- 
ing costs are much lower online than in the ‘real’ world, trading 
overheads — usually incurred by the sellers but ultimately passed 
on to shoppers — are also commensurately lower: there is a reason 
that a new DVD or book bought on eBay is cheaper than the 
same book bought at the Trafford Centre. In short, cheaper trad- 
ing connections, enabled on a vastly increased scale, are the raw 
ingredients under digital and networked capitalism for a massive 
expansion in platform rentierism. 

So, while platform rents in the UK today are not only digital- 
platform rents, they are increasingly digital — and perhaps already 
predominantly 
so. 
This crucial techno-economic 
transition 

applies with full force to the business with which | opened the 

chapter: the stock exchange business. The opening image of trad- 

ers in the trading pit may be iconic, but it is now thoroughly 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
183 

outdated. Financial trading long ago ceased to be a largely tactile, 

physical, face-to-face activity; it occurs overwhelmingly online, 

in and through computer networks. To maintain their rent- 

generating intermediary roles in this changing world, stock 
exchange operators such as LSEG have had to move with the 

times or risk rapid disintermediation. 

Instead of providing a superior physical platform for financial 

trading, then, exchange operators must provide a superior digital 

platform; companies’ willingness to continue listing their securi- 

ties on the London Stock Exchange, and to continue paying 
handsomely for the privilege, is entirely dependent on the LSEG 

furnishing an optimal technological trading environment for the 

world’s major financial institutions. And so, today, LSEG is an 

IT business as much as a securities-hosting business, earning 

rents not just for admitting and listing securities, but for connect- 

ing customers to its networked market infrastructure. The gold 

standard of these connectivity services is its Exchange Hosting 

product, which enables customers to collocate their equipment 

alongside LSEG’s servers in the latter’s own data centre, essen- 

tially renting space within it. In the brave new world of high- 

frequency trading, where millionths of seconds are all-important 

to trading profitability, collocation reduces ‘latency’ — the time 

taken to execute electronic trades — to a minimum. Such services, 

in any event, are indicative of the techno-economic frontiers of 

platform rentierism as we enter the third decade of the twenty- 

first century. 

Platform rentiers come in innumerable shapes and sizes, and 

over the past decade or so of rapid innovation in digital and 
networking technologies, they have proliferated at a dizzying 

rate. Arguably the most meaningful and useful way to categorize 

these rentiers is according to the nature of the trade that their 

particular platforms serve to intermediate: What is it that is 
bought and sold through the platform? The answer typically 

takes one of four generic forms (see Table 4.1).

First, there are platforms through which what is bought and 

sold is primarily human labour-power. Crystallizing what is 
often referred to as the ‘gig economy’, these labour platforms 
enable people or companies to connect to, and secure the paid 
services of, workers. The main difference between the various 
platforms operating in this subsector concerns the nature of the 
work being procured, which ranges from household service work 
(offered through TaskRabbit) to food delivery (Deliveroo), and 
from professional 
freelancing (Upwork) 
to, perhaps most 
famously, private car transportation (Uber). 

Notably, this trade in human labour-power often coexists with 

trade in the use of capital assets. Uber is a prime example: when 

an Uber rider procures the services of a driver through the Uber 

platform, she also thereby procures the use of that driver’s vehi- 

cle. Labour platforms, this is to say, frequently overlap with our 
second category: capital platforms — that is, platforms that enable 
and process the sale or, more commonly, letting of assets such as 

real estate, or indeed cars. The difference between the two plat- 
form types — labour and capital — is often one of degree: the 
former involve trade in labour-intensive activities sometimes 

relying on ancillary assets, while the latter involve trade in assets 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
185 

(or asset use) with little or no concomitant application of labour- 
power. Uber’s direct counterparts on the capital side are plat- 

forms such as Turo, which enable private car owners to rent out 

their vehicles — but not their labour. The archetypal capital plat- 

form, of course, is Airbnb, through which ‘guests’ search for and 
book homes for short-term rent listed by ‘hosts’. The ‘sharing 
economy’ label often given to the capital platform subsector is, 

needless to say, a misnomer, at least when applied to Airbnb and 

its ilk: if the Airbnb ‘host’ is ‘sharing’ her asset with her ‘guest’, it 

is only because she is being paid to do so. 

The third category is similar to the second, except that what 

are being sold — and it is generally sale rather than letting in this 

case — are not capital assets, but commodities. We are already 

relatively familiar by this point with such commodity platforms. 
The London Stock Exchange and eBay are both prominent 
examples, representing platforms for trade in, respectively, finan- 

cial commodities and . 
. 
. well, more or less anything under the 

sun (including, just to complicate matters, cars and houses — 

these categories are not watertight). While eBay and other 
marketplaces — online, or in the form of ‘real world’ shopping 

centres — are very obvious examples of commodity platforms, 
inasmuch as the nature of the trade conducted there is easy to 

grasp, there are also much less obvious but no less important 

examples. Consider, for instance, in the UK context, a business 

such as the London Stock Exchange-listed Flutter Entertainment, 

whose Betfair Exchange facilitates online betting directly between 

customers (rather than with a bookmaker). The commodity 

being bought and sold through this exchange? Financial risk. 

Fourth, there is a range of platforms facilitating trade in 
another very special, non-obvious type of commodity, whose 

collective importance is such that it warrants separating out as a 

category in its own right. This category includes such behemoths 

as Facebook and Google, but also companies ranging from 
Moneysupermarket 
to Rightmove. Everybody knows what 

Facebook and Google do (or rather, as we shall see shortly, they 

186 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

think they do). Moneysupermarket, meanwhile, is the UK’s larg- 

est price-comparison website, specializing in financial services 

(insurance, mortgages, savings products, and so on), while 
Rightmove operates the UK’s largest online real estate portal, 

carrying listings of property for sale or rent from over 20,000 

estate agents across the country. Crucially, what distinguishes the 

likes of Moneysupermarket and Rightmove from, say, eBay and 

Airbnb, respectively, is that no trade in financial products or real 

estate actually occurs through: 
the first two. ‘All’ these platforms 

are is search and listing sites; consumers wanting to buy insur- 

ance or an apartment are unable to do so on those sites them- 

selves. 
So what, 
if anything, 
is in fact traded through 
Moneysupermarket and Rightmove, if not the products or assets 

to which the listings pertain? The answer is attention. And the 
same is true of Facebook and Google. All four are fundamentally 

attention platforms. 

These distinctions can be clarified by considering how the 
platform owner makes money in each case. What is the revenue 
model? For the first three of these platform categories, the reve- 
nue usually consists of some form of transaction fee — a ‘tax’, if 
you like, on the value of the trade that occurs through the plat- 
form. Uber, for instance, charges a percentage commission on 
the ride fare; TaskRabbit takes a percentage commission on the 
value of performed tasks; Airbnb charges a percentage service fee 
based on the rental amount; Betfair Exchange charges a percent- 
age commission on winning bets — and so on. Sometimes, this 
variable fee based on transaction value is supplemented by a fixed 
charge: Deliveroo, for instance, charges a flat fee per delivery in 
addition to a percentage commission on the value of the food 
order. In all the above cases, however, the platform operator only 
receives money if a transaction takes place. 

Labour, capital and commodity platforms that levy fees irre- 

spective of whether any trade actually occurs are in a mingrity — 

and, interestingly, they tend to be (or to have evolved ftom) 

legacy ‘real world’ platforms, including some of those I have 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
187 

already discussed: LSEG, for example, charges securities admis- 

sion and listing fees irrespective of whether trade in those securi- 

ties takes place; and shopping centre owners such as Intu receive 

rents from the retailers they host irrespective of whether the latter 

sell anything.‘ In the online world, by contrast, labour, capital or 
commodity platforms aping this business model are scarce. eBay, 

for one, charges listing fees. But its sellers receive a capped (and 

relatively generous) number of free listings per month for most 
product categories, with the result that such fees are relatively 
marginal to eBay’s overall business proposition — the company 
makes the vast bulk of its revenue from percentage commissions 

on completed sales. 
: 
What, then, of ‘attention platforms’? How is attention priced 

and monetized? It depends. Sometimes according to the value of 
any trade — for instance, in commodities — to which the genera- 

tion of attention directly contributes. If for example, a consumer 

searches Moneysupermarket for a financial product using the 
price-comparison function, and then proceeds to click through 
and purchase one of the products turned up by her search, 
Moneysupermarket earns a ‘brokerage’ commission, which is 

either a flat fee (for example, in the case of car or home insurance 

policies, and credit card applications) or a percentage of the value 

of the purchased product (for example, in the case of loans and 

of travel or life insurance). 

Significantly, however, in order for Moneysupermarket to 
make money, it is not necessary for the attention its platform 

generates to trigger sales directly. For one thing, it earns click- 

through fees from some providers on some products (landlord 

insurance, for example) simply for generating leads, irrespective 

of whether anything ultimately comes of them. More impor- 

tantly, it earns money simply for listing products — or at least 

some of them. Ifa user selects a category (savings accounts, say) 

on the Moneysupermarket site, she will find that some compa- 

nies’ products are highlighted before any search criteria are even 

entered. These are sponsored products, whose providers pay fees 

188 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

to Moneysupermarket specifically for prominent positioning. A 

similar model is used by eBay for earning extra revenue, whereby 

it charges higher fees for the greater exposure afforded to its 
‘Promoted Listings. Meanwhile, Rightmove’s revenue model is 

entirely divorced from the question of whether site users end up 

purchasing or renting properties they discover using the site. 

Estate agents pay monthly fees to have their listings included — 

just as car retailers pay monthly fees to list vehicles on Auto 

Trader, another of the UK’s leading attention platforms — and 

are charged extra for enhanced listings (appearing for example 

as ‘Featured properties’ or ‘Premium listings’). Notwithstand- 

ing the substantive differences in their precise mechanisms of 

revenue-generation, however, the fact is that Rightmove and 
Moneysupermarket share the same underlying business model: 

generating attention for third-party providers (of property and 

financial products, respectively), and charging them for doing so. 

One of the most remarkable things about the platform-rentier 
business is that the revenue model is so frequently opaque to the 
platform’s consumer users. The main reason for this is simply 
that consumers rarely pay to use the platform — at least, not 
directly 
or 
consciously. They do not 
pay 
to 
search 
on 
Moneysupermarket or Rightmove. And if eBay or Uber take a 
small share of the amount the consumer pays for a DVD or ride 
purchased through the platform, the consumer is not told about 

it, and hence seldom knows about it. If a platform service — albeit 
not the product procured through its use — is ‘free’, why worry 
about how the provider of that service is managing to make ends 
meet? 

The classic examples of this opacity in action are of course 
Facebook and Google. Searching on Google is free, and yet 
Google — or rather its parent, Alphabet Inc. — is one of the world’s 
most valuable companies, earning revenues worldwide of $137 
billion in 2018.> It has achieved this by serving as an exemplary 

attention platform, connecting users to companies wanting to 
win our attention, and relentlessly selling our attention to them. 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
189 

Some 85 per cent of Alphabet’s revenue is advertising revenue, 
performance-based (earned when users engage with advertise- 

ments, for instance by clicking through) or otherwise (earned 
whenever an advertisement is displayed). The simple reason that 
Google can earn so much from advertising is that so many of us 
spend so much time on the site, which means it is easier (but 
accordingly more expensive) for advertisers 
to attract mass 
consumer attention on that platform than almost anywhere else. 

‘The same is true of Facebook, which is also free to use. In 
2014, when it had in the region of 1.2 billion monthly active 

users worldwide, the average user used Facebook for seventeen 
minutes each day; every day, nearly 40,000 years of individuals’ 
combined time was being spent on the site.° By the end of 2018, 

the number of monthly active users had jumped to 2.32 billion.’ 
That is a stock of aggregated consumer attention wholly unparal- 

leled in human history, and Facebook has exploited it deter- 
minedly to become perhaps the world’s paramount attention 

platform: no less than 98.5 per cent of 
its total global revenue of 
$56 billion in 2018 was from advertising — thus, a product of 

capturing and channelling users’ attention. ‘This advertising reve- 

nue was split, like Google’s, between revenue based on impres- 

sions delivered and revenue based on actions (clicks) taken by 

users. If Upwork is a platform for the aggregation and purchase 

of labour-power and Airbnb is a platform for the aggregation 

and purchase of rental accommodation, then Facebook and 

Google are platforms for the aggregation and purchase of eyeballs. 

Platform rentiers’ core revenue-generating service is intermedia- 

tion; but, as we have begun to see, they are seldom just interme- 

diaries. Facebook and Google, for example, provide tangible 

services to their billions of users; and even if we take the most 

cynical view possible — that they offer these services primarily or 

even only in order then to sell the eyeballs thus aggregated to 

advertisers — the fact remains that non-intermediation services, 

and often highly valued ones, are in fact provided. 

190 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Furthermore, intermediation ¢an in practice take many differ- 

ent forms, and the platform owner not only enables third parties 

to interact with one another but determines the conditions under 
which, and particular ways in which, they may do so. In other 
words, as Chris Forde and his co-authors have noted, platform 

rentiers do not just create markets, but actively shape them.® 
‘They do so, among other methods, through investment in plat- 
form design, whether the platform is a city-centre shopping 
complex, a website, or a smartphone app. While platform design 
may be the most visible dimension of the market fashioning 
undertaken by platform rentiers, it is in reality only one dimen- 
sion among many, several of which are as obscure as those rent- 
iers business models. A report dealing specifically with labour 
platforms, but of much more general pertinence, puts it this way: 

‘The position of the platform vis-a-vis the marketplace is more 

like that of a government that sets policies to encourage efh- 

cient market outcomes without dictating trades. The platform 

decides how often and in what context participants are exposed 

to each other, what information is collected by parties, and 
how this information is displayed. Platforms also set policies 
about what trades are permissible, how entry is gained, what 
contracts and prices are allowed, and so on. The platform may 

also make recommendations and set defaults.” 

Clearly, this is considerably more than just intermediation. 
Moreover, the platform owner is often at special pains to ensure 

that her intermediary function continues to be necessary even 

after buyers and sellers have been connected with one another. If, 

in the case of labour platforms, this means ‘lengthy and detailed 
contracts prohibiting practices such as direct contact between 

clients and workers’, then so be it.!° 

In a brilliant and perspicacious article published in 2010 — a 

lifetime ago in Internet years — the communications theorist 

Tarleton Gillespie highlighted some of the wider political

implications of the crucial fact that platforms are much more 

than mere platforms.'! Platforms’ ‘choices about what can appear, 
how it is organized, how it is monetized, what can be removed 
and why, and what the technical architecture allows and prohib- 

its, are all real and substantive interventions into the contours of 

public discourse’. In this respect, he noted, ‘ “platforms” are more 

like traditional media than they care to admit’.”” 

The very word ‘platform’, Gillespie argued, performs powerful 
work for today’s dominant intermediaries, which is why we need 

to be careful and critical when using it for analytical purposes. 

‘Platform’ suggests something singularly anodyne and innocu- 

ous: an operator providing a forum for others to do or say things, 
while itself remaining outside the fray. It is this sense of being 

‘open, neutral, egalitarian’ that, Gillespie claimed, makes the 

platform label so compelling for those companies that have 

enthusiastically claimed it. The ‘we are just a platform’ refrain 

also ‘fits neatly with the long-standing rhetoric about the democ- 

ratizing potential of the internet, and with the more recent 
enthusiasm for user-generated content, amateur expertise, popu- 

lar creativity, peer-level social networking and robust online 
commentary .'° 

In addition, platform rentiers often leverage their privileged 

position as market-makers to diversify into revenue-generating 

activities that are sometimes not themselves about intermedia- 

tion as such. Once again, LSEG is an excellent example. Alongside 

the fees it earns for securities admission and listing and for 
customer IT connectivity, it also makes large sums of money by 

providing services that are ancillary to the transactions facilitated 
by its exchange platforms. The key such services are trade clear- 

ing and settlement functions — ‘clearing’ being the process of 

updating the accounts of trading parties and arranging for the 

transfer of money and securities, the actual exchange of which is 

what is referred to as ‘settlement’. To clear and settle trades, for 

which LSEG earned £590 million in 2018 (significantly more 

than the £407 million earned from admission and listing 

2 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

services), is not to establish a market; it is to manage a market 

relationship that has already been established. 

And, more successfully perhaps than any other platform rent- 

ier operating in the UK today, LSEG has ventured even further, 

into revenue-generating territory more distant still from inter- 
mediation and market-making — namely data and information 

services. Over the past several years, LSEG has established an 
enormously successful business in providing clients like asset 
managers with data products ranging from market indices and 
benchmarks (in particular the FTSE Russell indices such as 
FTSE 100, FTSE All-Share, and so on) to real-time price and 
trading information. Control of the leading UK and Italian 
financial exchanges clearly gives LSEG a privileged position from 
which to run its data business, since much of the data it collects, 
consolidates and commercializes pertains to what is occurring on 

its own platforms.

In any event, LSEG’s data-subscription and licence fees 

totalled a whopping £841 million in 2018, making ‘Information 

Services’ easily its largest and fastest-growing division (see Figure 

4.1). The division is set to grow further still with the expected 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
193 

completion of its acquisition, for around $27 billion, of the trad- 

ing venue and data supplier Refinitiv, which was in negotiation 

at the time of writing. This acquisition, as Philip Stafford wrote 

in the Financial Times, is ‘all about data: ‘For the LSE the 

Refinitiv deal is about being able to combine data sets and 

distribute the information to the world.’'* I wrote earlier that 
LSEG is today an IT business as much as a securities-hosting 

business, but the Economist's recent take is perhaps even more 

apposite. ‘Europe’s largest trading venue’, it noted simply, ‘has 
become a data business.’ 

Indeed it has. Nevertheless, my suggestion that LSEG is in the 
vanguard of platform rentiers when it comes to generating reve- 

nue from the supply of information and data products may strike 
some readers as odd, possibly far-fetched. Surely data is the be-all 
and end-all — the lifeblood and key revenue source — of all 
contemporary digital platforms, many of which are of course far 

bigger businesses in revenue terms than LSEG? ‘The vast outpour- 

ing of breathless commentary on the “data revolution’ heralded 
by the rise of digital platforms would certainly suggest as much. 
But the answer to this question is: both yes and no. 

On the affirmative side, data is indeed at the very heart of 
what all digital platforms do, and is pivotal to the success of all 

those that succeed; digital platforms are data-driven platforms 

almost by definition, the ‘digital’ part referring to the fact that 
such platforms largely take the form of digital data. All interac- 

tions with digital platforms — from ‘likes’ on Facebook to ride 

requests on Uber, from property perusals on Rightmove to 
Google searches — generate data, and all digital platforms analyse 

this data in an attempt both to improve the platform ‘experience’ 

and, of course, to make more money. This has three immediate 

and highly significant implications. First, the world is increas- 

ingly awash in digital data: one market-research firm famously 

estimated in 2014 that, by 2020, the amount created and copied 

annually, which it termed the ‘digital universe’, would reach 

nearly 
fifty zettabytes.'° 
Second, 
this 
digital 
universe 
is 

194 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

increasingly held by platform owners, since theirs are the sites 
where most of our daily data-generation occurs. Third, to under- 

stand how these digital-platform businesses really work, one at 

least has to try to understand exactly how they put their data to 

work. 

In Facebook’s case, the primary use of user data, at least during 

the company’s history up to the present, has been to enable it to 

profile its users in extraordinary detail and depth, and thus to 

offer advertisers ‘an unprecedentedly precise tool for targeting 

their ads at particular consumers’, as John Lanchester has noted. 
He continued: “What Facebook does is watch you, and then use 
what it knows about you and your behaviour to sell ads.’ If 
LSEG, as the Economist suggests, is really in the data business, 
what business, then, is Facebook really in? Lanchester comes to 

the logical if somewhat scary conclusion that ‘even more than it 

is in the advertising business, Facebook is in the surveillance 

business. Facebook, in fact, is the biggest surveillance-based 
enterprise in the history of mankind. It knows far, far more about 
you than the most intrusive government has ever known about 

its citizens.’ Juxtaposing this sobering fact with Facebook’s 
predictably warm-and-fuzzy mission statement, which is ‘to give 
people the power to build community and bring the world closer 
together’, Lanchester speculates that there may never have been 
‘a more complete disconnect between what a company says it 
does — “connect”, “build communities” — and the commercial 
reality’.'’ He is right; and Google’s equally vapid mission state- 
ment — ‘to organize the world’s information and make it univer- 
sally accessible and useful’ — stands in equally stark contrast to its 
own commercial reality of data-driven attention-capture and 
sale. 

And yet, at the same time, the answer to my question — is data 

not the lifeblood and key revenue source of all contemporary 

digital platforms? — is also no. For all the bluster about ‘data revo- 

lutions and the ‘datafication’ of capitalism, few digital platforms 

are directly monetizing their accumulated data in the manner 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
195 

that most commentators seem to assume.'® As is often the case, 

the Economist is more perceptive on such matters than most. In 

a fascinating, long article that begins by comparing aspects of 

data-based platform capitalism with aspects of hydrocarbon- 

based natural-resource capitalism (see Chapter 2), there is an 
abrupt break: 

But another aspect of the data economy would look strange to 

dealers in black gold. Oil is the world’s most traded commod- 

ity by value. Data, by contrast, are hardly traded at all, at least 

not for money. That is a far cry from what many had in mind 
when they talked about data as a ‘new asset class’, as the World 

Economic 
Forum, 
the Davos 
conference-organiser-cum- 

think-tank, did in a report published in 2011. The data econ- 

omy, that term suggests, will consist of thriving markets for 

bits and bytes. But as it stands, it is mostly a collection of 

independent silos.” 

What is particularly striking, in other words, is precisely the 

absence of the data markets that most commentators expected 

the rise of digital platforms to engender (and that many people 

assume it has, in reality, engendered). 

Of course, this does not mean that platform operators are not 

using data in what are, at least for them, economically produc- 

tive ways. They are — internally, to refine and optimize mecha- 

nisms for profiting from platform-based trade in attention, 

labour power, capital and (non-data) commodities. But data are 

not often sold, even by Facebook: as the New York Times pointed 

out to its readers in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal 

— in which the political data firm hired by Donald Trump's 2016 

election campaign controversially gained access to private infor- 

mation on more than 50 million Facebook users — Facebook 

does not allow user data ‘to be sold or transferred “to any ad 

network, data broker or other advertising or monetization- 

related service”’.2° This, Facebook argued, was exactly what Dr 

196 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Aleksandr Kogan, an academic at Cambridge University, had 
done in providing the information to Cambridge Analytica. 

And as the Economist also noted, the reasons why platform 

operators, for all their expertise in making markets, have gener- 

ally not been making markets in data, are readily explicable: 

This absence of markets is the result of the same factors that 

have given rise to firms. All sorts of ‘transaction costs’ on 

markets — searching for information, negotiating deals, enforc- 

ing contracts and so on — make it simpler and more efficient 
simply to bring these activities in-house. Likewise, it is often 
more profitable to generate and use data inside 
a company 

than to buy and sell them on an open market. Their abun- 

dance notwithstanding, flows of data are not a commodity: 

each stream of information is different, in terms of timeliness, 

for example, or how complete it may be. This lack of ‘fungibil- 

ity’, in economic lingo, makes it difficult for buyers to find a 
specific set of data and to put a price on it: the value of each 

sort is hard to compare with other data.”! 

It is probably significant that the only platform rentiers that 
currently are substantially active in selling the data they harvest 

are those operating in markets where data has long been commer- 

cialized in this way, in which there therefore exists both a toler- 

ance — even enthusiasm — for such usage and, just as importantly, 

established methods for rendering abundant and heterogeneous 

data flows fungible. Stock prices and market indices — LSEG’s 
data products — are hardly new, after all, and neither are the data 
products retailed by the other platform rentier featuring among 
the top thirty London Stock Exchange-listed companies (Table 
Oclipa Aye Experiant 

One of the world’s leading credit-reporting companies, 
Experian may not typically be thought of as a platform,— but 

that, as we have defined that term here, is what it is, even 
if the 

> 
. 
. 
. 
. 
. 
. 
companys 
own 
articulation 
of | its 
intermediary 
function 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
ND. 

— ‘making it easier for consumers and businesses to interact’ — is 
horribly misleading, not just in its cheery tone but also inasmuch 

as Experian in fact connects businesses to other businesses, not 

to consumers. On one side of the platform, there are thousands 
of suppliers of credit history and repayment data pertaining to 
both individuals (over 1 billion at the latest count) and organiza- 

tions (over 100 million). On the other, there are the ultimate 
buyers of these data: banks, car dealerships, mobile phone opera- 

tors and others making decisions about lending and lending 

terms. And in the middle, the platform itself, Experian, packag- 
ing the multiply-sourced data into credit reports. 

In time, more substantial and widespread trade in data, medi- 

ated by digital platforms, may well develop. But, aside from 
prominent anomalous examples such as those of LSEG and 
Experian, it is not yet happening at scale. For now, at least, the 

datafication of capitalism is predominantly a phenomenon of 

capitalist production — occurring at the scale of and internally to 

individual capitals — rather than capitalist exchange. 

What, meanwhile, does LSEG’s own diversification beyond 
intermediation (and beyond services directly ancillary to inter- 

mediation) entail for our understanding of its modus operandi? 

It remains, in reality, a platform rentier through and through, as 

do other platform operators that have similarly branched out. 

Because, for all that some of what LSEG does is not about inter- 

mediation, intermediation remains the main pillar that it ulti- 
mately stands on as a business. LSEG could conceivably provide 

its other services were it not a platform intermediary; but it 
would do so with considerably less credibility and clout. Its plat- 

forms are foundations for its clearing, settlement and data 

services, as well as for intermediation, and the revenues gener- 

ated by the former — inasmuch as they ultimately are also 

payments occasioned largely by its platform assets, however indi- 

rectly — are also platform rents. And, for LSEG and all other 

platform rentiers of whatever degree of diversification, the plat- 

form, crucially, lives or dies on its success as an intermediary. If 

19S 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the platform ceases to intermediate successfully, then its owner 

will inevitably struggle to earn not only rents derived from inter- 

mediation as such, but ultimately all rents. 

Platform rentierism in its digital incarnations now reaches every- 

where where the Internet and capitalism combine — which leaves 

very few places. But, like the other forms of rentierism under 

consideration in this book, it does appear to be a phenomenon 

of particular importance in the UK; if the UK represents fertile 

territory for rentierism in general, this is seemingly as true for the 

newest form of it as it is for the most venerable. 

The significance of digital platforms in the UK, and the way in 
which it measures up relative to other countries, can be exam- 

ined from a number of angles. One is consumer usage. Here, the 
UK does not necessarily stand out: on most metrics, the UK 
appears fairly ordinary, although there is one glaring exception 

— e-commerce — where the UK has both the highest penetration 
(the proportion of the population regularly buying online) and 
the highest average online spend per customer.” 

The disproportionate significance of digital platforms is 

clearer to see in two other indices. The first is platform density 
and prominence. Alongside France, the UK has the highest 
number of active digital platforms in Europe (followed by 
Germany, the Netherlands and Spain).?> These platforms are 
unquestionably becoming more significant as commercial enti- 

ties. Imperfect it may be (most obviously, it excludes overseas- 
domiciled companies such as Facebook and Google), but the 

list of the biggest companies traded on the London Stock 
Exchange serves as a useful barometer of the changing climate 
of UK plc. Only two platform rentiers are in the top thirty 
(Table 0.1), but four others — Auto Trader, Flutter, Rightmove 
and Just Eat, the last of which is one of Deliveroo’s main rivals 
in the food-delivery platform space — join them in the top 
hundred. Six might not sound like much; but at the turn Bye the 
millennium there were none, and as recently as 2015 there were 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
HDD 

only two (Experian and LSEG having entered the top hundred 

in 2006 and 2007, respectively). Since then, there has been a 

veritable burst of platform entrants: Flutter in 2016, Just Eat in 
2017, Auto Trader and Rightmove in 2018. This is wholly new 

territory for UK ple. 

The second revealing index of the significance of platform 

rentierism in the UK is employment in platform work. Annarosa 

Pesole and her colleagues, in an important study for the European 
Commission published in 2018, looked at fourteen EU member- 

states (including the five largest), and found that the UK had the 

highest incidence of platform work whether the basis for assess- 
ment was frequency of employment (adults using platforms to 

source paid work at least once a month), income (those earning 

25 per cent or more of their income through platform-based 

work), or working time (those working via platforms ten or more 

hours per week) (see Figure 4.2). If, in short, we define an econ- 
omy in terms of how people make a living, then platform rent- 

iers control the UK economy more than they do any other major 

economy in Europe.
