RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Why might it be that platform rentierism has taken an espe- 

cially strong hold in the UK? The government and much of 

national industry would probably point to the UK’s lively 

‘entrepreneurial’ culture. But the notion that the UK is any 
more entrepreneurial than anywhere else is hogwash — and, in 
any event, most of the dominant digital platforms in the UK 

are 
not home-grown 
but overseas 
operators; 
indigenous 

successes such as Deliveroo and Just Eat are the exception rather 

than the rule. The fact that many of the leading digital plat- 

forms in the UK hail from the United States, and more specifi- 

cally from Silicon Valley, clearly plays a part in the UK’s relative 
prominence, given cultural and linguistic affinities. As Brian 

Fabo and his colleagues note, “Ihe UK is typically the first 
country in which international platforms originating in the 

English-speaking world try to gain a foothold in Europe.’ But 

eBay, Facebook, Google and so on are not known for hanging 

about; the UK may sometimes be a bridgehead, but, in Europe, 

France, Germany and other major markets are not far behind 

on the list of countries to colonize. 

To understand the platform rentier’s striking success in the 
UK, we must therefore look elsewhere. The most satisfactory 

explanation is that, from the earliest days of the commercial 

Internet, the UK has offered up a relatively benign and accom- 
modating political, regulatory and legal environment. There 
have been a few road bumps along the way, but commercial digi- 

tal platforms have mostly been given relatively free rein to create 
new markets and disintermediate existing ones — and to do so in 
the face of growing concerns around, for example, data privacy, 
labour practices and restraints on competition. When Nikita 
Malik noted in a 2018 opinion piece that the existing powers 
and regulations available in the UK to audit and regulate the 
Internet were ‘unclear’, she was putting it mildly.2° ‘Over a dozen 
regulators have a remit covering the digital world. But’ ~,as the 
House of Lords Select Committee on Communications Observed 
in a report published in early 2019 — ‘there is no overall 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
201 

regulator. Regulation of the digital environment is fragmented 

with overlaps and gaps.’”” 

The result is that curbs on digital platforms that have been 
introduced in various other jurisdictions, including in many 
European countries, have tended not to be introduced in the UK. 
One could point to Uber as an exception: in November 2019, it 

lost its licence to operate in London, which, with around 3.5 

million users and 45,000 drivers, makes the UK Uber’s biggest 
European market. But in fact Uber is not the exception it first 

appears to be. The UK has so far been an accommodating territory 

for digital platforms because its government has made it that way, 

and the decision to withdraw Uber’s licence or safety grounds — 

for the second time: it initially lost its licence in 2017, but had 

been granted two extensions — was not made by the (Conservative) 
UK government. It was made by the Labour mayor of London, 

Sadiq Khan, through Transport for London (TfL). 

In this respect, the decision was an outlier in every sense. 

Indeed, the Tories, concerned to present a friendly face to the 

world of global platform capitalists, have repeatedly made it 

plain that this is the case. In 2017, when TfL first attempted to 

clip Uber’s wings, the then prime minister, Theresa May, blamed 

Khan for what she called a ‘disproportionate’ action, hers being 

the most notable intervention in what one observer described as 

an ‘escalating . 
. 
. political war of words between Labour and the 

Conservatives over the US ride-hailing company’.** That war has 

continued, Uber becoming something of a lightning rod for the 

respective positions on digital platforms and their regulation of 

the ruling Tory party and the Labour opposition. When Ubers 

licence was again withdrawn in 2019, the Tory mayoral candi- 

date, Shaun Bailey, was just one of the Conservatives to attack 

Khan, saying he was ‘going after Uber to be popular.” The 

Conservative-supporting right-wing Daily Telegraph was sufh- 

ciently exercised to write a leader article, editorializing that 

Khan’s was an ‘ideological clampdown on Uber and a ‘harbin- 

ger of what a Labour government under Jeremy Corbyn would 

202 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

be like: ‘insular, over-regulated, resistant to innovation, protec- 

tive of vested interests and closed to global investment’.*° 

If you listen closely enough, you can just about hear Margaret 

Thatcher turning in her grave. The reason she abolished the Greater 
London Council (GLC) in 1986 was precisely to remove power 

over London and its economy from ‘socialist’ Labour upstarts — in 

the GLC’s case its leader, Ken Livingstone. The return of local 
London government in 2000, in the form of the Greater London 
Authority and a directly elected mayor, opened the way to the 

kind of metropolitan dissension and disconnection from national 
government policy that Thatcher had sought to eliminate — and 
which today, interestingly, is arguably as prominent in policy relat- 

ing to digital platforms such as Uber as in any other arena. 

In November 2019, in any event, despite ‘losing’ its licence, 
Uber was allowed to continue to operate in the capital during 
what will inevitably be a lengthy appeal process (ongoing at the 

time of writing). Meanwhile, Uber is either banned, restricted, 

or has been compelled to withdraw certain significant services in 

a large number of other European countries, including Denmark, 
Germany, Italy and Spain.*! 

The welcoming attitude of the UK, and especially of its 

national government, 
to digital-platform rentiers 
is perhaps 

partly a result of those rentiers’ lobbying efforts. We have already 

seen that financial, natural-resource and intellectual-property 
rentierism in the UK has been substantially abetted by industry 
lobbying power. What is true of those three sectors appears to be 
increasingly true of the digital-platform sector. Facebook, Google 
and Amazon doubled their UK headcount of policy specialists 
between 2016 and 2018 — Facebook naming Nick Clegg, the 
UK’s former deputy prime minister, as head of global affairs: one 
of the most senior lobbying roles at the company.” In November 
2018, the Internet Association — the influential US-based lobby- 
ing firm that represents the collective interests of the industry — 
announced it was opening an office in London.*? In early 2019, 

a leak of internal Facebook documents revealed that the company 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
203 

had ‘targeted politicians around the world — including the former 
UK chancellor, George Osborne — promising investments and 

incentives while seeking to pressure them into lobbying on 

Facebook's behalf against data privacy legislation’ 
.*4 

But the fact is that, if digital platform operators have indeed 

been actively seeking lenient treatment from the UK govern- 

ment, they have been pushing at an open door. Expressly deter- 
mined in its own words to make the UK ‘the best place to start 
and grow a digital business’ — the UK is never satisfied with going 
with the international flow; it always has to ‘lead’ or be ‘the best’ 

— the government has, by its own admission, been predisposed to 
permissiveness from the very start.” In its January 2016 response 

to an EU public consultation on digital platforms, the govern- 
ment set out its stall with striking clarity. Not only, it was argued, 

did digital platforms deliver ‘a wide range of benefits to both 

businesses and consumers’, leading the government to categori- 

cally reject ‘any form of regulation that would undermine [those] 

advantages’; the government also laid out its belief that the new 
breed of digital platforms themselves might actually serve as a 

quasi-regulatory force in the economy more broadly: they could 
do the work of regulators — and, somehow, do it better: 

These new business models challenge existing ways of doing 

business and empower consumers with unprecedented levels 

of knowledge about individual markets. Through networks, 

they are offering new answers to many of the challenges which 

previously we looked to regulation to tackle; such as how to 

hold traders accountable for the goods they sell (through 

review mechanisms) or how to maintain effective choice for 

consumers (through lowering the barriers to entry for new 

businesses). The need to have appropriate rules for how 

markets work will always remain, but platforms encourage us 

to think again about how to ensure these are proportionate 

and fit for the next few decades for all businesses, whether they 

have the characteristics of a platform or not.°° 

204 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

In hindsight, it was an extraordinary position to take. The 
government, notably, was especially keen to disabuse sceptics of 

the growing sense that digital platforms enjoyed monopoly 
powers, and that this, as much as anything else, represented 

reason to regulate them. ‘Platforms’, the government’s consulta- 

tion response insisted, albeit without offering any evidence, 

‘often face a much greater degree of competition than at first 
appears. *” A stake was being placed in the ground. 

And, if the growing influence of industry lobbyists has meant 

that the government has increasingly been operating in an echo- 
chamber on matters of digital-platform regulation, then the 
echo-chamber effect has been magnified by the fact that, for 

‘impartial’ advice on such matters, the government has frequently 
turned to those who have told them exactly what they want to 
hear — including, critically, on the question of competition. The 
most astonishing example of this came in early 2017 in the form 
of a report on competition in the digital-platform space. It was 
authored by Andrew Lilico and Matthew Sinclair of the economic 
consultancy Europe Economics, on behalf of the Department 
for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (which, significantly, 
was the department that had been responsible for the govern- 
ments EU consultation response the previous year). The report 
is not only borderline economically illiterate, containing such 
inherently contradictory statements as: ‘We find that dynamic 
competition can produce positive competitive outcomes, despite 
a lack of obvious competition’; many of its central assertions 
about the competition consequences of key economic dynamics 
in the platform milieu — such as, ‘We find evidence that network 
effects, which might otherwise act as a barrier to entry, encour- 

age dynamic competition’ — go against all accepted economic 

wisdom on the subject.°8 

As in all forms of rentierism — at least as defined in this.book — 

. 
. 
. 
te 
there are vital issues of monopoly power at stake in the platform 

space, and especially the digital-platform space. Google is, of 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
205 

course, overwhelmingly dominant in online search, and over 70 

per cent of total time spent by UK Internet users on social media 

sites is absorbed by Facebook (either on its eponymous site or on 
one of the other group properties, most notably Instagram).*° 
The result is that these two companies between them dominate 

the economy of online attention, taking more than half of overall 

digital advertising expenditure in the UK.” The landscapes of 
UK online labour, capital and commodity platforming may be 
somewhat less concentrated (the devil is in the detail of market 

definition and measurement), but not significantly so. The vari- 

ous sub-sectors within the labour platform space all tend to have 
dominant players (for example, Uber in private car transporta- 

tion); with regard to capital platforms, no one holds a candle to 
Airbnb; and, last but not least, eBay and Amazon Marketplace 

are clear market leaders in commodity platform intermediation. 

It is clear that leading digital platform rentiers in many cases 

have used many of the same competition-thwarting tactics that 

are easily recognizable from beyond the world of rentierism, in 

capitalist economic formations more generally. They buy up 

actual and potential rivals, for example, and act in other ways 

that serve explicitly to suppress competition. Google is a good 

case in point, though it is far from alone. It has acquired more 

than 200 other companies since 2001.*! Several forms of abuse 

of the market dominance sustained by this aggressive acquisition 

strategy have come to light. Indeed, several have fallen foul of 

competition regulators — though not, strikingly, UK competi- 

tion regulators, who have applied to the platform giants as ‘light 

touch’ a competition policy as possible (also known as doing 

nothing). Rather, it is the EU Competition Commission that has 

bared its teeth and taken the fight to Google, handing out fines 

totalling €8.2 billion across three findings of competitive miscon- 

duct by the company — ruled on in 2017, when Google was 

found to be favouring its own comparison-shopping service by 

deliberately demoting rival sites in search results; in 2018, when 

it was found to have been imposing restrictive terms on Android 

206 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

phone makers; and in 2019, when it was found to have suppressed 

competition in online advertising. Google’s infringements, the 

commissioner, Margrethe Vestager, noted, had been ‘serious and 

sustained’. 

However, as with the phenomenon of rentierism more broadly, 
monopoly power in the world of platform rentierism is not only 

a matter of such generic anti-competitive tactics — which can to 
some degree be found in essentially any industry sector. As I have 
argued, rentierism is anti-competitive by nature: rentiers are by 

definition those who generate income from scarce assets under 

conditions of limited or no competition. In other words, reduced 
competition is integral to, not contingent on, the rentier’s mode 

of being. As Martin Kenney and John Zysman put it in one of 

the best existing discussions of the rise of the digital ‘platform 
economy, ‘many platforms by their very nature prove to be 
winner-take-all markets, in which only one or two companies 
survive’.*’ In other words, monopolization is a feature, not a bug. 

Those, such as Europe Economics’ Lilico and Sinclair, who 

dispute this point, arguing that competition is in fact relatively 
healthy in the digital platform space, invariably point to one 

particular example to prove their point: the fate of MySpace, 
which was the largest social-media platform in the world in the 

latter half of the 2000s. This, for example, was what the Lords 

Select Committee on Communications was told by the UK’s 
most prominent free-market think tanks when taking evidence 

for its report on digital regulation: “Witnesses said that online 
platforms could not take their current market shares for granted 

in the face of future competition. The Entrepreneurs Network 
and Adam Smith Institute noted that “MySpace was previously 
seen as an unassailable monopoly before Facebook eventually 
won out.” “‘ But there is a good reason why contrarians, in main- 
taining that digital platform monopolies do not necessarily last, 
always invoke this same example of a monopoly that faltered: it 
has happened only once. ‘The evidence is overwhelming chats in 
the digital-platform world, monopoly power does indeed 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
207 

crystallize, and does ordinarily endure. For example, it is no 

coincidence that, during the same period when the digitization 

of stock exchanges and their intermediary role has taken place, 

there has also been a precipitous decline in the degree of compe- 

tition between those exchanges.” 

But this is not to say that the source of this inherent tendency 

towards monopoly is the same in the platform-rentier space as in 
other rentier domains. Platform rentiers’ assets are generally not 

scarce in the way that, say, oil companies’ development licences 

or pharmaceutical companies’ medicinal patents are — and nor 

are they insulated from competition by the same mechanisms. 
Anyone with the required technical knowhow, after all, can 

create a search engine. In principle, the barriers to entry in the 

digital-platform world are relatively low. If you can create a clever 

app to link possessors of unmet demand with possessors of spare 
supply capacity, in either a new market segment — “Uber for X’ 

— or even one containing existing players, you are in business. 

There are no absolute constraints: no single development licence, 

single patent, and so on. 

In what specific respects, then, is monopoly power inherent to 

platform rentierism? ‘There is now a relatively large body of anal- 

ysis on this question, and the vast bulk of it points to three criti- 

cal factors. The first concerns 
so-called network effects, or 
network externalities. Martin Sandbu offers a typically clear 

description: ‘Search engines, social media and shopping, match- 

ing or selection platforms all can perform their functions better 

the more people use the service. That makes it hard for new chal- 

lengers to compete. “° With every new user, the platform becomes 

both more valuable to its existing users and more attractive to 

further prospective users, in a virtuous circle that intrinsically 

locks competitors out. Jason Furman and his colleagues usefully 

distinguish between what they call ‘direct’ network effects, where 

all categories of user can benefit from growth in users, and ‘indi- 

rect’ network effects, which occur ‘when the benefits to users on 

one side of a platform market increase with the number of users 

208 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

on the other side of the market’. Platforms in which such indi- 

rect effects are prominent include online marketplaces and 

advertising-based attention platforms.” 

The second factor underpinning monopolistic tendencies in 

digital platform markets is economies of scale, where the often 

high up-front fixed costs of creating a service contrast with ‘low 

or near-zero marginal costs of additional users’. Economies of 

scale exist in many non-platform businesses, of course, but are 

especially pronounced online: ‘As digital platform companies 

user bases get larger, their average costs reduce significantly.’ 

Or, as Sandbu puts it, the work of matching buyers and sellers 
online is ‘inordinately cheap to scale up’. This helps early 
movers get ahead quickly, and stay there. 

The centrality to digital-platform business models of the 

extraction, analysis and utilization of data is crucial to the scale 
economies they enjoy. As US Senator Mark Warner, drawing on 

the work of the legal scholar Frank Pasquale, wrote in an influen- 

tial white paper on social-media and technology firms, ‘data 
exhibits economies of scale, enabling more effective data analy- 

sis, computationally intensive pattern recognition and computa- 

tional learning with greater collected data. As a consequence, 
firms with large pre-existing data sets have potentially insupera- 

ble competitive advantages over new entrants and nascent 

firms.’>° The UK’s Competition & Markets Authority (CMA) 
agrees. In its interim study of the UK online platforms and digi- 

tal advertising market, published in December 2019, it noted 
that Facebook and Google’s control of unparalleled volumes of 
data gives them ‘significant competitive advantages, and that 
potential challenger platforms’ inferior access to data likely repre- 
sents ‘a significant barrier to entry’.>! 

Third, alongside network effects and economies of scale, 

significant economies of scope also serve to entrench market 
dominance, insofar as they confer disproportionate returns to 

scale — in this case, by enabling companies to use scale in one 

type of activity to secure advantages (such as lower costs or higher 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
209 

service quality) in another (hence, ‘scope’). Google’s use — or, as 

the EU Competition Commission decided, abuse — of its domi- 

nant position in online search to gain advantages in comparison 
shopping is ‘an excellent example.’ Sandbu pictures digital- 
platform rentiers’ exploitation of these economies of scope in 

terms of ‘the colonisation of new tracts of the internet economy 
by those already dominant in one field’, and suggests that a 
primary source of such economies is — once more — the vast 

quantities of data held by the platforms in question, which are 

harvested in one sphere and then put to work in another.” Other 

sources include ‘use of existing customer and supplier relation- 

ships, branding [and] sharing of technical expertise.” 

To these three commonly-cited factors — network effects, econ- 

omies of scale and economies of scope — the CMA adds one more 

apparent basis for the monopolization tendency among digital 

platforms. It calls this the ‘power of defaults’. The digital econ- 
omy, the CMA says, has fundamentally transformed the way we 

interact with information. Inundated with instantaneous data, we 

increasingly place a premium of filtering out extraneous informa- 

tion, while becoming less tolerant of delays. The result is ‘default’ 

behaviour — ‘a propensity to avoid wasting time by accepting the 

default option presented to us, so that we can focus on what is 

important. Needless to say, this defaultism massively rewards 

those such as Facebook and Google that enjoy extensive default 

positions across the desktop and mobile landscape, while acting 

as a significant barrier to entry for other operators. Summarizing, 

the CMA concludes that the power of defaults has had nothing 

less than ‘a profound impact on the shape of competition in both 

search and social media’. It is a fourth factor rendering monop- 

oly power inherent to digital platform rentierism. 

These four fundamental forces engendering and enhancing 
monopoly power — supplemented where necessary by the 
monopolist’s standard arsenal of tools for batting away potential 

competitors — can rapidly make the digital platform into an invi- 

olable rent-generating asset, much like the other categories of 

210 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

rentier asset examined elsewhere in this book. What are the 

consequences? 

Furman and his colleagues point to several — none of which is 

particularly positive, except of course from the rentier’s perspec- 

tive. Choice and innovation tend to be suppressed as other firms 
become locked out — not just in their capacity as potential rival 

platform providers themselves, but in some cases as suppliers 
depending upon the dominant platform for access to consumers; 
such suppliers are at particularly high risk of exclusion where 

their supply role represents a direct threat to the platform owner.” 

There are also price-related harms. It is these that Furman and 

his fellow economists identify as the most significant potential 

negatives (or, in classic econspeak, ‘sub-optimal outcomes for 
consumers ). As we know very well by now, the rentier’s monop- 
oly power frequently buttresses monopoly pricing and monopoly 

rents. Thus, observing the same sub-optimal pricing outcomes as 
Furman and his colleagues, Kenney and Zysman write that, in 
becoming ‘a virtual monopolist’, the platform owner 

is able to appropriate a generous portion of the entire value 

created by all the users on the platform [because she has the 

power to] squeeze the platform community — the drivers or 

customers on Lyft or Uber, the content providers, the consign- 

ers, the customers, essentially any of the participants in the 
ecosystem who are instrumental in creating the value in the 

first place.” 

Leaving aside for the moment the impacts of monopoly pric- 
ing on workers, the fact that many of the services provided by 

digital platforms are free to use to the consumer means that — in 

the first instance, at least — those platforms’ monopoly prices 
must be shouldered by the business customers who pay the trans- 

action commissions and advertising premiums that represent 
platforms main sources of income. In this regard, Furman and 

his colleagues refer to a report commissioned by the Uk’s 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
PAD 

Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, which found 

that, as ‘a consequence of their high market share, ownership of 
key technologies and strong user data assets, Google and 
Facebook are, to some extent, able to set their own terms to 

advertisers and publishers’.°* They also point out, however, that 

the platforms’ business customers do not simply take this pricing 

hit on the chin: “Where fees and commissions are higher than 
they would be if markets were competitive, then these will be 
passed through to consumers to some degree.” 

My only quibble with these linked assertions is that, in ventur- 
ing that Google, Facebook and others set their own terms merely 

‘to some extent’, and that the companies on the 
receiving end of 

those monopolistic terms pass the burden on to consumers 
merely ‘to some degree’, Furman and his co-authors are alto- 

gether too equivocal. Google and Facebook are both absolute 

monopolists, and are thus able to set their own terms without 

hindrance. As Sandbu has said, if it were not for their unrivalled 

ability to extract economic (monopoly) rent, ‘the internet giants 

[would not be] so wildly valuable’. Meanwhile, the notion that 

Google and Facebook's business customers — the former's largest 

individual client is reported to be Amazon, its main customer 

category the finance and insurance sector, and neither is renowned 

for its charity — only pass those monopoly rents through to the 

consumer to a modest degree is ultimately just as fanciful. 

The highly concentrated nature of much of the digital-platform 

world also has consequences for workers — including, first of all, 

those employed by platform operators themselves. Just as market 
dominance enables Google, Facebook and the like, after Furman 

and his colleagues, to ‘set their own terms to advertisers and 

publishers’, so it enables them to set their own terms to their 

employees, except perhaps those few with skillsets in short supply 

but for which demand is strong. 

In other words, such companies have what I referred to in the 
Introduction as ‘monopsony power — the power that derives 

ALD 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

from being a dominant buyer — with respect to labour power. 

Frequently aimed ‘at the most vulnerable workers’, as Alan 

Krueger and Eric Posner have noted, and tending to crystallize in 

industries ‘dominated by a small number of huge companies’, 
monopsony power essentially represents bargaining power.°! 

Because workers in such concentrated industries have a restricted 

choice of employers, the latter have the upper hand and are able 

to suppress wages below the level that would obtain under a 

competitive labour market. 

Monopsony power is reinforced by the inherently ‘thin’ nature 
of most labour markets, by which it is meant that transactions 

occur relatively infrequently. Economists explain this thinness in 

terms of so-called matching frictions: only when both employers’ 
preferences and potential employees’ requirements ‘match’ will a 
hire be made. One important such friction pertains, writes Cass 
Sunstein, to job search: “Workers have to spend time and effort 
to find new jobs. For many low-income workers in particular, 
those costs can be high or even prohibitive, especially when they 
need to find suitable transportation and a new place to live.’® As 
Suresh Naidu and his colleagues point out in an influential recent 
paper on labour market power, matching frictions ‘both cause 
and reinforce the typically long-term nature of employment rela- 
tionships compared to most product purchases, leading to signif- 
icant lock-in within employment relationships’. Many observ- 
ers had anticipated that increasing digitization of the economy 
would thicken labour markets by loosening the frictions associ- 
ated specifically with geographical constraints. But, crucially, as 
the same authors note, this has not happened: 

[P]roducts are easily shipped around the country and world; 

people are not. While traveling is easier than in the past, and 

telecommuting has become more common, labor markets 
remain extremely local while most product markets are regignal, 

national, or even global. Most jobs still require physical prox- 

imity to the employer, greatly narrowing the geographic scope 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
213 

of most labor markets, given that many workers are not willing 

to move away from family to take a job. 

Nor, furthermore, is the power of digital platform operators 

over their workers solely a matter of industry concentration and 
labour-market thinness. Just as companies often make strategic 

corporate acquisitions in order to stifle competition in product 
markets, so they can turn to acquisitions when they fear compe- 

tition in the labour market. And digital platform operators have 
done exactly that: 

In recent years, tech companies have rushed to hire program- 

mers who specialize in machine learning. 
A common way of 

acquiring such talent is to purchase machine learning start- 

ups: Google bought DeepMind, Microsoft bought Maluuba, 

Apple bought Lattice Data. In contrast, the tech companies 

could have tried to hire workers directly by luring them from 

the incumbent employers using promises of high compensa- 

tion. It seems likely that the share of the gains accruing to 

workers (as opposed to investors and the few at the top of 

these start-ups) from open competition would have been 

greater than under an acquisition strategy.” 

This approach was thus another means of wage suppression. 

Further such sources include non-compete clauses in workers’ 

contracts — limiting workers’ mobility and their ability to press 

for higher pay — and explicit cartelization in labour markets. ‘The 

latter has been found to be rife, notably in Silicon Valley, where 

tech firms including Google have entered into no-poaching 

agreements with (nominal) competitors, whereby they agreed 

not to hire each other’s employees, thus preventing wage infla- 

tion. Indeed, the revelation of these anti-competitive agree- 

ments between companies in and around the digital platform 

space, and of ‘the casual way in which such major firms, with 

sophisticated legal staffs, engaged in such a blatant violation of 

aes 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

[antitrust] law’, was a pivotal moment in the ongoing unravel- 

ling of the erstwhile consensus — at least within mainstream 

economics — that labour markets are competitive.” 

The upshot of all this is that digital-platform operators find 

themselves at the centre of the growing concerns I| highlighted in 

the Introduction regarding capital’s increasingly absolute ascend- 
ancy over labour — both generally across the capitalist world, and 

also specifically in the UK. Naidu and his colleagues, in their 

paper on labour market power, forcefully make this general case, 

highlighting, among companies that seemingly ‘have achieved 
such powerful monopsonies that they should be broken up... 
platform-based firms that receive vast flows of valuable data 

services without any compensation 
(such as Facebook and 

Google)’.°* Diane Coyle makes the UK case, albeit more tenta- 

tively, flagging as a potential concern for policymakers ‘the theo- 

retical scope for platforms to become monopsony buyers in the 
labour market. The discussion of their market dominance in the 
literature focuses on the product market side. However, it would 
also be possible for them to become dominant in certain 
geographic labour markets.’ 

‘To be sure, the notion that the digital-platform space might be 

the locus of rapidly escalating inequalities between capital and 

labour clashes with the popular image of ‘tech bros’ setting up 
platform companies, taking them to IPO (initial public offer- 

ing), and earning vast financial rewards in the process. But to 
imagine that all workers employed by Facebook, Google and the 

like are on six-figure salaries is to neglect various critical dimen- 
sions — temporal, geographical and structural — of labour rela- 

tions at such companies. John Lanchester, in his essay on 
Facebook, emphasizes the temporal aspect: that is, ‘the never 
publicly discussed issue of the huge gulf between early employees 
in a company, who have often been made unfathomably rich, 
and the wage slaves who join the firm later in its story . He cites 
Bonnie Brown, a masseuse at Google in the company’s early 
days, on the fact that ‘a sharp contrast developed between 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
BUS, 

Googlers working side by side. While one was looking at local 
movie times on their monitor, the other was booking a flight to 

Belize for the weekend. How was the conversation on Monday 
morning going to sound now?” 

The geographical and structural dimensions, meanwhile, are 

closely interlinked. The key structural issue is that many of the 
‘wage slaves’ to whom Lanchester refers are not directly employed 
by the platform operator, though they undoubtedly carry out 
work for them. Rather, drudge work is often outsourced, mean- 
ing that this low-wage corner of company operations is, to a 

significant extent, hidden — which is why many people simply 

are not aware that it exists.”! 
; 
Not only do many digital-platform wage slaves work at one 
remove from the platform operator structurally; they also often 
work at one or more removes geographically. Hans Block and 

Moritz Riesewieck’s award-winning 2018 documentary 
The 

Cleaners, for example, examined the work of moderating content 
uploaded to leading Western social-media platforms thateis 

carried out ‘in the developing world, in darkened offices, by low- 
wage workers who must view 25,000 disturbing images in a 

single shift, focusing particularly on workers in Manila, in the 

Philippines, where much of the outsourced content screening is 

done.” These workers are, in a sense, doubly out of sight and out 

of mind, spatially as well as structurally sequestered. But their 

work is essential to digital platforms, making it impossible to 

analyse the dynamics of, say, UK platform rentierism — and espe- 

cially its labour-related dynamics — at the bounded scale either of 

the company, or rentier, itself or indeed of the UK as a geograph- 

ical territory. Rentierism spills over those artificial boundaries. 

It may well be true, for example, that Google's full-time, 
employed UK staff earn average annual wages of over £150,000 

— but that does not mean Google UK is not a machine for the 
empowerment of capital over labour.”? The machinery is trans- 

national and extra-corporate, and, because some workers — such 

as Google’s UK staff or Lanchester’s early arrivals (at Facebook 

DG. 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

they even have numbers, like ‘employee number 29’, Naomi 

Gleit) — earn very large sums of money indeed, it engineers not 

just ‘a shift in incomes from labour to capital’ but also, as 
Martin Sandbu has noted, ‘a more intense inequality of labour 
incomes’. In any event, if corporate power in the world of 
digital-platform rentierism is indeed contributing substantively 

to the former shift, it is probably not the only characteristic of 
the platform model that is doing so. Because, while it is true 
that platform rentiers, like many other companies, frequently 
mask their real ‘employee’ numbers through outsourcing, it is 
nonetheless also true that they tend to be less labour-intensive 
overall 
than most 
‘traditional’ 
businesses.?> 
This matters, 
because, as Sandbu says, such rentiers’ ‘vanishingly small need 
for human employees relative to the value they capture means 
that very little of the returns to investment need to be dissi- 
pated to pay for labour’.”° 

Much of the debate over the implications of the rise of platform 
rentierism for workers has dealt, unsurprisingly, with what I 

identified earlier as labour platforms — those where what is 
bought and sold through the platform is primarily human labour 
power itself, in what is often referred to as the gig economy. Such 
platforms — the likes of Uber, TaskRabbit, Deliveroo, Upwork, 
and so forth — essentially make, or rather remake, labour markets, 
insofar as they connect buyers and owner-sellers of labour power 
and the services it can deliver. 

One of the key concerns voiced by employment lawyers and 
gig economy workers themselves has long been that, because 

individuals securing work through a platform intermediary are 

not — or at least have generally not been legally recognized as — 
employees of the platform (or even of companies to whom the 
platform operator might outsource drudge work), they do not 
enjoy employee benefits, and are thus uniquely vulnerable to 
monopoly pricing in the form of elevated commissions. As 
Kenney and Zysman wrote in 2016: 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
ANGE 

Uber converts taxi company employees or former medallion 

owners into contractors, whose access to income is through 

the 
Uber 
platform 
... 
Are 
these 
contractors 
mini- 

entrepreneurs, employees in all but name, or yet something 

else? 
.. 
. Many are now concerned that rather than creating a 

new source of productivity we are legitimating a new form of 

putting out. Can Uber drivers be self-supporting contractors 

in a 1099 economy rather than stable workers in an employ- 
ment economy, or are they just extremely vulnerable gig work- 

ers? And, more broadly, as Ruth Collier asks, what will be the 

consequences for mass politics and political structures? Are we 

generating labor market flexibility, or a precariat that resem- 

bles a cyberized Downton Abbey replete with a small elite 
composed of the platform owners and a new and sizable 

underclass?”’ 

There has certainly been robust resistance to the immiseration 

of gig economy workers, much of it centred on precisely this 

question of employment status.’* Moreover, there have been 
some noteworthy, headline-grabbing wins. In 2016, for instance, 

an employment tribunal ruled that Uber’s London drivers should 

be treated as employees rather than self-employed contractors, 
and were therefore entitled to holiday pay, paid rest breaks and 

the minimum wage.” 

Yet Uber and its ilk, in their turn, have stubbornly resisted all 

efforts to constrain their ability to squeeze gig-economy workers 

and deny them their rights. Uber, for example, immediately 

appealed the 2016 employment tribunal ruling. When the tribu- 

nal upheld that ruling in 2017, Uber appealed to the Court of 

Appeal. And when, in December 2018, that court, too, upheld 

the original decision, Uber said it would take the case to the 

Supreme Court.” All the while, until the company actually 

implements worker status under the force of law, Uber drivers 

have had to continue to operate as self-employed contractors, 

and they will presumably have to do so until Uber has exhausted 

BGS 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

all of its legal avenues for appeal — no doubt at the snail's pace 

that the law typically allows. 

The overall picture of working conditions 
in the UK’s 
platform-mediated gig economy remains grim, as a welter of 
evidence shows. In a report on the platform economy in eight 
European countries, including the UK, published in 2017, Chris 

Forde and his colleagues found that the much-vaunted worker 
autonomy offered by that economy is largely a myth, as workers 

in reality have limited influence over either the content or variety 
of their work.*! “What is new about the gig economy’, Katrina 

Porrester has noted, ‘isn’t that it gives workers flexibility and 
independence, but that it gives employers something they have 

otherwise found difficult to attain: workers who are not, techni- 

cally, their employees but who are nonetheless subject to their 

discipline and subordinate to their authority.’ 

Pay in the European gig economy is ‘significantly lower’ than 

national minimum wage rates; access to social protection schemes 

is ‘very low’; and the greater the level of financial dependence on 
platform work, the lower the access workers have to such protec- 

tions.** Frequently, as with Uber in the UK, this is because work- 

ers are categorized as self-employed contractors rather than 
employees. But Forde and his colleagues found that, even where 
platform workers are theoretically entitled to employee benefits, 
in many cases ‘relatively low levels of hours or income mean that 
in practice they may not reach the necessary income or hours 
thresholds to access social protection’. Annarosa Pesole and her 
co-authors’ 2018 study of platform workers in Europe (again, 
including the UK) came to similar conclusions: 

[D]igital labour platforms typically rely on a workforce of 

independent contractors whose conditions of employment, 

representation and social protection are at best unclear, at 

worst 
clearly disadvantaged. 
In most 
cases, independent 

contractors are not covered by the labour rights and welfare 

support applicable to dependent employment. Health and 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
ZU 

safety regulations and social security contributions are typi- 

cally the responsibility of independent contractors alone. Both 

the platforms and the platforms’ clients tend to discharge 

themselves of any responsibility with respect to the conditions 

of work and employment of the independent contractors. 

This can result in a cheaper and more flexible supply of labour 

services, but at the expense of precarious conditions of work 
and employment for workers.* 

If the UK government was minded to turn a blind eye to such 

conclusions, it will have become harder for it to do so since the 

publication in February 2018 of a report on the experiences of 
individuals in the gig economy specifically in the UK, which 
came to similarly damning conclusions — albeit featherbedded 
with the odd nugget of positivity — and which was commis- 

sioned, what is more, by its own Department for Business, 

Energy and Industrial Strategy. Where the gig economy repre- 

sents the main source of a worker’s income, such individuals 

suffer from ‘precariousness in terms of a lack of employment 

rights’. The majority of gig-economy workers receive ‘no formal 

training and limited informal or on-the-job training’. There is 

scant opportunity for career progression. Pay is low. There is a 

lack of security in terms of work and working hours. And many 

workers, working through the platform rather than with 

colleagues, suffer from loneliness and social isolation.*° 

Many of these concerns were brought home with unusual inten- 

sity in a coruscating 2019 article by Aditya Chakrabortty on the 

working lives of car drivers securing taxiing work not through 

Uber, but instead through its UK competitor Addison Lee, owned 
by the Carlyle private equity group.*” Like Uber, Addison Lee is a 

platform operator, earning revenue primarily by levying charges 

on its drivers; also like Uber, it has been ordered — twice — by an 
employment tribunal that it should treat those drivers as employ- 

ees, recognizing their right, among other things, to holiday and 

sick pay; but, like Uber, Addison Lee has dragged its heels by 

220 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

appealing those judgements. Among the drivers interviewed by 
Chakrabortty was one man who — Addison Lee having increased 

the rent it charges for his car to £220 per week and its commission 
from 30 to 35 per cent of fare value — had seen his take-home earn- 

ings plummet by early 2019 to a measly £2.48 per hour for a week 
when he drove for sixty-five hours. The following week, when he 
secured less work, the man’s earnings were negative. 

Pondering this tragic story, it is hard not to concur with Alexis 
Madrigal’s avowedly ‘unkind’ summary of the state of affairs to 
which the ascendancy of the digital-platform rentier, and espe- 

cially the labour-power platform rentier, has given rise — a 
summary that, while focusing primarily on the United States, 
speaks to dynamics, including the centrality of surveillance and 
the crucial role of investment groups like Carlyle, that are no less 
applicable in the UK: 

‘The haves and the have-nots might be given new names: the 
demanding and the on-demand. These apps concretize the 

wild differences that the global economy currently assigns to 

the value of different kinds of labor. Some people’s time and 

effort are worth hundreds of times less than other people's. 
The widening gap between the new American aristocracy and 
everyone else is what drives both the supply and demand of 
Uber-for-X companies 
. .. What the combined efforts of the 
Uber-for-X companies [have] created is a new form of servant, 
one distributed through complex markets to thousands of 

different people. It was Uber, after all, that launched with the 
idea of becoming ‘everyone’s private driver, a chauffeur for alll. 
An unkind summary, then, of the past half decade of the 
consumer internet: Venture capitalists have subsidized the 
creation 
of platforms for low-paying work that deliver 
on-demand servant services to rich people, while subjecting all 
parties to increased surveillance. These platforms may unlock 
new potentials within our cities and lives. They've definitely 

generated huge fortunes for a very small number of people. 

MAKING AND SHAPING MARKETS 
BBS 

But mostly, they’ve served to make our lives marginally more 
convenient than they were before. Like so many other parts of 

the world tech has built, the societal trade-off, when fully 

calculated, seems as likely to fall in the red as in the black.** 

For the time being, at least, platform rentierism is among the 

smallest of the various forms of rentierism that increasingly 
dominate the UK economy. In terms of digital-platform rentiers 

specifically, for example, Facebook and Google are clearly among 

the largest — and yet their annual reported UK revenues in 2018 

were only £1.6 billion and £1.4 billion, respectively.” The rela- 

tively small scale of the UK platform-rentier domain appears 
more striking still if measured in terms of profit rather than reve- 

nue. Facebook’s reported 2018 UK profits were a paltry £97 

million, representing a profit margin of about 6 per cent; Google's 

were £245 million, giving it a margin of about 17 per cent. These 

are large absolute numbers to you and me, certainly; but they are 

hardly worth getting out of bed for among companies in other 

rentier domains, accustomed to profits in the billions rather than 

millions of pounds, and to margins of 30 per cent or more. 

Two important points need to be made about these revenue 

and, especially, profit numbers, however. The first concerns the 

place of profitability in the business strategy of many digital- 

platform rentiers. The prevailing wisdom among such rentiers 

_ 
and (equally importantly) their investors has for a long time been 

that growth comes before profit — at least until the business has 

reached ‘maturity’. Management’s focus is thus predominantly 

on scaling up and securing market dominance at almost any 

investment cost — and then worrying about realizing a surplus 

later. Uber, for example, was valued at over $80 billion when it 

floated on the stock market in 2019, and its global revenues 

stood at over $10 billion per annum — but it had never turned a 

profit.” No matter; some 84 per cent of US-based tech compa- 

nies that went public in 2018 had also never made a profit.”’ 

OD? 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

To understand extant profit levels as a measure of the true 

significance of the platform-rentier economy is to misread both 

the nature of the underlying business model and the scope for 
monopoly and monopsony power in the sector eventually to 

yield handsome returns. Mature UK-based platform rentiers 

such as Auto Trader (which was a ‘real world’ platform operator 

long before converting to a digital model), Experian, Rightmove 
(founded twenty years ago) and LSEG are cases in point. In 

2018, Experian had to make do with operating profit margins of 

23 per cent; but LSEG’s margin was 39 per cent, and Auto Trader 

and Rightmove — with essentially identical businesses save the 

fact that one lists cars and the other residential properties for sale 

— registered scarcely believable returns on sales of 67 and 74 per 

cent, respectively. 

The second important point concerns the geography of trans- 

national platform rentiers’ profit recognition. Profit is ultimately 

a fiction. ‘This is to say not that the flows of revenues and expen- 

ditures to which it refers are not real, but rather that these reve- 

nues and expenditures can be accounted for in so many different 
ways — and different geographical jurisdictions — that the result- 
ing profit figures are always a product of accounting techniques 

as much as they are of business realities. In particular, the fact 
that corporate tax rates vary significantly between different terri- 

torial jurisdictions represents an incentive for any business to 
allocate

Outsourced: Contract Rents 

i 

‘The people of Goldman Sachs’, boasted the bank’s then chief 

executive, Lloyd Blankfein, in 2009, ‘are among the most produc- 

tive in the world.”! It was an audacious claim to make. The global 
banking sector itself might by that time have recovered some 

spring in its step after the turmoil of 2007-08, but the wider 

global economy, not to mention most of those working in it, had 

not, and banks — Goldman foremost among them — were rightly 

held responsible. Goldman Sachs was not, on any reasonable 

reckoning, productive. 

But statistically, at least, Blankfein was right. Banks typically 
do very well on standard measures of employee productivity — 
revenue or profit per head — and Goldman Sachs typically does 

— 
better than other banks. Ben Walsh showed this in a fascinating 

blog post in late 2013: on these metrics, Goldman beat out all 
major peers, including Morgan Stanley, Citigroup and others. 

Still, it did not quite rule the roost: both on revenue per employee 

(over $2 million) and profit per employee (just short of $500,000), 

Apple comfortably exceeded Goldman. It also comfortably beat 

other major US technology companies such as Cisco, Dell and 

IBM.’ 

How might we account for the high productivity performance 

of the workforces of companies such as Apple and Goldman? 

228 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

There are numerous contributory factors, but a key one, as Walsh 

himself noted (though Blankfein, needless to say, did not), is that 
much of the work performed in providing Apple products and 
Goldman services is not carried out by Apple and Goldman 

employees, but by other workers at other companies working 

under contract with Goldman or Apple. In other words, revenue 

or profit per employee is a misleading measure. If, to provide 
your particular product or service, you contract out — 
or 

‘outsource’ — much of the work involved to third parties, then, of 

course, all other things being equal, you are going to appear more 

‘productive’ than if your own workers do all of the work in-house. 

Leading banks have long been assiduous outsourcers of ‘non- 

core’ functions, ranging from IT to payroll. This includes UK 

banks — the biggest, HSBC, has around 2,500 ‘critical vendors’, 

with which it spends about 80 per cent of its procurement 

budget; and it has smaller contractual arrangements with ‘many 

thousands more’. These numbers, notes Penny Crosman, ‘are 

typical for large, global banks’.’ 

But Apple puts even banks in the shade. Over the years, it has 

contracted out essentially all manufacturing and assembly opera- 

tions, leaving only strategy, design and marketing in-house. 
Around the world, there are dozens of enormous companies 
whose business is in significant part to fulfil Apple contracts. 
When rumours begin circulating that Apple is considering bring- 
ing some of these contracted operations back in-house, the value 
of the companies in question plunges. In a report published in 
2017 on the ‘dark, quiet, and massive archipelago of tech compa- 

nies that supplies Apple with parts that go into its iPhones and 
computers’, Jim Edwards identified no fewer than eighteen 
companies whose contracts with Apple earn them in excess of $1 
billion per annum. At the top of the pile was the legendary 
iPhone manufacturer Foxconn, whose $68 billion in annual sales 

to Apple represents around half of its total revenue. And 
Edwards list did not even include two of Apple's major suppli- 

ers, Sony and Samsung. The Wall Street Journal reported in the 

OUTSOURCED 
DEY) 

same year that Samsung’s contracts to supply the OLED display, 
NAND 
flash and DRAM chips in the new iPhone X would earn 

it an extraordinary $110 for each phone sold — or, in total, if the 
X sold as expected, around $4 billion more than from sales of its 
own phones.’ Contracting, clearly, is big business. 

Crucially, if Goldman Sachs and Apple are themselves corpo- 

rate rentiers — financial rentiers (Chapter 1) and intellectual- 
property rentiers (Chapter 3), respectively — so too are their 
myriad major contracted suppliers. These companies’ revenues 

derive, as those of all rentiers do, from control of scarce assets, 
which in this case are precisely the contracts they have entered 

into with their customers. A contract, in the most general terms, 

is a legally binding agreement for the exchange of goods, services 

or money. Samsung, for example, contracts to provide OLED 

displays and other iPhone components; Apple, in exchange, 

contracts to pay Samsung for them. For Samsung, the contract is 

an asset, because its control and fulfilment promises an income 

stream; as long as Samsung meets its side of the bargain, Apple 

has to pay. The contract may not be a licence to print money, 

but, insofar as revenue is guaranteed, it is not far short. 

The contract is specifically an asset, as opposed to something 
more fleeting, because, like all assets, it embodies futurity: the 

contract refers to future rather than historic or immediate (‘spot 

market’) exchange, and the value of the asset to its holder is the 

value of the future net cash flows it will elicit. Given, further- 

more, that control of the asset is wholly monopolistic — it is 

explicitly Samsung's, not another company’s, contract, and only 
Samsung is entitled to receive the revenue specified by the 

contract — the income stream it generates contains economic 

rent in one of its very purest forms. Compare Samsung and 

Foxconn and their gargantuan Apple contracts, on the one hand, 

with manufacturers producing components for subsequent sale 

off the shelf, on the other. The latter's products have to compete 

with the products on the shelves above and below them; 

Samsung's and Foxconn’s, for the duration of the contract, do 

230 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

not. Unlike Samsung and Foxconn, off-the-shelf manufacturers 
have no guarantee that their products will be sold. Potentially 

alike in terms of the types of products they produce, then, these 
two different sets of companies in reality practise very different 

types of capitalism, between which the exclusive possession of 

rent-yielding contract assets is the distinguishing feature. 

Of course, there has always been some degree of contracting out. 
Few if any companies have ever done everything in-house — or, 
where they have bought in goods or services, have always done so 

on an ad hoc basis, without contractual agreements in place. A 
good example of activities that companies have sourced to outside 

suppliers under contract more or less for as long as those activi- 

ties have existed would be specialist business services such as legal 

and accounting work, or consultancy of a specialist or technical 

nature.° Public-sector organizations have also been longstanding 

outsourcers. As a recent report by the Public Administration and 
Constitutional Affairs Committee of the House of Commons 
notes, 

The UK Government has always purchased some assets and 

goods from the private sector. In the 18th and 19th Centuries, 
governments purchased some public services from the private 
and voluntary sectors: such as, criminal justice, defence and 
education. Although governments brought some services in 
house during the first three quarters of the 20th century, they 

still purchased a variety of goods and services from the private 

sector, including construction services and weapons systems.” 

When they bought such services and systems, governments 
always did so through contractual arrangements. 

But while, under capitalism, there have always been contract 

rents and contract rentiers, the significance of the latter has 
increased dramatically during the neoliberal era, and nowhere 

more than in the UK — making contracts a vital component of

the wider story of the contemporary resurgence of the rentier in 

that nation. Indeed, the step change in the significance of 

contracts in recent decades has been sufficiently large to seep into 
many observers’ definitions of ‘outsourcing’. The Oxford English 

Dictionary defines outsourcing generically, as obtaining goods 
and services by contract from an outside source — the broad defi- 

nition I use in this book. But, for Oxford Economics (OE), a 
major economic consultancy that has authored several insightful 

reports on UK outsourcing, the phenomenon is more specific 
than that. It is essentially the contemporary surplus in levels of 
contracting-out over and above that which was typical of the 

period prior to neoliberalism, which is treated as the baseline, as 

it were, of third-party contracting: the historic capitalist ‘norm’. 
Outsourcing, by this understanding, is ‘the supply of services 
governed by an ongoing or time-specific agreement involving a 

degree of delegation of management responsibility, where that 

service would more typically be provided, or would in the past 
(UK 1950s—2000s) have been more typically provided, by an 

in-house team of the customer themselves’. Thus, while I treat 

financial audit, for example, as an outsourced activity, OE would 

not, as audit is not and never typically has been performed 

in-house. 
- 
Even if it is not the approach taken in this chapter, OE’s choice 

to exclude what it describes as ‘traditional procurement’ — ‘business- 

to-business and business-to-government activities which have as 

a general rule always been provided by outside suppliers’ — is 

understandable, because the shift that has occurred under neolib- 

eralism really has been remarkable, transforming private- and 

public-sector entities alike. 

Let us begin with outsourcing by the private sector. For several 

decades now, it has been received strategic wisdom that compa- 

nies should focus exclusively on their ‘core competences’ — those 

things not only that they do best, but which constitute the 

essence of their business model — and contract out everything 

else. ‘Moving noncore jobs out of a company, notes Lauren

Weber in an excellent piece on outsourcing, ‘allows it to devote 
more time and energy to the things it does best.” That is the 

theory. It is also conventionally held that outsourcing improves 
performance (handing over things a company does less well to a 

third party that can do them better) and reduces costs (not least 

future pension liabilities). All manner of corporate business func- 

tions have been subject to the outsourcing trend: payroll services, 

catering, recruitment, facilities management, IT support, logis- 

tics, security, and much else besides." 

Over time, as ever more operations have been contracted out, 

those newly outsourced operations have progressively encroached 

on the more ‘core’ business, and the ‘core’ that is left has conse- 

quently shrunk. Indeed, those companies whose business it is to 
perform the tasks outsourced by others have gone from claiming 
that they are superior performers of non-core activities to argu- 
ing that they are superior at the core functions as well. ‘Weve 
shown’, says one, ‘we can do core parts of [companies’] business 
better than they can do it themselves.’!! Notably, the wisdom of 
contracting out has been propagated perhaps most forcefully by 
those who stand to make among the greatest gains from its enact- 
ment, which is to say management consultants — since one of the 
activities most widely contracted out in recent decades has been 
management, or strategy-setting, itself. ‘Outsource, outsource! 
That is McKinsey and the prophets!’, as Marx might have said. 

The geography of private-sector outsourcing is an important 

consideration. Much of the discussion of outsourcing in the 
media, and indeed also by scholars, has focused on the contract- 

ing out of operations to lower-cost overseas territories.!2 As 
Weber notes, prototypical cases include the moving of apparel- 
making jobs to China and call-centre operations to India.’ But 
while these are perhaps the best-known examples of corporations 
contracting out, and are clearly enormously important for all 
manner of reasons, cross-border outsourcing represents the 
exception rather than the norm, at least where its enactment by 
UK companies is concerned. As Ursula Huws and Sarah Podro

The second key point, however, is that, for all the variation, there

Private-sector outsourcing of the type taken to extremes by the 

likes of BP has occurred to some degree across all Western econo- 

mies. While BP may be in the vanguard in the oil sector, there is 
nothing particularly notable about the UK experienge more 

generally. Where the UK does stand out, however, is in public- 

sector outsourcing, where it has indisputably led the way. To be

AS) 

clear, this is not about privatization. The UK has been a leader 

there, too (see Chapters 6 and 7); but outsourcing and privatiza- 

tion are different phenomena. 

It is worth pausing to consider the key differences between 

outsourcing and privatization, because they certainly share some 
dynamics, and the borders between them are blurred, which 
makes things more complicated than a simple dichotomy 

suggests. Privatization, as we will see in Chapters 6 and 7, is 
fundamentally about the transfer of an asset — very often an 

infrastructure asset — to the private sector; ownership of the asset, 

not just its operation (in the case of infrastructure), changes 

hands, and the state’s role is reduced to that of a regulator, if that. 

Public-sector outsourcing, by contrast, fundamentally concerns 

the public sector securing the provision of goods and services by 

contract from outside of the public sector — whether or not the 

ultimate consumer of those goods and services happens to be the 

contracting public body. 

The picture is complicated partly by the fact that the good or 

service being procured under a public-sector outsourcing contract 

can often itself be an asset (a new prison or hospital, for exam- 

ple), the operation and maintenance of which is then also 
frequently contracted out to-a private company. In addition, 

privatization and outsourcing often go hand-in-hand, 
and 

cannot be readily disentangled. The transformation of the UK’s 

rail sector, beginning in the mid 1990s, is arguably the quintes- 

_ 
sential example. Much of the sector, as we will see in Chapter 6, 

was privatized, including both the track and station network — 

although, to make matters even more confusing, this infrastruc- 

ture was subsequently renationalized — and the trains themselves 

(‘rolling stock’). But the remainder of the sector, in the shape of 

the operation of rail services, was not privatized, but rather 

outsourced — specifically, to private train operating companies 

(TOCs) that bid for contracts (generally of seven years’ duration) 

let by the Department for Transport through a tender process, 

and that lease their rolling stock. 

236 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

The final complicating factor is that, if the question of whether 

the asset enters private ownership generally provides a good rule 

of thumb for determining whether privatization or outsourcing 

is taking place, it is not always an easy question to answer. 

Consider the approximately one-third of state schools across 
England that have transferred to ‘academy status since the early 
2000s (22 per cent of primary and 68 per cent of secondary 

schools).'* Are they privatized or outsourced? It is not clear; or, at 

least, neither concept quite fits. First: What, exactly, is the asset? 

Is it the ‘business’ of running the school (the reason for scare- 

quotes will become apparent in a moment), the land and build- 

ings, or both? Second: What is the ownership status of these 

assets? As far as the ‘business’ is concerned, the owner is the trust 

that runs the academy; in terms of the land and buildings, the 
owner is sometimes the academy, but sometimes the local author- 
ity, with the academy holding the site on a long lease for a nomi- 
nal charge.'? Last but not least, is the academy trust a genuine 
private-sector business? This is hard to say: legally, it is a non- 
profit charity (raising the further question of whether an ‘asset’ is 
an asset if it cannot yield profits), and yet it may receive support 
(financial or in kind) from personal or corporate ‘sponsors’, in 
addition to its core contractual funding from central govern- 
ment. In short, this is a conceptual and definitional minefield, 
exceeding the simplifying categories we nonetheless need to use 
to try to make some sense of the neoliberal UK. Here, I will be 
treating academization as outsourcing (whereby the government 
procures a service by contracting and paying for it); but it could 
equally well be considered a form of privatization. 

In any event, since the end of the 1970s, the UK has been at 

the forefront of public-sector outsourcing, in the process creating 

vast stocks of new contract assets to be mobilized for economic 
gain by an expanding army of contract rentiers. When Margaret 
Thatcher came to power in 1979, local government wag first in 

the firing line: it was not local authorities themselves that initially 

elected to outsource local services — contracting out was foisted

Sh 

upon them. The principal mechanism was so-called compulsory 

competitive tendering (CCT), first introduced for construction, 
maintenance and highways work by the Local Government, 
Planning and Land Act (1980). Under CCT, a local authority can 

carry out activities in-house only if the work has first gone out to 

tender and been won in open competition (which it seldom is). 
Over time, CCT has been extended to encompass ever more local 

services, among them refuse collection and ground maintenance 

(in 1988), sports and leisure management services (1989), and 

professional services (1994—95).*° School academization, begun 

in the early 2000s but put into higher gear in the following decade 

— all schools are able to convert, but since 2016 those judged 

‘inadequate’ must do so — merely continued the trend of downsiz- 

ing the sphere of operation of the state at a local level. 

At the same time, the outsourcing phenomenon has been 
extended to other parts of the public sector; anything that can 

conceivably be contracted out has been — including considerable 
amounts of activity for which outsourcing would long have been 

considered inconceivable. Practically nothing has been spared — 

not even what is widely deemed the jewel in the national public- 

sector crown, the NHS. As early as 1982, health authorities were 

instructed to introduce competitive tendering for support services 

such as catering, cleaning, portering and building maintenance. As 

the decades have passed, however, contractors have been invited to 

encroach, as in the private sector, on increasingly ‘core’ domains, 

_ including primary and secondary care services. The 2012 Health 

and Social Care Act and the new public contract regulations of 

2015 are widely considered to have been especially significant in 

broadening the scope of NHS outsourcing. Any contract for care 

worth more than £615,278 over its lifetime has had to be put out 

to tender, leading to a ‘massive expansion’ in the amount of care 

being provided under contract by private companies.” 

The rationale typically given for public-sector outsourcing has 

partly mirrored that generally given by private companies that 

elect to contract out, which I examined earlier. That is, it is about

because the contracting authority believes that it will help

ity of the service . 
. 
. Getting a specialist to deliver services can

The language is very familiar. But public-sector outsourcing, it is

the private sector, away from the public sector and the taxpayer. 
These were two of the primary stated objectives of contracting

Yet underlying these stated rationales, and sometimes creeping 

explicitly into the light, has been a simple, deep-seated anti- 

statism. Outsourcing, in other words, is ideological. It is, after all, 

a centrepiece of UK-style neoliberalism; and, at the heart of the 
neoliberal project, especially in the UK, there has always been a 
conviction not only that the state should own as little as possible 

(see Chapters 6 and 7), but also that it should do as little as possi- 

ble. This is because the public sector, presumed to be mired in 
bureaucracy and wastefulness, is deemed inherently inefficient, 
both in absolute terms and — more importantly — relative to an 
idealized private sector. That which can be contracted out should 
be, simply because it will be done better. Becky Francis’s assess- 
ment of the government's true rationale for school academization 
—‘a strong dislike of local authority influence, and a faith in auton- 
omy and marketisation’ — can probably be safely extended to 
public-sector outsourcing more generally.”

phenomena, over the course of three or four decades, have 

together spawned an entire new class of contract rentier, practis- 

ing what is today a major form of economic activity: contract 

capitalism. Some contract capitalists are specialists, either taking 

on particular outsourced functions (for clients of various types) 

or servicing clients in particular industry sectors (and perform- 

ing a range of functions for them). An example of the former 

type of specialist would be Automatic Data Processing, Inc., 
which provides HR services for over 600,000 companies around 

the world, including in the UK, and whose payroll unit pays 
approximately 40 million workers. An example of the latter type 

of specialist would be oil service companies, which provide 

services to the oil exploration and production sector but do not 
generally produce oil themselves. These include the likes of 
Schlumberger and Weatherford International. 

Alongside these specialists are legion generalist contractors, who 

will essentially do anything for anyone. To the extent that these 

companies even have a business model, it is negatively defined: 

they do what others, in both the private and public sector, elect 

not to do themselves. A prime UK example of such a generalist 

contractor, as a piece on UK outsourcing in the Economist recently 

noted, is Serco. Serco’s major contracts at the time the article was 

written included the provision of catering services to the state 

education sector and conveyance of the country’s nuclear subma- 

rines; its other public-sector contracts included running six pris- 

ons and operating the sleeper train from London to Scotland. The 

Economist wryly observed that the range of work Serco performed 

ran ‘from serving school meals to serving up Armageddon’.” 

Indeed, if the UK is notable for having been in the vanguard 

of public-sector outsourcing, it is also notable for the promi- 
nence and relatively large number of these generalist contractors. 

Alongside Serco, other major names include Amey, Capita, G4S, 

Kier and Interserve. If it is possible to provide a positive defini- 

tion of their business model, then it is the one given by Colin 

Crouch, who has recognized more clearly than anyone that what 

240 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

these companies do is fundamentally what all rentiers do — that 

is, attempt to acquire and exploit assets, in this case contracts. 

Getting new assets on to the balance sheet is the central objec- 

tive; while Crouch 
writes 
specifically about 
public-sector 

contracts, his description of generalist contractors’ typical busi- 

ness model applies equally to their zeal for winning new private- 

sector business: ‘[T]heir core business is not a particular field of 

activity in which they have expertise, but knowing how to win 
government contracts: how to bid, and how to develop contacts 

with officials and politicians. This becomes a form of network 

externality; on its basis they can undertake contracts across virtu- 

ally any field where government has decided to outsource.””° 
When simply securing new contract assets becomes companies’ 

raison a 
étre, the adequate performance of the work stipulated by 

those contracts tends to become a secondary consideration, 
something to be worried about after the fact. I will examine the 
consequences of such skewed incentives and priorities later in 
this chapter. Meanwhile, one notorious recent episode captured 
the absurdity to which the latter-day rise to prominence of the 
do-anything generalist contractor ultimately tends: in December 
2018, the UK government awarded a contract to run a ferry 
service required in the event of a no-deal Brexit to a company 
that had neither ships nor any history of trading. 

Contract capitalism, or contract rentierism, accounts for a major 

slice of the contemporary UK economy —~ a bigger slice, all told, 

than any of the other forms of rentierism examined in this book, 
including behemoths like financial and land rentierism. But it is 

devilishly difficult to put a number on it, because it is very hard 

to delimit and examine it. As we have seen, contract capitalism 
does not represent a single industry sector in standard industrial 
classification systems, in the way that, say, financial and land 
rentierism largely do. Rather, contract rentiers Operate.to some 
extent in almost all sectors of the economy, practising a modality 
of business enterprise more distinctive for its combination of 

OUTSOURCED 
24] 

relational form (arms-length and contractual) and balance-sheet 

imperative (asset accumulation) than for the nature of the prod- 

ucts or services it provides, which is the basis of standard schemes 

of sectoral classification. The ‘professional and support activities’ 

sector 
identified 
in standard classifications 
is essentially a 

contract-rentier sector; but contract rentiers are highly active and 

influential elsewhere, too — in particular, in manufacturing, 

construction, transportation, information and communication, 

health and education. Contract rentiers are everywhere. 

Around a decade ago, OE attempted to determine the size of 

the UK outsourcing market, coming up with a figure of £207 

billion per annum (for 2009), which equated to approximately 8 

per cent of economy-wide output.” As we have seen, however, 
OE has a markedly restrictive definition of outsourcing: 
it 
excludes all those activities that have ‘always’ been contracted out 

— which is to say, those that were typically outsourced even before 

the recent historic upsurge in contracting out began, in the 

1980s. The question is thus by how much OF’s figure of £207 

billion underestimates the overall market — that is, the market 

including what OE refers to as ‘traditional procurement. 

While it is impossible to arrive at an exact figure, a rough indi- 

cation of the scale of this underestimation can be attempted. By 

OEF’s calculations, roughly 60 per cent of the £207 billion annual 
market it delimited represented outsourcing by the private sector, 

while the other 40 per cent — approximately £82 billion — repre- 

sented 
public-sector 
contracts. 
Cross-checking 
with HM 

Treasury data, we find that total public-sector procurement in 

2008-09 was £230 billion, comprising £188 billion in current 

resource procurement (goods and services) and £42 billion in 

capital procurement.” The National Audit Office has since 

confirmed that this total procurement figure indeed represents 

the government's expenditure on outsourcing, describing the 

£242 billion to which that expenditure had grown by 2014-15 

as the amount ‘that the public sector spends through contracts’, 

and noting in passing that the public sector ‘spends more money 

242 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

on contracts than it spends on providing services itself?.”? In 
other words, OE was only factoring in a little over a third of the 

total public-sector outsourcing market (£82 billion of £230 

billion), which has since expanded to £284 billion (in 2017— 

18).° If OE’s delimitation of the private-sector outsourcing 
market was similarly circumscribed, and if the latter has grown at 

a rate comparable to the growth of public-sector outsourcing 

over the past decade (two huge ‘ifs’, to be sure), one would expect 

a figure of around £430 billion for the private market today, and 
hence over £700 billion for the public and private markets 
combined. That might sound like an absurdly large figure, but 
total annual UK economic output is around £2 trillion, and the 
‘professional and support 
activities’ 
sector 
alone represents 
approximately 12 per cent of the economy (see Figures 0.1 and 
0.2, pp. 12-13). Ultimately, the exact numbers are almost irrel- 
evant. Whether the number is £700 billion or ‘only’ £500 billion, 
outsourcing in the UK is a gigantic business. 

We know much more about the structure of the public-sector 

outsourcing market than we do about its private-sector counterpart, 

because the government collates and publishes data showing which 

public bodies are outsourcing, what they are outsourcing, and some- 
times also the terms on which they are doing so. There is no compa- 

rable collation of information with respect to the private sector.

governments,

represents 
a significantly higher

items 
of non-procured 
state

of £75 billion in 2017-18. Second on the list, but a long way 

behind, was the Ministry of Defence, which is estimated to have

Different parts of the public sector use different models for hand-

NHS.

Figure 5.3 uses Treasury data to illustrate in more detail

Three separate analyses, however, help to shed further light 

on this question, at least if one triangulates between them (all

procurement categories across the public sector, and comforta-

OE provided its own categorization when estimating the size of
