Meanwhile, the form taken by the asset — the rent-generating 
contract — is, unsurprisingly, as varied as the specific service 
obligations assumed by the contractor. Sometimes the rent 

level is fixed: the contract is for a certain value. One example of 

this is the Aberdeen Western Peripheral Route road construc- 

tion contract, which Carillion and two partners were handed 
by Transport Scotland in 2015 for a fixed price of £550 

million.” In other cases there is a variable, often performance- 

related element to the contract. In 2014, for example, when the 

Ministry 
of Justice 
controversially 
outsourced 
probation 

services for low- and medium-risk offenders, one of the most 

eye-catching aspects of the contractual arrangements was a 

248 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Payment by Results scheme, under which a proportion of a 
contractors payment would be determined by the reductions 

in reoffending they achieved.*! In the most complex of contrac- 

tual cases, meanwhile, it is a major challenge even to begin to 
make sense of how rents are set. TOCs’ rail-services contracts, 

for example, not only license operators to earn passenger fares 
and sundry related income such as from on-board catering, but 

also grant them a more direct rental payment in the form of a 
subsidy from government. This subsidy has no fewer than three 
components: 
the net franchise payment 
(specified in the 
contract, but potentially adjusted for policy changes, and some- 
times negative — which is to say flowing to government), a reve- 
nue support payment (based on the TOC’s financial perfor- 
mance, and again potentially negative) and a network grant 
payment (a share of the direct rail support provided by govern- 
ment to Network Rail). 

Alongside variations in contract form, there is also a huge 

diversity in asset lifetime and value. In 2013, the National Audit 

Office undertook a fascinating analysis of the public-sector 

contracts held by what were at the time four of the biggest 

contractors to the state — Atos, Capita, G4S and Serco; such 

contracts accounted for a minimum of around a third (Capita) 
and a maximum of around two-thirds (Serco) of these compa- 
nies UK revenues. The NAO analysis found that their contracts 
with the UK public sector ranged from one to forty years in 
length, the average length of the public-sector contracts in each 
operators portfolio ranging from five years (Atos) to twelve 
(G4S). The average value of such contracts up for renewal in 
each one’s portfolio ranged from £54 million to £164 million. 
At around the same time, the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) 
examined 
contracts 
to 
the public 
sector 
specifically 
for 
outsourced IT, finding an average contract duration of seven- 
and-a-half years, rising to just over nine years when weighted for 
per-annum contract value, which tended 
to increase with 
contract length.“

More recently, the Institute for Government carried out a 
study of contracts across the whole public sector, looking at all 

contract types (not just IT) and all types of contractors (not just 

the biggest). The average length of published contracts in 2017 
was one year and nine months.” This much lower number 

reflects not just the fact that the analysis factored in contracts — 

typically shorter and smaller — awarded to smaller contractors, 

but also the wider range of contract categories: IT contracts are 

atypically long. 

Nevertheless, while long contracts are relatively few in number, 

their larger average value means they make a disproportionate 

contribution 
to contract-rentier 
income. The Institute 
for 
Government's researchers calculated that 25 per cent of the total 
value of public-sector contracts is accounted for by contracts of 

five years or more.*° Notably, only a handful of the very largest 
and longest public-sector contracts are awarded by local govern- 

ment and public corporations. Most come from central govern- 

ment, where the average value of contracts was recently estimated 

to be £35 million.” Examples of particularly large contracts 

include Capita’s £582 million deal with the MoD to recruit 

soldiers for the British army, and the twin contracts — with esti- 

mated values of £1.32 billion and £1.15 
billion — that the consor- 

tium of Balfour Beatty and Vinci were handed by the Department 

for Transport in 2017 for phase-one construction of the north- 

ern section of the HS2 line from London to Birmingham. And 

then there are true mega-contracts, the largest of all being the 

‘Aspire IT contract 
between HM Revenue 
and Customs 

(HMRC) and Capgemini, which was worth around £10 billion 

over its thirteen-year lifetime (2004-17). 

Just as there are large and small contracts, so there are large 

and small contractors; one recent report estimated that around 
200,000 different suppliers now deliver the services outsourced 
by the UK public sector — so that the number providing services 

to private or public buyers will be higher still, and inevitably the 

‘head’ constituted by a small number of very large contractors is 

250 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

attached to a lengthy industry ‘tail’ of small and medium-sized 

enterprises.” 

Whatever a contractor's size, however, its central modus oper- 

andi is the same. These companies are in the business of winning 

contracts more than they are in the business of fulfilling them. 

That might sound like an exaggeration or falsification, but it 
conveys an essential truth: you can win a contract without then 

fulfilling it 
— with consequences, to be sure, for remuneration 
and one’s possibility of securing further business; but you cannot 

fulfil a contract without winning it first. New contract business 

is a contractor's lifeblood, the assetized sustenance that nourishes 

its ongoing existence. 

As always, this essential truth is disclosed by a close reading of 

the annual reports and financial statements of the companies in 

question. In what follows, I draw on three examples, all of which 

are large and well-known contractors, including — to use the clas- 

sification I introduced above — one specialist and two generalists. 
‘The specialist is BAE Systems (see also Chapter 3), a defence, secu- 

rity and aerospace contractor, primarily for the public sector. The 

generalists are two companies we have previously encountered: 
Serco and Capita, the latter gloriously described by Joel Benjamin 

as ‘the Vampire Squid of business process outsourcing, its money 
grabbing tentacles extending through every layer of Government, 
from pensions to council finance, from parking and congestion 
charges to NHS GP primary care support, funeral services, and 
even the privatised food safety agency’. I have already identified 
some of Serco’s main contracts. Notable contracts held by Capita 

— which claims to be the largest provider of services to UK local 
government, including the famous ‘commissioning council’ of 
Barnet — alongside its MoD recruitment contract include admin- 
istration of the Congestion Charge and Low Emissions Zone for 
‘Transport for London, primary-care support services for the NHS, 
and electronic monitoring of offenders for the Home Office. 
Notable BAE contracts, meanwhile, include one to supply frigates 
and submarines for the Royal Navy.

These companies’ reports to their investors place a much 

stronger emphasis on securing new contracts, and thus shoring 

up existing stocks of rent-generating assets, than on the business 

of seeing those contracts fulfilled. The truly essential KPIs (Key 
Performance Indicators), whether the acronym is used or not, 

appear to be the size of the order book — unexecuted contracts on 

which rents have yet to be earned — and, especially, additions to 

it. Figure 5.5 shows these two metrics for all three companies for 

the 2017 financial year (which 
in each case matched the calendar 

year). It would be hard to imagine a more starkly powerful way 

of illustrating the relative health in which each of the companies 

found themselves. The crucial question is how successfully the 

_company replenishes its asset base — the stock of contracts that 

will deliver future income. In BAE’s case, the answer was: very 

well; new orders during the year, worth a cumulative £20.3 

billion, represented nearly half of the company’s £41.2 billion 

order book at year-end. Serco was doing less well, but still 

adequately: its ratio of asset reproduction was 32 per cent. But 

Capita was doing terribly, reproducing only 8 per cent of its asset 

base. The aggregate value of its new orders was down by 50 per 

cent year-on-year, at £676 million. It is little wonder, then, that 

its share price collapsed in January 2018. 

DP 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Alongside a preoccupation ‘with the number and value of 
proprietary contracts (especially new ones), one other recurrent 

concern in these companies’ reports is worthy of comment: a 

focus on contract length. All three go to some trouble to impress 
upon investors that the contracts they hold are disproportion- 

ately long ones. BAE, for instance, reported that 65 per cent of 

its 2017 revenue of £18.3 billion came from long-term contracts. 

For Capita, the equivalent proportion was 70 per cent, while no 

less than 98 per cent of the value of its £8.2 billion order book 
consisted of long-term contracts — clearly, it was doing at least 
something right. Lastly, Serco highlighted the fact that the aver- 
age length of the contracts in its order book was around seven 
years, rising to around ten years on a revenue-weighted basis; the 
securing during 2017 of a ten-year catering and cleaning contract 
with University Hospital Southampton, worth £125 million, 
boosted these figures considerably. 

How might we account for this emphasis on contract dura- 

tion? Part of the answer is straightforward: longer contracts are 

generally larger contracts, promising bigger rents. But this is 
surely not the whole answer. Various studies have indicated that 
longer contracts are not just bigger, but more profitable. The 
National Audit Office, for instance, came to this conclusion for 
UK public-sector contracts; Ernst & Young has noted the same 

for contracts in the UK construction sector.>! 

‘Then there is the question of risk. As Julie Froud has observed, 

contracts, by their nature, serve to protect contractors from 

exposure to ‘market risk of a kind that a private sector company 
would normally expect’, not least the risk that demand for what- 

ever product or service they deliver will dissipate during the 
period covered by the contract; and the risk avoidance function 
of contracts is, as Froud notes, especially valuable — and essen- 

tially impossible to replicate through alternative means — ‘over a 
contract lasting 25 years’ or similar extended duration. The 
contract, Froud concludes, ‘gives the private sector provider 
security far in excess of what would normally exist in commercial 

OUTSOURCED 
253 

arrangements.” And it provides such security in view not only 

of its mitigation of risk, but also, of course, of its mitigation of 

competition. As we have seen, the contract is an extremely pure 

rentier asset inasmuch as control over it is wholly monopolistic. 
Longer contracts thus deliver more extended insulation from the 

buffeting winds of competition. Competition, such an anathema 

to the rentier, is the question I will turn to next. 

The mere fact that control of an outsourcing contract is monop- 

olistic does not mean the contractor is always operating entirely 

free of competitive forces, though that is usually the case. When 

Serco wins a multi-year cleaning contract, for example, or BAE 
Systems wins a submarine engineering contract, 
the work 
performed in fulfilment of the contract is entirely unimpeded by 

competition. But where, in the case of the public sector, 

contracted services are supplied not #o the state but on behalf of it 

to third parties, competition can come into play, although it is 

typically of a limited nature. One might argue, for example, that 

academy schools compete to some degree with private schools. 

Meanwhile, in some areas of the country, contracted rail services 

face a small amount of competition, either where franchises 

overlap, or where two [OCs operate services between the same 

city pairs but on different routes, or where non-contracted ‘open- 

access operators’ are authorized to run services. But such compe- 

tition is not only very limited — it is also rare. The existing system 

_ of rail franchising ‘mostly creates regional monopolies once the 

contract 
is let’.»? Under contract capitalism, competition is 

unquestionably the exception rather than the norm. 

The government has long been aware of this problem, and has 

long acknowledged that it is indeed a problem, at least on the 

face of things. Not only, however, has it claimed that the prob- 

lem can be overcome; it has gone further, suggesting that the 

threat — of monopoly — can in fact be turned into an opportunity 

— namely, contracting out precisely to enable competition. ‘Thus, 

injecting a competitive spirit into service provision has long been 

U54 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

an explicit government rationale for outsourcing, just as it has 

been for privatization — where, it is fair to say, delivering such 

competition has been no less problematic (see Chapter 6). So 
how in theory was this paradox — the express commitment to 

foster competition in an economic context where it not only 
does not arise naturally, but which is in fact antithetical to it — to 

be resolved? 

The governments answer has been to distinguish between 
competition zm the market and competition for the market, and 

to emphasize the latter. It is true, the government has conceded, 

that, once the contract is let and a market — between contractor 
and contractee — is formed, competition is usually absent. But 
that does not stop companies competing for the market in the 

first place. All of the virtues that advocates of private property and 
markets ascribe to the magical powers of competition, such as 
innovation and cost-efficiency, can be ensured by making compa- 
nies compete for outsourced business. In the words of the National 
Audit Office, in its report on the public-sector contracts of Atos 
and the three other leading UK generalist contractors: ‘Competitive 
tension between providers of contracted-out services helps to 
bring innovation, to keep quality high and prices low . 
. 
. Most of 
the contracts for the four contractors were competitively tendered, 
either through “mini-competitions” with pre-selected contractors 
on a framework, or through an open competition.’ 

But the trouble is that, even if competitive contract tendering 
by the public sector does crystallize such benefits (which is far 
from self-evident), tendering has in reality not been especially 
competitive, and has become demonstrably less competitive over 

time. Even the National Audit Office, in the same report, 
conceded that there were obstacles to such competition. Some, 
such as the size and complexity of many public-sector contracts, 
which tend to winnow out small and medium-sized enterprises, 
applied whether a contract was new or being renewed.%, Others, 
such as officials’ proclivity to perceive incumbent providers as 

‘the safer and easier option’, applied specifically at renewal.°° In

investigating public-sector IT outsourcing, the OFT also found 

major barriers to competitive entry, including the high cost of 
bidding (exceeding £1 million on large contracts) and buyers’ 

propensity to aggregate contracts (which warded off non-scale 

players).°’ Barriers 
to switching, either mid-contract 
or at 
renewal, were even higher — these included penalties for early 

termination and the fact that some suppliers behaved ‘in such a 
way as to create or increase obstacles to public sector organisa- 

tions switching to other suppliers’.”* 

The upshot has been that the number of tenders for public- 

sector contracts receiving only one bid quadrupled between 
2012 and 2017.” Lack of competition has come ‘to be a particu- 

lar problem in rail service franchising, as the House of Commons 

Transport Committee observed in 2017, noting that successful 

franchising was 

contingent upon an adequate level of market interest for fran- 

chise competitions. The general consensus is that a minimum 

of three bidders is preferable. In the past, there had consist- 

ently been three to four bidders and it was not always the 

incumbent who won the contract. Recently, however, the 

number of bidders for franchises has fallen, with only two 

bidders shortlisted for the South Western and West Midlands 

franchises.” 

Note that all of this applies even before the issue of potential 
cronyism and corruption 
in the awarding of public-sector 

contracts is considered.“ 

Limited and falling levels of competition for public-sector 

contracts are reflected, inevitably, in a supply side that has 

recently been described as ‘concentrated and becoming increas- 

ingly concentrated’. Up to one-fifth of contract expenditure 

goes on the thirty or so companies that the government dubs its 

‘strategic suppliers, and this share has increased.% Levels of 

concentration are even higher in the provision of large and 

256 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

complex services, where the top five suppliers control nearly 60 

per cent of the market.“ In some highly specialist contract 

markets, concentration literally could not be higher: BT won all 
of the forty-four government contracts awarded between 2011 

and 2014 to deliver broadband to hard-to-reach rural areas, 

despite these being competitively tendered.” One need only 

turn back to those ever-revealing company accounts to see how 
uncompetitive contracting very often is: Serco’s bid win rates in 
2017 were 50 per cent for new contracts and over 90 per cent for 

re-bids and extensions (the latter representing contract rentiers’ 

version of the asset ‘evergreening’ by IP rentiers discussed in 
Chapter 3).°° Whatever those win rates might reflect, it is defi- 
nitely not competition. 

Frequently, moreover, the government itself has actively fore- 

closed the possibility of competitive tendering. Contracts have 

increasingly been awarded without a competition, in the form of 

so-called Direct Award Contracts or Single Tender Actions. The 
proportion of public-sector contracts awarded in this way jumped 
from 15 per cent in 2016 to 23 per cent in 2018.°” Direct awards 
were used, notably, for ten of sixteen passenger rail franchises 
disbursed between 2012 and 2015.® There may well have been 
good reasons for this, but clearly the direct-award mechanism 
militates against the ‘competitive tension’ lauded by the National 
Audit Office. Neither is it new. When, in 2018, the contract to 
build Type 31e general-purpose frigates for the Royal Navy was 
put out to competitive tender, Jag Patel noted that it was the first 
time a contract for fighting ships had been fought openly: 
‘Hitherto, the contractor to receive such a single-source design 
and build contract has always been selected on a preferential basis 
(from the Select Few).’® And the successful contractor had nearly 
always been BAE Systems; one of MoD’s explicit objectives in 
now using a tender process was precisely to break BAE’s monop- 
oly on Royal Navy shipbuilding.” 
= 

The consequences of weak and weakening competition for 

contract assets and rents, coming on top of the monopolistic

25/7 

nature of the contract itself, are largely what one might expect. 

First, contract rentiers, secure in their monopoly and compla- 

cent in their expectation not only that business is assured for the 

lifetime of the contract, but likely thereafter as well, have widely 
underperformed. The last decade, in particular, has seen a veri- 

table deluge of reported cases of underperformance by both 
major and more minor contractors. In calling in 2013 for stricter 

financial penalties to punish such poor service, the National 
Audit Office explicitly linked it to the increasing concentration 

of government’ spending with its ‘strategic suppliers’. Similarly, 

the Public Accounts Committee of the House of Commons has 

repeatedly emphasized BT’s contract monopoly in explaining 

its poor performance in rolling out rural broadband infrastruc- 

ture.’! Meanwhile, Amey was only three years into a twenty- 
three-year contract — an extraordinarily long period of monop- 

oly — for waste collection, street lighting and road cleaning with 

Trafford Council when it was penalized for poor service.” And 

the list goes on. Perhaps the most damaging performance-related 

impacts of limited competition have been experienced in the 

NHS. In 2013, Monitor, the NHS’s economic regulator, in a 

study of the effectiveness of local contracting in the health 

service, concluded that a ‘lack of perceived or actual competi- 

tion’ was ‘reducing [the] provider's appetite to perform to high- 

est standards’.”° 

The same report alluded to a second key consequence of 
limited competition within the contract market. The knowledge 

on both sides of the contractual relationship that the buyer ‘is 

reliant or critically reliant on the provider tends to limit how 

effectively contracts can be enforced.” If all the buyer's eggs have 

been placed in one basket (the monopolist’s), the former will 

naturally be reluctant to upset that basket. Too much is at stake 
—and a lack of competition is squarely to blame. Moreover, over- 

reliance on one or a small number of suppliers is inherently risky, 

and has been evident much more widely than just in the case of 

the NHS. As Benjamin noted, for example, ‘Capita don’t just 

258 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

provide a few services, they seem practically to run entire coun- 

cils’, Barnet being the prime example.” 

Having allowed the contract market to become increasingly 

concentrated, the commissioning public sector’s chickens came 
home to roost in January 2018, when Carillion, one of its strate- 

gic suppliers, entered liquidation, causing massive service disrup- 

tion. At the time, the company was in possession of some 420 

contracts with the state: 
‘Carillion held contracts with the 

Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Justice, Network Rail, HS2 

Ltd and various hospitals. The Local Government Association 

calculated that 30 councils and 220 schools were directly affected 
by the collapse of Carillion. When Carillion collapsed both the 
Scottish and Welsh Governments issued statements about their 
exposure to its failure.’”° It took until August of the same year for 
the last of Carillion’s contracts to be transitioned to new service 
providers.”” And Carillion had been only the sixth-largest supplier 
to the public sector; things could easily have been even worse.”8 

A third consequence of a lack of competition within UK 

contract capitalism has been monopoly pricing. In 2009, for 
example, the OFT imposed fines totalling £129 million on firms 

in the construction sector in England for colluding in the market 

for building contracts and, in the process, pushing up the prices 
paid by customers. The method of collusion was so-called ‘cover 

pricing’, where a bidder in a tender process solicits an artificially 
high bid price from a nominal competitor, giving the client the 

false impression that genuine competition exists, and that the 
price offered by the former bidder is a competitive one.”? Such a 

practice would not occur if competition were, in fact, genuine; 
and the particular nature of market formation in contract capi- 
talism — namely, tendering — is of course particularly susceptible 

to such abuses. 

The deleterious price effects of structurally limited competi- 

tion have been particularly notable in rail service franchising. 
Some two decades after the sector’s fundamental restructuring, 

the cost of peak and anytime tickets is among the highest in

259 

Europe: fares increased by over 20 per cent in real terms between 
1995 and 2016, and by over 40 per cent on long-distance 

routes.*” ‘The example of the Great Western Railway franchise is 

instructive. FirstGroup has run the franchise since 1996, and 

since 2013 on a direct-award basis. Between 2015 and 2018, the 

line earned it a dividend of £159 million despite deterioration in 
performance measures relating to reliability and punctuality. 

Nonetheless, the Department for Transport announced in late 
2017 that it was planning to extend the franchise until at least 
2022 (with a possible extension to March 2024), without a 

competitive tender.*! 

Beyond rail, in the realm of IT, the case of Capgemini’s 
monster ‘Aspire’ contract is also illuminating. Not only did the 
contracting public body, HMRC, eschew competition here too 

— it contracted with Capgemini ‘without first checking whether 

other providers could deliver a better deal’; furthermore, it ‘had 

evidence that it was paying above market prices’, which ulti- 
mately resulted in Capgemini and its subcontractor Fujitsu earn- 

ing lifetime contract profits that were double those originally 

envisaged.** None of this is peculiar to the UK: using govern- 

ment data on 2.8 million public procurement contracts in 

twenty-eight European countries 
for the period 2009-14, 

researchers found that single-bidder contracts were on average 

almost 10 per cent costlier than multiple-bidder contracts.*° 

If monopoly pricing has been endemic anywhere in the UK 
outsourcing space, it is in that cluster of public-sector contracts 

gathered together under the famed banner of the Private Finance 

Initiative (PFI). Introduced by the Conservative government in 

1992, PFI really took off under New Labour, frome 997e0in 

essence, PFI is contracting out with a twist. Instead of outsourc- 

ing construction, for example, of a prison or hospital to a private 

contractor, and meeting all the costs of work and materials as 

they are incurred — and usually having to borrow to do so — PFI 

enables the public sector to defer payment for the physical asset. 
The capital cost is paid over the life of the PFI contract (usually 

260 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

in the region of twenty-five to thirty years), as part of periodic 

‘unitary payments. Although such future unitary payments 

represent a liability to the public sector, this liability is usually 

recorded off balance sheet and is thus excluded from public debt 

calculations — which helps explain why the Treasury has always 
been fond of PFI.* The contractor is typically set up as a Special 
Purpose Vehicle (SPV), and the unitary payments it receives for 

the duration of the contract cover not only capital costs but also 
any services — generally subcontracted — such as maintenance, 

cleaning and catering that are provided under the contract once 
the facility is operational. 

There has been a welter of criticisms of PFI over the past two 

decades, of which the principal one concerns the high cost of 

the borrowing that payment deferral effectively entails. Even 
champions of the approach will admit that the government can 

access funds much more cheaply through direct borrowing in 

the capital markets than through the PFI mechanism. The stated 
rationale for PFI — whether anybody has ever really believed it is 
another matter — is that the higher cost of finance is more than 

offset by savings and benefits in other areas of PFI projects. 
More than a quarter of a century after PFI’s introduction, 
however, there remains a total absence of evidence to substanti- 

ate this supposition.” And it is abundantly clear that one of the 
reasons that PFI funds are as costly as they are is the limited 
degree of competition existing in a market that is notable for its 
high entry barriers and considerable complexity.°° Monopoly 
pricing, in short, results in monopoly profits. In 2012, the 
Public Accounts Committee concluded that the amount of 
money typically made by investors in PFI SPVs was evidence of 
‘excess profits being built into the initial pricing of contracts’ 
.°” 
Six years later, the story had not changed. ‘The same committee 
noted that ‘large returns’ remained common, citing the M25 
motorway PFI deal as an example, in which investors bad real- 
ised an estimated annualized return of over 30 per cent, oe ‘more 
than double the 12%—-15% annual returns expected over the life

261 

of most PFI deals’ ‘normal’ returns, one might add, that are 
themselves exceptionally healthy).** 

If investors have earned monopoly profits, who — in the cases of 

the 700 or more PFI projects contracted out by the UK state so far 

— has paid the price? (Where monopoly is present, there is always 
someone who pays.) [he answer, unsurprisingly, is the projects’ 

clients, and the clients of those clients — which is to say, the public. 
The Public Accounts Committee observed that costly PFI invest- 

ments had created ‘immense pain at a local level’ as government 
departments (the biggest users have been Defence, Education, 

Health and Transport) and other public bodies have laboured 

under the weight of crippling unitary-payment obligations.®” 

The inflexibility of PFI contracts has been a particular prob- 

lem. As the National Audit Office has noted, there is a good 
reason why the Treasury does not normally allow government 

departments to enter contracts lasting longer than seven years; 

times change, and so do service requirements and procurement 

options.”° But PFI contracts often last over twenty-five years, 
and during that period they can become millstones, ‘reduc[ing] 

the ability of the state to change its policy’”' Changes to 

contracts tend to be expensive (where they are even allowed). In 

the worst cases, under older contracts (particularly those signed 

before 2000), the public sector can be locked into paying for 

assets and services that are no longer even needed. Even the 

Treasury, for all its longstanding support for PFI, acknowledged 

_as early as 1997 that ‘commitments due under PFI contracts 

entered into by Departments represent inescapable expenditure 

to the Department concerned’.”* So it has proved: one notori- 

ous case has seen Liverpool City Council burdened with PFI 

costs of around £4 million per annum until 2028 — for a school 

vacated in 2014.” 

The NHS has been a notable PFI victim. National Audit 

Office analysis of PFI hospitals found zero evidence of improved 

operational efficiencies.“ Competition between providers has 

been limited, at best: analysing the 125 PFI contracts with private

For all that examples clearly exist of monopoly power crystalliz- 
ing monopoly pricing for contract rentiers, the wider story is 
simply not that straightforward, however. Even with conditions 
of 
limited and declining competition, the UK outsourcing sector 

— and especially that part of the sector focused on public-sector 

business — has, for long periods at various times, been afflicted by 
low levels of profitability. Instead of high prices, contractors have 
actually charged low prices. Why? 
% 
The reason for this partly has to do with the nature of the busi- 

ness model. If building an asset base is the sine qua non of an 

OUTSOURCED 
263 

organization's vitality — which, as I have suggested, it is for the 

contract rentier — the temptation to bid low to secure contracts 
and keep growing the order book is an ever-present one. But, 

crucially, this underlying predisposition to underbidding has in 

certain periods been compounded by public-sector purchasing 

strategies that have redoubled the propensity for low prices to be 

agreed. 

First, in the period from the early 1980s to the mid-to-late 

1990s, the introduction and extension of CCT normalized the 

prioritization of service cost among procuring public bodies: the 

unwritten rule was that the best bid was the cheapest one. Things 
changed with New Labour's victory in 1997: it replaced CCT 

with ‘best value’, which still required public bodies to outsource 
where they could, but encouraged them to consider factors other 
than cost alone. During the early 2000s, contractors were thus 

better able to exploit financially the monopoly powers they 

enjoyed. The financial crisis of 2007-8 and ensuing conditions 

of public-sector austerity saw things swing back decisively in the 

other direction, however. Cost was firmly back on the agenda: in 

investigating public-sector outsourcing in the wake of Carillion, 

MPs were repeatedly told that purchase decisions had long since 

reverted to being all about price.”” And as the Economist observed, 

contractors had been only too willing to oblige: 

Fearing that austerity would slash the number of contracts on 

offer, outsourcers have engaged in a race to the bottom. 

Underbidding, known in the trade as ‘suicide bidding’, has 
become common, 
as companies try to keep shareholders 

happy with the promise of new business. Outsourcers under- 

bid in the hope that subsequent amendments to the contract 

— extra charges here and there — will eventually yield some 

profits. But often they don't.”* 

The results of widespread ‘suicide bidding’ have been increas- 

ingly clear to see. Lots of contractors have struggled, and continue

and thus securing rent-generating assets — provides future guar-

the special case of PFI — profit.

But if the government's renewed preoccupation with bargain-

Indeed, in documenting widespread failure in the enforcement

the stakeholder group most often overlooked in media commen- 

tary, but arguably affected more directly and negatively than any 

other: workers. 

The employment conditions of people working for UK 

contract rentiers have been-a longstanding concern for those on 

the left, for two main reasons. One is simple economics: if a 

rentier secures a contract to deliver a good or service for a fixed 

price, then profit on that contract can be maximized by mini- 

mizing costs, of which labour costs are for most contractors the 

main element. The economic incentive to drive down labour 

costs was almost palpable in the 1980s and early 1990s, when 

the CCT approach invariably delivered new contracts to those 

who could come up with the lowest-priced bid. The other source 

of longstanding concern has been more structural, or organiza- 

tional. If workers providing services for, say, BP or the MoD are 

not employed by BP or the MoD themselves, but rather by 

contractors to them, or by subcontractors to those contractors, 

then it is possible that BP and the MoD may pay less attention 

2YO) 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

to the conditions in which those workers are labouring. Out of 

sight — or off-payroll — and out of mind. 

With the onset of austerity in the period after the financial 

crisis, such concerns — especially, but not only, around condi- 

tions for those working on public-sector contracts — have been 
voiced anew. John Tizard has captured them particularly well: 

[The public sector] can secure good terms and conditions for 

staff through contract terms and a willingness to pay for 
them . 
. 
. It is vital that we stop any return to the dark days of 

the worst excesses of compulsory competitive tendering where 

contracts were won on the basis of who could drive employ- 
ment terms and wages down the most. This was not clever then. 

It is most certainly not sustainable in a modern society. !*4 

But, sustainable or not, this, it appears, is precisely where things 
now stand: the ‘dark days’ referred to by Tizard have indeed 

returned, and with a vengeance. As early as 2012, Ursula Huws 
and Sarah Podro sounded the alarm, painting a dismal picture of 
employment conditions for workers on both public- and private- 
sector contracts.’ Job security was limited. The scope for collec- 

tive bargaining had been radically attenuated by the splintering 
of workforces. And, crucially, there was precious little evidence 
of either worker equality or cohesion, as even workers ‘perform- 
ing the same role on the same site, who were previously colleagues, 
found themselves on differing terms and conditions’ 
.!2° 
Two years later, the Smith Institute released an equally damn- 

ing report. Among the effects of contracting out were the reduc- 

tion or cutting off of career progression paths for lower-paid 

workers, worsened pension arrangements, and pay reductions — 

albeit not for managers and specialists, whose pay often increased, 
thus opening up greater pay differentials and resulting in greater 

inequality.'”” All of this, it should be noted, is not a bug.but a 

feature of contract capitalism — something written into the 

recipe, even if in invisible ink. As a perceptive UK employment

lawyer remarked in 2017: ‘Employees supplied to a client by an 

outsourced service provider, and able to claim parity with that 

client’s own employees’ terms and conditions, would undermine 

one of the key principles of outsourcing, which is to protect the 

client from employee liabilities.’ If working for a contractor were 

the same as working for the contractee, it would, she ventured, 

‘almost make outsourcing pointless .!”* Squeezing labour is partly 
what outsourcing is for. 

The Smith Institute nominated the adult social care sector as 

‘the most dramatic, whole-scale example of the role of outsourc-

finding in it ‘widespread non-compliance with the minimum

What has made matters considerably worse is that workers in 

the outsourcing sector have-in recent years been on the receiving

ening of employment protections. In 2010, in particular, the

private-sector

and 
which,

Thus, a two-tier workforce is what the UK undoubtedly now 

has. For example, Unison, the country’s leading health union,

An especially telling recent case concerned a group of security

ment conditions to those employed directly by the university, the

YS} 

negotiate directly with their de facto employer.’'® Such a possi- 

bility remains, for now, a dim and distant prospect. 

Given the well-publicized difficulties faced, and damage caused, 
by contract rentierism in the UK in recent times, it is unsur- 
prising that it has faced a backlash. Criticism of outsourcing by 

the public sector has been especially conspicuous and biting. 
Dozens of opinion columns have raged against the ‘spivvery’, 

to quote Aditya Chakrabortty, that ubiquitous public-sector 

contracting out represents.'*° And the government appears to 

have relented somewhat — for instance, terminating ahead of 

time the contracts of the private probation companies; cancel- 

ling the contracts of two TOCs and returning their passenger 

rail franchises (the Northern and East Coast lines, run respec- 

tively by Arriva and a Stagecoach—Virgin Group joint venture) 

to public-sector operation in the shape of the government's 

‘operator of last resort’; and greatly reducing the number of PFI 

projects since the scheme was relaunched as ‘PF2’ in 2012.'°” 

In early 2019, Will Hutton — an inveterate critic — felt sufh- 

ciently confident of a change in the climate to announce noth- 

ing less than the ‘death knell’ of the neoliberal British state's 

‘mania for hiving off public services’.'*® 

But Hutton was being wildly premature. Neoliberalism, in the 
UK at least, is alive and generally well; and so too is the public- 

sector outsourcing fetish at its beating heart. For all the criticism 

of the model, and notwithstanding the decline specifically of 

PFI, the public sector continues to outsource with abandon — 

albeit using public financing to fund outsourced construction 

projects, where in the past PFI might have been used. For every 

project or work package fulfilled internally or brought back 

in-house, many more are still contracted out, including big- 

ticket assignments in publicly sensitive areas. In 2019, for exam- 

ple, Serco won £1.8 billion of work on a new round of contracts 

providing housing for asylum seekers in the UK over a ten-year 

period.

CHAPTER SIX 

The X-Factor: Infrastructure Rents 

\ 

In my discussion of platform rentiers in Chapter 4, one digital 

giant — indeed, the biggest of them all by market value — received 

relatively little attention: Amazon. This was not intended to 

suggest that the e-commerce goliath, with UK revenues of 
approximately $15 billion per annum, is nota 
rentier. It certainly 

is, at least partly; and platform rentierism — in the form of 
Amazon Marketplace, which, like eBay, connects consumers to 

third-party sellers — 
is clearly part of the mix. Increasingly, 

however, Amazon is a different type of rentier, controlling a 

different type of asset base, and earning a different form of rent. 

Consider, firstly, Amazon Web Services (AWS), comfortably 

Amazon's most profitable business. In establishing and growing 

its marquee online retail operation — the Amazon we are all famil- 

iar with — in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Amazon developed 

formidable proprietary computing capacity located at server 

farms around the world. When, in the mid 2000s, Amazon began 

to make this capacity, which was originally solely for internal use, 

available to third parties, AWS was born: a business offering server 

space and distributed (cloud) computing facilities and function- 

alities to a wide range of corporate and public-sector clients. 

And consider, secondly, Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA). As well 

as 
building computer 
capacity 
to support 
its own 
retail 

278 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

operations, Amazon had also, from early on, built physical fulfil- 
ment and delivery capacity, and it began making this capacity 

available to companies selling via Amazon Marketplace around 

the same time that it opened up its server capacity to third parties. 

Thus was born FBA: Amazon's logistics and delivery business, 

offering sellers storage, packing and shipping services through its 

vast international network of warehouses, sorting centres and 

delivery stations. 

Both AWS and FBA are the fruits, in others words, of Amazon’s 

having built crucial infrastructures for the delivery of its own 

services, and then making those service-delivery infrastructures 
commercially available — one might say, renting them out — to third 

parties for the delivery of their services. They are both, that is, infra- 

structure rentiers. Indeed, inasmuch as part of the price paid for, say, 
books by Amazon's own retail customers is payment to cover the 

costs of the proprietary virtual and physical infrastructure assets 
that make such a transaction possible, Amazon has always been an 
infrastructure rentier to an extent. However, with the development 
and growth of AWS and FBA, this rentierism has become not just 
more explicit, but — more significantly — increasingly Amazon’s core 
enterprise. As Lina Khan observed, in one of the best pieces ever 
written about the company, Amazon has ‘emerged as central infra- 
structure for the internet economy’. Moreover: 

Reports suggest this was part of [chief executive Jeff] Bezos’s 

vision from the start. According to early Amazon employees, 

when the CEO founded the business, ‘his underlying goals 

were not to build an online bookstore or an online retailer, but 

rather a “utility” that would become essential to commerce.’ 

In other words, Bezos’s target customer was not only end- 
consumers but also other businesses. Amazon controls key 

critical infrastructure for the Internet economy — in ways that 

are difficult for new entrants to replicate or compete against. 
This gives the company a key advantage over its rivals: 
Amazon's competitors have come to depend on it.! 

THE X-FACTOR 
27/9 

Platform rentiers, of course, also control crucial infrastructures 

(see Chapter 4). But those infrastructures — the platforms them- 

selves — serve the sole purpose of intermediation, whatever the 

nature of the trade (in labour, capital, commodities or attention) 

that such intermediation is ultimately designed, directly or indi- 

rectly, to enable. Infrastructure rentierism is fundamentally differ- 

ent insofar as the infrastructure is integral to service delivery. 

Amazon is far from the only company to have established itself 

as a significant infrastructure rentier in the UK in recent decades 
by building, more or less from scratch, substantial proprietary, 
commercially exploitable service-delivery infrastructures. But if 
some major UK infrastructure rentiers are indeed self-made, 
having organically developed the infrastructures at the core of 

their business models, the majority are not. Most of the country’s 
infrastructure rentiers came into being through a very different 
and much more abrupt process. ‘That process was privatization. 

Since Margaret Thatcher kick-started the programme in the 

early 1980s, the UK has come to be seen as the world’s undis- 
puted privatization trailblazer, and is acknowledged as such both 
by those broadly supportive of the project — the Financial Times 

refers to ‘pioneering Britain — and those resolutely opposed — Joe 
Guinan and Thomas Hanna, for example, describing privatiza- 

tion as ‘a very British disease’. Less often recognized, though, is 

the fact that most major UK privatizations were privatizations of 

a very particular type. They involved the transfer to private 

ownership of state-owned enterprises with substantial asset bases, 

and more specifically substantial infrastructural assets; and those 

assets were typically used for the delivery to the public of services 

generally referred to as ‘utilities’, including but not limited to 

energy supply (electricity and gas), water and sewerage, teleph- 

ony, and certain forms of transport. 

Indeed, in the UK today, precious few utilities continue to be 

provided by public bodies controlling public infrastructures — 
noteworthy examples being below-ground rapid transit services in 
London (the responsibility of London Underground, which is a 

280 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

subsidiary of a statutory corporation, Transport for London) and 

water and sewerage services in Northern Ireland and Scotland (the 

responsibility, respectively, of Northern Ireland Water and Scottish 

Water, which are also state-owned enterprises). The fact that the 

biggest remaining public provider of an infrastructure-based util- 

ity, the owner and operator of most of the national railway network 

— Network Rail — is today in public hands only because privatiza- 

tion, and the creation of the notorious infrastructure rentier 

Railtrack, was an unmitigated failure and had to be reversed, tells 

its own story about the wider direction of travel in neoliberal 

Britain. ‘That story is the main subject of this chapter. 

Where privatization became a watchword of post-1970s UK 
governments, especially Conservative governments, nationaliza- 

tion had been a watchword of the Labour government that came 

to power in 1945 after the end of World War II. The UK’s major 
utility sectors were thought to be in need of privatization in the 
neoliberal era only because they had been brought under state 
ownership a few decades earlier. Moreover, as Chris Rhodes and 
his co-authors have noted, a ‘ “post-war consensus” between the

remained until the 1970s’? Even then, they continue (citing

Government that state industries should be privatised.’ In

nue raising measures introduced following negotiations with

only briefly referred to privatisation .

The decisive period of policy shift was 1979-83. By the latter 

date, following the 1981 privatization most notably of British 
Aerospace (the forerunner of BAE Systems, discussed in Chapters 
3 and 5), the position of the Tory government was explicitly that 

‘state ownership should be the exception rather than the norm’. 

This shift set the stage for ‘a rapid expansion of the privatisation

Table 6.1 lists the major privatizations that have since taken 

place, showing that they were concentrated in the period from 

1983 to the mid 1990s.‘ The date given in each case is the year in 

which the privatization took place — or, where it took place in

those privatizations that partly or wholly seeded significant infra- 

structure rentiers as I have preliminarily defined them here: that is, 

private companies exploiting exclusive control of service-delivery 

infrastructures (including mobile infrastructure assets, such as 

ferries). Two types of entities that feature in Table 6.1 but do not 

meet this definition (and hence are not shaded) warrant comment. 

Firstly, infrastructure rentiers do not include product manufactur- 

ers and their ‘infrastructure’ of machinery and factories, such as 

the privatized Rolls Royce, British Steel, or Rover Group; infra- 

structure rentierism is about service delivery. Nor, secondly, do 

infrastructure rentiers include high-street retailers (such as the 

privatized Tote), whose ‘infrastructure’ is simply land and build- 

ings (see Chapter 7) rather than anything more bespoke. 

If infrastructure rentierism is about service delivery, it is, more 

exactly, about the infrastructure of service delivery, and control of 

that infrastructure. The infrastructure itself is the core asset, 

control of which engenders rental payments in some form. To 

take the post-privatization rail sector as an example, the rolling- 

stock operating companies (ROSCOs), such as Angel Trains, are 

infrastructure rentiers, their business model being to lease the 

vehicles they own (the infrastructure) to train operating compa- 

nies (TOCs). The latter, by contrast, are not infrastructure rent-

of franchises issued by the Department for Transport, they are 

instead contract rentiers (see Chapter 5). 

The example of the rail industry is also useful in highlighting 

a final important definitional point, which is that an entity that 

controls infrastructure that is fundamental to delivery of a 

particular service does not itself have to deliver that service to 

qualify as an infrastructure rentier. Many such rentiers do provide 

the service: the UK’s water companies, for instance, which both 
own the infrastructure — the pipeline networks, waterworks, 
pumps, reservoirs, and so forth — and deliver the water and 

sewerage services routed by that infrastructure. But others, like 

the ROSCOs, do not. In their case, what the rentier is selling to 

third-party service providers (such as the TOCs) is access to infra- 

structure. This, if you like, is infrastructure rentierism in its 

purest, most unvarnished form: as in the case of Amazon’s AWS 
and FBA, the third party pays rent in return for use of infrastruc- 

ture that the asset owner finances and maintains. 

Where, as with the water companies, the asset owner is also the 

service provider, the company’s service provision ‘arm’ — I use the 

scare quotes because there is not an actual discrete such entity: the 
demarcation is mine — effectively pays an internal rent to the 

infrastructure ‘arm’, and that infrastructure rental cost is passed 

on to the customer (here, the consumer of water and sewerage 

services) without being visible as such. In some cases, however — 

often for regulatory reasons — there are in fact two such operating 

arms, institutionally incorporated as such and legally ring-fenced 

from one another; and the internal infrastructure rent is thus an 

actual, identifiable payment. A good example is a company we 

have already encountered, Arqiva, one arm of which owns, main- 

tains and sells access to the UK’s transmission infrastructure for 

radio and terrestrial television (comprising a mast and site network 

and shareable antenna systems), and another arm of which is the 

licensed operator of four of the eight network multiplexes into 

which signals are bundled for transmission. The latter arm pays 

fees (infrastructure rent) to the former on an arm’s-length basis.° 

284 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

The bottom line, at any rate, is that, in all cases of infrastruc- 

ture rentierism, the infrastructure is indispensable to the delivery 
of the service, and the controller is compensated accordingly. 
You cannot supply electricity without transmission networks 

(which transfer power from generating facilities to substations) 

and distribution networks (comprising smaller, shorter, low- 

voltage lines taking electricity from substations to businesses and 
homes) — those two types of networks, incidentally, being owned 
and operated independently of one another in the UK. Equally, 
you cannot broadcast television without a transmission network 

(terrestrial, cable or satellite-based); you cannot run rail services 
without track (still publicly owned in the UK) and rolling stock; 
and you cannot offer national mail collection and delivery 

services without a mail collection and distribution infrastructure 
(post boxes, mail centres, push-trolleys and vans). While some of 
these rent-generating infrastructures have been largely built by 
private companies, most, in the UK at least, have not: they were 
privatized in ready-made, rent-ready form, usually by way of 
public share offerings (as in the cases of British Gas, British 
Telecom and Royal Mail), though occasionally through sale to 

existing private companies or management-led buyouts. 

Whoever the original investors were, the privatization of the UK’s 

publicly owned, infrastructure-based service-delivery sectors repre- 

sented a bonanza from the start. As even the most ardent champions 
of such privatizations admit, the government rarely secured a good 

deal for taxpayers upon disposal. On Nigel Hawkins’s reckoning, for 
example, many of the enterprises were ‘grossly undervalued’.” 

Writing for the free-market Adam Smith Institute, Hawkins 
mentions in particular the regional electricity companies, which, he 
calculates, were subject to ‘severe underpricing’ when floated on the 
Stock Exchange in 1990.8 And the lessons were not learned. In the 

case of the UK’s biggest utility privatization of the new millennium, 
that of Royal Mail in 2013 — also conducted by way of a public'share 

offering — the extent of undervaluation was arguably even greater. 

THE X-FACTOR 
285 

The National Audit Office, the Public Accounts Committee and the 

Business, Innovation and Skills Select Committee all subsequently 

wrote scathing reports about the handling of the transaction, the last 

of these estimating the loss to the taxpayer at a cool £1 billion.’ 

Investment institutions had positively beaten down the door to get 

their hands on the underpriced Royal Mail shares — which were 
twenty-four times oversubscribed; the electricity companies’ shares, 
by way of comparison, had been ‘only’ ten times oversubscribed.'° 

Indeed, where the privatized utilities owners have been 
concerned, the post-privatization period has generally been one 
long boon: substantial profit-extraction opportunities were by 

no means limited to the privatization event itself. To begin to 
understand why infrastructure rentierism can be so lucrative, it is 

necessary first of all to explore in some detail the nature of the 

businesses concerned. Recall how I defined rent in the Preface: 
income derived from the ownership, possession or control of 

scarce assets under conditions of limited or no competition. Most of 

the private-sector infrastructure rentiers created through the 
privatizations itemized in Table 6.1 comfortably satisfy this 

‘limited or no competition’ criterion. Most of them, more 

precisely, are monopolists; and monopoly power, of course, 
frequently delivers monopoly pricing and profits. 

In fact, it is possible to be more specific still. Most of the 

companies in question are what economists refer to as ‘natural 

monopolists’, enjoying so-called natural monopolies. Writing in 

1968, Richard Posner defined a situation of natural monopoly as 

one in which ‘the entire demand within a relevant market can be 

satisfied at lowest cost by one firm rather than by two or more’."! 

Significantly, Posner’s main examples of industry sectors charac- 

terized by natural monopoly were exactly the ones that the UK's 

Conservative government would set about privatizing with such 

gusto a little over a decade later: gas, water, and electric power 

supply, and public transportation and telecommunications. It is 

not hard to see why natural monopoly obtains in these utility 

sectors. Consider the case of water supply within a geographically 

286 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

delimited area. Moving from a‘ monopoly to non-monopoly 
supply structure would entail duplicated infrastructure — for 
example, multiple sets of pipes — and duplicated costs, thus 
consuming more resources than are necessary. This, Posner said, 
would be an inherently inefficient outcome. Monopoly was ‘natu- 

ral’, then, specifically in the sense that it was most efficient. 

In some of the privatized utility sectors, the British government 

has sought to introduce elements of competition, most notably in 

electricity retailing. Today, suppliers — of which there are dozens — 
buy electricity from generators at wholesale prices in the competitive 

spot market. But electricity retailers are not infrastructure rentiers; 
they do not control transmission or distribution networks (or any 

other significant infrastructure assets). It is much harder to introduce 
competition into the transmission or distribution parts of the busi- 

ness, precisely because this is where conditions of natural monopoly 
apply. ‘Thus, there are still numerous natural monopolists active in 
the UK’s post-privatization utility landscape — including, although 
not only, in electricity transmission and distribution themselves. 

Nobody has captured the rentier characteristics of this post- 
privatization landscape as clearly, and with such a keen eye to the 
implications, as James Meek. Writing of the water sector, where 
the commercial English and Welsh operators enjoy regional 
monopolies, Meek describes 

millions of customers who have no choice of supplier, no 

choice but to take the water, and no choice but to pay for it. 

Millions of captive monthly payments in perpetiinjee a 
form of buy-to-let scheme, with us, the customers, as the 

tenants, paying water bills, like rent; the shareholders as land- 

lords, owning the water companies; and the company staff, 

like a property management agency, collecting the rent and 
maintaining the property .. 
. [If] we don’t like the property, 

the management agency or the landlords, or if we think the 

rent is too high, we don't have any choice. We can’t move to a 

cheaper property, or a better-run one; we're stuck. !2 

THE X-FACTOR 
287 

Hence, when the government privatized the water sector and the 

other public enterprises formerly charged with delivering the 

nation’s ‘essential services’, what it was ultimately selling off, 
Meek observes, was not only infrastructure, but captive ‘bill- 
paying citizens’.'° The former occasioned the latter, and it was of 

course the latter — specifically, citizens’ state of captivity and obli- 

gation to continue to pay — that gave value to the former. 

Crucially, moreover, the infrastructure business has a monop- 

oly tendency even if the strict condition of natural monopoly 

originally stipulated by Posner does not apply — which, outside 

the utility sectors, it often does not. This tendency, too, is easy to 

understand. 
Simply stated, 
infrastructure ‘is expensive. A 
company has to have deep pockets, or access to others’ deep 

pockets, even to consider playing in the infrastructure space. 
Generally speaking, the bigger the infrastructure business — the 
more customers it serves — the greater the cost of the infrastruc- 

ture, in the form of pipes, cables, ports, and so on. Not only are 

the entry barriers large, then; they tend to become larger with 

time as a market grows and matures, conferring significant 
advantage on the fabled ‘first mover’, and ineluctably reducing 

the likelihood of the emergence of new players. 

Amazon's two infrastructure rentier businesses — Fulfillment 
by Amazon and Amazon Web Services — are excellent examples 

of businesses displaying these non-natural monopoly tendencies. 

Replicating the vast infrastructures underpinning either one 

would be prohibitively costly. Writing about AWS, for example, 

Tom Krazit recently noted that ‘its first-mover advantage has 

lingered well into its second decade’ — its share of the market 

having held steady at around one-third for several years — precisely 

because ‘it takes an enormous amount of investment to create a 

cloud infrastructure network that can compete with AWS’."4
