THE X-FACTOR 
289 

The consequences of monopoly power being widespread among 

the UK’s leading infrastructure rentiers are broadly those one 
would expect, and with which we are already familiar. Three sets 

of consequences stand out. 

The first is monopoly pricing. The water sector is the example 
most commented upon. By 2015, retail water bills had increased 

in real terms by an average of some 40 per cent since the sector 

was privatized in 1989, the steepest price increases occurring 
during the 1990s.'° The water sector’s experience is closer to 

being the norm than the exception. When the Financial Times's 
Martin Wolf — hardly noted for his socialism — declared in 2008 

that ‘Britain’s utility model is broken’, one of his main criticisms 

of the ‘flawed’ model whereby infrastructure-based 
public 
monopolies had been transferred into the hands of private 
companies ‘that own, run and develop the assets’ was that it had 
proved ‘excessively costly to consumers’ not just in the water 

sector but also, among others, in the cases of ‘airports, nuclear 

power, electricity and gas networks’.'° 

Writing seven years later, also from a free-market standpoint, 

Nigel Hawkins agreed. Because of ‘the lack of competition in many 

utility sectors, the UK’s great utility-privatization experiment had 

led to ‘marked real price increases’ more or less across the board.'” 

Indeed, for both Wolf and Hawkins, there was only one substantive 

exception to the rule: telecommunications, where, partly thanks to 

the advent of mobile telephony, meaningful competition had 

emerged since privatization; and where, accordingly, consumer 

prices had, observed Hawkins, ‘fallen materially’."® 

The second set of consequences is closely related to the first. As 

we have seen in earlier chapters, the possession of monopoly 
power tends not only to encourage price rises, but also to elicit a 

certain indolence. Monopolists do not need to innovate and 

invest to remain in business; with captive customers, they can 

relax. Again, both Wolf and Hawkins serve as powerful witnesses 

for the prosecution. Wolf's second main criticism of Britain’s 

290 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

‘broken’ utility model was precisely that it had served as ‘an 

obstacle to investment — that is, an obstacle to investment in the 
physical infrastructures of service delivery themselves, not in the 
companies that owned and operated those infrastructures — an 

important distinction to be borne in mind in what follows. 

Privatized utility providers, cossetted by monopoly conditions, 

had, according to Wolf, been sweating their infrastructure assets 

rather than improving and upgrading them.” 

Hawkins’s assessment — telecoms again excepted — was perhaps 

even more damning. “Despite some efforts to provide incentives 

for innovation, he wrote, ‘the fact remains that R&¢D expendi- 

ture in the electricity, gas and especially the water sector is 

extremely modest. By way of example, Severn Trent, currently 

capitalised at almost £5 billion, invested just £5 million in R&¢D 
in 2013/14. That equated to 0.1 per cent of the company’s 
value — or 0.3 per cent of 
its revenues of £1.9 billion in the same 
year. Meanwhile, 
Railtrack, 
the private company that had 
assumed ownership of the bulk of the fixed railway infrastructure 
(track, stations, signalling, tunnels, bridges and level crossings) 
upon the sector’s privatization, was, noted Hawkins, ‘widely 
believed to have heavily underinvested’ prior to its collapse in 
2001. Hawkins also made special mention of the former airport 
owner and operator BAA plc, a ‘disproportionate part of whose 
investment budget had evidently ‘been directed at providing 
expensive retail facilities rather than improving airport infra- 
structure’.”! Rent-seeking, in short, has been rife. 

Indeed, BAA makes for an interesting case study. Created 
through the privatization of the British Airports Authority in 
1987, BAA originally owned and operated seven UK airports 

(Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted in England, and Aberdeen, 
Edinburgh, Glasgow and Prestwick in Scotland); charges to 

airlines for take-off and landing slots represented the lion’s share 
of its revenues. Being commercially sensitive, these charges — 

classic infrastructure rents — are notoriously opaque. But the slots 

are sufficiently valuable and scarce for the European Union, for 

THE X-FACTOR 
BOIL 

example, to operate an 80/20 rule, whereby, under normal 

circumstances, airlines must use 
a minimum of 80 per cent of 

the slots they have been allocated or risk losing them to a compet- 

itor; and information as to the scale of the rents that such slots 

generate for airport operators does occasionally seep into the 

public domain, either when airlines trade the slots among them- 

selves and report the amounts paid, or when airlines go bust and 

their rivals swoop in to feed on their carcasses. In the latter 

scenario, airport slots are normally the only valuable assets that 

remain — other than any proprietary aircraft.” In 2017, when 
Monarch Airlines collapsed, British Airways acquired its twenty 
prime slots at Gatwick for a rumoured £50! million, giving a 
good indication of how much Monarch had originally paid 
Gatwick’s owner for them. More recently, EasyJet paid £36 
million to buy slots at Gatwick and Bristol airports from the 

collapsed travel operator Thomas Cook.” 

Despite the ‘regular’ surfacing during the two decades follow- 
ing the privatization of the British Airports Authority of what 

two observers later described as ‘concerns over BAA’s dominant 

position in the UK’s civil aviation market’, no steps were taken 

to address that dominance until as late as 2008, when an inquiry 

by the Competition Commission concluded that, because of 

their common ownership, there was ‘no competition’ between 

BAA’s UK airports, which at the time controlled over 80 per cent 

of London’s runway capacity and serviced over 60 per cent of 
UK passengers.” Monopoly, the inquiry found, had massively 

dulled any competitive instincts the company might have had. If 

BAA was a case study in anything, it was commercial torpor. The 

chairman of the inquiry remarked: “We are particularly concerned 

by [BAA’s] apparent lack of responsiveness to the differing needs 

of its airline customers, and hence passengers, and the conse- 

quences for the levels, quality, scope, location and timing of 

investment and levels and quality of service’.” 

The third and final consequence of the fact that monopoly 

conditions 
have 
long permeated 
the UK 
landscape 
of 

DOP 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

infrastructure rentierism is that the landscape has also long been 

a magnet for financial investment institutions. And it is no 
wonder. While most such institutions offer bland generalities 
and buzzwords when describing their investment strategies — 
well-balanced and diversified portfolios, sustained returns, long- 

term value growth, and so on — a rogue individual occasionally 
departs from the party line and explains what it is that really 

attracts investors. Ihe answer is monopoly — monopoly protected 
by barriers to entry, and generating, in turn, monopoly prices 
and profits. Here, with a refreshingly honest statement, is Mark 

Kiesel, deputy chief investment officer of the global investment 
giant PIMCO: 

At PIMCO, we have refocused our bottom-up credit analysis 

on identifying industries globally with pricing power and/or 
compelling growth prospects . 
. 
. That is why high barriers to 
entry are an important characteristic for the sustainability of 
attractive economic profits. If an industry’s structure discour- 

ages new entrants, it passes an important screen in our invest- 
ment process and therefore warrants further assessment. While 
an industry with high barriers to entry does not automatically 
generate excess profit, it does offer competitive shelter — and 

the higher the barrier to entry, the greater the prospect for 

above-average returns.”° 

Capital, 
as David Harvey has observed, 
is ‘in love with 
monopoly 
.”” 

Given what we know about the high barriers to entry and 
monopoly tendencies that characterize infrastructure-intensive 

utility industries, it is unsurprising that such industries — ‘energy, 

wireless telecom, cell towers, cable, satellite’ — featured promi- 

nently on the list of sectors that Kiesel identified as meeting 
PIMCO’s stringent investment criteria.22 Where in the world 
have opportunities for footloose investment institutions such as 
PIMCO to invest in these industries been especially abundant in 

THE X-FACTOR 
2935 

recent decades? In the UK, of course. Jonathan Ford, City editor 

at the Financial Times, has articulated this mouth-watering 

national investment proposition particularly well: 

Imagine you are a Canadian pension scheme or a private 

equity group, spinning your globe thoughtfully, looking for 
some utility investments to place all those savings you are 
looking after. Where does your thumb land? More likely than 

not, you alight on Britain. It is the obvious choice. Few states 

have embraced privatisation of essential services with quite as 
much enthusiasm. What started in 1984 with the sale of 

British Telecom has been steadily extended over the decades to 

include water, 
electricity, 
gas, airports and even 
critical 

communications networks, such as television transmission.” 

And so, while there have been hardly any new operational 

entrants to the business of infrastructure rentierism in the UK 

since the heyday of privatization, the reverse is true of investor 

entrants, because what precludes the former — barriers to entry 

— entices the latter. Having scrambled to get hold of shares when 
monopolist public enterprises were originally privatized, as we 
saw in relation to the electricity companies and Royal Mail, 

investment institutions have continued throughout the interven- 

ing years to tussle for UK infrastructural equity. 

Table 6.2 demonstrates this clearly: the ownership picture of 

the UK’s biggest infrastructure rentiers is today dominated by 

major financial investment institutions from around the world, 

as yield-hungry capital has been lured to the country’s vast pool 

of infrastructure-based monopoly rents like a moth to a flame. 

Two important patterns 
to 
this institutional 
investment 

tableau merit comment. First, it is striking how many infrastruc- 

ture companies that were once publicly listed no longer are. 

Cadent Gas, UK Power Networks, Western Power Distribution, 

Associated British Ports (ABP), Anglian Water and ‘Thames 
Water (and many other UK infrastructure rentiers not shown in 

294 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the table) are all examples of ptivately owned companies that 

were — or that have emerged from the combination of companies 

that were — floated on the Stock Exchange at privatization, but 

have since been taken private. No longer content with the limited 

financial gains and — no less importantly — limited operational 

influence afforded by small minority stakes, major investment 

houses have swooped to take control of these rentiers — some- 

times independently, but more often as part of investment 

consortia. 

Second, just as strikingly, the table reveals a remarkable, 

tangled web of cross-investment. Allianz Capital Partners owns 

stakes in Cadent Gas and Porterbrook Leasing Company; IFM 

Investors owns stakes in Anglian Water and Arqiva. Other insti- 

tutions that hold investment positions in two different sectors 

include Dalmore Capital and OMERS Infrastructure (an invest- 
ment house, despite the name). But the prize goes to the Canada 
Pension Plan Investment Board, which owns significant stakes in 
companies in no fewer than three different sectors: ports (ABP), 
telecoms 
(Arqiva) and water and sewerage 
(Anglian). CK 
Hutchison also holds stakes in companies in three different 
sectors — two via CK Infrastructure Holdings, of which it is the 
majority owner; but it is an operating conglomerate rather than 

a financial investment institution. 

Why would a financial institution — or, for that matter, a 
conglomerate like CK Hutchison — make major strategic invest- 

ments simultaneously in sectors as diverse as ports, telecoms, and 

water and sewerage? The answer, of course, is that the same 

essential business model applies in each case. On the surface, you 
might appear to be buying very different businesses, with very 

different infrastructures. After all, what — in Hutchison’s case — 
do electricity distribution networks, train rolling-stock and 
mobile telephony assets have in common? At heart, though, as 
James Meek recognized, what the likes of Hutchison and the 
Canadian pensions fund manager are actually buying in all these 
instances is always the same: bill-paying customers and the 

THE X-FACTOR 
oF 

captive rents that, directly or indirectly, they pay to monopoly 
infrastructure owners. 

But let us return to the one infrastructure sector identified by 
Martin Wolf and Nigel Hawkins as a substantive exception to 

the post-privatization rule of rising consumer prices and weak 

investment: 
telecommunications. 
As 
Hawkins 
notes, 
UK 
consumers of telecoms services have benefited from both falling 

prices and significant investment-fuelled innovation since BT’s 

privatization (as British Telecom), in 1984. Hawkins argues, 

surely correctly, that the arrival of mass-market mobile telephony 
played a key role, representing as it did ‘a new aggressive compet- 

itor to fixed-line telecoms operators’, and thus keeping BT on its 

toes. Where other utility sectors have seen no new entrants of 

any significance in recent decades, telecoms — specifically the 
mobile market — has heralded new names. As Hawkins says, BT’s 
privatization took place ‘just two years after the incorporation of 

Vodafone as a subsidiary of Racal Electronics; within a decade, 
Vodafone had become a leading mobile telecoms company’. It is 

also noteworthy that, while in other sectors investors have made 

hay at the same time as consumers have fared poorly, investors in 
BT — whose consumer telephone charges have fallen substan- 

tially in real terms since 1984 — have not been so fortunate. Its 

return to shareholders since flotation has, Hawkins says, been 

‘dire’.*° 

Telecoms’ exceptionality extends, moreover, to the method of 

allocation to the private sector of key public assets — if not in the 

case of BT itself (the privatization of which was via the ‘standard’ 

route of a public share offering, again beset by claims of under- 

valuation), then certainly in the important case of radio spec- 

trum. Over recent decades, spectrum has emerged as a signifi- 

cant locus of infrastructure rentierism. Referring to a particular 

range of frequencies of electromagnetic energy that can be used 

for various types of communication, radio spectrum is often 

likened to land; it represents, so to speak, virtual real estate. Like 

296 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

land, it is a finite, and thus scarce, resource; and, like land, any 

part of the spectrum can accommodate only a limited number of 

uses, primarily due to the potential for interference. ‘The result is 

that, in most countries, the state, which ‘owns’ radio spectrum, 

licenses exclusive rights to use certain frequencies for certain 

purposes over specified geographical areas and for specified peri- 

ods of time. Where those uses enable licensees to generate reve- 

nues, the latter clearly constitute rents, insofar as they derive 

from exclusive commercial control of a scarce asset: usable spec- 
trum. Today there is a wide range of commercially viable uses for 

radio spectrum. Broadcasting of radio and television is one; 

provision of mobile Internet services is another. 

Governments methods for allocating spectrum to commercial 

licensees vary somewhat between countries. Traditionally, the 
preferred method was a so-called ‘beauty contest’, in which 

candidates submitted business plans for use of the infrastructure, 
and the government awarded licences to those it believed best 
met its published criteria. During the 1990s, beginning in the 
United States in 1994, preferences shifted towards allocation via 
auction, which has since become the default method interna- 

tionally. In the UK, the government 
first used an auction 
approach in 2000, awarding five licences for third-generation 
(3G) mobile services. Further major auction rounds for mobile 
services (auction-based licensing of spectrum for radio and tele- 
vision has occurred in parallel) concluded in 2013 (4G services) 
and 2018 (4G and 5G). 

Certainly, 
there 
are 
legitimate grounds 
to question 
the 
approach used. For one thing, some observers, including the 

Culture, Media and Sport Committee in 2011, have worried 

that the heavy focus of spectrum policy on mobile Internet 

services has prevented other users and uses from getting a look 

in.*' Relatedly, the prioritization of ‘efficiency’ considerations at 
each mobile auction has essentially reduced ‘best business plan’ 

to ‘highest bidder’, thus erecting formidable barriers to’ new 
entrants. Indeed, only in the 2000 auction did a non-incumbent 

THE X-FACTOR 
DY. 

(in the shape of the CK Hutchison-owned 3 Group: hardly a 
minnow) take a licence — and then perhaps only because one 

licence was reserved for a new entrant. Nevertheless, one thing 

the UK government cannot be accused of in the case of spectrum 

allocation is undervaluing the assets in question. Each mobile 

auction round has brought in vast sums from bidders. In 2000, 

the government raised an eye-watering £22.5 billion, in what the 
economists who designed the auction subsequently described as 

the world’s biggest auction ‘since the Praetorian Guard knocked 
down the entire Roman Empire to Didius Julianus in AD 195’. 

But even 
in the ‘exceptional’ telecommunications 
sector, 

recent years have witnessed increased rumblings of discontent 

about widespread instances of what amounts, in the final reckon- 

ing, to rent-seeking — and in forms uncannily similar to those 

visible in other UK infrastructure sectors. In 2018, for example, 

the price-comparison website Billmonitor published a report 

claiming that UK small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) 

were overpaying for mobile services by £1 billion, due to a lack 

of competition in the market. Sampling 356 business accounts 

with the ‘big three’ providers (BT/EE, Vodafone and Telefénica/ 

O2), it estimated that around half of businesses were paying 
more than twice what they should have been.*° 

Price, however, has been less of a concern than investment and 

service. Two particular sets of criticisms on these latter grounds 

have become headline news. The first pertains, again, to mobile 

services. Here, the charge is that providers of both voice and data 

services generally offer only very patchy coverage. An influential 

2016 report by a cross-party group of MPs calling itself the 

British Infrastructure Group (BIG), for example, found that, on 

average, mobile users could access 4G services only around half 

the time.*4 At the end of the following year, it was reported that 

only 43 per cent of the UK by area could receive a 4G signal 

from all four main mobile operators. Lord Adonis, chair of the 

government's National Infrastructure Commission (NIC), called 

the figure ‘deplorable’.° Rural areas were found to be particularly 

298 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

poorly served, with an estimated 28 per cent of rural Britain 
remaining without coverage from any operator in 2016. Just 35 

per cent of mobile users in Wales, for instance, were able to access 
4G services.*° 

BIG, for its part, blamed a lack of competition in the under- 

served regions for this state of affairs; but a better word than 
competition is probably ‘incentive’. The UK’s mobile operators 
have been geographically selective in building out their networks, 

cherry-picking densely populated hot-spots. In sparsely popu- 

lated rural areas (the so-called ‘not-spots’ without coverage), the 

subscriber rents potentially available from service provision 
simply do not justify the necessary infrastructure investment. 
Think of it as another type of ‘rent gap’. Like financial rentiers, 

infrastructure 
rentiers 
are exclusionary. To paraphrase Joan 
Robinson, from a consumer's perspective the only thing worse 
than paying rent to a rentier is not even having the opportunity 

to do so. 

The second set of criticisms, meanwhile, relates to fixed-line 

services, and more specifically to BT. BT owns and — through its 
Openreach division — operates the UK’s core fixed-line transmis- 

sion network, as well as the vast majority of local access networks 

— the so-called ‘local loops’ that connect customers to their local 
exchanges. Customers are connected up by Openreach engineers 
irrespective of whether they buy their telecoms services from BT: 

for over a decade, the UK local loop has been ‘unbundled’, which 
means that rival operators, now numbering in the hundreds, can 

offer fixed-line broadband and phone services over BT’s infta- 
structure, in effect paying Openreach a rent for network access. 

Recent years have seen a welter of criticisms of Openreach, 

which, it is said, offers subpar Internet (slow speeds have been a 

particular bugbear) and poor customer service, and has massively 
underinvested in the network. Some of these criticisms should 
perhaps be viewed with caution inasmuch as they have been 
made by rivals — Sky, for example, complained in 2015 that it 
was taking Openreach up to ten days to connect its new 

THE X-FACTOR 
299 

broadband customers.*” But similar criticisms have increasingly 
been levelled by more neutral observers. Another BIG report 
from 2016, for example, found that around 5.7 million people 

in the UK ‘had Internet connections that did not reach the 
10Mbps judged an ‘acceptable’ minimum speed by the industry 

regulator, Ofcom, of whom around 3.5 million lived in rural 

areas. ‘Whilst rural SMEs and consumers are left with dire 

speeds, or even no service at all’, the report thundered, ‘Openreach 
makes vast profits and finds little reason to invest in the network, 

install new lines or even fix faults in a properly timely manner.’** 

Subsequent research backed up this appraisal. In particular, a 

report by the Culture, Media and Sport Committee published 

later the same year remarked: ‘Openreach’s historically poor 

service record has failed to improve’, while the company had 
been ‘significantly under-investing in the access infrastructure 
and services on which a large part of the public rely’, leaving ‘a 
patchwork of premises that have not been reached [by superfast 

broadband]’. BT, the Committee insisted, ‘should therefore take 
immediate steps to invest further in Openreach infrastructure 
and services’.*? The following year, BT was fined £42 million for 

failing to compensate rival operators for significant delays in 

installing Ethernet lines during 2013-14. 

How, then, might we seek to understand these various appar- 

ent failures in the hitherto exceptional telecoms space? What has 

been going on? As we have seen, lack of competition has previ- 

ously been advanced as an explanation for both poor mobile 

coverage and the alleged overpricing specifically of SME mobile 

services. It is notable, therefore, that the same explanation has 

been wheeled out in relation to BT and Openreach. The Culture, 

Media and Sport Committee, for example, blamed an ‘embed- 

ded conflict of interest between BT as service provider and 

Openreach as local access infrastructure subsidiary for ‘stiflling] 

local competition’.“’ BIG, in turn, asserted that the record of 

‘systemic underinvestment stemmed from ‘the “natural monop- 
oly” of BT and Openreach’.” More precisely: 

300 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

BT are merely trying to eke out what life there is left in an 

outdated network system instead of planning for the future 
and upgrading to a fully fibre network. 
. 
. Rather than acknowl- 
edging the need to comprehensively rethink their broadband 

investment strategy, they are instead effectively postponing the 

decision and trying to strain every last bit of profit they can 
from the outdated and struggling copper network.” 

A dearth of competition in certain parts of the UK telecoms 

sector is undoubtedly part of the explanation for that sector’s 
having become in recent years more like the country’s other 

infrastructure-rentier sectors — that is, afflicted by poor service, 
weak investment and monopoly pricing. But it is far from being 

the full explanation. To approach a fuller explanation, it will be 
helpful first to briefly recap. 

My analysis to this point has focused on the underlying reasons 
why the UK has long represented what Jonathan Ford, specifi- 

cally in the context of utility infrastructure ownership, felici- 

tously calls ‘a rentier’s paradise’.“4 One such reason, of course, 

was a volume consideration — what Ford refers to as ‘the wealth of 
opportunities available’. The UK has sold off almost every public 
service-delivery infrastructure that could conceivably be sold off, 
advancing much further down that road than most other 
advanced industrial nations, the US included. Simply stated, 
rent-generating infrastructure assets abound. The other reason, 
meanwhile, was a value consideration — one that is by no means 
specific to the UK. Infrastructure rents make for a highly attrac- 
tive investment proposition because monopoly — ‘natural’ or 
otherwise — inheres in the infrastructure business. 

Largely unexamined so far, however, is the enormously impor- 

tant question of how UK governments have attempted to address 

those underlying tendencies towards monopoly. Did the govern- 
ment simply sell all those public monopoly infrastructure owner- 
operators to the private sector and then leave them to theit own 

devices? Of course 
not. Even the most ardent free-market 

THE X-FACTOR 
301 

champions in the Conservative Party of the 1980s and early 

1990s — in fact, perhaps especially them, given free-marketeers’ 

traditional suspicion of monopolies — accepted that handing 
monopoly businesses to private owners and hoping for the best 
would be asking for trouble. What, then, did the government 

do? How, broadly speaking, did it confront the monopoly prob- 

lem? This is the question to which I will now turn. Answering it 

will provide a fuller explanation not only of the latter-day emer- 

gence of rent-seeking in the ‘exceptional’ UK telecommunica- 

tions sector, but also of enduring patterns of rent-seeking across 

the rest of the UK’s infrastructural economy. 

t 

In a very small number of cases, the infrastructure-intensive 

enterprises that have been privatized in the UK have operated in 
what were already competitive markets at the time of their trans- 

fer to the private sector. British Airways, the airline operator 

floated on the Stock Exchange in 1987, is perhaps the best exam- 

ple. But British Airways was very much the exception. If the 
government had little need to worry about market power and its 

potential abuse in this case, there was considerable cause for 

concern elsewhere. 

From the outset, however, there was an extraordinary degree 

of confidence in the future of competition. Where, as in most 

cases, competition did not exist, it was believed that it would in 
time materialize, either by dint of market forces — ‘monopoly 

produces competition’, Marx once wrote of the tendency for 

capital to flow into sectors where monopolistic conditions afford 

above-average profits — or by virtue of the government managing 

to lever it into place.” Dont worry, the government repeatedly 

told naysayers; British Telecom, British Gas and the like might be 

monopolist for now, but they wont stay that way. 

In the meantime, the government further reassured doubters, 
regulatory bodies would be created to keep the monopolists in 

check. In this sense, regulation was only ever deemed a stopgap 
—a temporary measure required until such time as the market 

302 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

and its disciplinary regimen took’ over. Watchdogs for the differ- 

ent industries (water, energy, telecoms, and so on) ‘would simply 

hold the fort for the consumer until competition arrived like the 
US cavalry’, as Jonathan Ford and Gill Plimmer have put it. 
What was the express objective of these regulators, other than to 

substitute temporarily for competition? More than anything else, 

it was to prevent the two maladies identified by Martin Wolf in 

his critique of Britain’s utility model: namely, overpricing and 
underinvestment. In Ford and Plimmer’s words, the key to an 

effective regulatory architecture for the privatized infrastructure 

sectors would be ‘giving consumers a fair price while also offering 

private owners incentives to innovate and find efficiencies’.“° Or, 

more succinctly still, the task was to ensure the necessary network 
investment at a reasonable price to the consumer. 

But the problem was that, over time, all of these key premises 

animating the great privatization push would be revealed to be 
fundamentally flawed. Firstly, competition typically did not arise. 
The past few decades have, in reality, seen persistent reluctance on 
the part of successive UK governments — Tory and Labour alike — 

to introduce greater competition to the sectors in question, even 
where it is possible to do so. This qualifying clause is important. As 
I have noted, in many of these sectors, because of their natural 
monopoly characteristics, introducing competition would be hard 
enough, and frankly difficult to justify, even if the political appe- 
tite were there: Why add extra costs, which would inevitably be 
borne largely by consumers, taxpayers, or a combination of the 
two, simply on point of principle? But the fact that the UK has not 
managed to render competitive pure natural-monopoly businesses 
— ownership and operation of electricity transmission and distri- 
bution infrastructures, say — is not the central issue. The real issue 
is that, in some sectors, greater infrastructure competition has 
been possible, and continues to be — even if only at the margins; 
yet the government has nonetheless consistently dragged its heels.

infrastructure 
represents a 

prime example. ‘The UK government has long been well aware of

nals owned and run by different operators, were not pursued,

In any event, the requirement that BAA sell three of the seven

alin into the sclerotic veins of UK infrastructure rentierism.?

More commonly, the government has refrained from taking 

action to boost competitive forces. In fact, it has more often 

actively authorized a reduction of competition than it has sought 

to stimulate it. 

This latter instinct has been especially noteworthy in relation 

to media and communications network infrastructures. When 

the owners and operators of the UK’s two direct broadcast satel- 

lite networks, 
British 
Satellite 
Broadcasting and Sky TV,

two years later, Arqiva announced plans to acquire National Grid 

Wireless, the all-too-predictable approval that followed saw the 
UK’s only two integrated terrestrial broadcast transmission 
companies become one. This created another monopoly — and 

this despite the Competition Commission having found that the 
combination ‘would lead to a substantial lessening of competi- 

tion in the provision of broadcasting transmission services to 

television and radio broadcasters [that] could lead to higher 

prices and lower service quality’.”* It was thus little wonder that, 
when Nigel Hawkins sat down in 2015 to itemize the most nota- 

ble failings of the UK’s overall privatization programme, number 

one on his list was: “Endorsing long-term monopolies’. ‘The 

government has not only failed to break such monopolies apart; 

it has readily sanctioned their deliberate assembly. 

If the Tory privatizers’ original assumption that competition 

would eventually materialize was flawed, so also was the associ- 

ated notion that regulation would keep infrastructure monopo- 

lists on a tight leash in the meantime. It has, quite simply, cate- 

gorically failed to do so. This regulatory failure is a vital 
component of the wider explanation for the persistence of

successful rent-seeking by the’ UK’s infrastructure 
rentiers, 
including in the nominally ‘exceptional’ telecoms sector. 

Plenty of observers of the UK’s privatized infrastructure scene 
have worried about a phenomenon widely observable elsewhere 

in the world in industry sectors overseen by government- 
appointed watchdogs: regulatory capture. Indeed, concern about 

the possibility of capture was one reason for the original political 
determination that regulation should only ever be a temporary 
stopgap, to be supplanted in the long term by market competi- 

tion. ‘Permanent regulation’, as Jonathan Ford and Gill Plimmer 

note, ‘is vulnerable to industry capture. “The problem is that the 

regulator spends all its time talking to the company and its inves- 

tors, says [the academic David] Hall.’ And there are certainly 

those who believe that, in the eternal interregnum preceding the 
promised emergence of competition, the UK’s privatized network 
industries have indeed to some extent captured their respective 
regulators. One of them is Diane Coyle, who has noted the fact 
that entire teams are employed by infrastructure companies to 
handle regulatory relations.” 

Nevertheless, whether or not capture has taken place is almost 

beside the point if one is primarily interested, as we are here, in the 
substance of regulation — and, more importantly still, its effects. 
Captured or not, the reality is that regulation has been singularly 
unsuccessful in its objective of stimulating infrastructure invest- 
ment while protecting customers from inflationary price rises. It 
has instead been weak and accommodating, as numerous commen- 

tators attest. Regulators, Coyle says, have been ‘clearly far too leni- 
ent with “their” companies’.°” Investors have thus managed to ‘run 
rings around the watchdogs set up by the government to regulate 
the industries’.* Ford, perhaps, captures the overall picture best. 
Wielding flimsy ‘light-touch’ regulatory tools, the UK’s infrastruc- 
ture watchdogs have for four decades shown ‘myopic largesse’ to 
those they are charged with controlling.» 
is 

The UK has thus long represented a ‘paradise’ for infrastruc- 

ture rentiers not only because of the wealth of investment 

THE X-FACTOR 
307 

opportunities and the durability of endemic monopoly condi- 

tions sustained by a failure on the part of government to stimu- 

late competition, but also because of lax regulation.® Regulators 
—and the government that is responsible for regulating them in 

turn — have bent over backwards to make infrastructure rentier- 

ism pay. Having handed over rent-generating assets to the private 

sector at knockdown prices, they have proceeded to safeguard 

and even strengthen those assets, thus entrenching the ability of 

those assets owners to extract rents from them. 

A good example of this regulatory safeguarding and strength- 

ening can be found in the telecommunication space, and specifi- 

cally in radio-spectrum assets. The very nature of the spectrum 

assets licensed by government has changed over time, precisely as 

a result of regulatory action. “Prior to 1998’, as a useful Culture, 
Media and Sport Committee report on spectrum allocation and 

use points out, ‘the then regulator issued licences for specific tech- 

nologies and purposes on the basis of an assessment of their social 
and economic usefulness. This was very much a “command and 

control” model, whereby the regulator managed all spectrum 

usage.”°! The asset was ring-fenced; licensees were commercially 

constrained. Thomas Hazlett and his economist colleagues cite 

the example of terrestrial television broadcasters: “Transmission 

technology, business model (ad supported, not subscription), 

service (broadcast video, not two-way broadband), and even the 

location of transmitters were specified by regulators.’ 

Since its creation as the UK’s new media and communications 

super-regulator in 2003, however, Ofcom has been dedicated to 
spectrum liberalization, doggedly loosening ‘licence constraints 

wherever possible and allowing the market greater freedom to 

determine spectrum usage rather than determining usage itself’. 

Today, minimalist licenses define band contours and attempt to 

mitigate interference risks; but otherwise they ‘delegate the 

choice of technologies, services, and business models largely to 

the licensee’. The result is predictable enough. ‘Mobile phone 

and other modern licenses’, writes Hazlett, ‘convey airwave rights 

308 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

tantamount to spectrum ownership. This is the very definition 

of ‘light touch’ regulation. 

This regulatory cossetting of infrastructure asset owners has 

not been limited to one sector or one asset type; it is a much 

more generalized phenomenon. In fact, it would be difficult to 

overstate either the depth or breadth of the government’ and its 

regulators’ longstanding subservience to infrastructure-oriented 

rentier capital. 

This compliant stance is nowhere more evident than in the 

government's National Infrastructure Plans, published annually 
between 2010 and 2014 and then succeeded in 2016 by the five- 

year National Infrastructure Delivery Plan (NIDP) for 2016-21. 

“The government and regulators’, the NIDP insists, ‘continue to 

ensure regulated infrastructure networks remain an attractive 

place to invest’. That this has long been a strategic priority is 
beyond doubt. The government freely admits that, ‘when assess- 
ing changes to the regulatory policy or regulatory frameworks’, it 
pays ‘particular regard to the effect on investor confidence’. So 
concerned is the government not to scare investors away through 
heavy-handed regulation that it even provides guarantees — a 
total figure of £40 billion was cited in 2014 — if it fears that 
‘major infrastructure projects may struggle to access private 
finance’. A willingness to take project risk onto the government's 
own balance sheet, then, is clearly at least part of what is meant 
by the ‘stable risk and return profile’ that the UK regulatory 
environment offers to infrastructure investors. 

That financial investors are uppermost in the government's 
mind when it immodestly invokes ‘a framework of economic 

regulation [of infrastructure industries] that is among the best in 
the world’ is underlined not just by its reference to ‘certainty for 

a number of years for investment’, but by the fact that, for exter- 

nal validation of its framework, it turns not to a consumer group, 

or even to an industry body, but rather to Moody's Investors 

Service; Moody’s rates the regulatory regimes administered by 
Ofwat (water) and Ofgem (electricity and gas) as ‘amongst the

309 

most stable and predictable in the world’ — for investors, that is.” 
Most telling of all, though, is the fact that, in trumpeting the 

‘attractiveness of UK infrastructure’ to investors, the government 
shamelessly emphasises exactly those qualities which, as we know 
from PIMCO, financial institutions themselves most covet in 

potential investment propositions: “Strong competitive posi- 

tions, natural monopolies or high barriers to entry’. Fair 
enough, you might think. But what about the government's 

putative decades-long commitment to promoting competition 

between rival networks? It was plainly hot air all along. In short, 
when Danny Alexander, chief secretary to the treasury, exclaimed 

in his foreword to a 2014 Treasury report on “Investing in UK 

Infrastructure’ that the UK was ‘open for business’, this was very 
much an understatement. The UK could scarcely be more 

open, or more obliging, to investors. 

The first constituency to be negatively affected specifically by 

weak, investor-friendly regulation of the infrastructure business, 

needless to say, are customers. Consider, for example, the issue 

that has animated much of the growing chorus of criticism of the 

UK’s mobile telephony network operators: low levels of regional 

coverage. This is explicable not — or not only — in terms of limited 

competition; it is also a function of regulatory failure. Ofcom, as 

we have seen, has aggressively liberalized spectrum licenses; the 

last thing it has wanted to do is impose ‘burdensome’ require- 

ments on licensees. Therefore it has attached no, or only modest, 

coverage obligations. 

In advance of the 2013 4G auction, when Ofcom was propos- 

ing to implement a 95 per cent (population) coverage require- 

ment, but only on one of the licences, the members of the Culture, 
Media and Sport Committee cried foul. Not only, they said, 

should coverage obligations be attached to two or more licences, 

in view of the ‘risk that, by only applying a coverage obligation to 

one licence, consumers in the rural areas that would receive the 

extended coverage may still be limited in their choice of network

provider’; they also claimed — citing, of all sources, Arqiva — that 

the proposed 95 per cent threshold was ‘an obligation so unad-

Alongside service let-downs, and indeed connected directly to 

them, another way in which customers have suffered from regu- 

lators’ privileging of investors has been through maladapted 
distributions of risk. As Ford witheringly notes: 

‘The purpose of privatisation was to pass the operational and 

financial risks of utilities to the private sector. In practice, over 

the past three decades, no business has lost its licence for oper- 

ational or financial failures. Instead private owners have been 
allowed to transfer these risks on to the shoulders of consum- 

ers, who have no ability to manage or mitigate them.” 

Though not alone, the water sector is the prime example of this 
regulator-countenanced risk transfer. Under the ownership of 
Macquarie bank, which bought it in 2006 and exited a little over 

a decade later, Thames Water's financial and operational risk 

piled up: £2 billion of extra debt was loaded onto the company’s 

balance sheet, and what one judge described as ‘inadequate 

investment, diabolical maintenance and poor management led

to ‘extensive pollution of the Thames, and other rivers, with

Over the course of several years, furthermore, Ofwat had 

repeatedly warned ‘Thames (and other water companies) about

Ofwat’s lament that ‘water companies have been warned time 
and again that they need to be better at planning ahead to deal

the bite to back up its bark. 

Financial risk has been a pervasive issue within the UK’s infra- 

structure sector in recent decades. The accumulation of what two 

observers recently described as ‘stratospheric debts’ has been one 

of the sector’s signal features in the post-privatization period; the 

same authors referred to a veritable ‘orgy of borrowing.” BAA’s 

owners led the way in many respects, loading the company with 

£11 billion of debt by 2008.78 Arqiva has been another prolific 

borrower; at mid 2018, its long-term debt totalled just under £3 

billion — roughly three times the company’s revenue.” And then,

£42 billion three decades later.*°

because the gearing is high and therefore the equity is low, the

As the Financial Times’s commentators on the UK infrastruc- 

ture sector have repeatedly insisted, the utilities regulators bear at 

least some of the responsibility for this state of affairs. Regarding 

Arqiva, they have observed that ‘the regulator has allowed the 
owners to build up extreme levels of leverage’;** regarding the gas 

sector: “The regulator is not powerless to intervene in these finan- 

cial escapades’;** and regarding the infrastructure sector as a

Ifinvestor-friendly regulation has harmed customers by permit- 

ting poor service and skewed distributions of risk, however, the 
primary axis of harm has undoubtedly been price. This is partly 
because regulators have usually allowed the UK’s infrastructure 
companies explicitly to charge customers for major investment 

initiatives — rather than paying for such investment out of profits,

313 

at a cost to shareholders. Without wanting to pick on Thames

More generally, price harms have reflected the pricing models 

that regulators have devised to try to preclude price gouging by 

infrastructure companies operating in monopolistic markets. 
Ever since privatization, the UK’s preferred regulatory approach 

has been to cap prices rather than profits; apparently the idea of 

the latter model, used for US privatized utilities and elsewhere, 
particularly offended ‘Thatcher’s principal economics adviser, 

Alan Walters, who exclaimed: ‘We can’t do this. It’s socialism!’*® 
So price controls have been the tool of choice. But they — or at 

least the form they have taken — have been controversial from 

the start. 

BAA, for example, was a classic case of regulatory magnanim- 

ity, benefiting, as Nigel Hawkins later noted, ‘from relatively 
generous price regulation from the Civil Aviation Authority 
(CAA) in being granted real price increases for its landing charges; 

these eventually feed into passenger fares’.*” Notably, BAA 

conjured — and ruthlessly exploited — improbable visions of 

heavy-handed regulators scaring off external investors. In the 

early 2000s, it repeatedly ‘threatened to shelve major investment 
programmes ... 
if it did not receive sufficient financial incen- 

tives’. These scare tactics were successful: the CAA forced airlines,

Other watchdogs have been similarly generous with their pric- 
ing models. Understanding why these models have typically 
worked to the benefit of the UK’s infrastructure rentiers and 

their shareholders requires us to know a little bit about their 

basic form. Generally, this has followed the famous ‘RPI minus 
x formula, first devised and used for the privatized BT. The rents 
that can be charged by asset owner-operators are thereby ‘indexed 

for inflation (the retail price index) less a certain amount each 

year (x) to spur them to drive productivity.” 

Where is the problem with that, one might ask? Surely driving 

productivity is a good thing; and consumers benefit because 

prices rise slower than inflation. But, as we saw at the outset, 

prices ultimately have not risen slower than inflation (except in 
telecoms), mainly because companies have ordinarily been 
allowed to pass on network investment costs in the manner of 
Thames Water and the Tideway Tunnel. And even if prices had 
only risen at the rate implied by the standard formula, consum- 

ers would still have got a raw deal. Why? 

Imagine a hypothetical privatized utility, operating in a 3 per 

cent RPI environment. Its regulator, believing potential produc- 

tivity gains are limited, stipulates that it can increase prices at 

2.8 per cent per annum (x’, in other words, is 0.2). In the

event, however, our utility actually manages to reduce its costs

low; on the other, as James Meek notes of the privatized elec- 

tricity companies, but as has in fact been true much more 
broadly, the UK’s infrastructure companies have found enor-

The significance of all of this cannot be stressed enough. 
Mainstream economists are fond of arguing in favour of privati- 

zation on the grounds that privatized businesses have proved 
more efficient than their publicly owned predecessors.” Yet they 
invariably fail to say anything about which class fractions capture 

such efficiency gains. Under the US profit-cap model, there is 
potential for such gains to be shared relatively equitably; but not 

in the UK. Consumers’ share in any gains is strictly capped at ‘x’; 

and, true to form, UK regulators have not wanted to burden the 
countrys infrastructure rentiers with challenging productivity 

expectations, so x has consistently been squeezed. Efficiency 

gains have nonetheless been substantial, and 100 per cent of the 

‘extra’ gains — real cost reductions minus the limited quantum 
presumed by ‘x — have accrued to capital.” 

In 2016, the government essentially acknowledged, albeit 

probably unwittingly, that UK regulatory policy (and especially

privileged investors over consumers. In the NIDP published that 

year, it explained that it was ‘taking a new direction for energy 

policy which puts consumers first’ — implying, of course, that the 

previous course it had pursued did not put consumers first, 

which we know to be true.”® Specific regulators such as Ofwat 

and Ofgem, stung by repeated accusations of indulgence towards 

those they regulate, have also increasingly been talking tough. 

Indeed, ‘tough’ was the exact word that Ofwat used to describe 

new measures that it introduced in December 2019 to cap pay-

and the companies they regulate have appropriated the differ- 

ence as rates have fallen. One study published in 2017 estimated 

that, over an eight-year period, Ofgem’s overestimation of inter- 

est rates had padded the profits of the UK’s electricity and gas 

network operators by more than £3 billion.'° 

Lastly, and most controversially, regulators have made glaring 

— and hugely consequential — errors when estimating infrastruc- 

ture companies’ relative mix of debt and equity finance, as well 

318 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

as the respective costs of each type. For a long time, regulators 
assumed that this mix would be relatively equal. In reality, 
though, as we have seen, the companies widely loaded up on 

debt, operating on the basis of wafer-thin equity. This matters, 

because, as any financier will tell you, debt is typically substan- 

tively cheaper than equity; thus the companies’ actual financing 

costs turned out, once again, to be significantly lower than the 
estimated costs — predicated on an equitable balance of equity 
and debt — incorporated in ‘x’. The economist who first revealed 

this ‘large-scale financial arbitrage’, Dieter Helm, did not blame 

the companies themselves for acting as they did; it was, he said, 

a ‘rational response to a badly designed regulatory regime’: with 
‘RPI minus x’ the regulators had offered up ‘an extraordinary 
open goal’, and the companies, predictably, had taken full advan- 

tage.'°° Call it what you will — Martin Wolf described this ‘licence 
to print money as nothing short of a ‘scandal’ — but the result 
was the same — namely, a boost in rentier profits ‘worth up to 
£1bn a year, at the expense’, of course, ‘of customers, predomi- 
nantly in [the water sector]’.' 

‘RPI minus x’ has also been enormously damaging for constitu- 

encies other than consumers. Consider what types of strategic 

imperatives the model incentivizes for those companies to which 

it applies. Already lacking motivation to improve service, insofar 

as their customers are generally captive and thus obliged to keep 
paying whether they like it or not, ‘RPI minus x’ further disin- 
centivizes service improvement because price rises — for which 

service enhancement might be one justification — are capped. 
What would be the point of offering a better service if it 
was not 
remunerated accordingly? By contrast, the model powerfully 
incentivizes cost-cutting, since all ‘extra efficiencies get to be 
privatized by the company, which pockets the difference if actual 

costs are lower than the costs implied by the regulator’s x. And 
what, alongside network maintenance costs, are infrastructure 
rentiers main operating cost heads? Labour costs, of course. 

THE X-FACTOR 
319 

‘Thus, to these, the companies in question have widely taken a 
metaphorical axe. 

A 2017 report by Andrea Broughton and Chiara Manzoni for 

the Employment and Social Affairs Committee of the European 
Parliament has laid bare the extent of pain inflicted by the privat- 

ized utilities, which was considerably greater in the UK than 

elsewhere in Europe. There were colossal job losses in the water, 

gas and electricity sectors, ranging from around 20 per cent in 

the first of these to an extraordinary 60 per cent in the last — all 

such losses, remember, representing grist to the utilities’ profita- 

bility mill.!°° Moreover, hand in hand with substantial job losses 

went, inevitably, a decline of the unions, which, not by accident, 

was one of the Thatcher government’s principal motivations for 
embarking on the privatization programme in the first place. In 

the infamous Ridley Report of 1977, Nicholas Ridley, one of 
Thatcher's key advisers, had argued that, to effect broadly based 

privatization (referred to in the report as ‘denationalisation), it 
would be helpful where possible firstly to break up the national- 

ized utility industries into smaller parts, which would have the 
added advantage of breaking ‘the power of monopolicy public 

sector unions .!° 

In any event, for those fortunate enough to remain in a job 

after the privatized utilities had cut a swathe through these erst- 

while public-sector workforces, there was a predictable diver- 
gence in fortunes between those at the top — who rapidly bridged 

the divide between labour and capital — and those at the bottom. 
On the one hand, Broughton and Manzoni, drawing on research 
by David Parker, note, ‘senior management benefitted from 

stock options and profit-related bonuses; on the other hand, job 

losses, de-unionisation and changes to collective bargaining in a 

number of privatised enterprises produced a widening of pay 

differentials between unskilled workers and skilled workers and 

top management’.'” The electricity sector was one such case, 

seeing an increase in part-time employment and growing indi- 

vidualization of employment contracts. 
!°° 

320 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Another infrastructure-based ‘sector in which workers have 

suffered from weak regulation has been mail collection and deliv- 

ery — although here the story is somewhat different. Royal Mail 

was privatized in 2013 with what were, for a privatized utility, 
unprecedented pricing freedoms. This was partly because it was 

no longer a monopoly provider, the postal service market having 

been opened to competition in 2006. But Royal Mail took undue 
advantage of those freedoms. Just months after privatization, in 
January 2014, it proposed wholesale price changes that would 

have had the effect of massively penalizing its only major compet- 

itor in the bulk mail ‘access’ market, Whistl, which, with a distri- 
bution network covering only part of the country, relied on 

Royal Mail’s infrastructure elsewhere. The price changes were 
never implemented, but only because Whistl withdrew from the 
market — at the cost of some 2,000 jobs. Royal Mail’s actions, 
Ofcom has recently ruled, represented ‘a deliberate strategy of 
pricing discrimination against Whistl’.' A £50 million fine was 
imposed. 

The chief culprit in this case, one might argue, was not in fact 

a weak regulator so much as an abuse of power — its pricing free- 
doms — by Royal Mail; and Ofcom did at least fine the company. 
But it was the regulator that conferred those freedoms in the first 

place. Furthermore, despite instigating a ‘fundamental review of 
the regulation of Royal Mail in 2015 in the light of its return to 
monopoly-provider status in the access market, Ofcom in fact 
chose not to introduce price controls. The £50 million fine, 
meanwhile, was a relative trifle — just 0.5 per cent of Royal Mail’s 
revenues of £10 billion or more, compared with the maximum 

10 per cent of turnover that Ofcom is permitted to levy. And, 

last but not least, labour relations at Royal Mail have been 
‘re-regulated’ to detrimental effect: another crucial outcome of 
Ofcom’s 2015-16 review of the company was its recommenda- 
tion of greater workforce 
‘flexibility. The Communication 
Workers Union slammed Ofcom for effectively promoting “inse- 

cure and inferior employment standards’, to which the regulator 

THE X-FACTOR 
321 

replied that its role was to focus on the service and interests of 

postal users, not terms of employment.''® At the time of writing, 

three years later, Royal Mail workers have voted overwhelmingly 

to take industrial action over their ‘flexibilized’ employment 

terms.!!! 

Last but not least among those negatively affected by the govern- 
ment and regulators’ privileging of the UK’s infrastructure rent- 

iers and their owners has been the government itself — and, 
behind the government, the tax-paying public. As in many of the 

other rentier realms I have discussed in this book, the rentiers 
simply have not paid their fair share of tax, by any reasonable 

measure. One reason for this has been the provision of generous 

tax treatments, not least in the water sector. A fascinating if dry 
2016 review of taxation of the UK water companies for Ofwat 
by the tax specialists Alvarez & Marsal, for example, highlighted 

three key treatments then working to the benefit of the compa- 

nies concerned: a favourable 2011 change in the basis of taxation 

of infrastructure charge receipts; a favourable 2013 agreement 

with the tax authorities allowing capital allowances to be claimed 

for certain qualifying assets, including retrospectively; and policy 

allowing tax relief on the portion of pension scheme deficit 

recovery payments funded by companies.'” 

Far more significant for infrastructure rentiers’ tax position 

over the long term and across all sectors, however, has been the 

tax-minimizing 
impact 
of the enormous 
debt 
financing 
mentioned earlier. We will see shortly why it is that increased 

leverage reduces tax bills. But first it is important to understand 

that there has been a knock-on effect: because ‘x’ has not reflected 

the infrastructure companies’ preference for debt, nor therefore 

has it reflected the downward impact of that preference on their 

tax expenses. The result is that regulators have consistently over- 

estimated these costs as well as financing costs — with the differ- 

ence between actual and estimated costs, as we have seen, flow- 

ing entirely to profit.'"° 

O22 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

In any event, the effect of substantial debt financing on tax 

liabilities is straightforward. The key is that tax is paid on profit 

after rather than before interest costs. So, while it is true that 

interest rates have fallen, the sheer volume of debt frequently 

needing to be serviced has meant that, even for the most profit- 

able infrastructure rentiers, interest expenses have very often 
been sufficiently large to reduce operating profits to only very 
modest levels — or even to zero — before the inconvenience of tax 

enters the picture. Bluntly stated, the sector’s stratospheric debts, 

as Ford and Plimmer write, have actively ‘suppressed’ the govern- 

ment’s tax revenues.!!4 

Arqiva is a case in point. Across the three financial years to 
mid 2018, the company’s operating profits totalled £895 million, 
exceeding £275 million in each year. But, as we know, it has sky- 
high debt, and thus substantial interest costs. The result is that it 
paid zero tax in 2015/16, zero tax in 2016/17 — and received a 
tax credit of more than £224 million (‘a result of one-off tax 
adjustments including recognition of deferred tax assets 
following changes in tax legislation’) in 2017/18.!!5 Moreover, 
something in the order of half of the interest payments that 
served successfully to offset Argiva’s taxable profits went to its 
own shareholders, who had issued loans to the company bearing 
interest at ‘a juicy 13-14 per cent’.!'° 

Arqiva is far from alone in any of this. The water sector, once 

again, deserves special mention. A 2013 study indicated that the 

sectors use of this ‘debt tax relief’ mechanism had cost the 
Exchequer almost £1 billion in foregone receipts over the previ- 

ous three years.''” Not only, moreover, were the water companies’ 
tax-suppressing loans often issued by their own shareholders (as at 

Arqiva); but many of those shareholders, based offshore, were 
receiving the interest payments on these loans tax-free because the 
loans had been issued as quoted Eurobonds.''® At the time, prom- 
inent individuals, including the Tory MP Charlie Elphicke, called 
out the entire scheme for what it appeared to be — tax avoidance, 
and on an ‘industrial scale’, Labelling it ‘unethical, unacceptable 

THE X-FACTOR 
BBS 

and irresponsible’, Elphicke called for both the tax authorities and 
Ofwat to review the practices and ‘stop the culture of excessively 
high borrowing’.'!? But they did not stop it, of course. Five years 

later, it transpired that the debt-laden Thames Water, despite 
swimming in profit, had paid ‘almost no corporation tax’ for a 
decade. 
!”° 

We have seen how damaging feeble regulation and a lack of 
competition between infrastructure owners has been for UK 

consumers, workers and tax-payers. But the story would not be 
complete without evidence of quite how advantageous these 

conditions have been for infrastructure rentiers themselves, and 

for their owners. 

There are any number of studies in the public realm attesting 

to the super-profitability occasioned by the propitious condi- 

tions found in the UK infrastructure sector, protected as most 

operators are from meaningful competition, and indulged all the 

while by lenient regulators and a minimalist ‘x. To take just one 

example among many, 
in 2017 
the Energy and Climate 

Intelligence Unit published an insightful report titled ‘Monopoly 
Money’, examining the profitability of the UK’s electricity distri- 

bution network operators — the rentiers that own and operate the 

low-voltage networks taking power from the national high- 

voltage transmission network to UK homes and businesses, thus 

providing, in the report's description, ‘the capillaries to [the 

National] Grid’s arteries, the B-roads to its motorways’. Noting 

that these companies usually operate ‘out of the public gaze’, 

away from ‘media scrutiny’, the authors wanted to expose the 

sector’s financial performance to public scrutiny. They found 

that, between 2010 and 2015, operating profit margins in the 

sector had ranged from a low of 41 per cent to a high of 56 per 

cent, with a weighted average of 51.5 per cent. The authors’ 

description of these figures as ‘quite striking’ was a massive 

understatement. The numbers were, as the authors also wrote, 

‘huge by any standard’.'?!

THE X-FACTOR 
B25 

Such extraordinary infrastructure-rentier profits have been a 
consistent feature of the neoliberal era in the UK. Only once has 

the government found sufficient gumption to say: too much. In 
1997, Tony Blair’s Labour government imposed a windfall levy 

on the privatized utilities’ ‘excess’ profits. But, given the scale and 

scope of historical (not to mention future) profiteering, the 
amount levied, of around £5 billion collectively, was a pittance. 
And it was arguably just populist politicking: the levy, a one-off, 

was one of Labour’s manifesto commitments made during that 

years general election campaign; once safely ensconced in power, 
New Labour never again rocked the boat. 

Meanwhile, it is difficult to establish a clear’ picture of finan- 

cial performance for the owners of the UK’s infrastructure rent- 

iers. This is partly because it would be necessary to add apprecia- 

tion in asset value to dividend payments to establish total 
shareholder returns. But, as Nigel Hawkins noted when trying to 
do just that, the more significant obstacle to establishing the level 

of such returns is that there have been so many corporate trans- 

actions that muddy the picture — companies merging, companies 
being demerged, and, above all else, publicly listed companies 

being taken private, into a murky realm where shareholder 

returns are much more difficult to discern.'’? 

Still, the fact that, for decades now, global investment institu- 

tions have consistently flocked to the UK’s shores to grab their 

piece of the infrastructure-rentier pie tells its own story. As 

Hawkins, summarizing from the record to the extent that is 

possible, wrote in late 2015: ‘As a general principle, shareholders 

in UK privatized utilities have done well and, in some cases, 

outstandingly so.’ Expanding on this generalisation, Hawkins 

added that the owners of the water companies had done 

‘extremely well’ and those of National Grid had been rewarded 

‘massively’, while the electricity distribution companies, unsur- 

prisingly, had delivered ‘outstanding value to their sharehold- 

ers..!23 UK infrastructure, in short, has the ‘x’-factor.

CHAPTER SEVEN 

Ground Control: Land Rents 

One of the most distinctive of all UK privatizations was that of 

the National Freight Corporation (NFC), a collection of road 
transportation businesses, in 1982, which occurred not by way 

of the more common mechanism of stock market flotation but 

rather by employee buyout. The chairman at the time of privati- 

zation was Peter Thompson, who, after the eventual public list- 

ing of shares in 1989, penned a warts-and-all account of the 

corporation’s transformation, titled Sharing the Success.' (And 

what a ‘success’ it was: over 500 employees eventually pocketed 

more than £250,000 each.) What was the secret of this success? 

Well, much of it, it transpired, was serendipitous, predicated not 

on NEC's nominally core infrastructure assets, and still less on 

- 
management expertise, so much as on an asset that in 1982 had 

seemed almost incidental to the sale: land. The 1980s, in short, 

saw NEC become a property developer. Thompson recalled: 

Property development was almost thrust upon us. We acquired 

a land bank which with the UK property boom of the 1980s 

has proved to be more valuable than anyone imagined. We 

brought in the skills, not just to sell sites — which was all that 

we were allowed to do when we were state owned — but to 

develop them. 
In future we would act 
as the property 

328 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

developer. We have made increasing profits out of this activ- 

ity... We inherited the advantage of a first-class land bank. 

Thompson admitted to ‘a nagging doubt as to whether this is 

really our world ... the nagging doubt has remained with me, 

though not, I hastily add, with my colleagues’.* Given the wealth 

that inheritance of the land bank generated for Thompson's 

colleagues, 
their lack of introspection 
is probably not 
so 

surprising. 

NEC, whose vestiges today constitute an operating division of 

the international courier service company Deutsche Post, is far 

from the only former UK public enterprise to have generated 

substantial post-privatization income from land — the icing on the 

cake, as it were, of the core infrastructure rents explored in the 

previous chapter. When these enterprises were privatized, the assets 

transferred very often included large tracts of land along with 
network infrastructures, workforces, customer contracts, and so 
forth. Kevin Cahill has estimated that the privatizations of, most 
notably, water, electricity, coal and rail jointly shifted as much as | 
million acres (or 400,000 hectares), ‘some of it immensely valuable 
development land’, into private hands, ‘often without a proper 
evaluation, often without any disclosure as to its scale’? 

As the privatized successors of those land-rich public enter- 

prises have rationalized operations in search of production effi- 

ciencies in the years that have followed, they have very often 
found that they do not need all of the land that privatization 
bestowed upon them. In fact, in at least one case, they now do 
not need any of it. Few people perusing the website of the 
London Stock Exchange-listed property developer Harworth 
Group plc, owner of some 9,000 hectares of land valued at 
around £250 million, would be able to guess its origins. But 

there is a clue in the name: Harworth, in Nottinghamshire, was 
the base of UK Coal plc, formerly the UK’s largest coal mining 
business, and the main private offspring of the state-owned 
British Coal Corporation upon the privatization of the UK 

GROUND CONTROL 
B29 

mining industry in the mid 1990s. The property developer 
Harworth Group is all that remains today of UK Coal, now that 

all of its mining operations have been closed down, and the land 

that UK Coal owned is thus not needed for anything else. 

What has been done with all the ‘excess’ land belonging to the 
UR’s privatized enterprises? Some of it, as in the case of NFC — 
which in the years immediately after privatization relied almost 

entirely on property sales to make interest payments on the debt 

raised to finance the employee buyout — has been sold, either in 

an undeveloped or developed state, generating windfall gains 

that have in several cases been vast.* Harworth Group, for exam- 

ple, has sold 50 per cent of the approximately 18,000 hectares 

that, in its former incarnation as UK Coal, it owned a decade 

ago, when it was still mining 7 million tonnes of coal each year. 
Another illuminating case is that of Royal Mail. As if its privati- 

zation in 2013 was not contentious enough, the company poured 

fuel on the fire a few years later by selling three central London 

plots to developers to earn itself (and its shareholders) a tidy 

£400 million.» Even after those sales, which achieved market 

prices of between six and eight times book value, the net book 

value of Royal Mail’s huge freehold estate was £845 million, 

suggesting a total market value upwards of £5 billion.° 

The income raised by the likes of NFC and Royal Mail through 

such land sales can be understood as land (‘ground’) rent in capi- 

talized form — that is, the present value of the future rental 
payments that the land could be expected to generate if it were 

let.’ For the pure land rentier, with no interest in using land for 

her own operational purposes, this is always the question: to let 

one’s property, thus earning future rents, or, effectively, to cash 

those future chips in now? Ever more privatized enterprises with 

excess landholdings are looking to ‘release value for shareholders 

in this latter way. In late 2017, for example, the water company 

Severn Trent, which owns around 20,000 hectares of land, 

announced plans to generate £100 million of ‘extra profits’ over 

the following decade through the sale of 1,200 unused hectares.* 

330 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

And Severn Trent is not even close to being the biggest land- 

holder among the privatized UK water companies: that honour 

is held by United Utilities, which has over 56,000 hectares.” 

As well as selling excess land to realize capitalized rents, some 

of the former public utility providers have also become land- 

lords, renting their surplus properties out. National Grid, the 
owner and operator of the electricity transmission network in 
England and Wales and the gas transmission system across all of 

Britain, is a case in point. Indeed, of all the former public enter- 

prises to have had a property business ‘thrust upon’ them, 

National Grid has arguably taken to the task with the greatest 

facility, gusto and success; and what Nigel Hawkins described as 

the ‘massive’ rewards reaped by the company’s shareholders since 

privatization (see Chapter 6) have accrued in no small part 

thanks to this line of business. 

Quietly, away from public view, National Grid Property has 
been raking in hundreds of millions of pounds of actual and capi- 
talized land rents. As far back as 2007, it was reported that the 
company had been selling ‘about 
£100m of surplus land each year 
for the past five years’.'° Six years later, another report noted that a 
batch of further sales was expected to raise ‘more than £500m’."! 
Since then, the property business — which combines site develop- 
ment, disposal, and letting to third parties — has continued to hum 
happily along, regularly posting annual profits — not revenues — in 
excess of £50 million: in 2016/17 the profit figure was £65 million; 
in 2017/18, when the company sold forty-four sites and exchanged 
contracts on a further five, it was £84 million.!? The most extraor- 
dinary aspect of this story is that all of this historic activity appears 
to have barely made a dent in National Grid’s colossal land bank, 
which at the time of writing still contains 645 sites with a net book 
value — not market value — of £2.3 billion.'3 If National Grid is an 
infrastructure rentier, in other words, it is just as much a land rent- 
ier, and one so prodigious that it puts many of the Specialist land 
rentiers discussed below in the shade. 

GROUND CONTROL 
Bel 

The prominence of land rentiers is, of course, hardly a novel 
phenomenon in the UK. As I noted in the Introduction, land 

rentierism, alongside financial rentierism, is undoubtedly the 
form of asset control and exploitation with the deepest national 

historical roots. When, while writing Capital, Karl Marx saw fit 

to distinguish both the landed-property class and finance capital- 

ists ((money-lenders and usurers’) from industrial capitalists, it 

was on the basis of his examination of class structures and rela- 

tions specifically in capitalist Britain. Britain and land rentierism 

share a long, intimate history. The association of Britain with 
landed property and all the privileges that go with it is deep and 
indelible. 

Despite the historic centrality of land ownership and exploita- 

tion to social and economic relations in the UK, however, the 

neoliberal era has indisputably ratcheted things up by a notch or 

two. It has given the land rentier renewed impetus, allowing her 

to assume an arguably unprecedented national economic signifi- 

cance, certainly within the context of the past century. And it has 

seen land rentierism assume a new geography, too. When people 
think about landed property and Britain, they tend to think 

about rural England: country estates, landed gentry and tenant 

farmers. Today, however, land rent in the UK isa predominantly 

urban affair. 

It is also increasingly residential — and not only because resi- 

dential land is on average substantially more valuable than agri- 

cultural or industrial land. A century ago, when people in the 
UK rented their homes (which the vast majority did), the asset 

they were paying to let was almost exclusively the house itself — 

the bricks and mortar. But this is no longer the case. Brian Green 

estimates that, in England, the average proportion of the value of 

residential property accounted for by the land beneath it has 

increased from as little as 2 per cent in the 1930s to something 

in the region of 70 per cent today." In the most sought-after 

locations, like central London, it is even higher. Housing rental 

costs, in other words, are now largely ground rent — the costs of 

Be 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

renting land — making the label ‘landlord’ more and more appo- 

site as time goes by. 

In this chapter, in any event, by ‘land rentier I mean either 
landowning companies or private individuals explicitly in the 

business of earning land rents — rents on the land and its appurte- 

nances — whether through letting (repeat rental payments) or 

through speculative holding and sale (one-off capitalized rents). 
Admittedly, this is an imperfect definition, imparting to land rent- 

ierism decidedly fuzzy taxonomic boundaries. Owner-occupiers — 
companies or individuals occupying the properties they own, and 
whom I do not treat as rentiers — present the thorniest definitional 
conundrum. For example, to the extent that we live in ‘home- 
owner societies’, in which residential owner-occupiers regard their 
homes not just as shelters but as capital assets, the gains in value of 
which can be capitalized and captured through sale, we are all 
rentiers now — and nowhere more so than in the UK. 

Moreover, owner-occupiers — corporate or household — can also 

be thought of as earning regular rents just like landlords — albeit 

‘paid’ by themselves, or, in the case of companies, by the customers 

to whom those implicit rental costs are inevitably passed on as part 

of the product or service price.'® In the case of residential owner- 
occupancy, the value of this notional rent is actually included in 

national accounts (as ‘imputed’ rental income), deemed as it is to 

reflect the ‘service’ provided by the owner to the occupier, even 
though they are one and the same. In the UK until the mid 1960s, 
both residential and commercial owner-occupiers were taxed on 

this imputed income. It is one of the many ironies of the history of 
UK land rentierism, and is probably not entirely coincidental, that 

this tax was abolished just when the income in question was about 
to become truly significant. Still, in what follows, I generally leave 

to one side both the imputed rents and the capital gains associated 
with owner-occupancy. 

‘The growing economic importance of land rent in the UK was 
impressed upon observers especially forcefully in 2006, whén the 

Office for National Statistics (ONS) reported to the government
