All types of rent and rentierism, as we have seen in previous 

chapters, have been substantially succoured in the UK by its 

neoliberal policies. But among this wide cast of winners, land 

rentiers have seemingly been the biggest winners of all. 

Why have land rentiers done so well? Perhaps the main reason is 

that, as for infrastructure rentiers and financial rentiers, the stock 
of assets available for land rentiers to earn rents on has expanded 

significantly. At the beginning of the neoliberal period, the UK 

public sector, having been a net acquirer of land for the bulk of 

the twentieth century, performed an abrupt about-turn and 
became a net seller. In the four decades since Margaret Thatcher 

took power, in the region of 1.6 million hectares of public land, 

equating to around 8 per cent of Britain by area, have been sold 

off, in addition to the approximately 400,000 hectares that 
disappeared with the major enterprise privatizations.*! Almost all 

of this land has ended up in the private sector, either with compa- 

nies or households, as opposed to charities or community groups. 

This massive programme of land privatization has been driven 
and directed throughout from the commanding heights of 

central government. Persuaded by the neoliberal principle that 

private asset ownership is inherently superior to public owner- 

ship — and no doubt helped towards this conviction by the lobby- 

ing of private-sector rentier interests expounding precisely this 

dogma — Whitehall has used a variety of carrots and sticks to 

persuade the hundreds of erstwhile landowning public bodies 

either to rationalize their holdings or to liquidate them entirely. 

Local authorities have collectively sold in the region of 60 per 

cent of the land they owned in the late 1970s; for some govern- 

ment departments, the proportion has been even higher; the 

Department of Health, under unrelenting pressure, has privat- 

ized 70 per cent of its former estate. 

Certainly, some of the incremental private stock that land 

privatization has created has not ended up in the hands of land 

rentiers as I have defined them here; but most has. Very little was

Land privatization has been of fundamental importance to the 
good fortunes of land rentiers in the UK during the neoliberal 
period. In reality, however, it is only the centrepiece of a much 
broader and deeper story of exceptionally propitious times for 

the companies and individuals in question, in many ways mirror- 

ing the fortunes of infrastructure rentiers explored in Chapter 6. 
Not only did the state, in both cases, release valuable rentable 

assets to the private sector — land in one case, networked infra- 

structures in the other; in both cases, it also proceeded to make 

the released assets more valuable to rentiers by enacting powerful 

legal and/or regulatory work on the rights associated with asset 
ownership. Liberalization of radio spectrum licences was a prom- 

inent example of such work in the infrastructure space; perhaps 

the prime example in the land context has been a series of policy 

measures bearing on privately rented residential property. 

The 1988 Housing Act was a seminal intervention. It effec- 

tively signalled the end of rent controls in England and Wales, 

deregulating all new private rented tenancies created after January 

1989, and hence restricting regulated tenancies — those with ‘fair 

rents’ assessed by independent rent officers — to a pool of legacy 

lettings that by 2000/01 had declined to just 6 per cent of the 

private rental sector in England.*° Rents were henceforth set by 

the market. The 1988 legislation also initiated a process — one 

further progressed and reinforced by the Housing Act of 1996 

— of institutionalizing insecurity of tenure for private rental 

tenants, and thus, from the rentier’s perspective, institutionaliz- 

ing security of rent generation. Assured tenancies (‘which can 

run continuously provided the client complies with the terms of 

the lease’) were supplanted by assured shorthold tenancies (“fixed 

term tenancies that can be granted for periods as short as six 

months’).3”7 The 1988 Act introduced the latter; the 1996 Act 
made them the default. 

342 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

The twin 1988 and 1996 statutes also made it considerably 

easier for landlords to gain possession, in particular under the 

terms of the former’s widely reviled Section 21, which allows 

landlords to evict tenants without a reason after their fixed-term 
tenancy period ends.** As David Mullins and Alan Murie have 

observed, the overall effect of these various changes has been that 

the ‘balance of advantage was shifted from tenant to landlord’ 

— and decisively so. As if that were not enough, 1996 saw an 

additional boon to the residential property rentier in the form of 

the launch of the famous ‘buy to let’ mortgage, which was very 
lightly regulated and enabled small investors wanting to buy 
properties to rent out to borrow at much lower interest rates than 
had previously been available. These measures boosted the popu- 
larity of landlordism by making it much more profitable. 

Another significant parallel between the UK infrastructure 

and land stories is that, in both of these cases of large-scale 

public-sector asset privatization, the private sector has often 
acquired the transferred assets notably cheaply. An important 

reason that this has been true of privatized land is that when 
public-sector bodies have sold land they have frequently done so 
under pressure from Whitehall. As the Royal Institution of 
Chartered Surveyors advises, for market value to be achieved in 

a land transaction it is necessary that the parties to the transac- 
tion act ‘knowledgeably, prudently and without compulsion’. 
While it is unclear whether UK public bodies disposing of land 
have always acted knowledgeably and prudently, it is indisputa- 
ble that compulsion has frequently obtained, and that disposal at 

less than best consideration has been the result. Sometimes this 
compulsion has been explicit: a sale may literally be ordered; 
sometimes it has been implicit, and normally effected through 
the squeezing of budgets, which has given public bodies little 
option but to liquidate assets in order to stay afloat. 

In the early 1980s, for example, the imposition of financial 

constraints on the then still nationalized industries, such'as the 

railways, ‘created strong incentives to make [land] sales’. Sites

were therefore sold ‘before the time was ripe for them’ at ‘less 

than their full market price’.“” Charles Kennedy, later the Liberal

ing with publicly owned forest land: 

By publicly putting pressure on the [Forestry Commission] to 

raise money to help pay for the unemployment queues that

Meanwhile, limits on grants from central government and, for

balance their books. And under powers provided by the 1980 

Local Government Planning and Land Act, councils could be — 
and frequently were — forced to sell sites if they did not do so 
during the four months allowed to them to do so voluntarily.” 

Today, little has changed. The 2016 Housing and Planning 

Act not only revisited, revived and reinforced the powers of 

compulsion contained in the 1980 local government legislation, 

_ 
but extended them to land held by all other public bodies, too.” 

Moreover, the budgetary pressures on public-sector bodies have 

of course never gone away; indeed, since the global financial 

crisis, they have intensified. The London Metropolitan Police 

force is just one of many public bodies to have made significant 

sales of ‘surplus’ land and property in the post-crisis austerity 

period — in its case, almost £1 billion worth, including twenty- 

four police stations, between 2011 and 2017 — specifically in 

order to soften the blow of budget cuts.“ Local authorities and 
NHS trusts have been doing likewise.”

RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Perhaps the most significant category of public land sold at less 

than market value under conditions of compulsion is housing 

land, under the Right to Buy. In 1980, the Housing Act summar- 

ily removed local-authority discretion over whether council hous- 

ing should be sold.“ In this case, though, it is not such compul- 

sion — councils’ obligation to respect tenants’ right to buy — that 

explains the low prices paid; rather, discount is written into the 

very fabric of the policy. Increasing with the length of tenancy, 

discounts have ranged widely, both temporally and geographi- 

cally, but have been as high as 70 per cent off market value, which 

is more than even ‘Thatcher herself ever envisaged. 

A simple back-of-the-envelope calculation for the English case 

suffices to signal the extraordinary scale of the value not realized 
by the taxpayer on council house sales. Since 1979, around 1.9 
million properties have been sold under the Right to Buy scheme 
in England.” Let us assume an average discount against market 
value of 40 per cent, which is fairly conservative; other than 
during the period 2003-12, average discounts have consistently 
been above that level.“® If, for these 1.9 million properties, we 
assume an average market value at the time of sale, in today’s 
prices, of £100,000 (again, this is conservative: the halfway point 
of Right to Buy in terms of dwellings sold was reached in 1989— 
90, and the average UK house price in today’s prices had already 
passed £100,000 by 1986), then the cumulative absolute discount 
on these property sales, in today’s terms, is in the region of £75 
billion.” 

It is true that not all of this value has accrued to rentiers: many 
Right to Buy homes have remained in owner-occupancy, and 
many of those now in the private rental sector will no doubt have 
got there through sale by former council tenants after a seemly 
period of time. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that much of 
the government giveaway has indeed gone into the pockets of 

rentiers. Large numbers of Right to Buy homes have been let 
more or less immediately at market rates.° The rentier in such 

cases might be the former council tenant herself; it might be a 

GROUND CONTROL 
345 

company standing behind that individual;”' or it might be a 

landlord to whom the ex-tenant has ‘flipped’ the property at a 

profit: selling, of course, is the more immediate way for rentier- 
minded ex-tenants to monetize the discounts they have been 
granted. Certainly, discounts are supposed to be repaid if the 

exerciser of the Right to Buy sells her home within five years of 
buying it. But the amount of repayment declines by 20 per cent 

per annum, and there is enough evidence of Right to Buy homes 
being sold with unseemly haste — a BBC investigation carried 

out in 2019 unearthed 140 buyers who had resold within one 

month, of whom twenty had done so within one week — to 

suggest that the repayment rules do not in practice work as well 

as they are supposed to.” 

There are, furthermore, innumerable examples of public land 

being sold at substantially less than market value in situations where 
compulsion is absent — often to prototypically rentier institutions.” 

Where land privatization has occurred on the cheap, under 
conditions of compulsion or otherwise, buyers have clearly made 

windfall gains. Often, the full extent of under-pricing, and thus 

of the gains realized by buyers, has only become apparent later, 

as a phenomenon of much more general significance to land 

rentier fortunes has had time to kick in: namely, rampant land- 

price inflation. Given that future such inflation obviously cannot 

be anticipated and priced in by public bodies at the time of 

disposal, the government recommends that they insert clauses in 

sales contracts enabling a share of any subsequent value increases 

to be clawed back.*4 But these clauses have all too seldom been 

employed. In March 2018, for example, it was reported that 

property companies had made enormous profits through wind- 

fall gains on land acquired from the Ministry of Defence (MoD), 

and that ‘in most cases, the MoD failed to ensure that any of the 

windfall profits were returned to the taxpayer.” 

The crowning irony is that, having sold land to rentiers at 
below market prices, it has often been the state itself that has later 

enabled those rentiers to crystallize their fortuitous gains. One 

346 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

way in which it has done so is through the payment of Housing 

Benefit. Indeed, the proportion of tenants who receive Housing 

Benefit is typically higher in ex-council properties that are now 

privately rented than it is across the private rented sector as a 

whole; in 2015, in Renfrewshire in Scotland, some 43 per cent of 
Housing Benefit claimants in the private rented sector were found 

to be living in properties purchased under Right to Buy.’° Another 

state-facilitated mechanism of gain realization for rentiers has 
involved public bodies buying back, at inflated prices, the very 

land that they had previously privatized at a discount. This has 
happened with housing land: in the face of a mounting housing 

crisis, numerous local authorities have reacquired homes sold 

under Right to Buy — Ealing council in London, for instance, 
spending over £100 million buying back 516 properties origi- 
nally sold for less than £20 million.” And this has happened with 
other types of land as well. A striking example is railway freight 
sidings and yards. In the 1990s, the government gifted these to 
private-sector freight companies under rail privatization.’ But 
unforeseen growth in freight traffic in the decade-and-a-half 
following privatization saw Network Rail, the public body that 
once again owns and operates the core of the national rail infra- 
structure, buy back over a hundred sites in 2014. The cost was 
£220 million — representing pure rentier profit.”

time. This growth rate is more impressive still if one considers

‘Buy land; they're not making any more of it, in the famous 
words variously attributed to the American humourists Will 

Rogers and Mark Twain. This injunction has arguably never been 

more judicious than in the UK since the early 1990s; and yet the 

British government has throughout this period acted in diametric 

opposition to this advice. At the precise moment in UK history 

when the value of land was about to begin a sustained and strato- 

spheric rise never before seen in the country (real land prices 

increased at only around 1.5 per cent per annum between 1900 

and 1980), the government took the decision to commence a 

land-disposal programme that — even when discounts were not 

formally part of the policy — looks, in retrospect, increasingly like 

a giveaway of monumental proportions, and of monumental folly. 

While there is considerable debate over the exact reasons for 

this unprecedented price inflation, and over the relative contri- 

butions of the various factors in play, there is one factor on whose 

348 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

importance all commentators are agreed: the role of credit. 
Numerous scholars have described what has effectively become a 

mutually reinforcing feedback cycle tying together, on one hand, 

land markets, and, on the other, a credit system that has been 

substantially deregulated and liberalized since the beginning of 

the 1980s.°° Increased lending for property purchase has driven 
up land prices; and those land-price increases have been used in 

turn, implicitly if not always explicitly, to justify even more 

lending. 
. 

This cycle has affected the value of all types of land, but has 

perhaps been most evident in relation to housing land. Residential 
mortgage lending increased by over 500 per cent during the 

decade beginning in 1995 — which, as we have seen, was a decade 
of uninterrupted land-value growth.®! Around the time of the 
global financial crisis, mortgage lending dried up, and, as Figure 
7.4 shows, land-value growth stalled. After the crisis, however, 
the unconventional monetary policy known as quantitative 
easing (QE) helped reopen the lending taps, and keep them 
open, further lubricating demand and its upward pressure on 
asset prices. Indeed, Bank of England analysts have estimated 
that real UK house prices in 2014 would have been 22 per cent 
lower than they actually were had it not been for the stimulus 
provided by QE.” The government’s controversial Help to Buy 
programme has poured additional fuel on the credit-inflamed 
fire. 

For our purposes, however, the causes of this historic land- 

price inflation are less important than its consequences — specifi- 

cally for land rentiers — the most important of which can be 
simply stated: companies or individuals holding land for capital 

appreciation, as well as or instead of to earn rental income, have 
made out like veritable bandits. It therefore bears emphasis that 

capital gains are indeed a strategic objective for most property 
companies. For example, Land Securities Group — one 
of the 
UR’s biggest — says that it holds investment properties ‘either to 

earn rental income or for capital appreciation, or both’.

As Figure 7.5 makes clear, the increase in the price of land has 

caused land’s share of total UK non-financial wealth to increase 
markedly since the mid 1990s, from around a third to over a

such things — does land dominate the nation’s non-financial 

wealth to the extent that it does today in the UK.® Between 

1995 and 2017, the value of the UK’s intellectual property assets 

increased by 56 per cent; the value of its machinery, equipment

dential combined), excluding in each case the land beneath

increase in value was 460 per cent, blowing all other asset classes 

out of the water. For UK rentiers, a decent rule of thumb for 

profitable investment practice in recent decades would therefore 

simply have been: invest in land; for international land rentiers, 

it would have been to invest in the UK.

ring annual land value or property tax. That is reasonable enough, 
you might say; gains in the value of, say, inventories, intellectual 
property assets or weapons systems are not taxed either. But there 

is of course a crucial difference: all of those other assets are 
produced assets. When the value of the nation’s stock of intel- 
lectual property or machinery, or even dwellings, increases, it is 
often, albeit not always, because more of the asset in question has 
been produced: one of the reasons that the value of UK dwellings 
(excluding land) increased to the extent it did between 1995 and 
2017 (Figure 7.5) is that the number of dwellings increased by 
about 4 million. Alternatively, the quality of the stock of an asset 
is improved — dwellings are renovated, machinery is upgraded, 
intellectual property is strengthened. But land is land. No more 
of it is produced; and any improvements are made not to the 
land per se, but to its various appurtenances. 

It is for this reason that economists of more or less all persua- 

sions, following John Stuart Mill, regard the land value gains 

that accrue to landowners as ‘unearned’ increments. Landowners, 

Mill said, become enriched simply through the ‘ordinary progress 
of a 
society . 
. 
. independently of any trouble or outlay incurred 
by themselves. They grow richer, as it were, in their sleep, with- 
out working, risking or economizing. What claim have they, on 
the general principle of social justice, to this accession of riches?” 

GROUND CONTROL 
Sey 

This is why the UK’s meek taxation of land-value gains is note- 
worthy. Writing in 2010, for example, Martin Wolf, chief 
economics commentator at the Financial Times, remarked: ‘In 

1984, I bought my London house. I estimate that the land on 
which it sits was worth £100,000 in today’s prices. Today, the 

value is perhaps ten times as great. All of that vast increment is 

the fruit of no effort of mine. It is the reward of owning a loca- 

tion that the efforts of others made valuable.’®’ Wolf refers here 

to an economically extraordinary state of affairs: in contempo- 

rary London, and south-east England more widely, owners of 
homes (and thus of housing land) routinely ‘earn’ more from 

land-price appreciation than from their employment.” Noting 

that his enormous privatized capital gain was entirely tax-free, 
Wolf admitted that he was, therefore, despite himself, ‘a land 

speculator — a mini-aristocrat in a land where private appropria- 

tion of the fruits of others’ efforts has long been a prime route to 

wealth.’ “This appropriation of the rise in the value of land’, Wolf 

concluded, was plainly ‘unfair: what have I done to deserve this 

increase in my wealth?” In truth, the answer was: nothing at all. 

What makes British private landowners’ largely tax-exempt 

privatization of land-value gains particularly galling for critics is 

the fact that many of the interventions that lead to substantial 

increases in land values are state-led, and typically state-funded. 

One such intervention involves infrastructure improvements. 

Winston Churchill, for example, focused on these in his own 

famous tirade against land rentiers’ unearned increments: 

Roads are made, streets are made, services are improved, elec- 

tric light turns night into day, water is brought from reservoirs 

a hundred miles off in the mountains — and all the while the 

landlord sits still. Every one of those improvements is effected 
by the labour and cost of other people and the taxpayers. To 

not one of those improvements does the land monopolist, as a 

land monopolist, contribute, and yet by every one of them the 

value of his land is enhanced.”! 

B02 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Another important form of value-enhancing intervention 

occurs through the planning system. Landowners must first 

secure permission to develop land for commercial or residential 

use. Where planning applications are successful, the value of the 
permissioned land can increase by enormous multiples, literally 

at the stroke of a pen. Consider the government’s own 2015 esti- 

mates for the value of land in England in various types of use: 

agricultural land was estimated to be worth an average of £21,000 

per hectare, industrial land £760,000, and residential land £6.9 

million, rising in London to £29.1 million (over a thousand 

times agricultural value).” 

It is worth pausing briefly to consider the incentives generated 
by a system in which land-value gains are substantially deter- 
mined by state action but nonetheless captured overwhelmingly 
by private landowners. Wolf, as we saw, admitted to being a land 
speculator by default. But, clearly, if speculation pays, others — 
individuals and companies alike — will choose to speculate. And it 

is a lucrative choice. Since UK landowners pay no recurring tax 
on their land, they also, as Simon Tilford notes, ‘pay no penalty 

for sitting on it and waiting for the government — through infra- 
structure improvements or planning decisions or both — ‘to push 
prices up further.” It would be hard to design a system better 
suited to rentier interests. That rentierist behaviours result is 
wholly unsurprising. 

Furthermore, there is no reason to expect that speculative 
landowners would merely sit passively and hope for government 

action to inflate land prices. One would expect, at a bare mini- 
mum, coaxing, cajoling and lobbying. And this, observers 

suggest, is precisely what one finds: rentiers who acquire unde- 
veloped land then actively seek to influence political decision- 
making in sucha way as to elicit land-value gains. Guy Shrubsole, 

for example, has written about ‘land speculators acquiring 
chunks of Green Belt and then lobbying councils to chip away at 

it’, fingering in this regard one of the land-rich rentier institu- 

tions we will encounter later in the chapter — the insurance and 

GROUND CONTROL 
ye) 

pension company Legal & General.”4 Such behaviour, of course, 

represents the explicitly political dimension of what I have 

referred to as ‘rent-seeking’: that is, manipulating the political 

arena in order to generate economic rents. 

Nor is it an unmitigated disaster, moreover, for speculative 

individuals who buy agricultural land but fail to secure planning 

permission or other value-inflating state interventions. For one 

thing, they get to pass that land on to their children with inherit- 

ance taxes reduced at rates of up to 100 per cent under the exist- 

ing system of agricultural property relief; in 2015/16, 62 per 

cent of all such tax relief, or some £208 million, accrued to just 

261 families each with agricultural property assets worth more 

than £1 million.” Those rentiers also get to console themselves 

with the far-from-insignificant subsidies that for decades have 

been paid out to owners of UK farmland on the basis of the size 

of their landholdings under the European Union’s Common 

Agricultural Policy (CAP). This system of payments explicitly 

subsidizes the country’s biggest, most wealthy owners of agricul- 

tural land, including prominent, aristocratic parliamentarians 
such as the Duke of Norfolk, Viscount Ridley and Lord 
Rotherwick. The top 10 per cent of recipients receive almost 50 

per cent of total payments, which at the time of writing amount 

to approximately £3 billion per year.’° After the UK leaves the 
EU the CAP will no longer apply; but under proposals currently 

working their way through parliament, the UK government will 

continue to make comparable payments, slowly winding down 

the historic direct subsidies (between 2021 and 2027) and replac- 

ing them with payments contingent on using the land for envi- 

ronmental ‘public goods’ such as protecting bird habitats or 

preventing floods. For now and for the foreseeable future, farm- 

land rentiers really cannot lose; they win whether planning 

permission is forthcoming or not. 

One of the many significant ways in which the neoliberal 

period in the UK has distinguished itself from the post-war 

decades preceding it, meanwhile, is in the complete absence of 

Bot 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

any meaningful political effort’ to find ways for taxpayers to 

recoup some of the astonishing uplift in land value that occurs 
when planning permission 7s granted. On all three occasions that 
Labour regained power between 1945 and 1979, it swiftly intro- 
duced a legislative mechanism whereby some or all — usually the 

latter — of the uplift in question would be socialized. Granted, 
each time the Conservatives won power back they promptly 

abolished this legislation.’”” But New Labour, in what should 
unquestionably be seen 
as. another significant betrayal of its 

socialist predecessors, did not so much as raise a finger on the 

question of land-value capture during its time in power. That 

Thatcher's administration and its Tory successors have not done 

so either should go without saying. 

And the contrast is not just with the past; there are also impor- 

tant geographical differences, between the UK and its peers. 
Numerous other advanced industrialized nations have mechanisms 

to secure for society the uplift in land value that occurs when plan- 
ning permissions are granted; examples include Hong Kong, South 
Korea and Germany.’* Meanwhile, a more generalized mechanism 

for preventing, or at least limiting, unearned increments, in place in 
various other countries, takes the form of property and land-value 
taxes.” Even the United States levies property taxes, on both 
commercial and residential property. The UK is one of only a few 
advanced industrial countries that do not have any recurring tax on 
property or land values. As Tilford notes, a land-value tax not only 
‘would make it more expensive to speculate on future rises in land 

values’, but would mean that, when such rises occur, ‘some of those 
gains would be captured by the government 
’.® 

‘The reason the UK does not meaningfully tax privatized land- 

value gains is not that such taxation is impractical (as the experi- 

ence of other countries has shown). It is not even because main- 

stream economists, to whom the government so often appeals to 

justify its private-sector-friendly fiscal policies, warn against land 
taxation — in fact, most strongly support the idea, deeming it 
much more efficient than many other taxes. The reason the UK 

GROUND CONTROL 
Sy) 

does not substantively tax land is simply that to do so would 

represent a sharp departure from its consistent cossetting and 

privileging of rentiers in general and land rentiers in particular. 

Indeed, as if to prove the point, the UK has recently done what 

one might have thought impossible, which is to make the fiscal 
environment even more favourable to land-rentier institutions 
than it already was. Specifically, in 2007, Tony Blair's Labour 

administration introduced Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) 

to the UK. To be eligible, companies must be publicly listed and 
must carry on a property-rental business. The main appeal of 
REIT status to rentiers is that all income of the qualifying prop- 

erty-rental business — both profits and capital gains — is exempt 
from corporation tax. Investors in the REIT are subject to income 

tax on distributions; but, as the REIT itself is not subject to tax, 

there is more income available to distribute. In any event, the 

attractiveness of this tax-shelter mechanism was readily apparent: 
many of the UK’s largest listed property companies converted to 
REITs immediately upon the introduction of the regime, and 
numerous others have followed. At the time of writing, these land 

rentiers par excellence number in the region of seventy-five.*! 

Alongside REITs, who are the UK’s other main land rentiers? 
What types of assets do they own, and how much rent do those 

assets generate? Let us begin by looking at corporate rentiers, 

including REITs. There are, I would suggest, six main categories 

of rentier institution operating in the UK land market, although 

one of those is a catch-all ‘Other’ category within which I have 

erouped together companies that do not fit into one of the other 

pools, but which nonetheless play a significant rentier role. One 

of the main reasons for including this ‘Other’ group is simply to 

emphasize the important fact that land rentiers come in forms 

other than the five main ones I have identified. Table 7.1 intro- 

duces the categories and gives two examples of prominent rent- 

iers within each, together with pertinent information about the 

scale of their respective land-rent operations.

Before looking in a bit more detail at each category, it is worth 

highlighting a vital characteristic that is common to all of them: 

the business of these rentiers is primarily in commercial property 

— retail, office and industrial — and undeveloped land. Residential 

lettings are marginal. Research carried out by Tony Key and his 

colleagues for the Investment Property Forum estimates that, of 

the £1.15 trillion of UK residential property held within the 

private rental sector, only around 4 per cent, or £49 billion, is 
owned by corporate rentiers; the rest — the lion’s share — is held 

in the buy-to-let market by small-scale landlords.*” 

Among the few corporate rentiers with a substantive presence 

in the residential sector, all of which belong within my ‘Property 
company category, 
are Annington, Grainger and Grosvenor 
Group. Annington is the largest, owning over 40,000 homes with 

an asset value of over £7 billion, the vast majority of which were 

acquired (controversially) from the MoD in 1996 before being 

leased back under a long-term contract; in the year to March 
2018, these homes generated rental income of £193 million.* 

Grainger owns around 4,500 residential rental properties, which 

are valued at £1.9 billion and delivered rental income of £59 

million in the year to September 2018.*4 Grosvenor’s residential 

assets were valued at £2 billion at the end of 2016, although it is 

unclear what proportion are UK-based — around half of the 
groups overall property portfolio is located overseas.” 

Property companies and REITs, my first two categories of 

_ corporate land rentier, can be considered together; tax status is the 

only meaningful difference between them. ‘This is institutional 

land-rentierism 
at its most straightforward: 
essentially, such 
companies buy property, let it out, and, where a profit can be 

made, sometimes sell it. In the year to March 2018, for example, 

British Land, which earned rental income of £441 million, raised 

£78 million from property sales. It also generated £66 million in 

service charges and realized a gain, on paper, of £202 million 

simply through upward revaluation of its retained property port- 

folio.86 Offices and shopping centres are the principal assets of

Group — owner of nearly one-hundred acres of property at Canary

The third category is financial investors. Two major UK finan- 

cial institutions with particularly significant interests in land rent- 

ierism are Aviva and Legal & General. Substantial investment by 

financial institutions in UK land dates back to the late 1960s and 
early 1970s. In their epic 1978 study of capitalism and land in 

Britain, Doreen Massey and Alejandrina Catalano referred to this 
emergent dynamic, featuring insurance companies, pension funds 
and banks, as a form of ‘financial landownership’.*” A few years 

later, David Harvey theorized it in terms of the treatment of land 

as a pure financial asset.** Land, Massey observed, had become for 
financial institutions ust another sector to invest in®® She 
conjectured that the new breed of financial landowners was 

GROUND CONTROL 
Sow, 

interested more in the value of land as a capital asset than ‘in the 
immediate potential for production or current rent levels’.°° But 

if that was true then, it is clearly not true today. The likes of Aviva 

and Legal & General invest in land for both capital gain and 

current rent: as Table 7.1 shows, they earned, between them, 
more than £1 billion in rental income in 2017. 

The fourth category is property developers-cum-housebuilders. 
To the degree that these companies acquire and own land purely 

as raw material for their housebuilding operations, they do not 

constitute rentiers as I have defined them in this chapter, and 
they would undoubtedly bristle at the label. Yet, rentiers, to some 

extent, they indisputably are. Much of the land they acquire does 

not have planning permission in place, and securing planning 

permission — and the vast capital gains it yields — represents a 

pivotal element of their business model. Indeed, various close 
observers of the UK property-development sector go so far as to 

suggest that rentierism — the seeking of capital gains through a 
combination of buying and selling land and navigating the plan- 
ning system — is today not just one aspect but the main part of 

developers’ business. “Larger UK housebuilders’, Matt Griffith 

writes, ‘have become more focused on land trading and adding 

value through the planning system than the actual business of 

building houses.””! 

A glance at the ‘land banks’ of major UK housebuilders, such 

as Persimmon and Taylor Wimpey (Table 7.1), is telling in this 

respect. Their holdings are split into three components. First, 

and least certain, is the long-term ‘strategic pipeline’. Not only 

does this land not have planning permission, but the house- 

builder does not own it; it is controlled under option or promo- 

tion agreements, which give the company the ability to purchase 

it if and when permission is secured. ‘Taylor Wimpey, for exam- 

ple, has approximately 90,000 plots in its ‘strategic’ bank. 

Second, there are plots that are owned, but also without yet 

having permission, of which Taylor Wimpey has around 27,000 

— the ‘long-term’ owned bank. Finally, in the ‘short-term’ bank, 

360 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

are owned and permissioned plots, sitting and awaiting develop- 
ment; Taylor Wimpey has around 57,000 of these. The relative 
worth of ‘Taylor Wimpey’s short- and long-term banks tells its 
own story about the value of planning permission, and, in turn, 
about why speculation on the outcomes of the planning system 

is so central to housebuilder businesses. The unpermissioned 
plots are estimated to be worth around £3,350 each; the permis- 
sioned plots are each estimated to be worth approximately 
£40,620. It was plainly not building houses, in any event, that 
principally enabled Persimmon, Taylor Wimpey’s peer, to earn 
sufficient profit to pay its chief executive a bonus in 2017 of 
£110 million — later reduced to a more modest £75 million in 
the face of political and shareholder protest; it was capital gains 
— which is to say, capitalized land rents. 

The fifth category of land rentier is one I examined earlier: 

infrastructure rentiers (see Chapter 6). As we have seen, numer- 

ous former utility-providing public enterprises were major land- 
owners when they were privatized, and have been able since 
privatization to free up some of this land either to rent out or, 
more commonly, to sell. 

Sixth, and last, is my ‘Other’ category. In this group belong 
companies that do not fit elsewhere in my schema, but which are 

nonetheless, wholly or in part, land rentier institutions. I have 
picked two examples to illustrate the range of companies that the 
category encompasses. One is Big Yellow Group, a self-storage 
company with around 100 locations across the UK. Essentially, 
Big Yellow is a property company that buys land and lets it out; 
what makes it different is simply the fact that the land is let for 
the specific purpose of storage, and is configured accordingly. 
Like many other UK property rental businesses, Big Yellow 
converted to REIT status at the earliest Opportunity, in 2007. 

The second company illustrating the ‘Other category is Tesco. 
Here, ‘last but not least’ is particularly apt: Tesco’s property port- 

folio is in fact more valuable than that of any of the land rentiers 

profiled thus far, with a net book value of some £16 billion. 

GROUND CONTROL 
Bol 

Certainly, Tesco is in significant measure an owner-occupier; but 

it is also a land rentier. For one thing, it lets, and earns substan- 

tial rents on, many of the sites it owns but which do not house a 

Tesco store; these number, it has been estimated, over 300.9? And 

then there is a more indirect form of rentierism. In an investiga- 

tion completed in 2007, the UK’s Competition Commission 
found extensive evidence of leading grocery retailers such as 

Tesco buying land in the vicinity of their own existing stores 

specifically to prevent competitors from acquiring and building 

on it. As one commentator noted at the time, the guilty parties 

were found to be using ‘all the tricks in the book to control the 

relevant land: exclusivity arrangements, restrictive covenants, 

leases to friendly third parties and so on’; it was ‘anti-competitive 
behaviour on a magnificent scale’, and brought ‘new meaning to 

the retailers’ axiom that their business is all about property and 

location’.”°

How much rent in total do the UK’s corporate land rentiers 

earn each year? It is impossible to say for sure, but a ballpark 

figure can be estimated. It is probably somewhere between £30 

billion and £40 billion. Figure 7.3, above, provided estimates of

£60 billion, £34 billion and £0:5 billion for UK annual residen- 

tial, commercial and farmland rents, respectively, in 2017. 
Corporate rentiers dominate commercial rents; unincorporated 

individual (or, in national accounts parlance, ‘household’) rent- 

iers dominate residential rents. If individuals’ modest share of 
commercial rents is broadly comparable to companies’ modest 

share of residential rents, then we would be looking at corporate 
rents of in the region of £35 billion. ONS data for gross operat- 
ing surplus (GOS) earned from property rental broadly support 
this estimate. These data are charted in Figure 7.7, for both 
companies and households. As it shows, companies’ GOS from 
rental was £28 billion in 2016 (the last year for which the data 
are 
available). GOS 
represents 
output minus intermediate 
consumption and employee compensation — essentially, it is a 
gross profits figure, and thus lower than revenues, but not as low 
as operating profits. Whatever the exact revenue number, corpo- 
rate land rentierism in the UK is evidently a very good business 
to be in. 

Needless to say, many individuals have become extremely wealthy 
by working for or owning equity in successful UK land-rentier 

institutions. We have already encountered one such individual: 

Jeff Fairburn, the Persimmon boss who pocketed a £75 million 
bonus (and eventually paid for it with his job on account of the 
negative publicity that this egregious award generated for the 
company). But similar stories, if not always with quite the same 
staggering numbers, can be told about individuals running all of 
the types of institutional rentiers I have examined in this book. 
The companies have done extravagantly well, and hence so too 
have those who have managed them and owned parts of them. 
Yet land rentierism is, in important respects, different. Unlike 
in any other rentier sector, with the exception of financial rent- 
ierism (Chapter 1), individuals represent significant land rentiers 
in themselves. Sometimes they do so through a recoghizable 
corporate entity. ‘The best-known example of this is the Grosvenor 

GROUND CONTROL 
363 

Group, a property company I discussed earlier. The company is 
owned in its entirety by the Seventh Duke of Westminster, Hugh 
Richard Louis Grosvenor, and his family. The company is essen- 

tially a vehicle for the exercise of the family’s rentier interests. 

This makes it fundamentally different from a company like 
Persimmon, which may for several years have danced to Fairburn’s 

tune, but which is anything but a mere facsimile of individual or 

family wealth; his unceremonious exit, instigated by the institu- 

tional shareholders that own most of the company’s equity, 
demonstrated as much. Other major UK institutional land rent- 

iers that represent vehicles of individual or family rentierism 
include Cadogan Estates (owned by Charles Gerald John 
Cadogan, the Eighth Earl Cadogan, and his family) and the 
Howard de Walden Estate (owned by the Howard de Walden 

family). 

In other cases, meanwhile, individuals or families own substan- 

tial land empires more directly, without the trappings of a 

substantive corporate infrastructure. When the Sunday Times 
publishes its UK Rich List each year, these individuals are placed 

in the media spotlight — the list is packed with those whose 
personal wealth is held predominantly in land and its appurte- 

nances. Interestingly, two of the highest on the list in recent years 

are pairs of brothers: the Reuben brothers, David and Simon, at 

number four on the 2018 list, estimated to be worth around £15 

billion; and the Barclay twins, David and Frederick, at number 

fifteen, estimated to be worth £7.4 billion. The prominence of 

these two sets of brothers demonstrates, if nothing else, that not 

all major UK family property empires are rooted in inheritance. 

In both cases, the brothers’ property fortunes were accumulated 

more or less from scratch, which is certainly something that 

cannot be said for the current generations of the aristocratic 

Grosvenor, Cadogan and de Walden families, whose land wealth 

is in all cases centuries-old and inherited. 

Whether their wealth is inherited or not, all of these individuals 

and families represent rentiers in the classical sense described by 

364 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Thomas Piketty.** They are the descendants — sometimes literally 

— of the wealthy rentiers who lorded it over what Piketty describes 

as the ‘hyperpatrimonial’ Western societies of the late nineteenth 

century, in which the overall income hierarchy was dominated by 

high incomes from assets, and especially inherited assets.°” None 

of these individuals or families, clearly, needs to work — at least not 

in the familiar sense of selling their labour-power to capital. Where 

Piketty’s nineteenth-century rentiers earned rents primarily on 

agricultural land, the Reubens and Cadogans of the world have a 
more diversified asset base. While agricultural land is still often 

part of the overall portfolio (particularly, of course, for the aristo- 

crats among the tribe), the major sources of land rents today for 

these high-net-worth individuals and families is commercial prop- 

erty: retail, offices and hotels. Residential property, meanwhile, is 
marginal, just as it is for the institutional land rentiers discussed 

earlier. Grosvenor has a significant (if opaque) residential property 
portfolio, but one can count on one hand the other major indi- 
vidual or family UK land rentiers whose wealth consists in any 
meaningful part in residential assets. Next to Grosvenor, the 
Portman Estate, the fiefdom of Christopher Edward Berkeley 
Portman, the Tenth Viscount Portman, which includes around 
500 upscale residential rental properties in central London, is 
perhaps the most significant example. 

If the Goliaths of contemporary individual land rentierism in 

the UK are largely absent from the residential market, however, 
individual rentiers more generally clearly are not. As I noted 
above, the private rental sector has grown rapidly in recent years, 

to the point where it now contains around 20 per cent of all 

dwellings, collectively worth over £1 trillion (including, of course, 

the land beneath them) — and this is a sector in which corporate 

rentiers play only a very minimal role. So, if not the Goliaths, 
who exactly does own and profit from the 96 per cent of residen- 

tial rental property held by individuals and households? _ 

‘The answer is what Piketty calls ‘petits rentiers’ (see Chapter i). 

The most revealing source of information about this rentier class 

GROUND CONTROL 
365 

is the annual Private Landlord Survey published by the Ministry 

of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG).”° 
The one drawback to this survey is that it covers only England; 

nevertheless, it provides invaluable insight into who these rent- 

iers, now numbering in the region of 1.5 million, actually are. It 

turns out that they are indeed ‘petit’. Around half of individual 

landlords in the English private rental sector own only one rental 

property; 85 per cent own between one and four.” Figure 7.7, 
showing the ONS’s estimates for the gross operating surplus 
earned by UK households from property rental, gives an indica- 

tion of the overall scale of this business (household earnings from 

commercial property rental are, as discussed, relatively small). 
The key point to notice is the strong growth — a compound annual 

rate of 5.4 per cent between 1997 and 2016. This growth has 
been driven partly by increases in rental prices, but much more by 

the rapid increase from the early 2000s in the number of residen- 

tial properties being privately let (Figure 7.2). 

The growing multitude of small-scale UK landlords 
fits 

Piketty’s description of petits rentiers to a T. These are definitely 

not his classic rentiers, living wholly, or even primarily, off recur- 

ring capital income. In England, only 4 per cent of individual 

landlords let property as a full-time business, and thus represent 

rentiers tout court. The MHCLG estimates that individual land- 

lords’ average reported gross rental income of £15,000 per year 

represents around 40 per cent of their total gross income; but it 

comes with greater deductions than other sources of income — 

around 60 per cent of individual landlords fund their rental 

operations wholly or in part with interest-bearing debt.”* In 

other words, rentierism, for this class, is generally a complement 

to employment rather than a substitute for it. 

The only caveat to this observation concerns pensioners. A 

third of individual landlords are retired.” Strictly speaking, these 

individuals are pure rentiers, earning land rents on top of finan- 

cial rents. As I argued in Chapter 1, however, it is problematic to 

view pension payments as an expression of rentierism; they are 

366 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

arguably better understood not as financial rents but as delayed 
income from labour. In any event, the fact remains that, even 

with the recent historic growth in the UK’s small-landlord class, 

wages from employment dominate the income-generation of the 

country’s highest-income households in a way that they did not 

in the rentier societies of the late nineteenth century (see Figure 

1.10, at p. 91, in which property rental income is part of the 
‘Other income’ category). 

What the growth of the UK private rental sector has certainly 
done since the early 2000s is increase wealth inequality. Writing 

just prior to the neoliberal revolution, Massey and Catalano 

observed that, in Britain, ‘while the least wealthy have the least 

access to land, at the other end of the wealth spectrum no form 
of wealth is as heavily concentrated in the hands of the richest 
individuals’.!° The rise in homeownership levels through the 
1980s and 1990s served somewhat to reduce this stark land- 
wealth inequality: millions of erstwhile renting households from 
across the wealth spectrum became owner-occupiers. Since the 
turn of the millennium, however, as homeownership levels have 
fallen back, things have gone into reverse where property-wealth 
inequality is concerned. 

It is not difficult to see why. By definition, the nearly 10 per 

cent of UK homes that have moved from the owner-occupied to 

the private rental sector in the past two decades have been 
acquired by the rentier class (as Will Self says, ‘there can be no 

renter without a rentier’).'°' The rentiers in question, moreover, 
have been disproportionately drawn from the ranks of the already 
relatively wealthy, and specifically the already relatively land- 
wealthy. This broadly stands to reason: many people cannot 
afford to buy a primary residence, let alone one or more second- 
ary properties. Thus, over 20 per cent of households in the UK’s 
top housing-wealth decile now own one or more rental proper- 

ties (levels of landlordism below the top decile are far lower), 
while approximately half of all landlord households are located 
within that top decile of housing wealth.! 

GROUND CONTROL 
367 

Boosting the wealth of the UK’s burgeoning petit-rentier class 

all the while, and in the process exacerbating wealth inequality, has 

been the land price inflation discussed earlier; the unearned wealth 
increments that this landlord class has disproportionately realized 
have been truly eye-watering, often far exceeding any rental income 

that has been generated. In 2015, the estate agent Savills estimated 

that, between 2009 and 2014, the value of existing privately rented 

residential stock (stock already in the rental sector at the former 

date rather than entering it during that five-year period) increased 
by £177 billion.'°’ Four years later another estate agent, Hamptons 

International, revealed what headline numbers such as these meant 

in terms of actual individual wealth gains realized upon disposal: 
having held rental properties on average for approximately ten 

years, private landlords in England and Wales who sold up in 2018 
made an average gross gain per property of £79,770 — a figure that 

increased to £248,000 (around £25,000 per year of ownership) in 
London.'™ It is thus little wonder that, between 2006-8 and 
2014-16, 
Britain’s Gini coefficient 
for net property wealth 

increased from 0.62 to 0.67.'° Wealth, in short, begets wealth. 
The growth of petit property rentierism in twenty-first-century 

Britain has been, at the same 
time, the growth of wealth 

inequality. 

Having considered the growth of the private residential rental 

sector from the perspective of the petit rentier, it is important to 
consider it also from the other side of the fence. What has all of 

this meant for the UK’s renting households? 

I have already noted that rents in the private rental sector are 
perhaps a third higher in real terms today than they were in the 

early 1990s. But this number, indicating only modest inflation, 

fundamentally fails to convey the real extent of increase in rental 

costs that the UK’s renting households have experienced in recent 

decades. The reason is obvious: there has been a pronounced shift 

in the respective shares of overall residential rental stock located 

in the private and social-rented sectors. The private sector's share 

368 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of total stock has more than doubled, from a quarter in the early 

1980s to just over a half today. And private sector rents are signifi- 

cantly higher than social rents: an average of 87 per cent higher in 

England in 2017-18, for instance.!°° Thus, the UK’s renting 
households collectively have seen average rents rise partly because 

rents within each individual sector have risen — they have risen in 

the social rented sector as well as the private rental sector — but 

also, and more importantly, because the more expensive private 

sector has captured large quantities of stock from the state.!©”

Figure 7.8 illustrates the collective increase in rents. It shows

each year from 1985 (the first year for which the ONS provides

nominal terms — from £9 billion to £87 billion — or nearly 300 per 

cent in real terms.'* Certainly, the overall number of dwellings 
being rented across Britain also increased during this period, from 
approximately 8.4 million in 1985 to approximately 10,4 million 

in 2018. But that is an increase of only about 25 per cent. So, to 
summarize, there has been moderate growth in the number of 

GROUND CONTROL

renting households, but a massively increased overall payment 

burden, and thus an almost-as-massive increase in the average rent 

being paid by each renting household, which, in real terms, has 

risen by well over 200 per cent — that is to say, trebled. No amount 
of sprucing up of the housing stock can justify such a hike. 

Thus, just as the outsourcing of rail services to contract rent- 

iers has led to increased passenger rail fares (Chapter 5), and the 

sale of water and electricity networks to infrastructure rentiers 

has led to increased household utility bills (Chapter 6), so Right 

to Buy has led to increased housing rents. Much more than in 

either the rail or utility contexts, however, the housing phenom- 
enon has had deeply differential social consequences. Everyone 

has to pay water and electricity bills, and most people travel by 

train sometimes. It is true that utility bills and transport expenses 

account for a much bigger chunk of disposable income for poor 
households than for rich ones, and thus that the former house- 
holds are much more affected by increased utility and transport 

costs than the latter. But the costs of renting one’s home are of a 

different order of magnitude. And, just as significantly, if not 

more so, not everyone rents.

In the UK, the poor mostly do rent, while almost no rich people 

do. Figure 7.9 illustrates this difference graphically, showing not

substantially privatized, is thus of almost no consequence to the 

rich — except, of course, insofar as they are the ones hoovering up 

those increased rents — but has been calamitous for the poor, who 

largely — and increasingly — rent their homes.

Figure 7.10 demonstrates this disparity of outcomes. For 

households at the fifth percentile of the income distribution, 
housing costs — which, for these low-income households, mean

Wage increases have been modest, but rents have increased 

dramatically — and these are predominantly renters. Meanwhile, 

the picture looks very different as one ascends the income distri- 

bution. Even at the median income level, the impact of rising 

rents is already indiscernible. Not only are there far fewer renters, 

but wage increases have been stronger and mortgage interest 

rates — a major determinant of housing costs for such households 

— have been in long-term decline. Hence, housing costs have in 

fact fallen for this ‘average’ British home, from around 17 per 

cent to around 14 per cent of post-tax income. And they have 

fallen even further — in fact essentially halved as a percentage of 
(rapidly growing) income — for households at the ninety-fifth 

percentile of the income distribution. 

If the growth of the UK private rental sector under neoliberal- 
ism has increased wealth inequality, then, it has also clearly 

increased income inequality. On one hand, at the top end of the 
income distribution, there is a growing class of petits rentiers in 

the privileged position of seeing their income from employment 
supplemented by income from residential rental property (see 

Figure 1.10). Meanwhile, at the bottom end of the income scale, 

there is a class of renters burdened not just with low incomes but 
with the indignity of having to hand over nearly half of their 
meagre monthly take-home pay either to the state or, increas- 

ingly, to the private rentier class at the top of the income scale 

(Figure 7.10). 

Indeed, when one pauses to think about it, measures of income 
inequality that do not factor in the varying costs of housing — 
which the official, reported measures do not — are highly mislead- 

ing as an indicator of ‘real’ inequality, by which I mean inequal- 

ity as it is experienced in reality. One does not get to choose 

whether to spend money on shelter or not; housing costs are not 

‘discretionary in any meaningful sense of the word. They are, in 

this sense, like tax; although it is true that, unlike with tax, one 

is able to decide — within certain very real constraints that are 

more constraining the less you earn — how much one spends on

income really is; but it is clearly closer to income after housing 

costs than to income before such costs.

Since housing costs are proportionally so much larger for low- 
than high-income UK households, inequality is inevitably 

considerably higher after than before those costs are factored in. 
Figure 7.11 
vividly demonstrates 
this, illustrating income 
inequality in terms of the ratio of household incomes at the 

ninety-fifth and fifth percentiles of the distribution. But it also 
shows the more significant fact: that income inequality after 
housing costs — which is to say real income inequality — has 
increased consistently over the past four decades. The ‘before 
housing costs’ line shows the standard account of income inequal- 

ity, based on household survey data, and as circulated by most 
commentators in the media, which is that UK income inequality 
essentially plateaued from around 1990. The much more mean- 
ingful ‘after housing costs’ line shows that, during the 1980s, 
inequality had already risen more than the conventional measure 

GROUND CONTROL 
8/3 

indicated. It then simply carried on increasing. In 1980, after 
housing costs, households at the ninety-fifth percentile earned 

4.6 times as much as their peers at the fifth percentile; by 2017— 

18, they were earning 11.2 times as much. Real income inequal- 

ity has not just increased — it has more than doubled. 

Land rentierism, specifically in the form of petit rentierism in 

the residential sector, thus occupies a special place in the wider 

story of growing inequality under rentier capitalism in the neolib- 

eral UK. For all the reasons explained in the Introduction, the 
ascendancy of rentierism in general has generated in the UK 

increased inequalities of both income and wealth. But the substan- 

tial Right to Buy—facilitated expansion of private rental housing 

— housing owned and let predominantly by petit-rentier land- 

lords — is clearly special. Not only has this expansion dramatically 

exacerbated the inequalities that rentierization more generally has 
opened up. More fundamentally, 
it embodies those growing 

inequalities. That is, land and land rent respectively represent in 

significant measure the physical and social forms in which those 
growing inequalities are manifested. At the top end of the scale, 

surpluses of wealth are held in significant part in the form of land, 

and surpluses of income are derived in significant part from the 

land. At the bottom end, nothing today bespeaks exclusion from 

the ‘common wealth’ more than being locked out of homeowner- 

ship — and nothing bespeaks the likelihood of remaining excluded 

more than paying half of one’s income in rent. 

One individual long vexed by the institution of private landown- 

ership under capitalism was Karl Marx. It never quite made sense 

to him. Under feudalism and in predominantly agrarian socie- 

ties, the landowner was certainly ‘an important functionary in 

production. But this was not so, Marx reckoned, under mid- 
nineteenth-century industrial capitalism, which had reduced the 

landowner to little more than a ‘useless superfetation’. What 

specifically puzzled Marx was that, despite this uselessness, 

industrial capitalists not only tolerated the landowner’s existence 

374 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

but shared with her (and with bankers) the surplus value 
produced by workers, which was apportioned between rent, 

interest, and profit of enterprise. Why not do what Marx thought 

the dominant industrial class should logically do, which was to 

turn privately owned, partitioned land ‘into the common prop- 

erty of the bourgeois class, of capital’?!'® 

Marx advanced a couple of possible reasons, of which arguably 

the most persuasive was that private ownership of land served to 

legitimize private ownership more generally. David Harvey, in 

his own discussion of these issues, has expanded on this point. 

Private property in land, he suggested, following Marx, ‘performs 

an ideological and legitimizing function for all forms of private 
property. Insofar as this is true, Harvey continued, ‘we can 
regard rent as a side-payment allowed to landowners in order to 
preserve the sanctity and inviolability of private property in 
general’.''’ Private landownership is the ideological bulwark of 
private property ownership in toto. 

This argument is deeply suggestive with respect to the recent 

history of the UK. Why did the 1980s and 1990s not see more 

concerted resistance to the advance of neoliberalism and, with it, 

to the broadly based elevation of private property rights, mani- 

fested among other things in the privatization of more or less 
everything that could be privatized? I hazarded one answer in 
Chapter 2, in the form of the country’s North Sea oil-and-gas 
dividend and _ its cushioning welfare provisions for workers 
thrown onto the metaphorical slagheap. But Right to Buy is 
plainly also part of the answer. 

Right to Buy was, in many respects, Thatcher’s defining achieve- 

ment. It was the privatization that gave many of those perhaps 

most inclined to kick against neoliberalism a personal stake in the 

neoliberal project. In doing so, it disinclined them to protest 
against all those other privatizations — not least those examined in 
Chapter 6 — that not only gave them zero stake (the UK never did 
become a share-owning democracy, least of all on former council 

estates), but actually robbed them of the public wealth they had 

GROUND CONTROL 
By 

formerly owned. Borrowing terms from Harvey, we might say 

that Right to Buy, and the land privatization it entailed, performed 

a legitimizing ideological function for neoliberalism more broadly 

— to which, in the UK, privatization always was central. 

The transformations in the housing sector to which Right to 
Buy was so central lubricated the neoliberal shift in other ways, 

too. As we have seen, deregulation and liberalization of the mort- 
gage market, which had been necessary to enable Right to Buy, 

precipitated unprecedented growth in residential land prices 
from the early 1990s. This financial boon to the growing popula- 

tion of homeowners — owner-occupancy rates rose from 55 per 

cent when Thatcher entered Downing Street to approximately 

70 per cent at their 2002 peak — papered over all manner of 
cracks that neoliberalism was busily opening up in other dimen- 

sions of household economies. Through mechanisms such as 

equity release, it compensated for stagnating incomes. It was also 

increasingly relied upon to soften the impact of economically 

stressful life events — childbirth, divorce, unemployment — for 
which a diminished welfare state no longer made much provi- 

sion.!'* Welfare was now ‘asset-based’. 

And yet the very same credit-fuelled boom in residential land 

prices that made many people feel like neoliberalism’s winners — 

and helped them to ride out its vicissitudes — has ultimately pushed 

homeownership beyond reach for younger generations, dragging 

owner-occupancy rates back down to around 60 per cent and crys- 

_tallizing the grievances of millions of renters who not only feel but 
know themselves to be neoliberalism’s losers.'!* The Resolution 
Foundation estimated in 2016 that the UK’s millennial generation 

born between 1981 and 2000 will on average have spent £44,000 
more on housing rent by the time they reach 30 than the baby- 
boomer generation born between 1946 and 1965 did.'* “The 

current housing crisis’, Will Self is therefore right to conclude, 

is not so much emblematic of a transmogrification from a 

social market economy to a neoliberal one. It is constitutive of 

370 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

that process: the asset transfer from the state to the rich; the 
pump-priming of the value of those assets; the forcing of the 

poor into more expensive private rental accommodation — all 

of which measures are underpinned by a financial system 

heavily dependent on mortgage lending.!!° 

In a sense, Right to Buy, in aiming to reduce levels of rentier- 
ism (albeit public-sector rentierism), was always a contradictory, 
doomed project. Rentierism, as this book has shown, is integral 

to what neoliberalism is; it is coded into its DNA. That credit- 
based land-price inflation would eventually lead to the materiali- 

zation of a new rentier class and a new class of disaffected renters 
seems, at least in retrospect, the entirely predictable result. The 
Thatcherite homeownership project could only resist the inher- 
ent rentier-privileging dynamics of neoliberalism for so long. 

The same set of processes that first dampened but then revivified 

land rentierism, then, having originally buttressed the shift to neolib- 

eralism, is now underwriting growing opposition to it within 

‘Generation Rent’. It would be hard to imagine a better example of 

Karl Polanyi’s famous ‘double movement’, which entailed widespread 
marketization and privatization followed by vigorous social resistance 

to those twin dynamics, specifically where what had been privatized 
and marketized was land or one of the other so-called ‘fictitious 
commodities’.''° On a Polanyian reading, at any rate, landownership 
and its associated rentier dynamics would have to be seen as central 

not just to UK neoliberalism’s formative successes, but also to its 
current difficulties — and perhaps to its eventual failure. 

On such potential failure, finally, it is worth recalling Marx, 
who not only understood what made capitalism and its ideology 
of private property so successful (private landownership being one 

pivotal factor), but was convinced that in the secrets of its success 

lay also the foretelling of its demise. ‘[T]he rule of the bourgeois 
democrats, from the very first, will’, Marx prophesied, ‘carry 
within it the seeds of its own destruction’."!7 Perhaps the same will 
prove true of the ‘home’ rule of the UK’s bourgeois neoliberals. 

Coda 

In 1987 Ian Jack published a brilliant collection of essays, Before 

the Oil Ran Out: Britain 1977-86. It offers as rich a picture of 

Britain in the early years of Thatcherite neoliberalism as one 

could imagine.' Reflecting on that book a quarter of a century 

later, Jack noted that the main question on which he had erred 
was signalled by the book's title. “My estimate that by about 2010 

Britain would “probably cease to be a significant producer of 

oil”’, he admitted in 2013, ‘was hopelessly wrong.” The oil has 

still not run out today, even if oil-based tax revenue — which, as 
Jack also recollected, had bought Thatcher and the country a 
measure of social peace in the early-to-mid 1980s through tax 

cuts and welfare benefits — largely has (see Chapter 2). 

Where his book held up better, Jack observed, was in its 
gloomy prognosis for the future of the national economy in the 

light of a failure to invest the spoils of the oil boom strategically. 
He picked out one particular sentence from the book — ‘[G]iven 

the lack of industrial investment during Britain’s peak oil years, 

it is difficult to see what will provide our living’ — as having ‘the 

comfort of rightness’. Successive governments have since made 

the exact same mistake with the spoils of the financial services 
boom that followed hard on the heels of the oil boom. Jack's 

prognosis in 2013 was thus equally gloomy: ‘Neither Big Oil nor 

378 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

the Big Bang has saved us — what will, O Lord, what will?’? Jack 

was, of course, right; neither Big Oil nor the Big Bang has saved 

the UK economy, which, seven years later, remains in a parlous 

state, especially for those working in it. In this book I hope I 

have made a contribution to explaining exactly why. 

The core problem, I have suggested, lies not with the specific 

sector — which is to say, not with oil or finance, and their respec- 

tive idiosyncrasies — although both clearly have problematic char- 

acteristics. It does not even: principally lie with the fact that the 

tax revenues earned from oil and finance have not been prudently 

invested in the industrial base, although clearly that has not 

helped. The basic problem lies with the general capitalist model of 
which the oil and finance sectors represent quintessential exam- 

ples. It lies, in other words, with the rentier model. Since they are 
rentier sectors, oil and finance could not help but fail to save the 
economy, for reasons fleshed out at length in this book. So what 
about intellectual property? Or platforms, contracts, infrastruc- 
ture and land? None of these sectors, all of them thoroughly rent- 

ierist, is going to come to the nation’s rescue either. 

‘The reasons for this failure stem largely from the fact that the 

rentier, as I noted in the Preface, sweats monopoly from every 

pore. Monopoly is in the rentier’s nature, integral to her very 
being. A key consequence of this in many sectors, as we have 

seen, is profits far above those that would be attainable in 
anything approaching a competitive economy. The UK’s leading 
infrastructure rentiers, IP rentiers and land rentiers, for example, 
have been shown to enjoy levels of profit that would turn most 

capitalist firms green with envy. These profits have translated 

into a bonanza for the shareholders and managers of the UK’s 
leading rentier institutions. 

Nevertheless, monopoly profits arguably are not the main prob- 
lem with a rentier economy such as the UK’s; the problem is what 

comes with them, and the monopoly power that underwrites them. 
A monopoly economy, economists have long recognized, is an 
economy constitutionally prone to stagnation and low levels of 

CODA 
By) 

innovation and investment. We have seen repeated evidence of 

such torpor in this book, both at the level of individual rentier 

sectors and at the scale of the UK economy more broadly. 

National macroeconomic metrics for the neoliberal (that is, rent- 

ier) period bespeak mounting evidence of monopoly and its chronic 

ills. Levels of capital investment and research-and-development 

intensity have steadily fallen (Figure 0.4, p. 33). Accordingly, as the 

rentiers grip on the economy and its asset base has tightened, levels 

of growth have also fallen (Figure 0.5, p. 34). Indeed, output growth 
began falling just around the time Before the Oil Ran Out hit the 

shelves in the nation’s bookstores. If the UK economy did not run 

out of oil, then, it did — as Jack also predicted — run out of steam. 

There is nothing in the longer historical record to suggest that 

national growth prospects are likely to improve while the rentier's 

grip remains vice-like. As Rutger Bregman has cautioned: “One 

thing is certain: countries where rentiers gain the upper hand gradu- 

ally fall into decline. Just look at the Roman Empire. Or Venice in 

the 15th century. Look at the Dutch Republic in the 18th century. 

Like a parasite stunts a child’s growth, so the rentier drains a country 

of its vitality.“ 

Needless to say, declining economic growth such as the UK 

has experienced in recent times puts pressure on all incomes, 

including household incomes. ‘The latter, however, have come 

under particular pressure in the UK in this period, due to another 
phenomenon related directly to the rentier’s monopoly power. 

Monopolist rentiers exercise power not just in the markets in 

which they sell products and services, but also in those in which 

they are active as buyers — including, crucially, as buyers of 

labour-power. As the UK economy has ‘rentierized’ under neolib- 

eralism, so UK capital — rentier capital — has taken a steadily 

increasing share of national income at the expense of workers. 

Thus, labour has experienced a double squeeze. Incomes pres- 

sured by sluggish economic conditions have been further pres- 

sured by capital’s improving ability to capture disproportionately 

the proceeds of whatever growth is achieved. 

350 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

All of this, though, has beén experienced highly unequally. 
Workers at the top, if not necessarily executives at rentier institu- 

tions then often ‘petit’ financial and/or property rentiers them- 

selves (Chapters 1 and 7), have done just fine. The pressure has 
been concentrated, rather, on those at the sharp end, as the types 
of precarious employment associated most notably with plat- 
form and contract rentierism have proliferated (Chapters 4 and 

5). The aggregate result has been a substantial increase in UK 
income inequality in the age of rentier capitalism.’ 

Furthermore, as the work of Thomas Piketty, most famously, 

has shown, rentierism such as now dominates the UK economy 
has implications for wealth inequality, too.° Piketty’s central 
argument is that, under capitalism, the generalized excess of rates 
of return on assets (his 7) over rates of growth in economic output 
(his g) serves to increase levels of wealth inequality because assets, 
which are unequally distributed to begin with, deliver greater 
returns to their owners than employment does to the ‘owners’ of 
labour-power. Pursuing this argument further, Piketty notes that 
increases in wealth inequality will inevitably be greatest when g is 
suppressed and r is inflated. 

We have just seen that the first of these conditions has character- 

ized the UK under monopolistic rentier capitalism: output growth 

has been falling. And as I have emphasized repeatedly, the latter 
condition has also widely obtained. Piketty’s r has been inflated by 

all manner of factors and forces, some of which have applied to 

specific types of assets held by specific types of rentiers, while others 

— not least low and declining rates of inflation and low and declin- 
ing levels of taxation of wealth and capital gains — have been more 
general. Hence, alongside and intimately connected to growing 
income inequality, the UK has been witness to growing wealth 
inequality.’ This, in short, is the dual cross that a rentier nation has 

to bear; inequality is woven into the political-economic fabric.

To return to Ian Jack’s question, if neither Big Oil nor the Big 
Bang saved the UK economy — and if, in light of their rentier 

characteristics, IP, platforms, contracts, infrastructure and land 

are unlikely, individually or collectively, to do so either — what 

will? To put the issue more prosaically and pragmatically, what 

positive steps could be taken to dig the UK — and especially the 

vast majority of the population for whom rentierism delivers no 

tangible benefits — out of the hole into which four decades of 

rentier-privileging neoliberalism have sunk it? 

It will come 
as no surprise that there is no magic fix. 

Nevertheless, there are at least four areas in which action could 

be pursued that would help to redress the gross existing political- 

economic imbalance between rentiers — institutional and indi- 

vidual — and everyone else, and thereby to restore a modicum of 

health to the national economy and polity. None would be likely 

to be remotely sufficient individually — but in combination, 

feeding off one another, meaningful transformations in these 

four areas would certainly facilitate a loosening of the rentier’s 

stranglehold. Moreover, promising ideas on each score are already 

in circulation, and in some instances already being implemented 

— in other countries, if not always in the UK. Obviously, the UK 

is not the only country afflicted by rentierism, and the question
