RENTIER CAPITALISM 

of what can be done to move beyond rentierism is as urgent in 
many places outside the UK as within it. 

To speak of moving ‘beyond’ rentierism is of course to raise a 

rather significant question. If rentier capitalism, for all the reasons 

discussed in this book, is something to be rejected, what should 
be proposed in its stead? What could or should take rentier capi- 

talism’s place? In laying out in the following pages the four key 

areas in which action clearly needs to be taken, I will try to sketch 

out an answer to this question. 

The first area is competition policy. If the rentier enjoys 
monopoly power, then policymakers’ principal instrument for 

diluting such power should be utilized to the full extent of its 
capacity in order to limit the various negative consequences of 
pervasive monopoly described earlier. Certainly, there are some 
rentier sectors in which, as we have seen, it is very difficult to 
introduce market-based competition even if the political will is 
there. Land (Chapter 7) is one; infrastructure, and especially the 
‘natural’ monopolies existing in the supply of many public utili- 
ties (Chapter 6), is another. In these cases, alternative mecha- 
nisms for limiting pervasive rentier dynamics would be neces- 
sary, and I will come to these shortly. 

Nonetheless, for all the evident sectoral limitations on the 

effectiveness of competition policy, it is clear that much more 

can be done than has been attempted. Why, one might ask, does 

the UK have such a highly concentrated financial services sector 
(Chapter 1)? Why are UK IP rights typically tantamount to 
monopoly rights, and often in perpetuity (Chapter 3)? And why 
do so many of the new breed of digital-platform operators enjoy 
positions of untrammelled market dominance (Chapter 4)? In 
none of these sectors is monopoly power ‘natural’ or inevitable 

— even if, in some (such as the platform space), there are admit- 
tedly structural characteristics favouring the aggregation of such 
power. Instead, the answer is that policymakers have actively 
enabled rentiers’ accumulation of monopoly control — or, at the 
very least, failed 
to forestall 
it when presented with the

opportunity to do so. UK IP rights are expansive and robust

their own 
devices.

ment began with various prominent UK economic commenta-

A necessary part of the mix in a more progressive post-rentierist 

future would be a very different type of tax system. The UK’s 

existing system, as I have shown, is aligned exceptionally well 
with rentier interests, both in terms of general tax rules — 

in which the series of historic, rentier-friendly amendments to 

capital-gains tax stands out (see Introduction) — and in terms of 

tax provisions applying to specific sectors of the economy. The 

CODA 
389 

UK tax system is long overdue for a radical overhaul to rid it of 

its increasingly rentierist bent. 

In the first place, such an overhaul would be designed to end 

the cossetting of rentiers who scarcely require the additional 
support they currently receive. Rentiers should be made to pay 

their fair share of tax, which, on any reasonable reckoning, many 

— perhaps most — do not currently do. This is not just a question 

of taxes on income: rentierism is a form of economic existence 

predicated on control and exploitation of exclusive assets; the use 
and value of those assets is as important as the value of the income 
streams they generate. The centrality of assets is what distin- 

guishes rentierism from non-rentierist modes of economic 

production, and thus taxes on assets — which, alongside taxes on 

income, have long represented a primary instrument in govern- 

ments’ overall fiscal toolkit — need particularly close considera- 

tion when what is at stake is designing a fairer tax system specifi- 

cally for a rentier nation. 

Nor is this a question only of simple tax rates (on income, 

assets, or both); as we have seen, the tax system is much more 
complex than that. Part of the reason why rentiers have thrived 
under the tax regime that has emerged in the UK under neolib- 

eralism is that a broad range of customized fiscal supports has 

been made available, ranging from the capital allowances afforded 

to infrastructure rentiers (Chapter 6) to the reliefs on qualifying 

productions afforded to the nation’s creative industries (Chapter 

3), and from the exemptions available to landowners (Chapter 7) 

to the subsidies still — scandalously — handed out to fossil-fuel 

companies (Chapter 2). Modifying the tax system in such a way 

as to limit rentiers’ ability to earn excess profits should be a matter 

of reducing the existing tax-based subventions supporting rent- 

iers as well as, or perhaps instead of, simply increasing tax rates 

—which is of course a very different proposition in terms of 
polit- 

ical optics and public (let alone corporate) tolerance. 

Rethinking and redesigning the tax regime to enable a more 

proportionate contribution 
from 
rentiers who 
are 
currently

accustomed in many cases to capturing monopoly profits would in 

turn increase the government’ tax revenues. This would allow the 
government not only to support more effectively those whom rent- 

ier capitalism has largely left behind, but to invest actively in the 

production of an alternative, less-rentierist or even non-rentierist 

future. Boosting the state’s fiscal capacity would be a positive move 

at any juncture, but would be especially beneficial at this historical 
moment, when the UK has among the worst public finances in the 

Western world: large debts, substantial future pension liabilities, 

and, in the wake of the privatizations described in this book, few

In arguing for an overhaul of the UK tax system in light of the 
damaging contemporary dominance of the rentier, it is nonethe-

revenue. Increasing government tax income would be a positive 
outcome, but ultimately it would not be the primary objective.

Piketty estimates that the return on assets (7) globally before 

tax has always been greater than the rate of economic growth 

(zg). And, for most of capitalist history, r after tax has also been 

greater than g — hence Piketty’s claim that, ceteris paribus, 

wealth inequality increases under capitalism. What was differ- 

ent about the period from around 1910 to 1980 was that, for 

the first time in history, g exceeded net (post-tax) 7, thus reduc- 

ing inequality — thanks partly, at least during the three decades 

following World War II, to ‘exceptional growth’, but mainly as 

a result, across the whole period, of ‘progressive tax policies’. It

is tax, then, that principally explains ‘the unprecedented era 
during which the net rate of return on capital was less than the 
growth rate’, and during which wealth inequality accordingly 

fell.2! It is therefore no wonder that higher tax on assets is 
Piketty’s main policy proposal to bring r back below g, and thus 
counteract surging wealth inequality today. Only in this way, 
he argues, will it be possible — in Monbiot’s words — to break 
the power of patrimonial capital and the vicious circle of wealth 
accumulation and inequality.

There is one further dimension of taxes that is also highly 

pertinent to the constitution of the economy and the possibil- 

ity of shifting it, in the UK case, away from its existing rentier- 

ist disposition. Taxes 
are 
not 
a merely reactive 
political- 
economic technology, taking the tapestry of economic activity 

for what it is and then extracting various levels of tax from 
economic actors based on their varying levels of assets and 

income. Taxes also shape the economy: what economic actors 

decide to do with their existing assets and competences depends 

partly on their understanding of the different tax implications 

of different courses of action. As we have seen repeatedly, UK 
governments of the neoliberal period have not just feather- 

bedded rentiers with generous tax treatments but have also, in 

the process, actively encouraged them to be rentiers: perhaps 

those companies that have ploughed vast resources into drilling 

for hydrocarbons in the North Sea (Chapter 2) or into applying 

for patent extensions in order to ‘evergreen’ drugs nearing 
patent expiry (Chapter 3) would have used their resources 
differently if tax subsidies supportive of both these activities 
had not been available. 

The possibility clearly exists, in any event, to reconfigure taxes 

not just to make the rentier pay her way, and not just to tackle 
the soaring inequality to which rentierism is fundamental, but 

also to channel rentiers — existing and potential — away, from 
rentierism. Simply stated, taxes on incomes earned from non- 

rentier activities could be lowered, utilizing what economists 

CODA 
393 

refer to as the ‘negative reinforcement’ aspect of taxation: remov- 
ing an aversive stimulus in order to strengthen what is deemed to 

be a positive behaviour or outcome. Meanwhile, taxes on rentier 

assets and income streams could be introduced or, where they 

already exist, increased, thus discouraging rentierism. A prime 
example of such a tax would be a land-value tax, which, as we 

saw in Chapter 7, the UK does not currently levy. The lack of 

such a tax is one reason why the country is notable for such inef- 

ficient and plainly unproductive allocations of capital to land, 

with speculative ‘investors’ buying land and retaining it without 

developing it, purely in the hope that its value will increase, 
knowing that they are able to hold it tax-free. A land-value tax 

would act as another kind of negative reinforcer — motivating 

landowners to use their land, or pay. More broadly, a tax system 

is required that incentivizes productive investment and actively 

disincentivizes the crowding-out of such investment through 

forms of rent-seeking such as land speculation. 

This brings us to the third arena in which action should be taken 

to release the UK and its economy from its rentier vice. Moving 
beyond rentierism can never be only about burying — euthaniz- 

ing, to use Keynes's famous term — the rentier. If rentier institu- 

tions and their activities were eliminated from the contemporary 
UK economy, as this book has shown, there would not be much 

left. Something has to take their place. A non-rentier or mini- 
mally rentierist economy will not rise magically, phoenix-like, 
from the ashes of the rentier edifice. It will need to be built, 
which will require investment. 

The government would certainly need to play a pivotal role 

in stimulating appropriate private-sector investment, channel- 
ling companies and individuals away from the lure of rent — 

precisely by making it less alluring — and towards other types 

of economic production (see below). ‘The fact that the political 
mainstream in the UK has, in recent years, rediscovered indus- 

trial policy is probably a positive signal in this regard, although

omy. Although the bank, which will make long-term invest- 
ments in Scottish companies, will be a limited company oper- 
ating at arm's length from the government, the latter will own 
and fund it, and ‘ministers [will] be “given the power to guide 
its strategic direction” by “setting missions” for it to “tackle 
socio-economic challenges” ’.*° A similar institution established 
by the UK government would have the potential to contribute 
towards seeding and funding a transition away from rentierism 

at the level of the UK as a whole. 

CODA 
OM) 

Given the scale of the challenge, however, a little nudging here 

and there is almost certain to be insufficient. Rentierism is not 

some epiphenomenon in the UK; it essentially constitutes the 
economy, with both deep roots and pervasive reach. ‘The fashion- 

ing of a new economy will require the government to do more 

than merely incentivize certain alternative types of private-sector 

activity. It will require the government to grasp the nettle and 

invest on a significant scale in its own economic assets, skills and 

activities. Ihe government, in short, will have to take a leading 

role. As Mariana Mazzucato and Martha McPherson have writ- 

ten about the equally daunting ‘re-direction 
plan for the entire 
economy necessitated not by the problems of rentierism but 

rather by the need to both foster and prepare for a low-carbon 

transition: “This requires more than tax incentives: it requires 

bold investments like those witnessed in Roosevelt’s New Deal in 

the wake of the Great Depression.’*” 

Mazzucato’s own work is important for showing that large- 

scale, productive, intelligent state investment driving positive 

economic transitions is not the left-wing, pie-in-the-sky fantasy 

it is often represented as. Just like the conventional view of 

government industrial strategy (that it is misguided folly), the 

conventional view of ‘a boring, lethargic State versus a dynamic 

private sector is, Mazzucato has demonstrated, ‘as wrong as it is 

widespread’. The Entrepreneurial State shows that, historically, 

the state in many countries, the United States included, has 

served ‘not just as an administrator and regulator of the wealth 

creation process, but a key actor in it’, making truly transforma- 

tive investments to create ‘entirely new markets and sectors, 

including the Internet, nanotechnology, biotechnology and clean 
energy 
..*® The state, in other words, has driven major economic 

transitions through its own economic actions, rather than just 

through what it countenances or facilitates in the private sector. 

Mazzucato cites Keynes: “Ihe important thing for government is 

not to do things which individuals are doing already, and to do 

them a little better or a little worse; but to do those things which 

396 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

at present are not done at all.” It would, of course, be an exag- 

geration to say that, in the UK today, economic activities not 
saturated with rentier dynamics are ‘not done at all’, but it would 
only be a minor one. 

It is not an exaggeration, however, to say that an entrepre- 

neurial British state, taking the lead in the creation of an econ- 
omy not dominated by rentierism, would represent a major 

departure from the present. Not only is the current British 
government, like all its predecessors since the early 1980s, firmly 

on the rentier’s side; it has increasingly distanced itself from 

proprietary investment per se, whether of a rentier-hostile or 

rentier-friendly variety. As Figure C.1 illustrates, UK govern- 
ment investment as a share of GDP has been on a downward 

trend since the end of the 1970s, notwithstanding a brief uptick 

in the immediate aftermath of the global financial crisis. And as 

Figure C.2 shows, this downward path has meant that, relative to 

the size of the national economy, UK government investment in 

recent years has been significantly below the levels achieved by 

the majority of its OECD peers. This, clearly, would need to 
change.“

Where, then, should the UK government be investing? And 
where should it be encouraging the private sector to invest? I 
have said that investment needs to be redirected away from the 

rentier economy, but what might that entail in terms of where 
investment would be focused instead? This is obviously a consid- 

erably harder question, raising the issue of what a modern UK 
economy not beholden to the rentier would look like. I do not 

have any comprehensive answers, but three points seem particu- 

larly important. 

First, if rentierism is defined largely by exclusive control of 

assets, then non-rentierist activity is by definition that which is 

either non-asset-intensive or in which assets are fundamental but 

not exclusively controlled. The latter possibility speaks to issues I 

have either addressed already (competition policy) or to which I 

will be turning shortly (ownership), so I will focus on the former. 
What are ‘non-asset-intensive economic activities? Indeed, are 

there such things? There are. Much of what goes on in the services 

sector, 
not 
to mention 
significant parts of manufacturing, 
produces incomes not predicated in any meaningful way on asset 

398 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

mobilization, unless one counts workers as assets. Indeed, the 
position and value of workers represents a key point of distinc- 

tion. In a rentier economy such as the UK has today, workers are, 
to a significant extent, secondary, valuable not so much in them- 
selves but for their servitude to scarce non-human assets, enabling 
the latter — the real assets — to continue to throw off cash come 
what may. An economy based less on rent would be an economy 
based more on people, where what attracted investment would 
in some significant measure be workers and their skills, rather 
than non-human assets and their protection from competition. 
Second, this emphasis on people would extend from people as 
economic producers to people as consumers — but not, crucially, as 
individual consumers whose ‘needs’ are those produced by the 
market, and whose ability to realize those needs is determined by 
individual market income. Rather, the consumption to which invest- 
ment would primarily be directed would be collective consumption 
of essential, or what some are calling ‘foundational’, goods or services. 
Noting that the provision of such goods and services for collective 
consumption is not guaranteed by high and rising incomes (the 
market ‘fails’), the so-called Foundational Economy Collective 

describes this ‘foundational economy’ as comprising 

the goods and services which are the social and material infra- 

structure of civilised life because they provide daily essentials 

for all households. These include material services through 

pipes and cables, networks and branches distributing water, 

electricity, banking services and food; and the providential 

services of education, and health and social care, as well as 
income maintenance. These are welfare-critical activities for 

all households in the sense that limited access has a significant 

effect on the welfare of households and social economic oppor- 
tunity for citizens.*! 

The ideas are a bit vague, for now at any rate; but the central 

point 
is an 
important 
one: 
the foundations 
of ‘civilized’ 

CODA 
399 

(honourable?) life for large swathes of the UK population have 

been eroded under rentier-privileging neoliberalism, and renew- 

ing such foundations would be fundamental to the construction 
of an economy not organized around rentier interests. 

Third, a UK economy beyond rentierism must be green; it has 

to be a carbon-neutral economy, and soon. As climate crisis esca- 

lates by the day, it is really as simple as that. All manner of ideas 
and proposals have been advanced for the nature of the investment 

required to make this transition, with proposals for a Green New 

Deal currently circulating widely, but there is one thing all such 

proposals share: a realization that at the heart of the necessary 

investment would be massive investment in infrastructure — new 

infrastructure for, among other things, clean energy extraction and 

production, and for energy-efficient transportation, industry and 

homes.” To raise the issue of renewed infrastructure, however, is to 

beg the question not only of who would pay for it all — most 

commentators accept that the state would have to step up to the 

plate — but also of who would own and operate this new genera- 

tion of infrastructure assets. Ownership, in a post-rentier UK, not 

just of climate-friendly infrastructure but of economic assets in 

general, is thus the final issue to which I will now turn. 

While competition policy, taxation and investment would all 

play an important role in reconfiguring the UK economy in a 
manner 
that militated against ongoing rentier dominance, 
ownership is probably the consideration that underpins all the 

others. What, after all, is rentier capitalism if not a mode of 
economic production and reproduction in which the bulk of 

societys valuable economic assets are owned by capital? If the 

private sector does not own an asset, it is, in general, much less 

likely to be able either to control the way in which that asset is 
mobilized economically, or to privatize the benefits of any such 

mobilization. 

The rentier’s astonishing rise to prominence in the neoliberal 
period has been largely a function of ownership transformations. 

400 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

An extraordinary range and wealth of key assets have been privat- 

ized, including most notably land and housing (Chapter 7), 

infrastructures for the provision of public utilities (Chapter 6) 
and contractual responsibility for carrying out tasks previously 
discharged by the public sector (Chapter 5); as the economist 
Diane Coyle has observed, ‘the belief the public sector should 
own as little as possible’ has become nothing less than an ‘article 
of faith’ among successive administrations in Whitehall, New 
Labour included.* At the same time, the rights attached to the 
burgeoning stock of privately owned assets, from natural resource 
reserves (Chapter 2) to IP assets (Chapter 3), and from radio 
spectrum (Chapter 6) to rental housing (Chapter 7), have been 
widely strengthened, in the process changing the practical mean- 
ing and substance of ‘ownership’. If there is to be any meaningful 
prospect of a shift away from rentier capitalism in the UK, there- 
fore, the direction of such ownership transformations must, to 
some extent, be reversed. More than anything else, taking on the 
rentier means shrinking the portfolio of exclusive proprietary 

assets on which she is able to earn private rents. 

The objective of doing so would not only be to spread the 
economic rewards of asset ownership away from the privileged, 
propertied few; asset ownership does not furnish solely economic 

advantages. Insofar as the future of a society is built upon the 

assets it comprises in the present, the owners of a society’s assets 

have, almost by definition, the power to shape, or even dictate, 

that future, which is a matter of politics as much as economics. 

‘This is another dimension of rentier capitalism to which George 
Monbiot is more alive than most. “The economic power of the 
owners of wealth translates’, he has argued, ‘into political power. 
The richer a tiny segment of society becomes, the better it is able 
to capture politics and undermine democracy. Eventually, we get 
a government of the elite, by the elite, for the elite. Does that 
sound at all familiar?‘ Indeed it does: this is effectively the situ- 
ation in which the UK, with its extreme and growing concentrs 
tion of wealth (assets) in rentier hands, finds itself today. It is an 

CODA 
40] 

exemplar of what Paul Krugman calls a ‘rentier regime’, where 

the ‘rule by rentiers*of which he has also written is political as 

well as economic rule. As Martin Wolf has recently observed, 

there is nothing at all accidental about the fact that the tise of 

rentier capitalism has occurred simultaneously with the materi- 

alization of ‘an increasingly degraded democracy’ 
.“° 
Thus when it comes to the question of the objectives of reform- 
ing ownership away from rentier dominance, what is at stake is 
power and politics as much as pounds and pennies. It is about 
who gets to have a say in determining the future. Mathew 

Lawrence and Nigel Mason made much the same point in a 
2017 report on proposals for broadening ownership in the UK 

economy, which, while focused specifically on company owner- 

ship, has a much broader resonance. “The aim of ownership 

reform’, they maintained, ‘should be two-fold: to give more 

people a share of capital, both as useable wealth and for its 

income returns; and to spread economic power and control in 

the economy, by expanding the decision rights of employees and 

the public.” In the context of the full range of types of rentier 

assets discussed in this book, I could not agree with this senti- 

ment more strongly. 

What might all this mean in practice? One question relates to 
new assets — those that do not yet exist but that will come into 
being in the future being adumbrated here. I have already 
touched on the issue of what precisely, in a post-rentier economy 

of the future, must be invested in, but without addressing the 
ownership of those new assets. I have noted that a green econ- 
omy, scaffolded by new carbon-neutral infrastructures, will inev- 

itably be asset-intensive. The same is true of the ‘foundational’ 
economy, which, as its visionaries suggest, would comprise (as 

we noted earlier) ‘cables, networks and branches distributing 

water, electricity, banking services and food’, alongside buildings 

to house ‘the providential services of education, and health and 

social care’. So, if the green and foundational economies — which 

in practice will be a single green foundational economy — are 

402 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

substantially made up of assets, who will own them? Following 

the logic laid out in this book, the answer must be: not, for the 
most part — and certainly not by default — the private sector. ‘To 
avoid further enclosure and monopolistic rent extraction, it is 
essential that the public sector return to building, owning and 
operating the assets that undergird collective social life — assets 
such as transportation infrastructure, hospitals and genuinely 
affordable housing. 

Meanwhile, perhaps the more thorny questions, politically at 

least, concern not future assets but existing ones — that is, those 

that today belong largely in private rentier hands. Should these, 

or some of them, be expropriated? It is hard to see how the UK 

can otherwise move beyond rentierism. If so, which ones, how, 
and at what cost? These are very much current questions in the 
UK, on the Left if not necessarily elsewhere. There seems to be a 
growing groundswell of opinion in favour of expanded public- 

sector asset ownership, and exciting new ideas are being proposed 

for how exactly such expansion might be achieved. Think tanks 

— including niche entities such as Common Wealth and We Own 

It, alongside larger generalists such as the Institute for Public 

Policy Research (IPPR) and New Economics Foundation — are 
leading the way. 

Some of these proposals call for nationalization of what have 
always been private assets built and operated by private-sector 

rentiers. A good example is the digital platform rentiers exam- 

ined in Chapter 4, such as Facebook and Google. Nick Srnicek, 
among others, argues that, given that they perform increasingly 
essential (or at least publicly pervasive) services and benefit from 

powerful network effects, expropriation of such assets would be 

appropriate: 

In the past, natural monopolies like utilities and railways that 

enjoy huge economies of scale and serve the common good 

have been prime candidates for public ownership. The solu- 

tion to our newfangled monopoly problem lies in this sort of 

CODA 
403 

age-old fix, updated for our digital age. It would mean taking 
back control over the internet and our digital infrastructure, 

instead of allowing them to be run in the pursuit of profit and 
power.*8 - 

More commonly, however, it is assets that were previously 
publicly owned but have succumbed to the privatization frenzy 

of the neoliberal period that observers increasingly believe should 

be nationalized — or renationalized. We Own It, for example, 

makes the case for renationalization of the full range of assets | 
examined in Chapters 5 (services outsourced on a contractual 

basis) and 6 (privatized infrastructures and associated service- 

delivery). It articulates its mission thus: ‘We want to end privati- 

sation for good so that people come before profit. Public services 

should belong to all of us — whether that’s the NHS, schools, 

water, energy, rail, Royal Mail, care work or council services.’ 
Common Wealth, for its part, adds to this list the crucial asset 

whose widespread privatization I examined in Chapter 7: land, 

and the housing that sits on it. ‘Land’, its website says, ‘is nature’s 

gift. Yet its enclosure is at the heart of many of the challenges 

confronting us. From a broken housing system to deep inequali- 

ties of wealth, from financial instability to environmental break- 

down, unequal patterns of land ownership and use drive the 

UK’s dysfunctional economic and social model.’*° 

Indeed, these latter-day champions of ownership transforma- 

tion in the UK push the case further still. It is, they argue, not only 

rentier-owned assets that need to be considered. ‘The ownership- 

transformation agenda should be wider, and should take in private 
companies in general — whether rentiers or not. Lawrence and 
Mason's report on company ownership opens as follows: “The 
unequal ownership of capital in the economy is a powerful driver 
of inequality. With the share of national income going to capital 
having increased in recent decades, and likely to rise further, new 
models of company ownership are needed to reduce inequality 

and ensure the benefits of growing national wealth are widely 

404 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

shared.”*! Among their specific policy suggestions for broadening 
company ownership are a Citizens’ Wealth Fund (which would 
own shares on behalf of the public) and an expansion of coopera- 

tives, mutuals and employee ownership trusts. 

Nor are these ideas emerging in a vacuum, isolated from real- 
world developments. They are gaining traction partly because 

things are happening on the ground, both in the UK and beyond. 
Owners of UK companies, occasionally very high-profile ones, 
have handed ownership and control to employees.” And, more 

directly relevant to our account, asset ownership is being retaken 
from rentiers — albeit, at present, on a relatively small scale and 
principally at a local level. Many such examples concern the 

provision of local utilities returning from private to public 

ownership. Some of the most prominent instances of such ‘remu- 

nicipalization’ pertain to international cases; Aditya Chakrabortty 

has written about the notable case of Wolfhagen in Germany, 
where the local grid has returned successfully to municipal 

control, noting that this is just one of over 500 examples across 

continental Europe since the year 2000 of (predominantly local) 

public services being taken back into public ownership, ranging 

across energy and water supply, waste collection, social care and 

local transportation services.” 

But even in the UK, for so long a place of unchallenged ideo- 

logical supremacy and material security for the rentier, moves are 
now afoot. An important report compiled by Olivier Petitjean 
and Satoko Kishimoto has identified sixty-four UK remunici- 

palizations across education, energy, housing, transportation and 
more.” The bulk of these cases, as David Hall and Cat Hobbs of 
We Own It have noted, relate to councils bringing individual 
outsourced services back in-house when contracts fail or prove 
problematic (see Chapter 5).°° But there have also been more 
ambitious and probably more enduring remunicipalizations. 
Local authorities have established municipal energy companies 

in Nottingham, Leeds and Bristol — all major cities — where new 

public-sector suppliers already cover over 2 million people.” 

CODA 
405 

While these remunicipalizations have been by the public 

sector, and indeed most of the emergent proposals for ownership 

transformation referred to above likewise pertain to the expan- 

sion of state ownership, it is important that our thinking on 

these matters not be constrained. Public-sector ownership of key 

assets is not the only alternative to private rentier ownership, and 
should not necessarily always be the default answer to the ques- 

tion, ‘If not private ownership, what else?’ One of several reasons 

that the UK’s privatizing governments of the 1980s and 1990s 

were able to sell off the state’s assets as readily as they were, and 

with relatively little public dissent, is that the 
UK public was for 

the most part not greatly enamoured with public-sector owner- 

ship and management of the assets in question in the first place. 

Where land was concerned, for example, public-sector owners 

were sometimes woefully poor stewards. Meanwhile, British 

Rail, lest we forget, was hardly a poster-child for the ostensible 

merits of state ownership and operation. 

Private ownership and operation of privatized assets has, as I 

have argued, been largely a disaster for the UK, lining the pock- 

ets of rentier households and institutions, and their shareholders, 

while delivering remarkably — or perhaps not so remarkably — 

little in the way of discernible benefit to the population at large. 

But public-sector ownership prior to privatization was not a 

panacea either, and it is at best naive to assume that it would be 

a panacea in a future scenario of widespread renationalization. 
We should not romanticize state ownership in the way that rent- 

iers and their intellectual, ideological and political apologists 

have long romanticized and fetishized private asset ownership. 

Public-sector ownership, in short, is only one alternative to 

the status quo. Another, in the cases of some types of asset at any 

rate, 
is community ownership. Here, 
too, the think tanks 
mentioned above, for all their emphasis on the possibilities asso- 

ciated with state ownership, are doing important work. Whereas 
We Own It exclusively champions public-sector control, for 

example, Common Wealth — as its name intimates — sees much 

406 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

more scope for communal owneiship. Employee ownership of 
companies arguably fits this category (it is not nationalization, 

after all; and if a company does exist as a community then it is 
surely primarily in the form of its workers).”” So also, to some 
extent, do the local infrastructures for public services springing 
up amid the wreckage of the dominant privatized model. 
Chakrabortty has discussed two examples. One, albeit partial, 
pertains to the municipal reassumption of local electricity distri- 
bution in Wolfhagen, Germany discussed earlier: a quarter of the 
municipal supplier is held by a local citizens’ cooperative that has 
seats on the board of the company, ‘giving residents a direct say 
over how their utility is managed’.** The other is a patchwork of 
emerging local community bus services in the UK, appearing in 
areas left unserved either by private operators, for whom the 
routes in question would be unprofitable, or by local authorities 
hamstrung by budget cuts.” 

But perhaps the most obvious and promising asset for commu- 

nity ownership is land. Land is, in a sense, the original commons, 

and its enclosure the original source of capitalist rentierism — the 

model, as it were, for all enclosures and rentierisms that have 

followed, and one condemned by Polanyi as stridently as by 
Marx. To reclaim land for the community would be to strike a 

blow of symbolic as well as material significance against the rent- 

ier — a blow against rentierism as such, more than against one 

type of rentier, inasmuch as land has for so long been the rentier 

asset par excellence. Rent, after all, was originally and rent; and 

as David Harvey remarks, ‘private property in land . 
. 
. performs 
an ideological and legitimizing function for all forms of private 
property 
.° 
Community landownership in the UK is, for now at least, a 

relatively marginal phenomenon. But community groups have 
been agitating for many years for stronger claims on land that, in 

their view, is not being used in ways that benefit local people. 
Community land trusts are an increasingly favoured model for 
bringing these claims to fruition. While governments in both 

CODA 
407 

England and Scotland have been making increasingly positive 

noises about community landownership, however, the reality is 

that only in the latter territory do these noises currently counte- 
nance community acquisition 
of private land. The UK’s 
Community Right to Reclaim Land gives communities the right 

to contest the use only of land owned by public bodies. Scotland’s 
Community Right to Buy, by contrast, gives communities a pre- 

emptive right to buy certain types of land regardless of who owns 

them, and growth in community landownership in Scotland 

since the 1970s has occurred principally through buyouts from 

private estates, mainly in the north and west Highlands and 

Islands. By 2012, an estimated 76,000 property assets — includ- 

ing housing units, village halls, community facilities and farm 

estates — were owned by over 2,700 community-controlled 

organizations. Collectively, these assets covered some 187,000 

hectares, equating to a little over 2 per cent of Scotland’s land 

area.°! The challenge in a post-rentier UK — or, more accurately, 

the challenge of bringing a post-rentier UK into being — would 

be to build on these initiatives and rapidly scale them up. 

Ultimately, it is clear enough that moving beyond rentier capi- 

talism in the UK would, above all, be a question of breaking the 

ideological and substantive: dominance of private ownership, 

whatever the exact mix of ownership types that replaced it. It is 

wrong and destructive that, as is currently the case, one type of 

asset ownership is elevated above all others — private ownership, 

which naturally buttresses rentierism. But it would probably be 

no less problematic to replace the hegemony of private owner- 

ship with another dogmatic approach relying on a single answer, 

such as state ownership. The value of alternatives in general to 

private ownership needs to be acknowledged. 

A mixed, plural ecology of ownerships is probably the best 
objective — and is certainly the most politically and economically 

viable outcome. On one hand, this would probably result in 

certain assets staying in private hands, for instance some — but 

not all — financial assets, IP assets and housing. ‘The political 

408 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

challenge in this regard is to ensure, through a combination of 

competition policy and taxation, and perhaps other means as 

well, that those private owners are not encouraged and enabled 

to be rentiers. On the other hand, it is inescapably necessary to 
ensure that more assets are owned either by the state, whether 
locally or nationally, or by communal bodies — including many 
of those assets currently in private, rentier hands. 

Insofar as private ownership is the institutional centrepiece of 

capitalism, of course, a significant transformation of the land- 

scape of asset ownership of the kind I have gestured towards here 
would be enormously meaningful. To return, then, to the ques- 

tion I raised earlier: What ‘system’ should the UK move towards 

in moving beyond rentierism? To the extent that key economic 

assets, including but not limited to the means of production, are 

taken out of private hands, one would in practice be moving 

away from capitalism itself and towards something else. The 

further the hegemony of private ownership is eroded, the less the 
mixed ecology that takes its place will look like capitalism. 

The advocates of augmented competition policy whose argu- 

ments I discussed earlier — such as Philip Stephens at the Financial 
Times and Andrew Tyrie at the CMA — all agree with Ian Jack 

that the UK economy is not ‘working’, and needs urgent reform. 

But, on closer inspection, significant differences become clear in 

their understandings of what specific purposes such reform 
would serve. To use Jack’s framing, with which I began: Who or 
what, in short, needs saving? Jack says it is ‘us’, the people: ‘what 
will provide our living?’ This, however, is not Stephens or Tyrie’s 
concern, at least not ultimately. For them, what needs saving, 
rather, is capitalism — specifically, from ‘capitalists’ (Stephens) or 
itselBelyaie)e 

Pursued energetically and substantively, the four sets of trans- 

formative actions outlined above would I think together repre- 

sent an attempt to build something — call it what you will — that 

it would be impossible to label simply ‘capitalism’ in any of the 

CODA 
409 

various senses in which we have come to use the word. It is not 

capitalism, therefore, that one would be saving. The state would 

be much more active, involved and — not least — invested in the 
economy than it is under capitalism. Society’s economic resources 
would be subject to much more dispersed and democratic control 

than they are under capitalism. 

In fact, I would go further. If capitalist rentierism is success- 

fully subdued, what remains cannot be capitalism as we know it. 

This is because, as Piketty has argued, rentierism is effectively 

hardwired into capitalism. Capital, he writes, is ‘risk-oriented 
and entrepreneurial, at least at its inception, yet it always tends 

to transform itself into rents as it accumulates in large enough 

amounts — that is its vocation, its logical destination’. What we 

call ‘capitalism is, or inevitably becomes, rentierism. 

This is not only a function of the fact that, in David Harvey's 

words, capitalists prefer ‘the certainties, the quiet life and the 

possibility of leisurely and cautious changes that go with a 
monopolistic style’, although that is certainly all true.°? More 

fundamentally, it is a function of the relative rewards available 

under capitalism — aside from during the few exceptional mid- 

twentieth-century decades of expansionist taxation 
— from 

investment in new production, as opposed to earning rents on 

existing wealth. “The logic of r > g’, in Piketty’s precise formula- 

tion, ‘implies that the entrepreneur always tends to turn into a 

rentier." Another way of putting this is to say that, if rentierism 

is more rewarding than entrepreneurship, what rational capitalist 

would choose not to be a rentier? 

Issues such as ownership, competition and taxation are, after 

all, of central significance to capital. In fact, they are nothing less 

than existential questions, pivotal to the essence of what capital 
and capitalists represent — especially, though not exclusively, in 

their rentierist guise. If rent is capital’s vocation, in any event, 
meaningfully suppressing rent and rentierism while thereby — in 

Stephens and ‘Tyrie’s terms — saving capitalism is a logical impos- 

sibility. To euthanize the rentier is to create a political-economic 

410 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

system with a different ethos, a different ‘logical destination’. 
Only by doing so can we — Jack’s ‘us’ — be saved. 

But if this, very broadly, describes what needs to be done, who 

is going to do it? It will not be capitalists themselves. This is a 
much less obvious point than it might sound — there are in fact 

very good reasons for capital to favour at least 
a measure of 

de-rentierization. But an endemic collective-action problem 

militates against capitalists pursuing such an outcome. 

Consider, for example, the ‘narrow issue of monopolization 
and its negative impact on the labour share of income. Neither 

excessive monopoly power nor excessively squeezed wages are, in 

reality, propitious for capital — inviting, as they do, stagnation 

while dampening overall effective demand. Nonetheless, monop- 
oly and cheap labour are wonderful for the individual capitalist 
company that happens to enjoy them. Certainly, not all compa- 

nies do; but, just as many individuals languishing below the 
economic elite think they will advance to its ranks one day, so 

too do many companies that are not successful rentiers hope and 

expect to be so in the future. This is just one reason that capitals 
typically fail to come together to act politically as a class to work 

in the collective interest of capital as a whole. 

Then there is the more generalized Keynesian fear of what 
might happen when, as one might well argue is the case in the UK 

today, poverty becomes so widespread and so dishonourable as to 
approach the point of becoming socially intolerable. This is not a 
promising scenario for capital, either — or indeed for Keynes's 
ever-precarious ‘civilization’. Keynes knew this, and thus, as Mann 

observes, he insisted ‘that capital must “sacrifice” in the interests 
of the social order, in the interests of stable accumulation’. But it 

never does. Why is this? Because, according to Mann, citing 
Keynes, to the extent that capital ever does act ‘as a class’, it is 
‘dogmatic, myopic 
. . 
. It is not sufficiently worried that the emer- 
gence of the rabble will lead to a oh Sater derrdcunn of 
existing economic forces in their entirety”’.© Is rentier capital in 

CODA 
41] 

the contemporary UK worried about gross inequality and dishon- 
ourable poverty and their potentially destructive implications for 

capitalism — and prepared to sacrifice accordingly? It does not 
appear to be remotely as worried as it arguably should be, still less 

contemplating sacrificial undertakings. 

Capital, then, will not move to transform the existing order — 

even in ways that would ultimately be beneficial for capital and 

capitalism, much less in the profound ways I have argued are 

necessary, and which on the whole would not be beneficial for 

capital. Neither is the political Right — which, if we include New 

Labour, has been in government in the UK for four decades now 

— going to rid the UK of its rentierist bent. Marx wrote in The 

Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, originally published in 
German in 1852, that ‘the Tories in England long fancied that 

they were in raptures about royalty, the church and the beauties 

of the ancient constitution, until a time of trial tore from them 

the confession that they were only in raptures about rent.’ It 

was a typically shrewd and acerbic insight, and his assessment of 

where the interests of the Tories of the early nineteenth century 

ultimately lay applies with equal force and accuracy to today’s 

Conservative Party. It is, perhaps more than anything else, a 

party of and for rentiers, existing first and foremost to defend 

rentier interests much more than the interests of productive 

capital. 

Indeed, the Conservative Party’s rentierist disposition proba- 
bly goes some considerable way to explain why, after 2016, it 
emphatically became the party of Brexit. All reasonable commen- 

tators believe that Brexit will be enormously deleterious for 

productive capital based in the UK — harmful, in Simon Wren- 

Lewis's words, to ‘most productive capital and those who work 

with it: the capital embodied in firms that trade for sure, but also 

the capital that produces stuff for firms that trade and so on. In 

so far as Brexit will impoverish the UK as a whole, it is also harm- 

ful to any firms that produce for the UK market.’ Furthermore, 
productive capitalists themselves fully recognize these likely 

412 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

harms, and voiced their opinion’ in no uncertain terms. “Who 

backs Brexit?’, asked David Edgerton. ‘Agriculture is against it; 
industry is against it; services are against it.’°’ So why, Wren- 
Lewis asked, was ‘the party that has traditionally been thought of 

as supporting UK productive capital, the Conservative party’, 

also ‘the one promoting Brexit’??® Why, in Edgerton’s words, did 

the Conservative Party take ‘a course regarded by every reputable 

capitalist state and the great majority of capitalist enterprises as 
deeply foolish’?”’ 

The most credible answer is surely the one I have hinted at: the 
Conservative Party is not the party of productive capital, but of 

rentier capital, and had the interests of the latter, not the former, at 

heart. Productive capital’s concerns about Brexit were thus largely 

shrugged off. Edgerton suggested the same. “Ihe modern British 

state’, he explained, ‘has distanced itself from the productive econ- 
omy, 
resulting 
in 
‘increasing 
disconnection 
between 
the 

Conservative Party and productive capital.”! Where I would quib- 

ble with Edgerton — with due deference to his acumen as an eminent 

historian, which I am not — is in his reading of historical change. 
Edgerton maintains that the UK once was a nation of ‘great manu- 

facturers’, and that the Tory Party once was the party of productive 

capital.” For a very brief period in the mid twentieth century, 
perhaps so, but otherwise I am not convinced. I side rather with 
Perry Anderson, who, as I noted in the Introduction, makes a 
compelling case that the UK has always at heart been a nation of 
rentiers.” And I side also with Marx, and with his branding of the 
‘Tory Party as the party of rent — in the past no less than today. 

At any rate, the fact that Brexit is likely also to be harmful to at 

least some rentier capital interests — finance capital, for example — is 

probably lost on the Tories, whose understanding of the economy 

has never lived up to the billing they like to give it.‘ It may also be 

lost on some of those rentier capitalists themselves. But whatever 

the political-economic arithmetic informing Brexit, the simple and 

vital truth is that the Conservatives are rallying behind rentiers 
now, as through history. George Monbiot is thus wholly correct to 

CODA 
413 

insist that, in the UK, ‘the right will never break the power of patri- 

monial wealth, because the right exists to defend it’.”° 

The political movement to move the UK beyond rentierism 

must therefore come from the Left, which, Monbiot maintains, 

exists (when it remembers what it’s for’) to ‘confront’ patrimoni- 

alism.’° In this regard, there have been eminently hopeful signs 
from the current opposition. Under Jeremy Corbyn, its leader 

since 2015, Labour has been talking about plans for transforma- 

tions in taxation, investment and ownership that align closely 

with those described above, and that derive from broadly similar 

concerns.’/ 
: 

Under existing policy proposals, a Labour government would, 

for example, aim to renationalize, at a minimum, water, energy 

and rail services, as well as to rebuild the UK’s denuded stock of 

public land by using revised compulsory purchase laws to enable 

the public sector to acquire sites from private owners at closer to 

existing-use value than is currently possible.”* A Labour govern- 

ment would also seek to instigate a ‘radically different approach 

to taxation’, one focused specifically on rentier wealth, including 

— through land-value taxation — rentier property wealth.”? And a 

Labour government would work to provide the UK with its own 

Green New Deal; in 2018, it unveiled plans for a programme of 

investment and transformation designed to achieve a 60 per cent 

reduction in emissions by 2030, while creating over 400,000 

skilled jobs.*° All of this would be undertaken with a view to 

reducing inequality and poverty, and especially dishonourable 

poverty, ‘shifting the balance of power back towards workers [to] 

achieve decent wages, security and dignity at work’, and treating 

those out of work with the ‘dignity and respect’ they have been 

denied by governments of the Right.*! On the other hand, though 

it would give workers a voice on the CMA and other public 

bodies, Labour has no substantive plans for the fourth pillar of 

anti-rentierist 
political-economic 
transformation 
I outlined 

earlier — competition policy. But you cannot have everything. 

414 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

Figuring out what needs to be done about rentier capitalism, and 
who needs to do it, is the easy part. Getting it done is, unfortu- 

nately, altogether more difficult. To tackle meaningfully issues of 
ownership, competition and taxation, not to mention the role of 

the state in the planning and operation of the economy, would 
be to strike at the very heart of capital and power in the rentier- 
ized UK. This power should not be underestimated. 

It is no secret that big capital has tremendous influence over 

the UK political economy as.a whole. In the 1930s, Keynes, as I 

noted in Chapter 1, declared that the euthanasia of the rentier of 

which he dreamed would represent the euthanasia of power — 

specifically, power to exploit the scarcity-value of capital — that 

was in his terms ‘cumulative’ (the power of the capitalist class) 
and ‘oppressive’ (the Oxford English Dictionary’s preferred syno- 

nyms are ‘merciless; harsh; exploitative; repressive’). Without 
wanting to make difficult comparisons between the balance of 

the political economy of the UK then and now, let us just say 

that the power of rentier capital is not evidently less cumulative 
and oppressive today than it was in Keynes’s era. Moreover, as 
Rutger Bregman has forcefully argued, rentierism is, ‘in essence, 

a question of power’: 

That the Sun King Louis XIV was able to exploit millions was 

purely because he had the biggest army in Europe. It’s no 

different for the modern rentier. He’s got the law, politicians 
and journalists squarely in his court. That’s why bankers get 

fined peanuts for preposterous fraud, while a mother on 

government assistance gets penalised within an inch of her life 

if she checks the wrong box.” 

Anyone in any doubt about either the power of rentier capital 

in the contemporary UK or its determination to thwart the types 
of anti-rentier initiatives envisaged by Labour under Corbyn 
would do well to consider the strength of the establishment 
backlash against the proposals elaborated by the party during the 

CODA 
AWS) 

course of 2018 and 2019. Two of the country's leading infra- 

structure rentiers, for example, on learning of Labour’s renation- 

alization plans, summarily shifted ownership of their UK opera- 

tions overseas ‘to defend themselves against Labour's policies’.* 

‘The reaction to the Labour-commissioned ‘Land for the Many 

report — published in mid 2019, and containing proposals for 

progressive land reform — was sufficiently fierce to lead a clearly 

shaken Monbiot, one of its co-authors, to write an article reflect- 

ing on the readiness of the UK’s ‘billionaire press’ to go into 

battle on behalf of the ‘ultra-rich’ and ‘oligarchic power’. 

Meanwhile, the Financial Times — which in many respects has 
given Corbyn a fairer hearing than the UK’s nominally left news- 

papers, such as the Guardian, during his time as Labour leader 

— had clearly had enough when it saw the contents of the party’s 
2019 general election manifesto: ‘punitive tax increases, sweep- 

ing nationalisation, and the end of Thatcher-era union reforms’. 

‘Mr Corbyn’s original sin’, the paper editorialized, ‘is to cast 

private enterprise as a necessary evil to be managed rather than 

being part of the solution to the problems his party has identi- 

fied. The assault on business is an attack on wealth creation.’® 

The fact that the manifesto was much better understood as an 

attack on rentierism than on wealth creation was entirely lost on 

the writers. The paper's insistence that the UK economy ‘is not 

broken’ also spoke volumes. Not broken for whom? Thus did the 

Financial Times return, then, to its role as the premier newspaper 

of capital, and not just of global capitalism. 

The extent to which rentier capital in the UK had been threat- 
ened by Labour's proposals became ever clearer in the immediate 
wake of the party’s eventual defeat at the ballot box. Friday 13 
December, 2019, the day after the election, was the busiest day 

of trading in shares in Britain’s biggest companies for more than 

two years. Not only did share prices in general leap; shares in 

rentier institutions saw especially large gains. As the Guardian 

reported, ‘banks, housebuilders and utilities’ — rentiers one and 

all — were among the main beneficiaries: “Shares in BT, which 

416 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

would have faced the nationalisation of its Openreach broad- 
band division under a Labour government, rallied by more than 
6%, while billions of pounds were added to the value of energy 
and water companies that were nationalisation targets including 

Severn Trent, Centrica and National Grid’.®° The existential 

threat posed by Labour had been averted. To be sure, the 

Conservatives’ victory made Brexit, and an overall negative shock 

to the UK economy, inevitable. But as Yanis Varoufakis remarked 

on Twitter the same day, “Brexit cut[ting] through supply lines 

and wreck[ing] services’ was nonetheless deemed preferable to 
Labour cutting off rentiers at the knees: ‘ “Investors” [are] happier 

with the shrinking of 
the overall pie than the prospect ofa Labour 
[government] that shifts some of their gains to the many, 

Varoufakis wrote. ‘Class war rules OK.’ 

Capital’s resistance to root-and-branch UK economic trans- 
formation, supported by apologists among the commentariat, 

clearly represents a major obstacle to change. Arguably more 

significant still, though, is resistance on the part of the ‘we’ whom 

Tan Jack had in mind when asking: “What will save us?’ — that is, 

the UK population as a whole. Labour’s electoral failure in 2019, 
on a platform that was implicitly if not explicitly anti-rentierist, 
should be cause for concern among all those convinced of the 
balefulness of contemporary rentier capitalism and by the need 

to supplant it. 

Just as in the case of support for Brexit, there are of course all 
manner of explanations, of varying degrees of plausibility, for the 

UK’s electoral reluctance to support Labour and Corbyn; but 
again, as for Brexit, rentierism itself is surely part of the explana- 

tion. That is, Labour lost partly because of its plans to rein in the 

rentier. Here, we would do well to listen to Bregman, who has 
made a crucial observation about the durability of rentier capital- 
ism in the face of its manifest unfairnesses. Rentier capital is safe- 
guarded, he writes, not just by its cosy relationship with official- 
dom and the mainstream media. Something arguably each more 
troublesome — Bregman says ‘insidious’ — plays a role. Capitalist 

CODA 
417 

corporations are not the only ones that aspire to be rentiers, 
frequently succeeding and profiting in that capacity. As Chapters 

1 and 7 demonstrated, many of the rest of us do, too. ‘We're all 
wannabe rentiers’, Bregman writes. Rentier institutions ‘have 
made millions of people complicit in their revenue model. 

Consider this: What are our financial sector’s two biggest cash 

cows? Answer: the housing market and pensions. Both are markets 

in which many of us are deeply invested.’ And ‘it’s hard to point 

fingers at a kleptomaniac when you have sticky fingers too’.’” 

As I suggested in Chapter 7, the individualized conflicts to 
which this paradoxical state of affairs can readily give rise — recog- 

nizing the problems of rentier capitalism, and perhaps even 
wanting to see it done away with, while simultaneously reaping 

its benefits in a personal capacity — 
are much less common among 
younger people in the UK, who are largely priced out of home- 

ownership. The political obstacles to taking on rentier capital in 

the court of public opinion may therefore not be as great, in the 

British case at any rate, as Bregman fears. As William Davies has 

recently observed, in another insightful essay: 

The young people of Generation Left are now habituated to 

an economy organised around rents, which they experience 

not just as tenants but through the dubious opportunities 

afforded by the ‘sharing economy. Work space, 
spare 

bedrooms, cultural ‘content’ and vehicles aren’t things to be 

owned, but hired on a time-limited basis. Conversely, with the 
demise of the ‘career’ as the dominant way of organising work- 

ing life, a young person comes to view him or herself as a rent- 

able asset, which finds its price on the market. ‘This is the logic 

that underpins Instagram-based celebrity as much as it does 

cycling for Deliveroo.** 

One of the reasons that younger people in the UK voted over- 
whelmingly for Labour in December 2019, in other words, is 

that they are generally not rentiers. They are renters, with 

418 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

nothing to lose and likely plenty to gain from Labour's tilt against 

rentierism. 

But, as Piketty might say, the problem for Labour was and is 

that the UK is today not a nation of a few classical rentiers — it is 

a nation of many ‘petits’ rentiers, and perhaps even more so a 
nation of very many (after Bregman) ‘wannabe’ rentiers. Davies's 
‘comfortable Télegraph-reading Hampshire retiree’ is only the 
most egregious example. There are countless other types. And 
they voted for the Tory party in 2019. Indeed, the rentier— 
non-rentier vote divide was arguably even more pronounced 
than the old—young divide, with which it was not identical; ‘even 
among older voters’, Davies noted, ‘the appeal of the Conservative 
Party doesn’t extend beyond the ranks of owner-occupiers: some- 
one who rents in their sixties is no more likely to vote Conservative 
than someone who rents in their thirties’.* 

As Davies has also written, it certainly seems to be the case 

that, to the UK’s assorted petits rentiers, just as to the country’s 

biggest rentier-capitalist institutions, whatever happens with 

respect to Brexit is much less worrying than the prospect of a 
Labour government: ‘Inflation or a stock market slump would 

certainly harm them, but they may have forgotten that these 

things are even possible. Jeremy Corbyn terrifies them even more 

than the prospect of Remain, as they believe he will tax capital, 

gifts and inheritance into oblivion.° That in fact he would not 
have done any such thing had he won power is almost beside the 

point; courtesy of the UK’s overwhelmingly right-wing press, the 
public appeared convinced that he would. As Monbiot tellingly 
recounted, for example, the press claimed that the ‘Land for the 
Many’ report that Monbiot co-authored had proposed a capital 
gains tax on people's main homes, even though it did nothing of 
the sort.”' A ‘spiteful raid that will horrify millions’, the Mail on 
Sunday screamed.” ‘The rest, as they say, is electoral history. 

Though making progress against and beyond rentierism may not 
be easy, it is nevertheless necessary. For everyone other than 

CODA 
419 

rentiers (of both the household and institutional varieties), capi- 

talism in the UK is patently not working. And there is every 

reason 
to believe that, unless substantive political-economic 
change comes soon, the problems explored in this book will 

intensify rather than abate. That, as Monbiot reminds us, is in 

the very nature of rentier capitalism: 

[When the return on capital increases faster than the growth 

of economic output, inequality spirals, social mobility stalls 
and the enterprise economy is replaced by a rentier economy. 

In other words, once you have money and property, you can 

use it to accumulate more money and property, taking an ever 

greater share of society's wealth, through the harvesting of 

economic rent ... By this means, through no enterprise of 

their own, the rich become richer and the poor become poorer. 

This process has no natural limits. Eventually, as we’ve seen in 

the past, the very rich can capture almost the entire produc- 

tion of society... This predicament is not a perversity of the 

system. It is an innate characteristic. It is bound to work this 

way, unless there is a political movement capable of breaking 

the vicious circle of wealth accumulation.” 

Only once in modern Western history, in the early twentieth 

century, has capitalism and capitalists’ tendential march towards 

the totalizing rentierism envisioned not only by Monbiot (fore- 
seeing capture by the rich of ‘almost the entire production of 
society ) but also by Piketty (with his description of rent as capi- 

tal’s ‘vocation’) been effectively checked. From around 1910, as 
we have seen, wealth inequality, which had been acute, began a 

secular decline, only beginning to escalate again once neoliberal- 
ism had been transformed from a niche obsession among a small 
band of Western intellectuals into an increasingly pervasive 
political-economic reality. 

I have noted, following Piketty, that a progressive tax system 
played an important role in the early-to-mid twentieth century 

420 
RENTIER CAPITALISM 

in checking the further deepening of the inequalities of the 
Gilded Age. Returns on assets were thereby restricted. But of 
course, the shift that occurred from around World War I was as 
much about a reduction in the quantity of assets — of capital in 
general — as a squeezing of returns on these. World War I was 
followed by the Great Depression and World War II; it was, 
remarks 
Piketty, an 
era of ‘violent 
military, 
political, and 
economic conflicts. Those conflicts effected a colossal destruc- 
tion of wealth: “By the middle of the twentieth century, capital 
had largely disappeared.”* Rentierism ceased to pay in large 
measure because there were now few rent-generating assets. 

It is in reflecting on these stark historical realities that Piketty 
makes what is one of his most significant observations. Contra 

all those histories demarcating its various 
‘ages’, capitalism, 

Piketty says, had not substantively changed between the periods 

before and after World War I. Rent was still very much capital’s 

vocation; but, because of conflict and destruction, rebuilding 

was required. ‘The notion that ‘capitalism had been structurally 
transformed’ is an ‘illusion created by ‘the wars of the twentieth 
century that wiped away the past’.”” 

And so here we are again now — not least in the UK — with 

rentier capitalism once again in the ascendant, bringing with it 
once again the stark inequalities that are its calling card. It would 
be easy, perhaps, to think about that historical precedent in a 
one-sided way — to recognize, with Piketty, that war and economic 
depression successfully stymied rentierism (their one positive 
outcome?), without considering the possibility that rentierism in 
some way contributed to those calamities in the first place. But 
Monbiot, 
for one, 
refuses that comfortable conceit. What 
happens, he asks, when, with the advancement of the rentier 
economy, inequality spirals, social mobility stalls, and, ‘as we’ve 
seen in the past’, the very rich capture ‘almost the entire produc- 
tion of society’? ‘At this point’, Monbiot warns, ‘the debt, desti- 
tution and unemployment that results can cause economic 
collapse: the Great Depression is a good example.’”° 

CODA 
42] 

Thus, on the one occasion in the past when the rentierist 
tendency has been checked, it required war and economic 

collapse to bring this about — and, if Monbiot is right, there was 
nothing accidental about that. If rent is capital’s logical destina- 

tion, social and economic devastation may in turn be rent’s logi- 

cal destination — the logical outcome of the economic and social 

fractures, not least the mass proliferation of dishonourable 

poverty, to which it gives rise. 

Unless the Left returns to power in the UK in relatively short 

order and is able to push through the transformations required 

to remove the rentier from her pedestal, it is entirely possible that 

it will require devastating socioeconomic ructions once again to 
impose the limits to rentierism that it does not contain within 

itself — and that, once again, rentier dynamics and the state’s 
encouragement of them will be partly to blame for those ructions. 

This is what Piketty sees in his crystal ball for the Western world 

more widely: ‘[I]f the trend over the period 1970-2010 is extrap- 

olated to the period 2010-2050 or 2010-2100, the result is 

economic, 
social and political disequilibria of considerable 

magnitude, not only between but within countries — disequilib- 

ria that inevitably call to mind the Ricardian apocalypse’.”” 

This time, however, there is an extra dimension of ‘disequilib- 

rium’ to be thrown into the mix. In the future, it seems inevitable 

that the kinds of political, military and economic turmoil that 

scarred the twentieth century, temporarily putting paid to rentier 

capitalism in the process, will be intimately bound up with envi- 

ronmental turmoil. Here, too — including in the UK, home as it 

is to carbon neoliberalism (Chapter 2) — rentierism plays a pivotal 

role. And if fossil-fuel rentierism continues unabated, of course, 

the disruptions that result this time may well be terminal — apoc- 

alyptic, in fact.

49. 

Before readers respond to my argument that Keynes explained interest rates in terms 
of supply and demand with howls of protest, let me be clear. His argument — most 

clearly and fully elaborated in ‘Alternative Theories of the Rate of Interest’, Economic 
Journal 47: 186 (1937), pp. 241-52 — that ‘the rate of interest depends on the 

NOTES FOR PAGES 68 TO 77 

430 

demand and supply of money’ (p. 241) referred to the demand and supply of monies 
of different types. Contra the ‘classical’ (Keynes said pre-1914) doctrine that the inter- 

est rate depends on the supply of and demand for credit (the rate being fixed at the 

level that equalizes the two), Keynes submitted that the key variables were the 
demand for credit and the supply of cash. Specifically, ‘the rate of interest on a loan 
of given quality and maturity has to be established at the level which, in the opinion 
of those who have the opportunity of choice — i.e. of wealth-holders — equalises the 
attractions of holding idle cash and of holding the loan’ (p. 250). As he explained to 
the many interlocutors who seemed to misunderstand him, this was a ‘liquidity- 
preference’ theory: holders of cash only lend it if the interest rate on loanable funds 
is sufficiently attractive to offset the liquidity downside of holding the loan instead. 
Thus, ‘it is precisely the liquidity-premium on cash ruling in the market which 
determines the rate of interest at which finance is obtainable’ (248). So, supply and 
demand — but, to be sure, not supply and demand in any simplistic sense. 
Keynes, General Theory, p. 375.

publishing.service.gov.uk. Might the CMA’s market study — ongoing at the time of 

this writing — see the UK take a more proactive stanceto monopoly power in the 

digital platform space? Perhaps: the interim report certainly makes it clear that the 
CMA, the UK’s competition regulator, believes both that competition is indeed 

constrained in this market and that Facebook and Google — earning profits ‘well 

above’ what one would expect in a competitive market — are the preeminent monop- 

olists. But it seems likely that the CMA will nonetheless stop short of making a full 

market investigation reference, which would give it the power to intervene itself. 

Instead, its current belief is that ‘the best mechanism for delivering reforms’ is for it 

to make recommendations to the government, leaving it to the latter to decide the 

appropriate course of action. Given the governments track record, it is difficult to 

share the CMA’s belief.

How did Britain’s economy become a bastion of inequality? 

UNCORRECTED PAGE PROOFS 

Rentier Capitalism 
Who Owns the Economy, and Who Pays for It? 

By Brett Christophers 

In this landmark book, the author of The New Enclosure provides a forensic 
examination and sweeping critique of early-twenty-first-century capitalism. Brett 
Christophers styles this as ‘rentier capitalism’, in which ownership of key types of 
scarce assets - such as land, intellectual property, natural resources, or digital 
platforms - is all-important and dominated by a few unfathomably wealthy 
companies and individuals: rentiers. If a small elite owns today’s economy, everybody 
else foots the bill. Nowhere is this divergence starker, Christophers shows, than in the 
United Kingdom, where the prototypical ills of rentier capitalism - vast inequalities 
combined with entrenched economic stagnation - are on full display and have led the 
country inexorably to the precipice of Brexit. With profound lessons for other 
countries subject to rentier dominance, Christophers’ examination of the UK case is 
indispensable to those wanting not just to understand this insidious economic 
phenomenon but to overcome it. Frequently invoked but never previously analysed 
and illuminated in all its depth and variety, rentier capitalism is here laid bare for the 
first time. 

Brett Christophers is a political economist and economic geographer, and the author 
of Rentier Capitalism and of The New Enclosure, which won the Isaac and Ta 
3
